World.title: South Africa: Suspect Sought as Police Probe Ekurhuleni Murders - South African News Briefs - September 16, 2026
World.content:
press review

Police Pursue Person of Interest in Ekurhuleni Murders

Police said that they are pursuing a person of interest in connection with the deaths of eight women in Ekurhuleni, reports EWN. Police have not disclosed the individual's identity or gender, and they have not confirmed which cases the person may be linked to. The women have been found since July, with several discovered half-naked and bruised. Investigators are examining whether the deaths are connected but have cautioned against concluding that a single person or group is responsible for all eight cases. A separate suspect arrested after the first body was found remains in custody.

Madlanga Commission to Hear Vetting Expert

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Madlanga Commission is set to hear evidence from an international vetting expert as it investigates allegations of criminal infiltration within law enforcement agencies, reports SABC News. The expert will testify about the processes used to assess the integrity and suitability of people appointed to law enforcement positions. The evidence could shed light on whether existing vetting systems effectively identify candidates suitable for senior roles, amid testimony on the conduct and integrity of senior law enforcement officials.

SASSA Grant System Faces Scrutiny Over Bank Checks

The South African Social Security Agency's automated verification system for the R370 Social Relief of Distress grant is reportedly causing problems for some applicants because bank transactions can be interpreted as income, according to Wits University legal expert Busisiwe Kamolane-Kgadima. The system checks applicants’ information against government and banking records to determine whether they exceed the income threshold. She said such checks are necessary to prevent people from receiving benefits they do not qualify for. She raised concerns about the heavy reliance on an automated process, which may not account for the nature or source of individual bank transactions.

World.title: Travis Kelce among pro athletes defrauded by Ponzi scheme that funneled funds into one stock
World.content:
Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce, 36, was officially identified as a victim in a $35 million Ponzi scheme run by a Texas fund manager.

During a Tuesday sentencing hearing in a St. Louis federal courtroom, prosecutors named Kelce among those defrauded by 38-year-old Siddharth Jawahar.

Jawahar operated Swiftarc Capital LLC, an investment firm that collapsed into a federal wire fraud investigation.

HALL OF FAME RECEIVER TERRELL OWENS ACCUSES LONGTIME MANAGER OF 'STEALING' FROM HIM: 'LIAR AND A THIEF'

According to the U.S. Department of Justice, Jawahar raised more than $35 million from investors between July 2016 and December 2023.

Instead of managing a diversified portfolio, he allocated roughly 99% of client capital into a single stock, Philip Morris Pakistan.

As that position tanked, Jawahar hid the losses, issued falsified statements and used funds from new investors to pay out earlier clients.



Federal prosecutors noted Jawahar actually invested roughly $10 million of the total funds raised. He spent the remainder funding personal luxuries, including private jet charters, upscale apartments in Austin and New York, high-end dining and exclusive private club memberships.

Court filings did not specify the exact financial loss suffered by Kelce.

Kelce was not the only professional athlete caught up in the operation.

A 2021 Forbes report previously linked Swiftarc funds to several NBA players, including Gary Harris, Tim Hardaway Jr. and Mason Plumlee.

Jawahar pleaded guilty to three counts of wire fraud in January 2026.

U.S. District Judge Zachary M. Bluestone sentenced Jawahar to 11 years in federal prison and ordered him to pay $31.35 million in restitution.

World.title: Republican congressman presses NHL over Alex Ovechkin’s appearance in Putin party campaign ad
World.content:
Rep. Joe Wilson, R-S.C., has a problem with Alex Ovechkin appearing in a campaign  for the Vladimir Putin-backed United Russia party, and he wants NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman to address it.

Wilson sent Bettman a letter Tuesday calling the Washington Capitals captain’s participation "shameful" and asking the league to review the matter. Capitals owner Ted Leonsis was copied on the letter.

Ovechkin does not speak in the ad. He stands behind Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in a United Russia campaign video ahead of Russia’s Sept. 18-20 parliamentary elections. Margarita Simonyan, editor-in-chief of the Russian state-controlled network RT, also appears in the ad.

"While Mr. Ovechkin has every right to hold personal political views, actively participating in campaign material for Putin’s oppressive party while serving as the captain of an NHL franchise in our nation’s capital raises serious questions about the standards expected of players who represent the League and their communities," Wilson wrote.

STEPHEN A SMITH WARNS POLITICS IS CAUSING 'DIVISION' WITHIN AMERICA'S LAST UNIFYING PASTIME

The letter does not ask Bettman to suspend or fine Ovechkin. Wilson wants the NHL to explain whether it has any policies governing active players who appear in political s for foreign parties or regimes.

He also wants the league and Capitals to make clear that Ovechkin’s participation does not represent either organization’s position.

Wilson was more direct on social media.

"It is incredibly alarming that [the NHL] and [the Capitals] have allowed Alexander Ovechkin to appear in a campaign  supporting the party of war criminal Putin," he wrote. "American hockey fans deserve better leadership from their star players!"

Wilson elaborated on the letter Wednesday during an interview with Fox News’ Dan Scully.

Asked what he wanted Bettman to do and whether he was seeking discipline for Ovechkin, Wilson did not directly answer.

"For Ovechkin to be campaigning for a person who is indeed the new Hitler of the 21st century, it’s just inconceivable," Wilson said.

Scully also asked whether Wilson had information that the NHL or Capitals knew about the  beforehand.

"Ahead of time, I’m not sure," Wilson said.

Capitals respond to Ovechkin ad

The Capitals said Ovechkin was approached while spending the offseason in Russia.

"This summer, while in Russia, he was asked by his country to participate in a video campaign," Capitals spokesperson Sergey Kocharov said in a statement to Reuters.

But who asked him?

The Capitals did not say. The team also did not answer questions from Fox News Digital/OutKick about whether it knew of Ovechkin’s participation beforehand or whether anyone within the organization approved or facilitated it.

Kocharov noted that Ovechkin lives with his family in Moscow during the offseason and plans to return there after his NHL career. He said Ovechkin and the Capitals are focused on the upcoming season and his continued impact in Washington.

WASHINGTON CAPITALS STAR ALEX OVECHKIN CRASHES A COUPLE'S WEDDING PHOTO SHOOT ON A HOTEL STAIRCASE

Ovechkin has publicly supported Putin for years. He founded "PutinTeam" in 2017 to rally support for the Russian president, and his Instagram profile photo remains an image of the two men standing together.

Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Ovechkin called for peace but declined to criticize Putin.

"Well, he is my president," Ovechkin said at the time. "But, like I said, I’m not in politics. I’m an athlete."

Wilson says Ovechkin should face ‘consequences’

Wilson argues that the Kremlin has a history of using athletes and international sporting achievements to promote the Russian government abroad.

"An NHL superstar appearing in campaign propaganda for Putin’s political party cannot simply be dismissed as an activity wholly disconnected from the League," Wilson wrote.

Wilson also writes that the broader United Russia campaign features Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia’s commissioner for children’s rights. The International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Lvova-Belova and Putin in 2023 over the alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from Russian-occupied territory.

Scully asked Wilson how Ovechkin’s appearance differs from an American athlete supporting a U.S. politician.

"The difference is that the American politician is not a mass murderer," Wilson said.

"Now, we can all disagree," he continued. "There is a right to free speech, of course, but there should also be consequences of being associated in promoting a war criminal."

Wilson did not say what those consequences should be. When Scully later asked directly whether he wanted the NHL to suspend Ovechkin, Wilson again did not answer.

Wilson also said he is working with Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jim Risch, R-Idaho, and that Risch agrees Ovechkin’s participation "is just not right." Wilson did not describe what action, if any, he and Risch intend to pursue.

The congressman said he has not received a response from the NHL but is willing to give the league time to answer.

Throughout the interview, Wilson repeatedly referred to Putin as a "convicted war criminal," echoing the handwritten message beneath his signature.

The ICC issued arrest warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova in 2023, but neither has been convicted by the court.

World.title: Dem insurgent turns on the charm with party establishment as Schumer leaves bitter feud hanging
World.content:

Michigan’s insurgent progressive Senate nominee ran as far as he could from Washington, D.C., but, on Wednesday, he traveled to the nation’s Capitol for a closed-door meeting with top Democratic brass as the race for power intensifies.

Abdul El-Sayed met with top Senate Democrats just hundreds of yards away from Congress, where lawmakers and the wunderkind candidate huddled to discuss his campaign and how to keep Michigan blue.

Many left boasting that the Wolverine State would not turn a shade of purple.

But few, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., would say whether the fences broken during El-Sayed’s primary fight had been mended.

SCHUMER DUCKS QUESTION ON CAMPAIGNING WITH SOCIALIST CANDIDATE WHO REFUSES TO BACK HIM AS LEADER

"Look, we have to win Michigan, and we had a great and friendly meeting," Schumer said when asked by Fox News Digital if he and El-Sayed had moved on from their differences.

Still, El-Sayed held court with Democratic brass for hours at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee’s (DSCC) headquarters in Washington, where a steady flow of lawmakers — both allies and skeptics of his Senate bid — milled in and out of the building throughout the day.

Schumer and Democrats are confident and determined that they can flip the Senate, which Republicans hold with a 53-47 margin. Losing Michigan to the GOP and former Rep. Mike Rogers would serve a mortal blow to that push.

"He’s gonna win," Sen. Kirstin Gillibrand, D-N.Y., who is also the DSCC chair, said.

The key mission for Democrats is getting independents and Republicans on the fence. But few, including Schumer, said they would actually hit the campaign trail with El-Sayed.

It all comes after El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., locked horns in one of the most bitter Democratic primary fights of this cycle that pitted the Democratic old guard versus a progressive movement gaining steam across the country.

SEE IT: DEM SENATORS RALLY BEHIND EL-SAYED BUT DUCK QUESTIONS ON PROGRESSIVE AGENDA

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., who initially endorsed Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow before she dropped out, told Fox News Digital, "Obviously, primaries can get really hot, and the Michigan primary got hot.

"This is what you do after a primary is you try to unite the party and then you do the work to reach out and cross over to independent voters and Republican voters," Murphy added. "So, I don't think anybody should be surprised that he's trying to build bridges after a heated primary. That's what good candidates, that's what winning candidates do."

Another McMorrow backer, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., painted a rosy picture of the closed-door session and noted it was "hard to hear in there because so many people were talking and laughing and wanted to hear about the campaign.

"He makes good connections because it's a lot of people in there who are talking about, ‘What can we do next? What can we do to lower costs for families? What can we do to make this government work better for working people?’ So, it was a very enthusiastic, very cheerful group of people."

Retiring Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., whose seat El-Sayed is gunning for, initially endorsed Stevens. Now, he’s shifting gears.

DEMS' LEFTWARD LURCH GETS LEGS AS EL-SAYED'S MICHIGAN SENATE VICTORY SPARKS PARTY DEBATE

"I'm endorsing him, and he's been getting support across the board in Michigan. The Democrats are coming together," Peters said in response to a question about whether the Democratic establishment was uniting behind El-Sayed. "We understand how important this election is."

Others were more keen to lend an assist to El-Sayed, including Murphy and Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., who said, "I’m gonna be in Michigan here in a couple of weeks."

Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., who is running for re-election in deep blue Massachusetts, said that Democrats’ strategy heading into the final stretch was pitching an affordability agenda, and El-Sayed "is the answer."

"I'm helping him. I think we're all gonna help," Markey said when asked if he would raise money for El-Sayed.

The specter of El-Sayed’s relationship with controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who helped to amplify his campaign in the primary battle, wasn’t something that Democrats focused on during their huddle.

"Hasan what?," Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin, D-Ill., told Fox News Digital when asked if he came up during the meeting. "I don’t even know who that is."

When asked if Piker came up or if Democrats encouraged El-Sayed to further distance himself from him, Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, "Not in terms of the conversation. Like I said, I was just trying to get to know him."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

After initially dodging Fox News Digital’s question on whether he would campaign with Piker, El-Sayed later told reporters, "This conversation is so far removed from what people are talking about.

"Everyday, in Michigan, people sit at their kitchen tables and ask, 'How am I going to make this work next month?’ That’s not a middle, right, left issue, that’s a basic affordability issue."

When further pressed, he countered that Michigan voters "really don’t care about that."

"They really don't," El-Sayed said.

A pair of young newlyweds were killed in an accident involving a water taxi in Venice just three months after they were married.

Gabriella Querino, 26, and Sean Michieli, 25, were killed Saturday morning in a collision involving a 5-ton water taxi, Jam Press reported.

The couple was in a boat that had departed from Burano, an island in the Venetian Lagoon, about 6 miles northeast of central Venice.

BELOVED CRUISE SPOT WILL BE OFF LIMITS THROUGH 2027 AS SAFETY CONCERNS LINGER

They had set out to collect bait for Michieli's work as a clam fisherman.

Shortly afterward, the couple's boat collided with the water taxi and sank.

Querino was reported missing in the immediate aftermath of the crash, and search efforts were hampered by strong currents and poor visibility.

Her body was eventually recovered from the lagoon.

Michieli was rushed to Venice-Mestre Hospital with severe head and facial injuries and other injuries across his body. He was pronounced brain-dead the next day.

CRUISES THROWN INTO CHAOS AS DROUGHT STRANDS SHIPS, LEAVES PASSENGERS SCRAMBLING

Querino, originally from Ribeirão Preto, Brazil, moved to Italy about two years ago.

She developed a passion for fishing alongside her husband, who was from Cavallino-Treporti, Italy, according to Jam Press.

She was working to obtain the necessary license to join her husband in the fishing industry, according to the outlet.

The couple was expecting their first child, Italian newspaper Il Resto del Carlino reported.

World.title: Gavin Newsom blames Trump for housing costs using chart showing massive increase under Biden
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom faced backlash Tuesday after taking a swipe at President Donald Trump for high housing costs, using a chart showing a massive cost spike during the Biden administration.

On his X account, Newsom, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, shared a post reporting that U.S. homes are "now the most unaffordable in history," along with a graph showing the income needed to qualify for a median-priced home from 2005 to 2026.

"Great work, @realDonaldTrump!" Newsom wrote.

CALIFORNIA DEM, FORMER LA MAYOR VILLARAIGOSA ADMITS TRUMP'S NOT TO BLAME FOR STATE’S HOMELESSNESS, COST CRISES

However, several X users pointed out that although the chart reached its highest level during Trump's second administration, it shows a substantial increase between 2021 and 2024, when former President Joe Biden was in office.

"Hey @GavinNewsom, who was president during the biggest uptick in home unaffordability?" the Libs of TikTok account asked.

Meteorologist Chris Martz wrote, "Evidently, @GavinNewsom doesn't know how to read graphs. Housing prices skyrocketed under Joe Biden's presidency."

"California is the most unaffordable state in the country to buy a house, and it’s only gotten worse since Gavin Newsom took over. And no one in the media will call him out for saying this," OutKick writer Ian Miller commented.

California Post opinion editor Joel Pollak wrote, "You would be ashamed if they broke it down by state."

"Gavin, I guess you can’t read a graph. The biggest spike was before DJT took office," actor Doug Davidson commented.

Author Jens Heycke joked, "Aspiring presidential candidate Gavin Newsom demonstrates that he is unable to read a simple graph. This level of numeric and economic illiteracy is disqualifying."

THE SURPRISING HIDDEN COST QUIETLY ADDING NEARLY $132K TO NEW HOME PRICES REVEALED

Other users compared Newsom's post to a since-deleted X post from the official Democratic Party’s account featuring a graph claiming that "U.S. Grocery Prices Reached Record Highs in 2025" with prices "higher today than they were on July 2024" in categories such as dairy, produce and meat.

At the time, users pointed out that the graph, in fact, showed prices skyrocketing in 2021, when Biden was president, and only leveling off at the end of 2024 when Trump was re-elected.

Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Newsom's post came as the California governor has been working to tackle housing affordability in his state. In 2025, he signed into law a housing package to exempt certain projects from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and streamline environmental review for qualifying housing and infrastructure development.

In July, he signed into law more housing affordability reforms focused on streamlining affordable-housing financing and project reviews.

TRUMP-BACKED HOUSING OVERHAUL TARGETING WALL STREET INVESTORS CLEARS SENATE

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital Trump is more "laser-focused" on affordability than the "incompetent" Newsom.

"Unlike incompetent Governor Gavin Newscum, President Trump has been laser-focused on making housing more affordable. The president signed an executive order prohibiting large Wall Street firms from purchasing single-family homes, directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to purchase $200 billion in mortgage bonds that helped drive rates to four-year lows and cut unnecessary red tape at a historic pace to boost supply, speed construction, and lower costs," Ingle said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The president will not stop fighting until the American dream of homeownership is within reach for every American, which is why he continues to sign bold new executive orders and calls on Congress to pass further legislation."

Fox News' Ashley J. DiMella contributed to this report.

World.title: Lawmakers say they are standing at the gates against 'Trojan horses' promoting malign foreign interests
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

WASHINGTON, D.C. — In a series of exclusive interviews with Fox News Digital, lawmakers on the House Foreign Affairs Committee sounded the alarm on a sprawling network of "Trojan horse" activists, nonprofits and social media influencers allegedly amplifying the hostile messages of foreign adversaries straight through the open gates of American democracy.

The warning came into sharp focus Tuesday when CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin and two fellow activists walked into House Rayburn 2172 for a hearing on covert foreign influence operations, then strategically positioned themselves behind witnesses in T-shirts supporting the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Communist Party of Cuba.

About 30 minutes into the hearing, South and Central Asia Subcommittee Chairman Bill Huizenga, R-Mich., stopped the hearing and had Capitol Police escort them out.

LAWMAKERS THROW OUT 'TROJAN HORSE' ACTIVISTS THEY SAY ARE ENGAGED IN AMERICAN SUBVERSION

"They're coming in, trying to look like one thing, but we know that once they're inside the gates that those doors are going to spring open, and there's a whole other motivation for what they're trying to do," Huizenga told Fox News Digital.

At the center of the controversy is communist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham, who married CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans in a tropical wedding in Jamaica in 2017, soon after funneling $285 million to six pro-China, pro-communist, anti-American nonprofits in the U.S., including CodePink, according to a Fox News Digital investigation.

Lawmakers say the answer is transparency and following the money and exposing who finances the alleged "Trojan horse."

In their series of interviews, Huizenga and other committee members explained how the modern "Trojan horse" isn't made of wood but rather a network of activists, nonprofits, social media influencers and other ostensibly American voices that foreign governments and foreign-linked actors can allegedly fund, amplify or exploit to carry their messages through the open gates of American democracy.

"They're coming in, trying to look like one thing, but we know that once they're inside the gates that those doors are going to spring open and there's a whole other motivation for what they're trying to do," Huizenga told Fox News Digital.

At the hearing, devoted to "Trojan Horses: Covert Foreign Malign Influence Operations in America," lawmakers expressed concern about how the Communist Party of China, Russia, the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Communist Party of Cuba spread their propaganda and influence in the U.S.

The phrase "Trojan horse" comes from the ancient Greek story of soldiers concealed inside a wooden horse presented to the city of Troy. Once the horse was taken behind the city's fortified walls, the soldiers emerged and opened the gates, destroying Troy.

Huizenga stressed that Americans can hold sincere beliefs while also having those messages funded or amplified by foreign actors without necessarily knowing it. He argued that the answer to foreign influence is exposing the origins of the messaging through transparency and robust debate.

Rep. Huizenga: 'It's really about theatrics'

Inside the hearing room, as Fox News Digital reported, Benjamin and her fellow CodePink activists offered a vivid illustration of the debate over how political messages are created and amplified.

They sat directly behind the witnesses, placing their T-shirts in the sight line of the official committee cameras.

Benjamin then turned toward a television monitor on the side of the hearing room displaying the official video feed. She pulled out her phone, zoomed in on the image of herself and a fellow activist appearing behind the witnesses and took photo after photo of the screen.

HOUSE PANEL PROBES FOREIGN ‘TROJAN HORSES’ AS SINGHAM SCRUTINY WIDENS

Huizenga said he viewed the episode as political theater designed for an audience beyond the committee room.

"This isn't about discourse. This is about disruption," Huizenga told Fox News Digital. "It's all planned out. You see people in the crowd filming with their phones, getting ready. You knew something was going to happen because, all of a sudden, the phones would come out.

"It's really about theatrics," he added, arguing that confrontations can subsequently be circulated on social media to attract attention, donations and volunteers.

The episode captured the central tension running through the hearing: How does the United States expose genuine covert foreign influence without treating protected American political speech as foreign subversion?

"Transparency. Transparency is the watchword," Huizenga told Fox News Digital. "We really need to make sure that people know not only the why, but the who is behind all this."

Rep. Baumgartner: 'We need to know who's behind it'

Rep. Michael Baumgartner, R-Wash., told Fox News Digital that America's open political system creates opportunities for foreign governments to try to influence legitimate domestic debates through social media, universities and other institutions.

"The American people need transparency and need to understand what is going on in these public policy discussions and whether it's podcast hosts, certain actors on social media or things going on our college campuses," Baumgartner said. "We need to know who's behind it and what their motivations are."

Baumgartner pointed to "clear transparency on this issue" as a solution, adding that if evidence showed organizations were acting on behalf of foreign governments without complying with applicable disclosure laws, the matter could potentially be referred to the Justice Department, which oversees the Foreign Agent Registration Act, or FARA. The law requires that people and organizations acting on behalf of foreign interests register with the Justice Department.

Rep. Randy Fine: Trojan horses ‘poison people’s minds’

Other lawmakers said the modern Trojan horse doesn't necessarily have to walk physically through the doors of Congress, but rather arrive via social media.

Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., described social media, influencers and protests as potential channels through which foreign governments influence American political debate. He said "it's a real issue, whether it's on social media, influencers, protests, these things are all designed to destabilize our country."

Fine characterized what experts call "cognitive warfare" as "using our information platforms to try to poison people's minds and to create division from within."

Rep. Darrell Issa: ‘It’s a network’

Rep. Darrell Issa, R-Calif., focused on another battlefield: artificial intelligence.

"Trojan horses are things like the announcement that we should slow down on AI," Issa told Fox News Digital, arguing that foreign adversaries can benefit when American political pressure slows U.S. technological development.

"We are in a war in which the other side uses all the clandestine tools," Issa said. "They use their, quite frankly, their social media to our detriment."

Huizenga similarly argued that Americans should view the organizations under examination not individually but as a network.

"It's a network. It's not independent organizations or even people," he said. "You will see some of the same people at different organizations, rallies, or protests."

‘Origins aren’t organic’

At the center of much of the hearing were findings from a Fox News Digital investigation into Neville Roy Singham, an American-born communist tech tycoon who lives in Shanghai and has pumped $285 million into six nonprofits, including CodePink, the People's Forum and other groups examined during the hearing.

Huizenga alleged in his official opening remarks that Singham uses his wealth and relationships in China to support organizations that promote communist ideology and destabilize American society. He explicitly described Singham, CodePink and a growing network of pro-communist, pro-China groups as "Trojan horses."

‘TROJAN HORSES’ IN AMERICA: CONGRESS PROBES INFLUENCE NETWORKS TIED TO CHINA, IRAN AND CUBA

Singham and CodePink have denied taking direction from the Chinese government. Singham has said his activities reflect his own political beliefs, while Benjamin has said CodePink doesn't receive money from the Chinese Communist Party.

As Fox News Digital reported in June, the Justice Department and the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York have convened a grand jury investigation into alleged money laundering, bank fraud and wire fraud by Singham and the organizations he has funded.

No criminal charges have been filed against Singham or CodePink with respect to those allegations.

Huizenga argued that the funding relationships deserve scrutiny.

"Oftentimes, it's frankly the origins aren't organic, or if there is a part of it being organic, this is getting fed by outside organizations, oftentimes even outside countries," Huizenga alleged.

‘Transparency is the watchword’

Being escorted through the committee room doors didn't end CodePink's political theater.

Outside the hearing room, Benjamin positioned herself beside the House Foreign Affairs Committee placard and began recording another video, pulling out a comb first to straighten her hair.

When Rep. Fine emerged from the hearing, Benjamin followed him down the hallway firing questions as another member of her team recorded the encounter.

After Fine disappeared into an office, Benjamin returned to the committee entrance, straightened her hair with a comb and resumed recording.

HOUSE COMMITTEE PASSES FOREIGN FUNDING TRANSPARENCY ACT TO EXPOSE FOREIGN DONATIONS TO NONPROFITS

About two hours after Capitol Police escorted the activists from the hearing, CodePink posted a carefully edited video of the day's confrontation on social media, where activists in the broader network began sharing it.

The physical protest was over, but the images it produced were just beginning to travel.

That sequence was precisely why lawmakers said Americans should look beyond the spectacle to who finances and amplifies political messaging.

"This is theater for many of these people," Huizenga said. He said he wanted Americans, through "transparency and disclosure," to understand "not just the what they are doing, but the who is financing them."

The lawmakers gathered to investigate modern "Trojan horses" said the lesson of the ancient story wasn't simply to keep the horse outside the gates but also to understand what — and who — might be inside.

"Transparency. Transparency is the watchword," Huizenga said.

Lawmakers say 'transparency and disclosure' are the best defense against influence campaigns exploiting America's democracy.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Fox News Digital's Reagan Schroeder and Brooke Curto contributed to this report.

World.title: Skid Row forgeries, illegal votes and a mayoral candidate: Election fraud cases pile up nationwide
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Trump administration continues to crack down on voter fraud cases, including a noncitizen who allegedly voted in a mayoral race he was fraudulently registered for and a noncitizen arrested for allegedly lying about her citizenship to vote in federal elections.

These allegations span a slate of federal election-related cases highlighted by the Justice Department in recent days, adding to a series of prosecutions targeting noncitizen voting, fraudulent voter registrations and other alleged election-related crimes.

The DOJ's latest announcements involve California, Kansas, Louisiana, Texas and Massachusetts, while federal prosecutors have brought a number of other cases across the country in recent weeks amid the Trump administration's broader efforts to bolster election security ahead of the midterms.

The White House pointed to the new cases that continue to pile up as evidence supporting the administration's crackdown.

DEMOCRAT NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR SAYS THOUSANDS OF NONCITIZENS DISCOVERED ON VOTER ROLLS, PURGED

"Despite extreme Democrats and the media claiming it never happens, the evidence of noncitizens registering and voting in our elections continues to pile up," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. "Any noncitizens found registering and voting in our elections will be arrested and held accountable. Only Americans should be electing American leaders."

The more than a dozen defendants charged in cases announced this week face allegations ranging from illegal voting and false claims of U.S. citizenship to fraudulent voter registration and identity fraud. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche warned that individuals "gaming the election system, voting illegally or committing voter fraud" will face prosecution, while federal prosecutors in Texas said their seven cases "send a clear message" that laws barring noncitizens from voting will be enforced.

Among the defendants were Louisiana mayoral candidate Bridget Johnson, who prosecutors allege fraudulently registered Jamaican noncitizen Michael Wedderburn before he voted in the 2024 federal election and the same mayoral race in which Johnson was a candidate. Johnson allegedly electronically submitted a Louisiana voter registration application in Wedderburn's name on July 14, 2024, falsely stating that he was a U.S. citizen, according to court documents.

ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT LEARNS FATE AFTER USING STOLEN IDENTITY TO VOTE IN US ELECTIONS FOR DECADES

Johnson was charged with fraudulent voter registration and voting by an alien, while Wedderburn was charged with voting by an alien. If convicted, Johnson faces up to five years in prison, while Wedderburn faces up to one year, along with potential financial penalties, according to federal prosecutors.

Other cases announced this week included allegations against three people in California accused in an alleged scheme that used stolen identities of registered voters to manufacture signatures on ballot initiative petitions.

California frequently uses ballot initiatives to put major policy questions directly before voters, with citizen-backed measures capable of changing state law or amending the state constitution. Recent initiatives have included Proposition 36, which increased penalties for certain drug and theft crimes, and measures dealing with the minimum wage and rent control.

Prosecutors allege James Brass and Courtney Price went to Los Angeles' Skid Row, where they handed people stolen identities belonging to registered California voters and paid them to copy those voters' personal information onto ballot petitions and forge their signatures.

Brass and a third defendant, Jateisha Herron, then allegedly falsely certified that they had personally witnessed the registered voters sign the petitions. Brass allegedly received about $41,600 from coordinators working with a petition-management company helping collect signatures, according to prosecutors.

EX-NEW JERSEY MAYOR, HER HUSBAND CHARGED FOR USING FAKE BALLOT SIGNATURES AFTER SHE PLEADED GUILTY TO DUI

The case is the second election-related federal prosecution announced this year involving alleged payments to people on Skid Row. In May, federal prosecutors charged a longtime ballot initiative signature collector with paying individuals, including homeless people living on Skid Row, to register to vote.

In Kansas, prosecutors charged 24-year-old Peruvian national and U.S. permanent resident Mariana Alexandra Dewey with falsely claiming U.S. citizenship, fraudulent election conduct and voting as an alien in a federal election after arresting her earlier this month.

In Massachusetts, federal prosecutors announced a case this week against Nigerian national Gladys Adaeze Okafor, who allegedly claimed to be a U.S. citizen while registering to vote before casting ballots in multiple federal elections.

A handful of cases were announced by federal prosecutors in Texas this week as well, including multiple cases where individuals registered to vote illegally when applying for a Texas driver's license. On the same day those defendants were indicted, a Mexican national was also sentenced to 36 months in federal prison for aggravated identity theft, false statements of citizenship, and illegal voting by an alien, according to federal officials.

INSIDE HOUSE REPUBLICANS' PLAN TO END RUN DEM OPPOSITION AND PASS TRUMP-BACKED VOTER ID

The cases add to the growing list of federal election-related cases brought in the past few weeks on top of other prosecutions earlier this year involving noncitizens accused of illegally registering or voting in U.S. elections. Less than two weeks ago, the Justice Department charged five people in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Wisconsin in cases involving alleged illegal voting or fraudulent registration tied to the 2022 or 2024 elections.

The DOJ separately charged an Indian national in Minnesota last week with falsely claiming U.S. citizenship in order to vote in the 2024 general election.

Despite the mounting prosecutions, the Trump administration also faced a setback this week in its efforts to boost election security.

The Supreme Court ruled Monday that the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) could not implement the president's stricter mail ballot requirements for the 2026 elections, leaving a lower court's nationwide injunction in place. The blocked rules would have required states to use specially designed mail ballot envelopes with unique voter barcodes, submit envelope designs to USPS for review and provide it with information about intended ballot recipients.

The ruling, however, did not block a separate part of Trump's March executive order directing the federal government to create citizenship lists for states to use in checking their voter rolls.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was appointed by Trump, agreed the rules should not take effect for this year's elections, writing that state and local officials did not have sufficient time to reasonably implement them.

Nonetheless, Kavanaugh said there was "at least a fair prospect" that the Postal Service ultimately has the statutory authority to impose the requirements. Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented.

Trump blasted the decision Tuesday as another "bad decision" from the Supreme Court and praised Alito and Thomas as "legends," while arguing the ruling would make cheating through mail ballots easier.

World.title: House passes bill to shield consumers from data center price hikes on energy
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Under pressure to act on unpopular data centers, the House on Wednesday overwhelmingly passed bipartisan legislation aimed at shielding consumers from higher energy costs when new data centers are built in their communities.

The vote was nearly unanimous, 417-3, with the only opposition coming from progressive Reps. Summer Lee, D-Pa., Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., and Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich. Because GOP leaders brought the bill to the floor under a fast-tracking procedure known as suspension, support from two-thirds of voting lawmakers was required.

The bill, dubbed the Ratepayers Protection Act, is the only legislation related to artificial intelligence that was scheduled for a vote this week as Congress considers its response to dire warnings from some former AI employees about its dangers.

With the House holding its final votes before the midterm elections on Wednesday evening, and the Senate only staying in Washington a few more weeks, not much more is expected to get done to address the AI issue until at least the post-election lame-duck session.

03:08 New poll on AI and data centers reveals how people feel on the topic 00:00 00:00

The data center bill was co-sponsored by Reps. Gabe Evans, R-Colo., and Kathy Castor, D-Fla., both members of the Energy and Commerce Committee.

It aims to put the onus and responsibility on tech and data center companies — rather than consumers — to pay for power upgrades required to operate new large data centers.

Specifically, the legislation would create a federal standard for state utility regulators to consider when creating rules for large, high-power data centers to cover the costs of power generation, transmission lines and other infrastructure upgrades needed to power these facilities, according to Evans.

Data centers provide the computing power and storage for artificial intelligence. The Evans-Castor bill, however, does not address any of the recent warnings from AI researchers: that the fast-moving technology could cause human extinction. And it’s unclear what the Senate will do with the bill, if anything. The upper chamber has its own set of data center bills, but it hasn’t moved any.

“Hardworking families should not have to subsidize the energy demands of data centers,” Evans said in a statement after the vote. “America needs the infrastructure to lead the world in AI and outcompete Communist China, but we cannot have that growth at the expense of hardworking families, farmers, seniors, and small businesses.”

Evans, in his first term, is one of the most vulnerable House Republicans of the cycle; Cook Political Report characterized his race against Democratic state Rep. Manny Rutinel in Colorado as a “toss-up.”

Evans and other at-risk lawmakers had been pressing GOP leaders for a vote on data centers, which have emerged as a key campaign issue in the November midterm elections.

President Donald Trump has fully supported the construction of new data centers, saying they are critical for U.S.-based AI companies to compete with China. But voters in swing districts and swing states have argued that data centers are springing up across America too fast, and they’ve begun mobilizing against their construction in many places.

A recent NBC News Decision Desk poll powered by SurveyMonkey found that nearly 70% of respondents oppose the construction of AI data centers in their neighborhood; 45% said they were strongly opposed.

The ratepayer bill was just one of a handful of energy-related bills the House took up in its final week in session before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The votes come as oil remains above $100 a barrel and the high cost of living and inflation remain the top issues heading into Election Day.

Many Democrats supported the measure, saying they didn’t view the bill as harmful, but they panned it as weak.

“Our communities and the people in our districts are so outraged, and they are understandably very angry that Congress isn’t doing enough” on data centers, Rep. Veronica Escobar, D-Texas, who represents El Paso, told NBC News before the vote. “I’m going to vote yes, but it is truly the bare minimum. In fact, it’s kind of pathetic that all we’re going to do is make them pay their own energy costs.”

“These data centers are going into communities like mine that don’t want them,” she added. “My community does not want data centers, loudly and clearly, and I agree with my community.”

Michigan Rep. Debbie Dingell, who heads Democrats’ policy and communications arm, voted yes but said, “It’s not enough in any way, shape or form.”

And former Progressive Caucus Chairwoman Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., who also supported the bill, pointed to Trump’s comments this week that the AI industry doesn’t need guardrails and that serious safety warnings about AI are a “hoax.”

“This is the same party that has a president that says that the AI threat is a hoax, and so I am worried about just allowing this to be, ‘Oh, we’ve solved it,’” Jayapal said. The effort “is a direct contradiction to what their president is continuing to say in opposing any real regulation.”

World.title: House passes Russia sanctions bill named for Lindsey Graham, sending it to Trump
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The House voted Wednesday to pass a major bill aimed at imposing sanctions on Russia and Iran, sending it to President Donald Trump for his signature.

The vote was 262-159.

The 61-page legislation, which passed the Senate 86-11 last month, was named the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, in honor of the late senator, who was an outspoken proponent of the cause before his unexpected death in July.

The bill takes aim at Russia’s energy sector by punishing the largest buyers of its oil and gas, allowing the president to impose tariffs on goods from those countries, which may include China and India.

The goal: to slash the revenue streams that fund Russia’s ongoing war on Ukraine, which began in 2022.

“The act’s most consequential new authority is its provision to place tariffs of up to 100 percent on third countries purchasing significant volumes of Russian energy,” according to the nonpartisan Center for Strategic and International Studies. “This replaces the blanket 500 percent tariff in the 2025 version with a more measured instrument, alongside a carve-out for countries taking significant steps to reduce dependence on Russian energy and whose imports amount to less than 15 percent of Russia’s annual natural gas exports.”

The Atlantic Council said the bill would “authorize the Trump administration to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on Chinese imports on national security grounds if China continues purchasing Russian oil. This approach assumes that tariffs will compel China to reduce imports of Russian energy.”

The measure would also target Russian government officials, as well as oligarchs, some family members and Russian financial institutions.

At Trump’s request, the package would also extend sanction authority aimed at slashing funding for Iran’s weapons and energy sectors.

Some top House Democrats criticized the bill, fretting that it would grant broad tariff authorities that Trump could abuse. But in the end, those hesitations weren’t enough to scuttle it.

“I have always been in favor of the Russia sanctions bill,” House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told reporters Monday. “But we had to build a consensus around it, and I think we have it.”

Daniel Balson of Razom for Ukraine, a U.S. advocacy group supporting Ukraine, called the bill’s passage “momentous.”

“It comes as Russian officials move towards full-scale mobilization and intensify their bombing campaign against Ukraine’s critical energy infrastructure,” he said in a statement. “This bill sends an unmistakable message: for so long as Putin continues to inflict suffering on Ukraine, Congress will continue to impose consequences on Putin.”

World.title: Merriam-Webster gives its dictionary a ‘glow-up’ with 1,400 new words and definitions
World.content:
Merriam-Webster is giving its dictionary another “glow-up,” adding 1,400 words and definitions.

The dictionary publisher announced the additions on its website Tuesday. The new words and definitions include “shapewear,” “looksmaxxing” and “meme coin.”

“The new entries reflect words and meanings that have demonstrated widespread use over time, offering a window into the world today,” it said in the release.

Other words and definitions that made it into the dictionary include “parasocial,” “compute,” “vibe coding” and “superfood” (food rich in nutrients, including salmon, broccoli and blueberries).

As temperatures drop across the country, Merriam-Webster fittingly added “cuffing season” to its dictionary. The company defines the term as “a time of the year when people who are not married or in a relationship begin looking for a short-term romantic partner to spend the colder months of the year with.”

And amid widespread fears in recent days about AI’s impact on humanity, the company added “uncanny valley” to its collection of definitions. Merriam-Webster defines the term as “that creepy feeling that results from something artificial appearing almost—but not quite—human.”

The nod to AI follows Merriam-Webster’s word of 2025, “slop,” which it defines as “digital content of low quality that is produced usually in quantity by means of artificial intelligence.”

Merriam-Webster has not yet announced a Word of the Year for 2026. The company typically makes the announcement in the final quarter of the year.

The company said on its website that it adds new words and phrases to its repertoire based on frequent, widespread and meaningful use.

“The definer must judge whether there is enough evidence to put a new word in; that judgment will be reviewed by more senior colleagues as the dictionary moves through the editorial process, but there’s no committee, no advocacy, no meetings for new word inclusion,” the company said.

World.title: Supreme Court pushes back against Trump and GOP ahead of the midterm elections
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court in the last week has delivered major blows to President Donald Trump and his fellow Republicans that suggest the justices will not be receptive to last-minute efforts to change election rules heading into the midterms.

With control of Congress at stake, the court on Monday night blocked Trump’s plan to exert federal control over mail-in ballots via a Postal Service regulation.

The decision came after the court twice last week ruled against Republicans by declining to revive a new congressional map in Missouri that would have eliminated one of two Democratic-held districts.

While the court has a 6-3 conservative majority that often rules for Republican priorities, there are limits to how receptive some justices are to more extreme requests, election law experts told NBC News. That’s especially true for cases that could disrupt voters when an election is close or already underway.

Justin Levitt, an NBC News contributor and election law expert at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles, said the recent decisions show “there aren’t five votes for abject chaos.”

“I think the court is going to pay very close attention to any extraordinary actions that destabilize the electoral process,” said Bob Bauer, who served as White House counsel under President Barack Obama. “There’s a signal here that this sort of late intervention is going to receive scrutiny.”

On the left, the Supreme Court has been viewed with particular distrust and alarm as it relates to election issues following a major ruling in the spring that further weakened the landmark Voting Rights Act.

In the aftermath, the court quickly allowed Republican states to draw new congressional maps that eliminated majority-Black, Democratic-held seats.

But now it is Trump who appears angered and frustrated by the court’s actions.

“It is a big loss for Republicans, and America itself, and makes cheating by the Radical Left ‘Dumocrats,’ on Mail-In Ballots, a much easier thing to do — And now they have an open field to do so!” he said in a Truth Social post on Tuesday, repeating his unfounded claims about widespread election fraud.

With some states already sending out ballots for the midterm elections, timing was an issue for Republicans in both cases.

The Missouri Supreme Court faulted Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins for delaying a decision on whether the new map could be challenged, ultimately finding him in contempt for defying its ruling in favor of plaintiffs.

As for the Postal Service, it pushed through the new regulation despite concerns raised by election officials that they would be unable to implement it in time.

“In both instances, the court said we’re not going to countenance that,” said Travis Crum, an NBC News contributor and law professor at Washington University in St. Louis. “I do think that the Missouri case is going to send the message that dragging your feet like this is not going to be rewarded by the Supreme Court.”

There are limits to how receptive the Supreme Court is to more extreme election requests, experts said. Matt Nighswander / NBC News file

As the November elections loom, efforts to make late changes to the rules, including any new proposals from the Trump administration relating to mail-in ballots, are likely to meet with a similarly frosty reception from the justices, experts said. They cautioned, though, that it is too early to say what new litigation could arise ahead of or after Election Day.

Among the concerns that have been raised by some election officials are that the Trump administration could post federal immigration agents near polling places, although officials have said they have no current plans to do so.

As he has done previously, Trump might also complain about mail-in ballots being counted after in-person votes, claiming voter fraud because the outcome might appear to change, even though it is customary for various jurisdictions to continue counting ballots after Election Day under state law.

States with competitive elections, especially those that could determine control of the Senate, could be a particular focus for any Election Day or post-election litigation. These include Texas and Georgia, two states under Republican control with competitive races. Alaska, where votes often take a long time to count, is another state that could attract litigation, with Democrats hoping to win the Senate race there.

One fear among election administrators is that the federal government could try to seize ballots and other voting records over claims of election fraud similar to those Trump and his allies raised, and courts rejected, following the 2020 presidential election. In January, the FBI searched an election office in Georgia, seizing 2020 election ballots.

But as the Supreme Court has shown in other cases, the conservative majority follows its own agenda, not Trump’s, and has delivered him major defeats this year on his sweeping tariffs and plan to roll back birthright citizenship.

“This court is radically conservative,” Levitt said, “but not actually in the tank for Trump’s particular version of personalist chaos.”

World.title: Ross Fire 100% contained after more than 3 weeks
World.content:
A wildfire that sparked near Ross in Palo Pinto County on Aug. 24 has burned roughly 90,000 acres and is 100% contained as of Wednesday, Sept. 16.

It destroyed more than 150 structures in the area, including homes, forced evacuations in neighboring Jack County and affected local schools, North Texas officials said.

The National Weather Service said the Ross Fire is the second-largest wildfire in North Texas.

How big is the Ross Fire and where was it burning?

The Ross Fire burned roughly 90,000 acres in Palo Pinto and Jack counties, with the fire burning near U.S. 180 and FM 919.

According to the Texas A&M Forest Service, the fire is 100% contained as of Wednesday, Sept. 16; 157 structures have been destroyed, 140 have been damaged and 453 have been saved.

Residents in Jack County along County Road 2210 toward Highway 281 were instructed to evacuate on Tuesday, Aug. 25; however, those mandatory evacuations were lifted a day later as conditions improved. Jack County Emergency Management warns returning residents to stay vigilant as the fire is still burning in neighboring Palo Pinto County.

The fire began near Ross in Palo Pinto County just before 1:30 p.m. Monday, Aug. 24, and was initially estimated at 25 acres, according to the Palo Pinto County Emergency Service District. It rapidly expanded to thousands of acres.

The Longhorn Council of Scouting America said many buildings at Worth Ranch in Palo Pinto were among the structures that suffered catastrophic damage, but no scouts, campers, or guests were at the property when the fire moved into the area, and the camp ranger, Pat Adams, was safely evacuated.

What areas were under evacuation orders because of the Ross Fire?

As of Monday, Aug. 31, all school districts in the area resumed normal operations.

The wildfire and evacuations affected schools in the area. Jacksboro ISD delayed the start of school by two hours on Tuesday, Aug. 25, but normal operations resumed the next day.

Perrin CISD canceled classes for Tuesday, Aug. 25, and delayed the start of school to 10 a.m. Wednesday, Aug. 26.

Jack County Emergency Management instructed Bryson ISD and Graford ISD to cancel classes that same Wednesday.

A Molson Coors spokesperson said the company had temporarily paused some canning lines at the Fort Worth facility out of an abundance of caution over the smoky skies.

"But beer lovers will see absolutely no impact," the spokesperson said.

The Texas Intrastate Fire Mutual Aid System (TIFMAS) Strike Team, along with the Texas A&M Forest Service, is supporting firefighting efforts with dozers and aircraft.

What roads closed because of the Ross Fire?

U.S. Highway 180 reopened after being closed to all traffic between South FM 4 and FM 919 because of the wildfire on Tuesday.

A Temporary Flight Restriction was in place over the fire area.

Where could livestock be taken during the Ross Fire?

CBS News Texas

The Graham Livestock Commission said that it was offering space for livestock displaced by the wildfire at the Old Mineral Wells Sale Barn at 2805 North Oak Ave.

The holding station is available to people who need a temporary place for livestock until other arrangements can be made.

The Humane Society of North Texas said it is helping the Mineral Wells Animal Shelter clear out its current shelter population to make room for pets displaced by the Ross Fire. Twelve dogs and 26 cats were expected to arrive at the shelter in Fort Worth on Wednesday.

Why is the wildfire risk high in North Texas?

Dry vegetation, a lack of measurable rainfall and gusty winds are creating elevated wildfire conditions across parts of North Texas.

The National Weather Service is monitoring several wildfires west of Interstate 35, with the Ross Fire among the largest.

After more than a month without measurable rainfall, fine surface fuels have become critically to extremely dry, making vegetation easier to ignite and allowing fires to spread quickly.

Residents are urged to avoid outdoor activities that could produce sparks or flames.

World.title: House passes Russia sanctions bill, overcoming Democratic opposition
World.content:
Washington — A sweeping Russia sanctions bill overcame opposition in the House on Wednesday, after many Democrats expressed concern that it would expand President Trump's tariff authorities.

The House passed the bill in a 262 to 159 vote on the final day that the lower chamber is in session before lawmakers leave Washington until after Election Day. Some 58 Democrats voted in favor of the bill, while seven Republicans voted in opposition.

The Senate passed the legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support in August after more than a year of negotiations that were spearheaded by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina. It now heads to Mr. Trump's desk.

"This bill sends a powerful message of American unity and gives the administration every tool in the toolbox to help bring this war to a just end, and we are proud to send it to the president's desk," House Speaker Mike Johnson said in a statement after its passage.

The effort to penalize top Russian figures and the biggest buyers of Russian oil over the war in Ukraine gained fresh momentum after Graham's sudden death in July. Graham died shortly after returning from a trip to Kyiv and announcing that a deal had been reached with the White House to move forward on an updated version of the legislation.

The bill, titled The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, allows the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil or natural gas. There are exceptions for countries that import less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia and are taking "significant" steps to reduce the imports. It also includes sanctions on Russian President Vladimir Putin, officials within his government, oligarchs and Russian banks and financial institutions.

China and India are the largest buyers of Russian crude oil, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air think tank. Europe has historically been Russia's largest natural gas customer, though the European Union has cut its imports significantly in recent years, and sales to China have grown.

At the request of Mr. Trump, the bill also extends sanctions on Iran's energy and weapons sectors.

It gives the president authority to waive the sanctions if he certifies to Congress that it's in the national interests of the U.S.

Several House Democrats in leadership positions were opposed to the measure in its current form. In a joint statement explaining their "no" votes, House Democratic leaders said Mr. Trump "has shown no willingness to be strong on Russia."

"He cannot be entrusted with new powers to impose tariffs that will further raise costs for American families," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Democratic Whip Katherine Clark and Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California said.

Another group of Democrats argued last week the bill would "dramatically extend presidential tariff authorities."

"These flaws would raise Americans' prices while undermining support for Ukraine in the long term," Democratic Reps. Gregory Meeks of New York, Don Beyer of Virginia and Richard Neal of Massachusetts said in a statement Friday after GOP leaders added the legislation to this week's floor schedule. "The President has ample authority to expand sanctions on those fueling Russia's war machine, including those targeted by this bill, and we renew our call on him to do so without further delay."

Meeks said after the vote he hopes Mr. Trump proves him wrong and implements the bill as intended.

"But, in the likely event he doesn't, I will do everything in my power to make sure Congress holds him to account, the American people do not get further crushed by his inflationary tariffs, and that Ukraine receives real support," he said in a statement.

Republicans noted during floor debate on the measure that it had the support of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

"As we've heard from President Zelenskyy's team, you can evade sanctions — which the Russians have done for years — but you cannot evade tariffs," Republican Rep. Michael McCaul of Texas said on the House floor. "Tariffs are a powerful way to amplify the impact of sanctions. That's why they are the teeth of this bill."

The legislation narrowly avoided a potential hurdle Tuesday during a procedural vote to tee the bill and several unrelated measures up for debate as a small group of conservatives voted in opposition or withheld their support. Two moderate Democrats — Reps. Jared Golden of Maine, who is retiring, and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington, who holds a competitive seat — split with Democrats in what is typically a party-line vote to help propel it forward.

"This is our last week in session until November. The stakes for Ukraine are too high to let this good bill — which already passed the Senate with overwhelming, bipartisan support — die as a result of a procedural vote," Golden said in a statement about the defection.

Gluesenkamp Perez pointed to her Ukrainian constituency, saying, "I'll always stand with my community's values."

World.title: Coast Guard and FBI boarded tankers due to cyberattacks. How big is the risk?
World.content:
U.S. Coast Guard personnel and FBI agents boarded two Texas-bound energy tankers last month after cyberattacks struck the vessels while they were traveling toward the United States, according to U.S. officials.

One of the vessels was the VL Prosperity, a 1,093-foot Liberian-flagged crude oil tanker headed to Galveston, Texas. Iranian state media identified the ship shortly after the incident and claimed hackers had gained access to its propulsion, navigation and cargo systems, knocking out communications for 30 hours.

The Coast Guard has not publicly pinned the attacks on Iran. But Rear Adm. Amy Grable, commander of U.S. Coast Guard Cyber Command, told CBS News in a network exclusive interview that investigators did find evidence of a malicious cyber actor.

"They started out by doing an assessment of the information technology and the other systems on board the vessel, and they did find malicious cyber activity," Grable said.

The U.S. is investigating whether the two cyberattacks are connected and whether Iran or another foreign adversary was behind the attacks.

What happened?

The VL Prosperity is what's known as a supertanker — more than three football fields long and capable of carrying roughly 2.3 million barrels of oil.

Public vessel data shows the ship departed Egypt's Sidi Kerir oil terminal on Aug. 1 headed for Galveston. U.S. officials say it slowed near the Strait of Gibraltar around the time of the cyberattack before continuing across the Atlantic and toward the U.S.

Iran's Mehr News Agency reported on Aug. 20 that the VL Prosperity had been attacked on Aug. 7 while transiting through the Strait of Gibraltar. Citing an unnamed crew member, Mehr alleged hackers breached the engine room, reducing engine cooling flow, increasing engine speed and interfering with fuel systems.

Rob Lee, CEO of Dragos, an industrial cybersecurity firm specializing in operational technology, said the Iranian report's details were technically plausible, but warned that authorities have not yet revealed who was behind the incident.

"The details that they published, from what we understand of these types of vehicles and ships and similar, is spot on," Lee said. "Everything they're saying is very realistic."

The next day, Aug. 21, Coast Guard cyber personnel, law enforcement officers, a vessel inspector and FBI Cyber Action Team operators boarded the ship for four days.

Grable said Coast Guard teams had been alerted by interagency partners and went offshore with the FBI to climb aboard — one of roughly 40 to 50 missions the Coast Guard's Cyber Protection Team has undergone in the past year.

She said investigators were hunting for malware and combing through information technology systems to root out malicious activity.

"The real thing we're concerned about is those IT systems being connected to other systems on the ship that control propulsion, navigation and other systems that are critical to the safety of that vessel," Grable added.

Typically, investigators collect data that is later analyzed, and Grable told CBS News that the Coast Guard plans to provide the vessel owner with recommendations for patching vulnerabilities. She stressed that response teams did not find any evidence indicating the ship had become unsafe to navigate when they boarded it.

How difficult is it to attack a ship?

The concern surrounding large cargo vessels and maritime critical infrastructure transcends stolen files or disrupted communications.

More and more, modern commercial vessels run on internet-connected systems, relying on them for navigation, propulsion, steering, ballast and additional critical machinery. A cyberattack that penetrates those operational systems could potentially be weaponized or manipulated.

"When these vessels are highly connected, they're susceptible to cyber threats," Grable said, warning that an attack could lead to "a vessel blocking a waterway or a pollution incident or any other number of safety and security hazards to our ports and waterways."

The danger that a large vessel could be compromised near an American port is something that authorities fear.

"Of course we're worried about a collision, an explosion, anything that blocks the channel for other vessels to safely enter and exit the port, pollution incidents — we're kind of worried about the whole gamut," Grable said.

The potential economic impact is also colossal. Grable said $5.4 trillion in commerce flows through U.S. ports annually — which could mean high economic stakes for even a relatively small disruption.

"Any small delay, because of a cyber breach, like, for example, if a port has to shift to manual operations, it causes a big delay with tankers and cargo vessels coming in and out of the port," she said.

Perhaps most concerning, Grable said the technical barrier may not be as high as the public assumes.

How sophisticated would an attacker have to be to move beyond breaking into a computer network to manipulating machinery aboard a modern tanker?

"Not necessarily that sophisticated," Grable told CBS News. "There is malicious source code that people can get their hands on."

Grable said that code is available right now, and added that "artificial intelligence is accelerating the rate at which we need to take action."

She urged operators to zero in on network segmentation, phishing attacks and basic cyber hygiene. "Just taking basic precautions would prevent most of these occurrences."

Just one firewall away

On many ships, the barrier between a satellite internet connection and critical onboard systems can be as fragile as a single firewall.

Behind that firewall, Lee said, can be a shared network containing "navigation, propulsion, ballast, steering, ship command — everything on one shared network."

Lee explained that artificial intelligence could make that problem worse because it can assist attackers in picking out weakly protected systems, speeding up attempts to breach internet-facing systems on energy carriers.

"The very thing that we think is our one protection — not that you should have one protection — is the very thing that AI is actually really good at," Lee said.

Still, experts concede that while older vessels may not have the same digitally connected control systems, even on modern ships, reaching critical machinery still requires some knowledge of the onboard environment.

Is 'remote hijacking' a real threat?

Asked whether cyber access to a ship could amount to a form of remote hijacking, Grable called it a fair description of the broader risk.

"That's a good way to characterize it, and yes, it is a concern," she said.

Lee agreed that the scenario is realistic if an attacker gains a foothold.

"I do think there's a realistic concern," Lee said, describing the possibility of remotely messing with a maritime asset, even running it aground.

But former Coast Guard cyber official Quinton DuBose seemed skeptical of the notion that hackers could simply take over an entire supertanker like a remote-controlled vehicle.

"I'd be kind of cautious about saying that somebody can just take control of the ship," DuBose said. "Ships are incredibly complicated systems."

The more realistic threat, he said, may be an attacker disrupting one or more critical subsystems enough to make the vessel unsafe.

"Rather than looking at it as, 'okay, I'm going to take full control of this thing,' it's, 'what systems can I disrupt to the point where it affects the safe handling and makes the ship less safe to operate,'" DuBose said.

Iranian state media claims under scrutiny

The U.S. has not publicly stated who is behind either cyberattack. But Iranian state media began pushing out content around the VL Prosperity incident before U.S. authorities even publicly acknowledged the boarding.

Four days after Mehr's initial report, Iran's Tasnim News Agency published an article with the headline, "No American Vessel Is Safe Anymore: Will Cannons Give Way to Codes?"

DuBose stressed that the Iranian narrative remains unverified, cautioning that Iranian-linked actors are often quick to oversell their cyber influence.

Attribution in cyberspace can take weeks or months, DuBose added.

According to Grable, investigators typically compare the attacker's tactics, techniques and procedures — effectively their digital fingerprints — against known threat actors.

"We look at things called TTPs, which are tactics, techniques and protocols that certain adversaries use — kind of like their trademark fingerprints on how they gain access to systems and what they do and what their payloads are," she said.

A warning to the maritime industry

For Coast Guard Cyber Command, the growing concern is that increasingly connected vessels create more porous entry points for attackers, as ships adopt satellite communications and connect IT networks with their onboard control systems.

"Because they're facing the internet, that is a vector for attackers to gain access and deploy malicious activity on the vessels," she said.

DuBose said the industry should take the threat seriously, while resisting the notion that all vessels are suddenly vulnerable to remote takeover.

He added that maritime infrastructure is so critical that the federal government "has increasingly imposed baseline cyber requirements across the sector."

Grable's warning to vessel owners and operators was blunt: "We need everybody to pay attention to this."

World.title: Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time since 2023
World.content:
The Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 on Wednesday, reversing course as the Iran war drives up global energy prices and fuels inflation.

The Fed raised the federal funds rate by 0.25 percentage points, bringing its target range to between 3.75% and 4% — its highest level since December 2025. The benchmark rate influences borrowing costs across the U.S. economy, including for credit cards, auto loans and personal loans.

In a set of quarterly projections, the Fed also signaled that its rate-setting committee expects to further raise rates later this year. The vote to hike rates was unanimous, the Fed said in a statement on Wednesday.

No rate hikes in 2027

For now, however, the Fed's move doesn't appear to signal the start of an aggressive rate-hiking campaign. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday that policymakers expect to hold rates steady throughout 2027.

"For more than five years, inflation has been running above target," Warsh said at a news conference after the rate announcement. "So our predominant focus is on the price stability side of our mandate. The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long."

About half of FOMC members predicted that rates would hold steady next year.

"We don't think this is the beginning of another major tightening cycle, and markets have too much tightening priced in over the coming year," Michael Pearce, chief U.S. economist at Oxford Economics, said in a research note.

By contrast, the central bank raised rates 11 times starting in 2022 as it sought to quash surging inflation as the economy was rebounding from the pandemic.

Still, the latest hike marks an about-face from the Fed's stance at the start of the year, when inflation was cooling, and as many economists expected the central bank to lower interest rates throughout 2026. Instead, monetary policymakers are brandishing their most potent weapon to curb prices. The Consumer Price Index rose at an annual rate of 3.4% in August, far above the Fed's 2% annual target.

President Trump has repeatedly called on the Fed to lower borrowing costs. But escalating conflict in the Middle East has disrupted crude oil production and supplies, pushing up fuel prices in the U.S. and driving up costs across the broader economy.

When asked on Wednesday how the president might react to the rate increase, Warsh said, "I've got nothing for you on a discussion with the president."

In a Truth Social post on Wednesday after the Fed policy statement, Mr. Trump said U.S. interest rates "should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World — BY FAR."

"LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!" he added.

Why stocks fell after Warsh comments

"Hiking was the right move, and it restores Fed credibility that the central bank will curb inflation no matter what the White House or anyone else says," Heather Long, chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union, said in an email. "The big news is that the vote was unanimous and the forecast only signals one more hike in 2026."

Higher interest rates can tamp down inflation because consumers pare spending and businesses reduce investment. That cools economic growth and tempers price increases as demand slows.

Stocks tumbled after Warsh said the U.S. economy "appears to be strengthening" and reiterated his pledge to tame inflation. Some investors interpreted his remarks as a sign that the central bank believes the economy can withstand additional rate hikes if they are needed to finally get inflation under control.

"Stocks declined after Warsh finished. Why? Warsh was hawkish today," Long said. "How many more hikes beyond that remains an open question that likely will depend on the war in Iran and just how insatiable the data center building boom is."

The Dow Jones Industrial Average slid 631 points, or 1.2%, to close at 51,462, while the S&P 500 lost almost 0.4%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq ended the day largely flat.

Higher borrowing costs

Banks are likely to respond to the latest Fed hike by boosting their interest rates on credit cards and other lending products, although a single 0.25 percentage-point increase might not significantly raise borrowing costs, according to financial experts.

Even so, the increase in borrowing costs comes as Americans are shouldering higher costs for gas, food and other essentials.

"Consumer sentiment is now 13% below where it was this time last year," said Heather Boushey, professor of practice at the Kleinman Center for Energy Policy at the University of Pennsylvania, in an email. The Fed's rate hike this week "will make it harder for families to borrow, raising the cost of car loans, credit cards, mortgages and more."
