World.title: Women farmers in Oaxaca, Guerrero report catastrophic drought
World.content:
Drought has devastated corn crops in Oaxaca and Guerrero, according to farmers in the two southern states.

Two associations of women farmers — one in Oaxaca and one in Guerrero — released a joint statement last week in which they reported the loss of up to 100% of agricultural production.

They said that drought is not only taking a toll on their crops but also on their economic well-being.

The National Water Commission’s most recent “drought monitor” report shows that large parts of Oaxaca and Guerrero are “abnormally dry” or experiencing “moderate drought.”

However, the women farmers’ associations — Red de Mujeres, Ejidatarias y Comuneras del Estado de Oaxaca and the Red Estatal de Mujeres Agraristas de Guerrero (REMA) — described the drought conditions as “severe.”

“The severe drought afflicting our states is on the scale of a catastrophe, similar to the damage caused by hurricanes, only without the wind and without [the public, media and political] spotlight,” they said.

“A hurricane destroys what is visible in a matter of hours; drought destroys our future and what sustains us over the course of months: the cornfields, water, seeds and our livelihoods,” they said.

The farmers’ associations said that communities in Oaxaca and Guerrero, in both coastal and inland regions of the two states, are “losing the capacity” to produce their own food.

Drought conditions “represent a direct threat to the food sovereignty of farming families,” they said.

The two farming associations called on state and federal authorities to declare a climate emergency in drought-affected areas of Oaxaca and Guerrero and establish programs aimed at guaranteeing food sovereignty and supporting female farmers, many of whom primarily grow corn to feed themselves and their families, but sell any surplus they have. They also asked for authorities to provide direct monetary resources to female farmers.

Women farmers in the two states are “in despair,” said Nancy Solano, a farmer and spokesperson for her fellow campesinas in Oaxaca.

She told the news outlet La Silla Rota that prices for corn and tortillas — a staple in Mexico — will go up due to drought-related maize shortages.

Adriana Paz, president of REMA, told La Silla Rota that the association she leads has requested a meeting with federal Agricultural Minister Columba López Gutiérrez to propose a comprehensive drought relief program that takes gender into account.

“A lot of the government’s public policies don’t have a gender perspective and exclude women,” she said.

“… Without women there is no corn and without corn there is no country,” Paz said.

With reports from El Universal and La Silla Rota

World.title: The Mexican Navy’s at-sea cocaine seizures are up nearly 50% this year
World.content:
Cocaine seizures by the Mexican Navy have increased significantly this year, rising 47.2% from 25.7 metric tonnes in 2025 to 37.9 tonnes this year as of Sept. 10.

“These results are the product of operations carried out by the Mexican Navy through surface, air and Marine Corps units, focused on monitoring the coasts and national waters, as well as detecting, intercepting, and seizing vessels linked to illicit activities,” the Navy (Semar) stated in a report.

Semar’s maritime operations aim to disrupt the logistical capacity of criminal organizations operating in the maritime domain, according to Semar.

In addition to the drugs seized, the Navy’s maritime operations this year have resulted in the confiscation of 26 vessels, one low-profile vessel (LPV) and 54 outboard motorboats, as well as the arrest of 86 suspects.

The seizure of the substances “contributes to reducing their availability and circulation, as well as preventing them from reaching communities and particularly affecting younger generations,” Semar said in a statement

“With this action, the Mexican Navy contributes to the protection of youth and the creation of safer environments for children and young people.”

In a related development, on Tuesday a coordinated effort of Semar and the National Customs Agency of Mexico at the Mexico City International Airport (AICM) confiscated 1 metric tonne of cocaine that had been declared as ground roasted coffee and hidden in over 3,000 bags.

“With these actions, the Navy, Customs, the Ministry of Security and Citizen Protection (SSPC) and other security cabinet institutions are strengthening inter-institutional cooperation and reinforcing control and oversight mechanisms to protect legality in foreign trade operations,” the authorities said.

With reports from Sin Embargo and La Jornada

World.title: State of democracy improved in Mexico in 2025 as region showed signs of deterioration
World.content:
The state of democracy in Mexico improved slightly in 2025 — President Claudia Sheinbaum’s first full year in office — compared to 2024, according to the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (International IDEA), an intergovernmental organization.

On Tuesday, the Stockholm-based organization released its annual report on the state of democracy in more than 170 countries around the world.

This year’s report, “The Global State of Democracy 2026,” is subtitled “Democracy in an Age of Conflict” in recognition of the wars currently being fought in various parts of the world. It focuses on the state of democracy in countries around the world in 2025.

International IDEA scores and ranks countries in four different democracy-related categories: representation, rights, rule of law and participation.

Compared to 2024, Mexico’s score improved in two of the four categories, declined in one and was unchanged in another. Mexico rose in the rankings in two categories, but fell in the other two. Its combined score across the four categories increased by 0.008 points to 1.778 out of 4 in 2025 from 1.770 in 2024.

In December 2024, less than three months after she was sworn in as president, Sheinbaum said that Mexico was “perhaps” the most democratic country in the world given that it would hold judicial elections in 2025.

However, International IDEA’s latest report indicates that Mexico is far from a global beacon of democracy. In the four categories assessed by the intergovernmental organization, Mexico is among the top 100 countries in just one of them.

However, the slight improvement in the state of democracy in Mexico in 2025, according to International IDEA, is, of course, preferable to a decline. The quality of democracy in many other countries is on the wane, according to the intergovernmental organization.

In the executive summary of its report, International IDEA wrote that in 2025, “the global challenges to democracy and the difficulty in stemming its erosion were both exemplified and compounded by political developments in the United States.”

“There, President Donald Trump quickly amassed power in the executive branch and wielded it to further a narrow set of personal goals and pursue retaliation against perceived enemies,” International IDEA said.

The intergovernmental organization also said that “Latin America has become the most politically polarized region in the world after a rapid rise in polarization over the past decade.”

“Highly contentious issues such as the economy, migration, and insecurity, as well as the increasing success of anti-establishment politicians who capitalize on divisive identity-based narratives and ‘us versus them’ politics, have contributed to an erosion of democratic dialogue,” International IDEA said.

Almost two years into her six-year term, Sheinbaum remains a very popular president, according to poll results.

However, there is political polarization in Mexico, and a significant number of Mexicans believe that the state of democracy in Mexico has declined during the presidencies of Sheinbaum and her predecessor Andrés Manuel López Obrador as a result of government-led initiatives such as the disbandment of various autonomous agencies and the election of judges affiliated with, or seen as sympathetic to, the ruling Morena party.

Mexico’s scores and rankings in the four democracy-related categories assessed by International IDEA are outlined below.

Representation: Mexico’s score and ranking declined

According to International IDEA, in the Global State of Democracy (GSoD) Indices, “Representation” is an aggregate measure of the extent of representative democracy, built from component measures of credible elections, inclusive suffrage, freedom to organize through political parties, the effectiveness of the legislature, and the practice of democracy at the local level.

Mexico scored 0.550 out of 1 on this measure to rank 83rd out of 173 countries.

Mexico’s score declined by 0.003 points compared to 2024, while it fell one spot in the rankings.

Nevertheless, Mexico achieved its best score and ranking in this category.

Mexico’s score in 2025 was on par with those of Paraguay and Hungary.

The top three countries in this category were Denmark, Germany and Costa Rica.

The United States ranked 51st while Canada ranked 25th.

Rights: Mexico’s score was unchanged, but its ranking declined

According to International IDEA, the “Rights” category is made up of liberal and social rights that support both fair representation and accountability. It is built upon four component measures — Access to Justice; Civil Liberties, including Freedom of the Press, Freedom of Expression, Freedom of Association and Assembly, Freedom of Religion, and Freedom of Movement; Basic Welfare; and Political Equality, including Gender Equality, Social Group Equality, and Economic Equality.

Mexico scored 0.407 out of 1 on this measure to rank 111th out of the 173 countries assessed.

Mexico’s score was unchanged compared to 2024, while it fell one spot in the rankings.

Mexico ranked one spot above Burkina Faso in this category and one position below Qatar.

The top three countries in this category were Denmark, Switzerland and Germany.

The United States ranked 42nd while Canada ranked 27th.

Rule of law: Mexico’s score and ranking improved

According to International IDEA, in the GSoD Indices, “Rule of Law” is an aggregate measure that includes assessments of the independence of the judiciary from government influence, the extent to which public administrators use their offices for personal gain, the predictability of law enforcement, and the degree to which people are free from political violence. Overall, the index provides a snapshot of the extent to which everyone is subject to the law and the level of safety that exists.

Mexico scored 0.370 out of 1 on this measure to rank 112th.

Mexico’s score increased 0.009 points compared to 2024, while it rose seven positions in the rankings.

Mexico ranked one spot above Thailand in this category and one position below Ukraine.

The top three countries in this category were Denmark, Germany and Switzerland.

The United States ranked 37th while Canada ranked 26th.

Participation: Mexico’s score and ranking improved

According to International IDEA, in the GSoD Indices, “Participation” is an aggregate measure of the extent to which people are actively involved at all levels of government. It is comprised of three factors that measure the space for civil society to operate freely (Civil Society), the extent to which people engage in political and non-political associations and trade unions (Civic Engagement), and voter turnout (Electoral Participation).

Mexico scored 0.451 out of 1 on this measure to rank 120th.

Mexico’s score increased 0.002 points compared to 2024, while it rose four positions in the rankings.

Mexico’s score in 2025 was on par with that of Papua New Guinea.

The top three countries in this category were Denmark, Switzerland and Norway.

The United States ranked 19th while Canada ranked 32nd.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Quintana Roo passes ‘Nicole’s Law,’ banning cosmetic surgery for minors
World.content:
The southeastern Mexican state of Quintana Roo this week passed a ban on invasive cosmetic surgery for minors, joining Durango in approving reforms known as “Nicole’s Law.”

The initiative takes its name from Paloma Nicole Arellano, a 14-year-old who died in Durango last September after cosmetic surgery. Her death exposed gaps in rules governing elective procedures for minors and intensified calls for state-level restrictions.

Two months later, Durango became the first Mexican state to enact a version of the law, with its legislators approving the measure 23-0.

The Durango law prohibits cosmetic surgery for minors except for reconstructive or medically necessary care It also strengthens penalties for people who practice medicine without proper credentials.

The federal entity of Mexico City followed suit in May, approving changes to Article 172 of its Health Law that invalidate authorizations for clinics to perform aesthetic surgery on minors.

The changes are state and city measures, not a single nationwide Mexican law.

The Quintana Roo Congress approved the reform on Monday, adding a provision to the state penal code that bars plastic, aesthetic and cosmetic surgeries on people younger than 18 when the purpose is solely to alter appearance.

The measure exempts reconstructive procedures with medical justification, including treatment for congenital malformations, cleft lip and palate, and other conditions requiring specialized care, such as accident-related injuries.

Doctors who perform prohibited procedures face six months to three years in prison, fines and suspensions from professional practice.

A congressional committee in Jalisco approved a similar package in August, though it has not yet received a final vote from the full legislature.

Coahuila could be the next state to approve a similar law. Deputy Jorge Valdés said his fellow members of Congress will debate and vote on a proposed Nicole’s Law during the current session.

Internationally, similar restrictions are uneven. The state of Queensland, Australia, has barred unnecessary cosmetic procedures for minors since 2008, and Norway also prohibits health professionals from providing higher-risk, nonmedical cosmetic procedures on minors, even with parental consent.

Comparable broad bans appear uncommon in the United States and Canada, where regulation generally centers on consent, medical judgment and procedure-specific age limits.

With reports from Excélsior, Infobae, La Jornada and N+

World.title: El Jalapeño: Mexico is only good for ‘tamales and tomatoes’ … and keeping the entire US economy functioning on a daily basis
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — After U.S. President Donald Trump said Mexico was only good for “tamales and tomatoes” last week, senior Mexican trade representatives held a press briefing Monday morning to clarify that while fresh tomatoes and steamed tamales are indeed foundational pillars of the national economy, Mexico also happens to provide the industrial, technological and automotive machinery that keeps the entire United States economy functioning on a daily basis.

The statement came after remarks from Trump suggested the United States could comfortably eliminate trade with its southern neighbor, omitting the fact that Mexico is the number one trade partner for the U.S.

“We want to reassure our northern neighbors that while our tamales remain world-class, our exports also include the computer servers powering their artificial intelligence, the advanced medical devices in their hospitals and the heavy auto parts keeping their assembly lines moving,” said Deputy Secretary of Trade Logistics Mateo Morales, presenting a series of charts detailing the US $60 billion in goods exported to the U.S. in July alone. “It turns out the nation feeding you lunch is also building the vehicle you drive to work.”

Morales emphasized that as the top trading partner of the U.S., Mexico’s commercial footprint extends well beyond agricultural goods, encompassing complex manufacturing networks that link factories from Monterrey to Detroit.

“If the flow of goods were to stop tomorrow, the issue would not merely be a shortage of menu items,” Morales noted. “It would be the immediate realization that half the light trucks on American highways were missing their transmissions.”

Trade officials concluded the conference by assuring consumers on both sides of the border that supply chains remain fully operational, confirming that shipments of high-tech machinery, auto components and fresh produce will continue shipping north on schedule.

World.title: In Grito, President Sheinbaum celebrates migrants, women insurgents and the dignity of Mexico’s diverse peoples
World.content:
Listen to this article

From the central balcony of the National Palace and in front of a huge crowd of celebrants gathered in Mexico City’s central square, President Claudia Sheinbaum delivered the national Cry of Independence (Grito de Independencia) on Tuesday night, the eve of Mexico’s Independence Day.

“Mexicanas, Mexicanos, long live independence!” Sheinbaum declared 216 years after priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla issued the Cry of Dolores (Grito de Dolores) — a call for revolt against Spanish rule.

En el 216 Aniversario del Grito de Independencia, exaltamos a los héroes y heroínas que nos dieron patria, como Antonia Nava. También destacamos a los pueblos indígenas y afromexicanos, así como a nuestros hermanos y hermanas migrantes. ¡Que viva México libre, independiente y… pic.twitter.com/bJXNXaB43m — Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) September 16, 2026

With the presidential sash draped over her torso, the Mexican flag in her left hand and her husband, Jesús María Tarriba, standing beside her, Sheinbaum issued a total of 21 arengas, or “cries of viva!“, each of which was met with a reciprocal “¡viva!” by those present in the Zócalo and Mexicans across the country.

A selection of Mexico’s independence heroines and heroes, the nation’s Indigenous and Afro-Mexican people and Mexicans living abroad were all wished long life by Sheinbaum, who made history a year ago by becoming the first female president of Mexico to deliver the Grito. In a year in which she has denounced U.S. interference in Mexican affairs, the president also issued an emphatic cry of ¡viva! in defense of Mexican independence and sovereignty.

“Long live Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla! Long live Josefa Ortiz Téllez-Girón! Long live José María Morelos y Pavón! Long live Leona Vicario! Long live Vicente Guerrero! Long live Gertrudis Bocanegra! Long live Guadalupe Victoria! Long live Antonia Nava!” Sheinbaum proclaimed.

“Long live the heroines and heroes who gave us a homeland! Long live the Indigenous and Afro-Mexican peoples! Long live our migrant sisters and brothers! Long live the dignity of the people of Mexico! Long live freedom! Long live equality! Long live justice! Long live democracy! Long live a free, independent and sovereign Mexico! ¡Viva México!”

Some of the people honored by the president, including Afro-Mexicans and the insurgent Antonia Nava, had never before been included in a national Cry of Independence.

After completing her second Grito, Sheinbaum rang the Campana de Dolores — the same bell that Hidalgo rang 216 years ago in the town of Dolores, Guanajuato — and waved the Mexican flag to the mass of people gathered in the Zócalo. The president received the flag from an escolta (color guard) made of up of six female military cadets.

After the Grito, a fireworks display lit up the sky above the Zócalo, where musical acts including the Grammy Award-winning Texan band Intocable played on Tuesday night.

Among the officials who witnessed Sheinbaum’s second Cry of Independence from National Palace vantage points were Attorney General Ernestina Godoy, Supreme Court Chief Justice Hugo Aguilar, Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez, Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard, Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla, Navy Minister Raymundo Pedro Morales and Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada.

Governors and mayors also issued Cries of Independence at ceremonies held on Tuesday night in cities and towns across the country.

No incidents reported at Mexico City’s 300,000-strong Independence celebration

The Mexico City government said in a statement that more than 300,000 people attended the Mexican Independence celebration in the Zócalo.

“The event took place peacefully and concluded without any casualties or incidents,” the government said.

“… Coordination between various agencies and the responsible participation of citizens allowed this commemoration to take place in an organized manner and in an environment of harmony,” the government said.

“The event also reflected the support of thousands of people for President Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo, who went to the Zócalo to participate in a day of profound significance for the history and identity of the country, as well as to hear a message to the nation in defense of our independence, dignity, and sovereignty.”

With reports from Reforma and La Jornada

World.title: Is Mexico’s soccer league a monopoly? Antitrust officials are looking to find out
World.content:
The National Antitrust Commission (CNA) has unilaterally opened an investigation into Liga MX, Mexico’s top professional soccer league and a massive cultural touchstone that captures the country’s passion for the sport.

An internal CNA document says the investigation aims to identify “the possible commission of relative monopolistic practices in the market of ‘affiliation, organization and access’ to professional federated football competitions in Mexico, as well as similar or related services.”

⚽ ¿Cómo investigamos el funcionamiento de un mercado?

José Manuel Haro Zepeda, titular de nuestra Autoridad Investigadora, explicó en @MVSNoticias las herramientas con las que contamos para analizar la organización y acceso a competiciones de fútbol profesional en México. pic.twitter.com/r2qgofrR9M — Comisión Nacional Antimonopolio (@AntimonopolioMX) September 15, 2026

In short, the CNA wants to know if a small group is violating the Federal Law of Economic Competition by unfairly controlling who can join, who can compete and how tournaments are organized, to the exclusion of other interested parties.

“After analyzing the events that occurred in recent months, the Investigating Authority determined that it has sufficient evidence to formally open an investigation on its own initiative for possible monopolistic practices in the professional soccer market in Mexico,” the CNA said in a public report.

The recent events referred to are likely related to a Liga MX decision in July to scrap promotion/relegation between the top-flight Mexican soccer league and the second-tier Liga Expansión. Liga MX also announced the end to payouts to the second-tier sides.

Promotion and relegation were scrapped in 2020 to insulate the clubs from the financial impacts of lost revenue during the enforced lockdown ordered due to the Covid-19 pandemic.

Liga Expansión officials fiercely disputed the decision, even filing a suit with the Court of Arbitration for Sport, which ruled that the 2026-27 campaign was the earliest point at which promotion/relegation ought to be reinstituted.

Critics have also identified the league’s policy regarding possession of television broadcasting rights by teams as a monopolistic practice.

The commission has sought to make clear that there are no defendants identified as yet and it hasn’t been determined exactly who will be investigated. Instead, the probe will simply review whether competition law is being followed.

The investigation can last up to 120 business days, but can be extended up to three times longer if necessary. During that time, the CNA can request documents, visit offices, summon people to testify and conduct inspections.

If guilt is determined, the Liga MX and its member teams could face a penalty of up to 10% of their annual income and would be required to correct any monopolistic practices detected.

With reports from ESPN, El Economista, El Universal and SportCa

World.title: Zambia Charges Two Former Education Officials Over US$259m Contract
World.content:
ZAMBIA · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Zambia’s Anti-Corruption Commission arrested and charged two former Ministry of Education officials on 16 September 2026.

— Who Henry Tukombe, 57, a former permanent secretary, and Jacob Masatunya, 53, a former head of procurement.

— The contract A supply contract with Mikalile Trading Company Limited, a Hong Kong-based firm.

— The numbers The contract principal is US$259.25 million. The total loan obligation attached to it is US$401.8 million.

— Who announced it ACC spokesperson Joseph Mwenya.

— Where they are now Both have been released on bond and are awaiting court appearance. Neither has entered a plea.

Two numbers are circulating in this case. They are not the same number, and the difference is the financing.

Zambia’s Anti-Corruption Commission has charged two former education officials.

Zambia’s Anti-Corruption Commission has charged two former Ministry of Education officials. The arrests were announced on 16 September 2026 and concern a supply contract with a Hong Kong-based company. The contract principal is US$259.25 million, within a total loan obligation of US$401.8 million.

Who Has Been Charged

Henry Tukombe, 57, served as permanent secretary at the Ministry of Education.

Jacob Masatunya, 53, headed procurement at the same ministry.

ACC spokesperson Joseph Mwenya announced the arrests on 16 September 2026.

Both men were released on bond and are awaiting a court appearance. Neither has entered a plea.

The Two Figures

Reporting has attached the number US$401.8 million to this case, and that figure is real but specific.

It is the total loan obligation: principal plus the financing costs Zambia would repay over the life of the facility.

The contract principal, the amount payable to the supplier, is US$259.25 million.

Using the larger number to describe the contract overstates what the company was contracted to receive.

The Counterparty

The supplier is Mikalile Trading Company Limited, registered in Hong Kong.

Supplier-credit arrangements of this kind bundle goods and financing into a single package.

They are common in African education and health procurement because they move faster than budget appropriations.

However, they also convert a purchase into sovereign debt, which is why they attract audit attention.

Why the Structure Matters

In a supplier-credit deal, the government is buying goods and borrowing at the same time.

The financing cost is embedded in the arrangement rather than negotiated separately in a competitive market.

That makes value for money harder to test after the fact.

It is also where the gap between US$259.25 million and US$401.8 million comes from.

The Anti-Corruption Commission announced the arrests on 16 September 2026.

The Currency Point

The amounts in this case are denominated in United States dollars, not kwacha.

That is normal for imported supply contracts financed offshore.

It also means Zambia carries the exchange-rate risk on repayment, without any hedge in the contract itself.

A weaker kwacha raises the domestic cost of the same dollar obligation.

The Political Setting

President Hakainde Hichilema came to office promising to prosecute corruption from the previous administration.

The ACC has brought a series of cases against former officials since 2021.

The commission itself has faced scrutiny, including over the conduct of its own officers.

Prosecutions of this kind therefore carry a double test: the evidence, and the perception that it is applied evenly.

Zambia’s anti-graft drive has run since President Hichilema took office in 2021.

What Is Not Yet Known

The ACC has not published the specific counts against each man.

It has not said when the contract was signed, or how much of it was disbursed.

Mikalile Trading Company Limited has not commented publicly.

An arrest is a charge, not a finding. The case has not been tested in court.

What to Watch

The first court appearance, which will set out the counts in detail.

Whether the contract itself is suspended, cancelled or allowed to run.

Any statement from the Ministry of Finance on the outstanding loan obligation.

And whether further officials or intermediaries are charged in the same matter.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was arrested in Zambia?

Henry Tukombe, 57, a former education permanent secretary, and Jacob Masatunya, 53, a former head of procurement.

Who announced the arrests?

Anti-Corruption Commission spokesperson Joseph Mwenya, on 16 September 2026.

How big is the contract?

The contract principal is US$259.25 million. The total loan obligation attached to it is US$401.8 million.

Why are there two figures?

The larger figure includes the financing costs of the supplier credit, not just the amount payable to the supplier.

Who is the supplier?

Mikalile Trading Company Limited, a firm registered in Hong Kong.

Are the two men in custody?

No. Both were released on bond and are awaiting a court appearance. Neither has entered a plea.

Sources: Zambia Anti-Corruption Commission statement of 16 September 2026 via spokesperson Joseph Mwenya, Zambian press reporting on the Mikalile contract.

World.title: Mali Opens Special Forces Headquarters at Sénou Near Bamako
World.content:
MALI · DEFENCE

Key Facts — What happened Mali inaugurated a headquarters for its special forces at Sénou, near Bamako, on 15 September 2026.

— Who presided General Assimi Goïta, president of the transition, according to the Malian armed forces.

— What it houses The Bataillon autonome des forces spéciales et des centres d’aguerrissement, known as BAFS-CA, on a 15-hectare site.

— The command The site also activates the Commandement des opérations spéciales, created by texts adopted in the Council of Ministers on 18 June 2025.

— The four units BAFS-CA, the Force antiterroriste, the Groupement de reconnaissance et d’intervention and the Force spéciale Air.

— The money The armed forces said the project was financed from the national budget. No cost has been published.

Mali has built its special forces a home and switched on the command that runs them.

Mali inaugurated a special forces headquarters at Sénou, near Bamako, on 15 September 2026.

Mali inaugurated a headquarters for its special forces battalion at Sénou, near Bamako, on 15 September 2026. General Assimi Goïta presided. The Malian armed forces said the 15-hectare complex was financed from the national budget.

What Was Opened

The complex at Sénou covers about 15 hectares on the southern edge of Bamako.

It holds administrative buildings, accommodation, a restaurant, sports facilities, storage and parade grounds.

It is the headquarters of the Bataillon autonome des forces spéciales et des centres d’aguerrissement.

The last part of that name refers to combat-hardening centres, the training sites where the battalion prepares its troops.

The Command It Activates

The ceremony also marked the activation of the Commandement des opérations spéciales, or COS.

The command was created by texts adopted in the Council of Ministers on 18 June 2025.

It has a command body and a centre for planning and running operations.

Four units sit under it: BAFS-CA, the Force antiterroriste, the Groupement de reconnaissance et d’intervention and the Force spéciale Air.

Why a Single Command

Before the COS, Mali’s elite units answered through separate chains.

Special operations depend on speed, and a divided chain of command costs hours that matter.

Putting air assets and ground units under one headquarters is the standard fix.

It also concentrates scarce equipment and intelligence in one place rather than spreading it thin.

The Security Picture

Mali faces armed groups linked to both al-Qaeda and the Islamic State across its centre and north.

Attacks on fuel convoys and rural garrisons have continued through 2026.

Bamako itself was attacked in September 2024, which changed how the capital is defended.

A special forces command is a response to that pressure. It does not by itself resolve it.

The new headquarters sits at Sénou, on the southern edge of Bamako.

The Financing Claim

The armed forces said the complex was financed from the national budget.

That is a political statement as much as an accounting one, given how much Sahelian security spending is externally funded.

No figure has been published, so the claim cannot be measured against the defence budget.

The Rio Times reports it as the army’s own account rather than as verified fact.

After the French Withdrawal

France ended Operation Barkhane in Mali in 2022 and the UN mission MINUSMA left at the end of 2023.

Mali has since rebuilt its force structure around national units and new partners.

Russian personnel have operated alongside Malian forces, a relationship neither government details publicly.

However, the Sénou project is presented by Bamako as a domestic build, and no external partner was named at the ceremony.

Mali faces armed groups linked to al-Qaeda and the Islamic State.

The Regional Read

Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger left the Economic Community of West African States and formed the Alliance of Sahel States.

All three have expanded special forces and centralised command since their respective coups.

The model is a smaller, better-equipped core force rather than a large conscript army.

Whether that produces results depends on intelligence and mobility, which are the harder inputs to buy.

What to Watch

Whether the COS is declared fully operational, and when. No timeline has been announced.

The tempo of special forces operations reported by the FAMa in the coming months.

Any published defence budget lines that would test the domestic financing claim.

And whether the training centres at Sénou take in units from partner states.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Mali open?

A special forces headquarters at Sénou near Bamako, inaugurated on 15 September 2026 by General Assimi Goïta.

What is BAFS-CA?

The Bataillon autonome des forces spéciales et des centres d’aguerrissement, Mali’s autonomous special forces battalion and its combat-hardening centres.

What is the COS?

The Commandement des opérations spéciales, created in June 2025 to run Mali’s special operations under one chain of command.

Which units does it cover?

BAFS-CA, the Force antiterroriste, the Groupement de reconnaissance et d’intervention and the Force spéciale Air.

How was it paid for?

The Malian armed forces said it was financed from the national budget. No cost figure has been published.

Is the command operational?

No official timeline for full operational status has been announced.

Sources: Malian armed forces (FAMa) communications on the 15 September 2026 inauguration, APA News, Malian Council of Ministers texts of 18 June 2025.

World.title: Ghana EPA Shuts Empire Cement Weija Plant Over Pollution Breaches
World.content:
GHANA · ENVIRONMENT

Key Facts — What happened Ghana’s Environmental Protection Authority ordered Empire Cement Ghana Ltd to shut its Weija plant in Greater Accra on 14 September 2026.

— Why Alleged air pollution breaches and missing environmental monitoring returns.

— The conditions cited Five: 5.1(1)(a), 5.1(a), 5.1(h)(i), 5.1(h)(iv) and 9.1 of the plant’s environmental permit.

— The deadline Outstanding quarterly environmental monitoring returns are due by 1 October 2026.

— Who runs the regulator The EPA is headed by chief executive Prof. Nana Ama Browne Klutse. The directive itself names no signatory.

— What is not known The EPA has not said what restart conditions apply beyond the returns, and the company has not responded publicly.

A cement plant on the edge of Accra has been told to stop. It is not the first time.

The Empire Cement plant sits at Weija, on the western edge of Greater Accra.

Ghana’s Environmental Protection Authority ordered Empire Cement Ghana Ltd to shut down its Weija plant on 14 September 2026. The regulator cited five conditions of the plant’s environmental permit and gave the company until 1 October to file outstanding monitoring returns.

The Directive

The EPA issued the shutdown order on 14 September 2026 over alleged air pollution breaches.

It named five permit conditions: 5.1(1)(a), 5.1(a), 5.1(h)(i), 5.1(h)(iv) and 9.1.

Those conditions cover emissions control and the duty to file environmental monitoring data.

The company has until 1 October 2026 to submit the outstanding quarterly returns.

What a Cement Plant Emits

Clinker grinding and bagging release fine particulate matter, the dust that travels furthest and lodges deepest.

Permits typically cap emissions at the stack and require continuous or quarterly measurement.

The measurement obligation is not a formality. Without returns, a regulator cannot tell whether a plant is within its limits.

That is why missing paperwork and alleged pollution appear in the same notice.

Where the Plant Sits

Weija is on the western edge of Greater Accra, near the Densu river and the Weija dam.

Residential neighbourhoods and the Panbros salt works lie in the same area.

Residents in McCarthy Hill, Tetegu and around the Panbros site raised dust complaints in reporting between 2020 and 2022.

Those complaints are the background to the current action, not part of the September directive itself.

The EPA cited five conditions of the plant’s environmental permit.

A Long Regulatory History

The EPA first shut the plant in June 2021 for operating without an environmental permit.

In 2022 Ghana’s trade minister said Empire Cement had been permitted to manufacture cement bags, not cement itself.

The plant has since operated under a permit with the conditions now cited against it.

This is therefore a second enforcement round rather than a first encounter.

The Industrial Policy Angle

Empire Cement is a Chinese-backed project and has been associated in local reporting with the One District One Factory programme.

However, the government withheld approval at points in that process, so the link is looser than headlines have suggested.

Public reporting supports an investment figure of about US$50 million. Lower figures circulating elsewhere could not be sourced.

Industrial policy and environmental enforcement sit in different ministries, and this case shows where they collide.

Who Is Affected

Plant workers lose shifts for as long as the shutdown runs.

Ghana’s cement market is supplied by several larger producers, so building sites are unlikely to feel a shortage.

Residents near the site gain immediate relief from dust if the order holds.

Chinese investors in Ghanaian manufacturing gain a data point about how enforcement works here.

Ghana’s EPA has become more visible on enforcement since its restructuring.

Why the Regulator Is Moving

Ghana’s EPA has been more visible on enforcement since being restructured from an agency into an authority.

Air quality in Accra ranks among the worst in West Africa on several monitoring datasets.

Mining and quarrying enforcement has taken most of the political attention, but industrial emissions affect far more people daily.

A shutdown notice is the strongest tool the authority has short of revoking a permit.

What to Watch

Whether the outstanding returns are filed by 1 October 2026.

Any statement from Empire Cement, which has not responded publicly.

Whether the EPA sets emissions-control conditions for a restart, beyond the paperwork.

And whether this becomes a pattern of enforcement against industrial emitters in Greater Accra.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why was Empire Cement shut down?

Ghana’s EPA cited alleged air pollution breaches and missing environmental monitoring returns, naming five permit conditions.

Which conditions were cited?

Conditions 5.1(1)(a), 5.1(a), 5.1(h)(i), 5.1(h)(iv) and 9.1 of the plant’s environmental permit.

When does the company have to respond?

Outstanding quarterly environmental monitoring returns are due by 1 October 2026.

Where is the plant?

At Weija, on the western edge of Greater Accra, near the Densu river and the Panbros salt works.

Has this happened before?

Yes. The EPA shut the plant in June 2021 for operating without an environmental permit.

Who leads the EPA?

Chief executive Prof. Nana Ama Browne Klutse. The September directive does not name a signatory.

Sources: Environmental Protection Authority of Ghana shutdown directive of 14 September 2026, MyJoyOnline and Graphic Online reporting, earlier Ghanaian reporting on the Weija plant from 2020 to 2022.

World.title: Sterling Bank Board Adds Two Independent Directors as Four Retire
World.content:
NIGERIA · COMPANIES

Key Facts — What happened Sterling Financial Holdings told the Nigerian Exchange that two independent non-executive directors have joined the board of its banking subsidiary.

— Who joined Laoye Jaiyeola, effective 17 August 2026, and Chinedu Ikwudinma, effective 20 August 2026. The Central Bank of Nigeria approved both.

— Who left Four directors retired in the same filing: Michael Ajukwu, Olusola Oworu, Olaitan Kajero and Tunde Adeola.

— The net effect Two independent directors in, two independent directors out. Board independence is unchanged, not increased.

— A separate board Olubisi Makoju and Olayinka Oni joined the holding company board in July 2026, which is a different body from the bank board.

— What is not disclosed The filing does not give effective dates for the retirements.

Two names in, four names out. The arithmetic matters more than the announcement.

Sterling Financial Holdings filed the board changes with the Nigerian Exchange.

Sterling Financial Holdings has appointed Laoye Jaiyeola and Chinedu Ikwudinma as independent non-executive directors of Sterling Bank Limited. The Central Bank of Nigeria approved both. The same filing records four retirements from the bank board.

The Two Appointments

Laoye Jaiyeola took his seat on 17 August 2026 and Chinedu Ikwudinma on 20 August 2026.

Jaiyeola brings more than 35 years in financial services, corporate governance and public policy.

He founded Hillside University of Science and Technology and previously led the Nigerian Economic Summit Group.

He also ran Kakawa Discount House and served as president of the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria.

The Risk Man

Ikwudinma spent more than 30 years in international banking.

He was group chief risk officer at Ecobank Transnational Incorporated.

Before that he spent over two decades at Citibank, including as chief executive in Uganda and executive director in Nigeria.

He was also the pioneer managing director of Nova Merchant Bank.

The Part the Headline Left Out

The same filing records four departures from the Sterling Bank board.

Michael Ajukwu and Olusola Oworu retired as independent non-executive directors on tenure expiration.

Olaitan Kajero, a non-executive director, also retired on tenure expiration.

Executive director Tunde Adeola retired on reaching the prescribed age.

Why That Changes the Story

Two independent directors arrived and two independent directors left.

Board independence is therefore flat, not strengthened, whatever the headline count suggests.

The board is also smaller by two after the departures of Kajero and Adeola.

That is a normal rotation on tenure limits, but it is not the governance upgrade it can be made to look like.

The Central Bank approved both appointments to the bank board.

Bank Board and HoldCo Board

Sterling Financial Holdings Plc is the listed parent. Sterling Bank Limited is its banking subsidiary.

These appointments are to the bank board, and the Central Bank approves them because the bank is a regulated entity.

Olubisi Makoju and Olayinka Oni joined the holding company board in July 2026.

Those are separate appointments to a separate body, and merging the two lists misstates who sits where.

The Regulatory Backdrop

Nigerian banks are working through a recapitalisation deadline that runs to March 2026 and beyond for some tiers.

The Central Bank has tightened its scrutiny of financial-crime controls and board fitness across the sector.

Tenure limits on independent directors are part of the same framework, which is why these rotations cluster.

A former group chief risk officer joining a bank board fits that supervisory climate closely.

Sterling Financial Holdings Plc is the listed parent of Sterling Bank Limited.

What It Signals

Sterling has spent recent years positioning itself around agriculture, health and education lending.

A board weighted toward risk and public policy suits a bank growing in regulated, capital-hungry segments.

However, board composition is a slow-acting variable and rarely moves results within a year.

The numbers that matter next are capital adequacy and cost of risk, not the names on the notice.

What to Watch

Sterling Bank’s capital position against the Central Bank’s recapitalisation thresholds.

Whether further non-executive appointments follow to replace the two seats now vacant.

The holding company’s next set of results and its cost of risk.

And any further tenure-driven rotations, which the filing schedule makes reasonably predictable.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who joined the Sterling Bank board?

Laoye Jaiyeola on 17 August 2026 and Chinedu Ikwudinma on 20 August 2026, both as independent non-executive directors.

Who approved the appointments?

The Central Bank of Nigeria approved both, as it must for a regulated banking subsidiary.

Who retired?

Michael Ajukwu, Olusola Oworu, Olaitan Kajero and Tunde Adeola. The first two were independent non-executive directors.

Did board independence increase?

No. Two independent directors joined and two left, so the count is unchanged.

What about Olubisi Makoju and Olayinka Oni?

They joined the holding company board in July 2026, which is a different body from the bank board.

What is Ikwudinma’s background?

More than 30 years in international banking, including group chief risk officer at Ecobank and senior roles at Citibank.

Sources: Sterling Financial Holdings Plc filing to the Nigerian Exchange, Nairametrics and Premium Times reporting, Central Bank of Nigeria corporate governance guidelines.

World.title: Nigeria Commissions 3.3MWp Solar Mini-Grid at Abuja University
World.content:
NIGERIA · ENERGY

Key Facts — What happened Nigeria commissioned a solar hybrid mini-grid at Yakubu Gowon University in Abuja on 16 September 2026.

— The numbers 3.3MWp of solar panels, 2MWh of battery storage, 3MW of alternating current output and 388 solar streetlights.

— Who did it Minister of Power Joseph Tegbe commissioned the plant. Abba Abubakar Aliyu, managing director of the Rural Electrification Agency, also spoke.

— The programme Phase 2 of the Energising Education Programme, covering seven universities and two teaching hospitals. Phase 3 is under way.

— Who it serves The minister put the campus population at 58,726 students.

— What is not clear Neither the cost of the installation nor the diesel volume it replaces has been published.

A campus that ran on diesel now runs on panels and batteries, with a national programme behind it.

Nigeria has commissioned a 3.3MWp solar mini-grid at a federal university in Abuja.

Nigeria commissioned a solar hybrid mini-grid at Yakubu Gowon University in Abuja on 16 September 2026. The plant pairs 3.3MWp of panels with 2MWh of battery storage and delivers 3MW of alternating current. Minister of Power Joseph Tegbe performed the commissioning.

What Was Switched On

The installation carries 3.3MWp of solar photovoltaic capacity and 2MWh of lithium battery storage.

Its alternating current output is rated at 3MW, which is the figure that matters for what the campus can actually run.

The project also delivered 388 solar-powered streetlights across the university grounds.

Yakubu Gowon University is the former University of Abuja, renamed in 2025.

The Programme Behind It

The plant sits in Phase 2 of the Energising Education Programme, run by the Rural Electrification Agency.

That phase covers seven federal universities and two teaching hospitals.

A third phase is being implemented, which extends the same model to further campuses.

Minister Tegbe said the plant serves a campus population of 58,726 students.

Why Campuses First

A large Nigerian university is effectively a small town with a single electricity bill.

Its load is predictable, its site is secure and its diesel spending is large enough to make the arithmetic work.

Laboratories, servers and teaching hospitals are also the loads where an outage costs most.

That combination is why federal campuses have been an early target for distributed generation.

The plant serves a campus the minister put at 58,726 students.

The Diesel It Replaces

Nigerian universities have run on diesel generators through decades of unreliable grid supply.

Diesel costs several times more per unit than solar generation over the life of a plant.

Battery storage matters because it carries the campus through the evening, when the panels stop and the load does not.

The government has not published how much diesel this installation displaces, so the saving cannot yet be measured.

Where the Money Comes From

Nigeria’s off-grid push leans heavily on multilateral finance.

The Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up programme, known as DARES, is backed by US$750 million from the World Bank.

The REA reported more than 200 mini-grids delivered under DARES by early 2025.

Figures circulating for a programme-wide mini-grid target could not be sourced to the agency and are left out here.

The Limits of the Model

A campus mini-grid is not a fix for the national grid, and nobody involved claims it is.

It removes a large customer from a stressed network, which helps, but it does not add transmission capacity.

Maintenance is the recurring weakness of Nigerian solar installations, and batteries have a replacement cycle of their own.

The test is whether this plant is still delivering 3MW in five years, not whether it delivered it on commissioning day.

Nigeria has the largest unelectrified population on the continent.

The Continental Frame

Mission 300, run by the World Bank and the African Development Bank, aims to connect 300 million Africans to electricity by 2030.

The banks say more than 50 million people across 40 countries have been connected so far.

Nigeria has the largest unelectrified population on the continent, so its numbers move the continental total.

Distributed solar is the cheapest route for communities the grid will not reach this decade.

What to Watch

Published performance data from the plant after its first dry season.

The rollout schedule for Phase 3 of the Energising Education Programme.

DARES mini-grid completions, which show whether the off-grid programme is scaling or stalling.

And the maintenance contracts, which decide whether these plants age well.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was commissioned at Yakubu Gowon University?

A solar hybrid mini-grid with 3.3MWp of panels, 2MWh of battery storage, 3MW of AC output and 388 solar streetlights.

Who commissioned it?

Minister of Power Joseph Tegbe, on 16 September 2026. REA managing director Abba Abubakar Aliyu also spoke.

What is the Energising Education Programme?

A Rural Electrification Agency programme powering federal campuses. Phase 2 covers seven universities and two teaching hospitals.

How many students does it serve?

The minister put the campus population at 58,726 students.

What is DARES?

A US$750 million World Bank-backed programme to scale distributed renewable energy in Nigeria.

What does the project cost?

The cost has not been published, and neither has the volume of diesel it replaces.

Sources: Nairametrics and Leadership reporting on the 16 September 2026 commissioning, Rural Electrification Agency statements, World Bank DARES programme documents.

World.title: Afreximbank PAPSS Expects China and India Links by Early 2027
World.content:
PAN-AFRICAN · FINANCE

Key Facts — What was said PAPSS chief executive Mike Ogbalu III said he expects the system to connect to payment networks in China, India and Brazil.

— When At a briefing in Lagos on 7 September 2026. The timeline he gave was the first quarter of 2027.

— What PAPSS is The Pan-African Payment and Settlement System, launched in January 2022 by Afreximbank and the African Union.

— What it does It settles cross-border payments between African countries in local currencies, without routing them through the dollar or the euro.

— What is not there yet No agreement has been announced, no counterparty named and no memorandum published. Afreximbank’s own statement of 11 September does not mention the plan.

— Why it matters If it happens, Africa’s trade with its two largest partners would settle outside the dollar system.

An expectation, stated at a briefing. That is a different thing from a signed deal, and worth keeping straight.

PAPSS was launched in 2022 by Afreximbank and the African Union.

PAPSS chief executive Mike Ogbalu III spoke at a briefing in Lagos on 7 September 2026. He said he expects the system to link to networks in China, India and Brazil by early 2027. No agreement has been announced and no counterparty named.

What Was Actually Said

Ogbalu spoke at a briefing in Lagos on 7 September 2026, ahead of a wider Afreximbank event.

He named China, India and Brazil as the systems PAPSS expects to connect with. The timing he gave was the first quarter of 2027.

He described this as an expectation rather than a concluded arrangement.

Afreximbank has published nothing since naming a counterparty, and its statement of 11 September does not refer to the plan.

Why the Distinction Matters

A payment-system link is a technical and legal arrangement between two central banks or two operators.

It requires messaging standards, settlement accounts, legal agreements and, usually, regulatory approval on both sides.

None of that has been announced. What exists publicly is a target date given by an executive.

The plan may well proceed, but at this stage it has not been confirmed by any party on the other side.

What PAPSS Does Today

The system was launched on 13 January 2022 by Afreximbank and the African Union.

It lets a buyer in one African country pay a seller in another in their own currencies.

Settlement between the two central banks happens later, in net terms, which is where the saving comes from.

Without it, a payment from Lagos to Nairobi typically travels through a correspondent bank in New York or London.

The Cost It Is Meant to Remove

Routing through a third currency means two conversions, two spreads and two sets of fees.

For a small importer, those costs can exceed the margin on the shipment itself.

They also add days, because the payment waits in a correspondent chain it does not control.

Cutting the chain is the practical argument for PAPSS, and it holds whether or not the geopolitics are discussed.

PAPSS settles cross-border African payments in local currencies.

Why China, India and Brazil

China is Africa’s largest single trading partner and India is among the top three.

Brazil matters for agricultural trade, particularly with West Africa and Angola.

China operates CIPS, a cross-border renminbi settlement system, and India has built a large domestic payments stack.

Those are the obvious counterparties for any African system looking outward.

The Case for Scepticism

PAPSS has taken several years to sign up African central banks, and adoption inside the continent is still uneven.

Connecting to an external system is harder, not easier, because sanctions compliance and capital controls enter the picture.

Chinese and Indian regulators set their own terms, and neither has said anything publicly about this.

A first-quarter 2027 date is ambitious for an arrangement that has not yet been announced.

Afreximbank is headquartered in Cairo and launched PAPSS with the African Union.

The Wider Contest

Payment rails have become a quiet front in the competition over trade and influence.

Beijing has spent a decade promoting renminbi settlement, while Washington’s leverage rests partly on dollar clearing.

African institutions have generally tried to add options rather than pick a side.

Connecting to several external systems at once, if it happens, would be consistent with that approach.

What to Watch

A statement from a Chinese, Indian or Brazilian operator or central bank, which is what would turn this into news.

Any memorandum published by Afreximbank naming a counterparty.

PAPSS transaction volumes inside Africa, the test of whether the core system is working.

And the number of African central banks live on the platform, which has been the slow variable throughout.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the PAPSS chief executive say?

He expects links to payment systems in China, India and Brazil by early 2027. He said so in Lagos on 7 September 2026.

Has an agreement been signed?

No agreement has been announced and no counterparty named. Afreximbank’s own release of 11 September does not mention the plan.

What is PAPSS?

The Pan-African Payment and Settlement System. Afreximbank and the African Union launched it in January 2022 to settle African trade in local currencies.

How does it save money?

It removes the need to convert through the dollar or euro, cutting two currency spreads and the fees attached to them.

Why those three countries?

China and India are among Africa’s largest trading partners, and Brazil is a major agricultural supplier.

Is the 2027 date realistic?

It is ambitious. Cross-border payment links require regulatory approval on both sides, and none has been confirmed.

Sources: Remarks by PAPSS chief executive Mike Ogbalu III at a briefing in Lagos, 7 September 2026; Afreximbank corporate statements; PAPSS platform documentation.

World.title: Kenya Livestock Project Gets US$55 Million More From IFAD
World.content:
KENYA · AGRICULTURE

Key Facts — What happened The International Fund for Agricultural Development approved an extra US$55 million, about Sh7.1 billion, for the Kenya Livestock Commercialization Project.

— What the project is KeLCoP, a rural development programme that helps smallholders sell sheep, goats, poultry and honey rather than keep them for subsistence.

— The size now IFAD puts the current total cost at about US$90.11 million. The design approved at launch was roughly US$81 million.

— Where it runs Arid and semi-arid counties where rainfall is unreliable and livestock is the main store of value.

— Who said it IFAD country director for Kenya Matteo Marchisio.

— What is not settled IFAD has not published a household target for the additional money, nor a county-by-county breakdown.

The UN farm fund is putting more money into Kenyan goats, sheep and bees, and less into cattle.

IFAD has approved an additional US$55 million for Kenya’s livestock commercialization project.

The International Fund for Agricultural Development has approved an additional US$55 million, about Sh7.1 billion, for the Kenya Livestock Commercialization Project. IFAD country director Matteo Marchisio said the money extends a programme running in Kenya’s dryland counties.

What KeLCoP Actually Does

The Kenya Livestock Commercialization Project works with smallholders who keep animals mainly as savings.

It funds breeding stock, veterinary services, fodder production and the market links that turn animals into income.

The value chains it covers are sheep, goats, poultry and beekeeping rather than dairy or beef cattle.

Those are the animals that survive a dry year, which is why a drought-exposed programme builds around them.

The Money, Corrected

The new approval is US$55 million, which at current rates is about Sh7.1 billion.

IFAD lists the project’s current total cost at roughly US$90.11 million, financed with the government and other partners.

The figure approved when the project was designed was closer to US$81 million.

The difference between those numbers is co-financing added since launch, not a single new cheque.

Why Goats and Not Cattle

A goat eats browse that cattle will not touch and needs far less water.

In a failed season a herder can sell goats in small numbers without losing the whole herd.

Poultry turns over in weeks, which gives households cash between livestock sales.

Beekeeping needs almost no land and pays in a commodity that stores well and travels.

The programme works in arid and semi-arid counties where rainfall is unreliable.

The Drought Context

Kenya’s arid and semi-arid lands cover most of the country’s land area and carry much of its livestock.

The region has moved through repeated failed rainy seasons over the past five years.

Each failure pushes pastoralists to sell animals cheaply at exactly the moment everyone else is selling.

Programmes like KeLCoP try to break that cycle by building markets that work before the crisis, not during it.

What the Money Buys on the Ground

Aggregation points where traders can buy in volume, which raises the price a herder receives.

Fodder and pasture work, so animals hold condition through a dry spell instead of losing weight.

Animal health services, because a treated flock is worth more than an untreated one.

And the paperwork of formal trade, which is what separates a market from a roadside sale.

The Case Against

Livestock commercialisation has critics, and their objection is not a small one.

Pushing pastoralists toward markets can concentrate herds in the hands of those who already have capital.

Researchers on East African drylands argue that mobility, not market access, is what keeps herders alive in a drought.

IFAD’s own evaluations of earlier Kenyan projects have flagged slow disbursement and weak county capacity.

Who Gains and Who Does Not

Households in the target counties gain access to services that commercial lenders do not offer them.

Traders and small processors gain a more predictable supply of animals and honey.

Counties outside the programme get nothing from this approval, which widens the gap between them.

And the gains depend on disbursement speed, which in Kenyan rural projects has often been the weak point.

IFAD lends on concessional terms alongside the Kenyan government and other partners.

Development Finance as Strategy

IFAD is a United Nations agency that lends on concessional terms to farm and rural projects.

Climate funds have moved into the same space, financing adaptation work that used to sit with aid budgets.

For Kenya, that means livestock policy is now written partly in the language of climate finance.

It also means the terms of the money shape which animals a herder is encouraged to keep.

What to Watch

The first disbursement, which shows whether the approval turns into money in county accounts.

Any published household target, which would allow the programme to be measured against a number.

Livestock prices in the target counties through the next dry season.

And whether the government matches the IFAD money on the schedule it has agreed.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did IFAD approve for Kenya?

An additional US$55 million, about Sh7.1 billion, for the Kenya Livestock Commercialization Project.

What is KeLCoP?

A rural development programme helping smallholders commercialise sheep, goats, poultry and beekeeping in Kenya’s dryland counties.

How big is the project in total?

IFAD puts the current total cost at about US$90.11 million. The design approved at launch was around US$81 million.

Who announced it?

Matteo Marchisio, IFAD’s country director for Kenya.

Why does it focus on goats and sheep?

Small stock survive drought better than cattle and can be sold in small numbers without breaking up a herd.

How many households will it reach?

IFAD has not published a household target for the additional financing.

Sources: International Fund for Agricultural Development project record for the Kenya Livestock Commercialization Project, IFAD Kenya country office.

World.title: Zimbabwe Power Utility ZESA Hires Former Eskom Operations Chief
World.content:
ZIMBABWE · ENERGY

Key Facts — What happened Zimbabwe merged its three state power companies into one utility, ZESA (Private) Limited, and named a new executive team.

— Who is in charge Cletus Nyachowe became group chief executive on 1 May 2026. Former Eskom chief operating officer Jan Albert Oberholzer joins as chief operating officer.

— The board Eleven members, chaired by Albert Joel Nduna.

— The owner The utility now sits under the Mutapa Investment Fund, Zimbabwe’s sovereign wealth fund.

— The pressure A transmission fault knocked out the national grid for about three and a half hours in July 2026.

— What comes next Harare is betting that consolidation and outside expertise can steady a grid that leans on imports.

Zimbabwe has folded three power companies into one and hired a South African utility veteran to run its operations.

Zimbabwe’s three state power companies have been merged into a single utility.

Zimbabwe has consolidated ZESA Holdings, the Zimbabwe Power Company and the transmission and distribution arm into one company. Cletus Nyachowe took over as group chief executive on 1 May 2026. Former Eskom chief operating officer Jan Albert Oberholzer joins as chief operating officer.

Three Companies Become One

ZESA Holdings, the Zimbabwe Power Company and the Zimbabwe Electricity Transmission and Distribution Company no longer exist as separate entities.

They have been folded into ZESA (Private) Limited, a single vertically integrated utility that generates, transmits and sells electricity.

The shareholder is the Mutapa Investment Fund, the sovereign wealth fund that now holds most of Zimbabwe’s large state assets.

A board of eleven, chaired by Albert Joel Nduna, oversees the new company.

The New Executive Team

Cletus Nyachowe was appointed group chief executive officer with effect from 1 May 2026.

Jan Albert Oberholzer, who ran operations at South Africa’s Eskom, joins as chief operating officer.

Oberholzer spent years inside a utility with problems Zimbabwe knows well: ageing plant, deferred maintenance and load shedding.

Hiring him is a statement that Harare wants operating discipline rather than another round of restructuring on paper.

What the July Blackout Showed

On 22 July 2026 the national grid collapsed and the whole country lost power.

ZESA blamed a fault on a transmission line and said supply was restored in stages.

Most customers were back within about three and a half hours, which is fast by regional standards.

The speed of the recovery was reassuring. The fact that a single line fault could black out a country was not.

A fault on a transmission line brought down the national grid in July 2026.

A Grid That Leans on Neighbours

Restoration drew on imports from South Africa’s Eskom and on Mozambique’s Cahora Bassa scheme.

Domestic generation came back through the Kariba South hydro station and the Hwange coal plant.

Kariba output rises and falls with the level of the lake, which drought can pull down sharply.

Hwange has been expanded with Chinese financing, but older units at the station remain unreliable.

Why Consolidation Is the Chosen Fix

Splitting generation from transmission was meant to bring competition and clearer accounting.

In practice it left three companies arguing over money that none of them had.

A single balance sheet makes it easier to price electricity, raise debt and plan maintenance.

It also concentrates responsibility. If the lights go out, there is now one company to answer for it.

What It Means for Business

Mines, smelters and irrigation schemes are the customers most exposed to unreliable supply.

Many already run diesel generators, which cost far more per unit than grid power.

Reliable supply would cut that bill and make Zimbabwean output more competitive against regional rivals.

Tariffs are the other half of the equation, and a utility that cannot cover its costs cannot maintain its plant.

Zimbabwe drew on imports from South Africa’s Eskom to restore supply.

The Regional Picture

Southern Africa trades power across borders through the Southern African Power Pool.

Eskom itself has spent years fighting load shedding, so its former managers are in demand across the region.

Zambia, next door, has rationed electricity through a drought that cut Kariba North output.

A stronger Zimbabwean utility would make the regional market less fragile, not only the domestic one.

What to Watch

Whether Oberholzer is given authority over maintenance budgets rather than a title.

Hwange availability through the dry season, and the level of Lake Kariba going into 2027.

The tariff review, which decides whether the merged utility can fund its own repairs.

And the import bill, the clearest measure of whether domestic generation is recovering.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who now runs Zimbabwe’s power utility?

Cletus Nyachowe is group chief executive from 1 May 2026. Former Eskom executive Jan Albert Oberholzer is chief operating officer.

What is ZESA (Private) Limited?

The single company created by merging ZESA Holdings, the Zimbabwe Power Company and the transmission and distribution arm.

Who owns it?

The Mutapa Investment Fund, Zimbabwe’s sovereign wealth fund, holds the shares.

How long did the July 2026 blackout last?

The national grid failed on 22 July and most customers had power again within about three and a half hours.

What caused it?

ZESA attributed the collapse to a fault on a transmission line.

Where does Zimbabwe import power from?

Mainly from South Africa’s Eskom and Mozambique’s Cahora Bassa scheme, alongside its own Kariba and Hwange plants.

Sources: ZESA (Private) Limited board announcement, Reuters reporting on the July 2026 national blackout, Mutapa Investment Fund, Southern African Power Pool.

World.title: Twelve students receive Refrigeration and Air Conditioning scholarships as Belize marks World Ozone Day
World.content:
Twelve students receive Refrigeration and Air Conditioning scholarships as Belize marks World Ozone Day

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Department of the Environment (DOE), through the National Ozone Unit, awarded 12 scholarships under the Refrigeration and Air Conditioning (RAC) Scholarship Programme.

The recipients are enrolled in RAC programmes at ITVETs in Belize City, Orange Walk, and Stann Creek, and will receive support for the 2026–2027 academic year, including tuition, a toolbox of servicing tools, and personal protective equipment.

Three of the twelve recipients are female trainees, marking a step toward greater participation of women in the RAC sector.

The ceremony coincided with World Ozone Day, observed annually on September 16. This year’s theme, “Global Action for a Cooler Planet,” marks ten years of sustainable cooling efforts under the Kigali Amendment.

The DOE said the scholarships reflect Belize’s ongoing transition toward lower-global-warming-potential refrigerants and more efficient cooling technologies, which requires a pipeline of skilled technicians.

Through the programme, the DOE said it is investing in the next generation of RAC professionals to help promote safe, efficient, and environmentally responsible cooling practices going forward.

The twelve scholarship recipients are Zadiel Dias, Patrick Zetina, Samuel Alamilla, Brandon Ysaguirre, Gerardo Magana, Milcar Ku, Rilma Urbina, Edwardo Coc, Cierra Teck, Jahleel Flowers, Erwin Colon, and Dorda Castillo.

World.title: Garbage dumped at Yo Chen Village entrance cleaned up, Department of Environment steps up surveillance
World.content:
Garbage dumped at Yo Chen Village entrance cleaned up, Department of Environment steps up surveillance

By Zoila Palma: The Department of the Environment (DOE) has cleaned up a garbage site at the entrance of Yo Chen Village following a media report regarding the issue.

The DOE said it investigated the matter promptly and worked with the Ministry of Infrastructure Development and Housing (MIDH) to address the concern.

The area has since been cleaned and placed under surveillance to help prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future.

The DOE is reminding the public that under the Pollution Regulations, it is an offence to place or permit refuse to be placed on any land without written permission from the department.

The DOE is encouraging community members to remain vigilant and report instances of illegal dumping at this or any other location.

World.title: Belize @45 History Tour brings dialogue on Independence to Orange Walk Town
World.content:
Belize @45 History Tour brings dialogue on Independence to Orange Walk Town

By Zoila Palma: The Belize @45 Magical History Tour made its way through Orange Walk Town on September 15, continuing a series of events aimed at encouraging dialogue and reflection on the country’s history.

The tour is led by the Institute for Social & Cultural Research (ISCR-NICH) in partnership with historian Dr. Assad Shoman, and focuses on Belize’s path to independence, the experiences that have shaped its national story, and ongoing conversations around decolonization.

During the day, the tour engaged students from New Hope High School, Muffles College High School, and Orange Walk Technical High School in discussions on Belize’s history, national identity, and the range of experiences that continue to shape the country. Students were given the opportunity to ask questions and share their perspectives on how the past connects to present-day Belize.

That evening, the tour held a public forum at the Banquitas House of Culture, bringing together community leaders and residents of Orange Walk Town. The forum allowed attendees to discuss the country’s shared history and consider how a deeper understanding of the past could inform Belize’s future direction.

ISCR-NICH thanked the students, educators, community leaders, and residents who took part in the day’s events, noting their questions and input as central to the tour’s goals.

The Magical History Tour is made possible through the National Celebrations Commission and the National Institute of Culture and History, along with partners including the University of Belize.

World.title: International News: Trump names Haiti security expert Austin Holmes as Ambassador nominee
World.content:
International News: Trump names Haiti security expert Austin Holmes as Ambassador nominee

By Zoila Palma: U.S. President Donald Trump has nominated Florida businessman Austin Holmes to serve as the next U.S. ambassador to Haiti, as the Caribbean nation continues to grapple with a severe political and security crisis.

Holmes’ nomination was submitted to the U.S. Senate on Monday, September 14, and he must receive Senate confirmation before taking up the diplomatic post.

Holmes has longstanding ties to Haiti through humanitarian and security work and has previously lived in the country with his family.

Earlier this year, he testified before a Senate appropriations subcommittee during a hearing examining U.S. security and foreign assistance priorities in Haiti.

During his testimony, Holmes said he has participated in security operations in Haiti, including kidnapping recoveries and emergency extractions. He cited the 2023 recovery of American humanitarian worker Jeff Frazier, who was kidnapped by gangs while participating in a food distribution mission and held captive for 43 days. Holmes said his team “successfully recovered” Frazier.

Holmes said his approach to operations in Haiti is based on local knowledge and long-term engagement. “Deep cultural fluency, long-term presence and operational leadership rooted in local context” have driven the results achieved by his teams, he said, adding that many of his personnel are Haitian and Haitian American with local experience, language skills and relationships.

World.title: Police intercept pickup carrying suspected uncustomed goods in Orange Walk
World.content:
Police intercept pickup carrying suspected uncustomed goods in Orange Walk

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police intercepted a pickup truck near the Blue Creek Dam in Orange Walk earlier this month and reportedly discovered several boxes and sacks of food products suspected to be uncustomed goods.

According to police information, personnel from the North HIT conducted a staging operation in the area between approximately 5:30 p.m. and 8:40 p.m. on Friday, September 4.

During the operation, officers intercepted a white Dodge Ram being driven by a 25 year old man from San Felipe Village.

A search of the vehicle reportedly led to the discovery of six boxes of oxtail, five sacks of cabbage and 15 sacks of onions.

The driver and the goods were subsequently escorted to the Orange Walk Customs Department.

Police say the matter was handed over to a Customs officer for further action.

No information was provided on the estimated value of the goods or whether any charges have been filed.

World.title: Police chase ends with reckless driving charge in Orange Walk
World.content:
Police chase ends with reckless driving charge in Orange Walk

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 24 year old Orange Walk man has been charged with reckless driving following an early morning police pursuit.

According to police information, officers were conducting mobile patrol on San Narciso Street at around 1:20 a.m. on September 15 when their attention was drawn to a black motorcycle with a defective rear light.

Police say the rider was signalled to stop but allegedly drove off and began swerving from side to side along the street.

Officers reportedly followed the motorcycle for approximately five minutes before managing to intercept the rider.

Police say the man told officers he had not been trying to escape.

A search was conducted and nothing incriminating was found. Checks on the motorcycle documents also reportedly showed that the licence and insurance were up to date.

The rider was then informed that he was being detained for reckless driving and was escorted to the Orange Walk Police Station.

Police identified him as Nathan J. Navarrete, 24, a labourer of Santa Familia Street, Orange Walk.

He was later formally arrested and charged with reckless driving.

World.title: Carmelita woman charged after police reportedly find 19.7 grams of cannabis
World.content:
Carmelita woman charged after police reportedly find 19.7 grams of cannabis

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 35 year old woman from Carmelita Village has been charged with possession of controlled drugs after police reportedly found 19.7 grams of suspected cannabis during a house search on Wednesday morning.

According to police information, officers executed a search warrant at a residence in Carmelita Village at around 9:30 a.m.
