Police say that while searching the kitchen area, the woman allegedly told officers that she had a small amount of cannabis in the house.

She then reportedly handed over a small blue transparent plastic bag containing green leafy substance suspected to be cannabis.

The substance was weighed and reportedly amounted to 19.7 grams.

Police informed the woman that possessing more than 10 grams of cannabis constituted an offence and placed her under arrest.

Officers continued searching the residence but reportedly found nothing else incriminating.

The woman was escorted to the Orange Walk Police Station, where the suspected cannabis was weighed again, sealed and labelled in her presence.

Police identified her as Cristine Cristylane Wade, 35, self employed of Carmelita Village.

She was later formally arrested and charged with possession of controlled drugs.

World.title: Family services shake-up
World.content:
The Ministry of Education has severed ties with the heads of two of its primary family services agencies — the Child Protection and Family Services Agency (CPFSA) and the National Parenting Support Commission (NPSC) — reportedly to undertake a major shift in their operations, the Jamaica Observer has learnt.

As part of that shake-up, chief executive officer of the CPFSA Laurette Adams-Thomas, who took the helm of the agency in October 2023, will demit office next month.

In a brief response to the Observer, Adams-Thomas said her contract expires on October 1, 2026 and she was “officially notified on July 23, 2026” that it would “not be renewed”.

The CPFSA is an executive agency which was formed from the merger of the Child Development Agency (CDA) and the Office of Children’s Registry (OCR). Adams-Thomas, an educator and social worker, took over its leadership following an eight-year stint as general manager of the largest infirmary in the Caribbean — Jamaica’s Golden Age Home — where she had oversight responsibly for protection and welfare services for more than 450 indigent people from the parishes of Kingston and St Andrew. Prior to assuming that position, she was interim executive director/registrar at the OCR, where her focus was centred on ensuring that an effective system was maintained to facilitate the confidential receipt, assessment, and referral of reports of known or suspected cases of child abuse.

She holds a master’s degree in business administration, bachelor of science in human resource management, and a number of certifications in leadership, corporate governance and strategic planning.

In the meantime, the Observer was reliably informed on Monday that NPSC CEO Kaysia Kerr “is no longer with” the entity. Efforts to get an official response from Kerr were unsuccessful. A pre-recorded message on her personal mobile phone directed all callers with queries related to the commission to contact the education ministry or the commission itself.

A source with knowledge of the development said the ministry had decided to disengage with Kerr due to a breakdown in relations.

She took the helm of the commission in 2017, succeeding Dr Patrece Charles. In an interview with the

Observer at the time, Kerr said she hoped to craft and design programmes for parents and children of all 13 categories of disabilities, move the organisation out of eastern Jamaica to serve other parishes, take some of the programmes internationally, and get the unit to a stage where it generates income.

The former NPSC head has a solid background in education and has completed studies in business and professional management at Nova Southeastern University, along with a first degree in special education and a master’s in administration and supervision from Western Carolina University.

The commission coordinates a wide range of services for parents and also delivers programmes that build parenting skills and promote parental involvement in education.

The Government of Jamaica mandated the establishment of the NPSC in response to the 2004 task force report on the status of education in Jamaica.

The NPSC began operating in January 2013.

World.title: Global aviation squeeze
World.content:
Jamaica Tourist Board (JTB) Deputy Director of Tourism for the Americas Philip Rose says Jamaica needs more airline seats to meet strong demand as carriers face aircraft shortages and higher fuel costs amid the impact of the war in the Middle East.

Addressing the media during the Jamaica Product Exchange (JAPEX) forum in Ocho Rios on Tuesday, Rose said Jamaica’s immediate challenge is not a lack of demand, but having enough airline seats to bring visitors to the island.

“The immediate thing that we do need is more seats into the destination. The good news is, and I really want this to land, the good news is the airlines know this. The airlines are preparing because they don’t want to leave business on the table. The airlines know that the demand is there. The airlines are preparing to put in additional flights,” he said.

His comments come as Jamaica’s tourism industry continues its recovery following last year’s Hurricane Melissa, with hotel capacity gradually returning and airlines looking to adjust their schedules accordingly.

Rose said the global aviation industry is itself under pressure, making it difficult for airlines to simply add capacity whenever demand rises. He pointed to higher fuel costs linked to developments in the Middle East, as well as problems affecting aircraft engines, servicing and maintenance.

“As you all know, there are global pressures now on the aviation space. What’s happening out there in the Middle East has really impacted oil prices, which impacts fuel prices. In the best of days, the margins are exceedingly thin for airlines. You’re going to add this increase in jet fuel, it puts additional pressure on the industry,” he explained.

“Along with that, there is a shortage of aircraft because of issues to do with the engines, which I won’t really bore you all with. There are some service and maintenance things that are going on, which means a lot of aircraft have been pulled out of service,” he added.

The result, he said, is that Jamaica cannot depend on unlimited airline capacity, even as demand remains strong

“Airlines across the world don’t have infinite aircraft. That means that seats are not infinite. When the seats are full, the seats are full. Because of the demand that we have been generating for Jamaica, the vast majority of the flights into Jamaica are full,” he added.

Still, Rose said the outlook for airlift is positive, with airlines preparing to increase service as more hotel rooms become available.

He said airlines are also preparing to return to the flight schedules that existed before Hurricane Melissa, although they first have to resolve their own aircraft availability issues and factor in Jamaica’s accommodation capacity.

World.title: Sugar Cain promises powerful music, deep message
World.content:
Members of the cast of Sugar Cain, Father Ho Lung and Friends’ upcoming stage production, rehearse the songs for the show, last Wednesday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

A sober message of moral commitment complemented by powerful music is in store for audiences at Father Ho Lung and Friends’ upcoming stage production Sugar Cain.

“It’s a show that I think everybody will be able to relate to, even if you are not Jamaican,” music director for the group Jody Anne Johnson told the Jamaica Observer last Wednesday, just before the start of rehearsals for the production scheduled to run over two weekends — October 3-4 and October 10-11 at the National Arena in St Andrew.

“There are a lot of emotions that we go through every single day that will be explored, and the music is powerful… in kind of fuelling those emotions and setting the stage for the whole story to unfold,” added Johnson, who described the music as a “kind of melting pot of different genres”.

“We have traditional Jamaican music; there’s mento, there’s reggae — a lot of nice Jamaican reggae. We also have a little bit of hip hop; there are ballads; a little bit of music from the 60s, 70s; and then it comes up to dancehall as well,” Johnson explained, adding that the show contains 20 songs.

The script and all 20 tracks were written by Ho Lung in keeping with the tradition of his stage productions over the years, but Johnson, who took over from Wynton Williams as music director in 2019 after joining the group in 2003, wouldn’t be drawn when asked whether Sugar Cain tops all the previous productions.

“You remember them for different things. I remember Moses for all the tech — all of the interesting lights and special effects. And the Messiah is remembered because it is the story of our Lord and Saviour when He was crucified and risen. So each story has a special kind of brand that it leaves on our audience. So, I wouldn’t want to compare,” she told the Observer.

“I believe, though, that the music in Sugar Cane is a little bit more current, because of the addition of the hip hop, and we have some dancehall and stuff like that. But I think it’s going to be a powerful story… and all the stories that Father Ho Lung has done are powerful,” Johnson added.

She reinforced Director Hugh Douse’s observation, shared in an earlier interview with the Observer, that the ego often associated with artistic personalities is conspicuously absent among the cast, whose members have instead embraced a spirit of humility and collective purpose.

“The persons in this group are very easy to work with. We’ve been doing this for a long time, so we kind of have an idea of how things are to go, exactly what is to be done. So a lot of those initial growing pains where you have different ideas and people getting at each other, it doesn’t really happen,” Johnson said.

World.title: KINGSTON BOOKSHOP’S $1-B EXPANSION
World.content:
Kingston Bookshop’s new distribution centre on Lyndhurst Road in St Andrew.

Kingston Bookshop has pumped approximately $1 billion into a new distribution centre on Lyndhurst Road in St Andrew as its wholesale business takes a larger share of sales.

The company told the Jamaica Observer that business-to-business (B2B) sales now account for approximately 25 per cent of revenue, up from just under 20 per cent about four years ago as it widens the range of products supplied to schools, bookstores, pharmacies, offices, and other businesses across Jamaica.

That growth had begun to stretch an operation that was still being run from three separate warehouse properties on King Street in downtown Kingston.

The new Lyndhurst Road facility, which became operational in May 2025, brings warehousing, purchasing, and business-to-business sales together in one location and gives Kingston Bookshop significantly more room to handle stock.

Director of Strategy and Innovation Shauna Fuller Clarke said the company had reached the point where its old warehouse arrangement no longer matched the scale of the wholesale business.

“As that side of the business grew, so did our warehousing and operational requirements. At one point we were operating from three separate warehouse locations, so the decision to develop the Lyndhurst Road facility was a strategic one,” Fuller Clarke told the Business Observer.

“It allowed us to consolidate our warehousing, B2B sales, and purchasing operations in one location, creating a more efficient operation and, importantly, enabling us to provide better service to our customers.”

The approximately 42,000-square-foot facility includes a 39,000-square-foot warehouse and another 3,000 square feet for the company’s B2B sales and purchasing teams.

Kingston Bookshop previously operated with about 34,000 square feet of warehouse space across 72, 74, and 80 King Street.

The gain at Lyndhurst Road, however, is larger than the difference in floor space suggests.

Fuller Clarke said the height of the building and the racking system allow the company to make far greater use of vertical storage, taking usable capacity to the equivalent of approximately 50,000 square feet.

“The investment was, therefore, about much more than simply adding square footage. It was about creating the infrastructure to operate more efficiently, improve inventory management, and better support our retail and B2B customers,” she said.

The expansion comes more than three decades after Kingston Bookshop first moved into wholesale distribution. The company said that business began with stationery in the 1990s and later expanded into textbooks, general books, games, and technology products. It has recently added sports gear and equipment, particularly for schools.

That widening product range has helped Kingston Bookshop deepen its relationship with existing wholesale customers rather than relying only on traditional book sales.

“As our customers seek to diversify their own product offerings, we have been able to respond by supplying more of what they need rather than limiting our B2B operation to traditional books and stationery,” Fuller Clarke said.

The company now supplies customers in all parishes through its own delivery fleet.

New plan for former warehouses

The move to Lyndhurst Road is also changing how Kingston Bookshop uses its downtown real estate.

The company has already vacated 72 King Street, which was leased, while an expansion of its retail footprint at the 74 King Street head office is under active consideration.

That leaves the other warehouse property, at 80 King Street — one of its busiest retail stores — as the likely candidate for a mix of Kingston Bookshop operations and commercial rental space similar to what the company has adopted in Portmore, St Catherine, with the Script Cafe. The location is particularly significant given its position along one of downtown Kingston’s main retail corridors, where a large volume of shopping activity is concentrated.

“One option under active consideration is expanding our retail footprint at 74 King Street, while another property may incorporate a mix of Kingston Bookshop operations and commercial rental space, similar to the mixed-use approach we have successfully adopted at our 31 East Plaza location in Portmore,” she said.

The possible expansion downtown comes after Kingston Bookshop closed its Boulevard location earlier this year, but Fuller Clarke said that decision should not be read as a pullback from physical retail.

She told the Business Observer that stores remain Kingston Bookshop’s largest sales channel, even as wholesale contributes more and online purchasing continues to grow.

“The two decisions should not be viewed as Kingston Bookshop moving away from physical retail. They reflect our ongoing assessment of how and where we deploy our resources across the business,” she said.

“Our physical stores remain our largest sales channel, while B2B now represents approximately 25 per cent of sales and continues to grow. We are also steadily seeing increased purchasing through our e-commerce platform.”

Kingston Bookshop is continuing to invest across those three areas, but Fuller Clarke said expansion will be driven by where the company sees a commercial case rather than simply adding more locations.

“Our focus is not expansion simply for the sake of adding locations. We are looking at how we can strengthen the business across our retail, B2B, and digital channels while improving the customer experience and the efficiency of our operations,” she said.

That investment is being made at a time when one of Kingston Bookshop’s most important retail periods has produced little growth.

Fuller Clarke disclosed that revenue from the company’s stores during the 2026 back-to-school period was broadly similar to 2025 and, after accounting for inflation, the company considers sales relatively flat year on year.

The company continues to see strong demand for early childhood and primary-level material, including supplementary resources for Primary Exit Profile preparation, but purchasing at the secondary level has become more selective.

Parents have access to the Government’s textbook rental programme, second-hand books, online resources, and are increasingly deciding which items must be bought immediately and which can wait.

“Given the cost of preparing children for school, particularly for households with more than one child, parents are understandably making very deliberate choices about what they purchase,” Fuller Clarke said.

According to the company, workbooks and other books considered essential tend to be purchased first, while stationery and other supplies are sometimes bought later.

The company is also reporting a rise in parents choosing to pay for purchases in instalments.

“We have also seen more parents taking advantage of our lay-away programme, which allows them to make a deposit and pay towards their purchases over time,” Fuller Clarke said. “That provides families with another way of managing the cost of back-to-school preparation without having to meet the entire expense at once.”

The investment at Lyndhurst Road also leaves Kingston Bookshop with additional capacity that could eventually support more business outside Jamaica as well.

The company has previously supplied special orders to customers in smaller Caribbean islands, although Jamaica remains its main wholesale market.

Fuller Clarke reasoned that while the new facility puts Kingston Bookshop in a better position to pursue opportunities elsewhere in the region, the cost of distribution will determine how aggressively it moves.

“The cost of moving stock across the Caribbean can be significant, so both demand and logistics are important considerations in determining where and how we expand. We, therefore, see the Caribbean as an area of opportunity, but one where expansion has to be driven by sustainable demand and commercially viable distribution arrangements,” she said.

World.title: Visual Vibe to take screens off-grid with solar partnership
World.content:
A Visual Vibe outdoor screen at Mandela Park in Half-Way-Tree, St Andrew.

Digital advertising company Visual Vibe Limited is moving to take its entire network of outdoor screens off the national grid as it seeks to halve energy costs and eliminate outage-related downtime.

Following a recent partnership with Florida-based renewables firm Rush Hour Engineering, the Kintyre Holdings (JA) Limited subsidiary is getting ready to install solar power across its network of outdoor advertising screens.

Kintyre Holdings founder, chairman, and CEO, Tyrone Wilson, who also heads Visual Vibe, said the plan is to have every screen in the network — existing and new — powered by solar energy.

Visual Vibe currently operates 14 outdoor digital signs, for which energy costs now averages about $24 million annually, but the company will be adding another 15 screens shortly, which Wilson said could push annual electricity costs to as much as $60 million as the network expands.

The solar roll-out is, however, expected to reduce those costs by at least 50 per cent, bringing yearly energy expenditure to about $30 million.

“Electricity cost has long been one of the digital advertising business’s largest single monthly expenses, and with the war pushing up gas prices, we don’t see that easing anytime soon. So we had no other choice than to tap into solar,” Wilson told the Jamaica Observer.

“If we can cut our electricity bill by about 50 to 60 per cent, that would lift Visual Vibe’s profits enough so that we can keep funding growth from our own cash flow instead of seeking outside investment,” he further said to the Business Observer.

Stressing the need to have more efficient systems, Wilson said the new partnership also allows Visual Vibe to offer greater reliability to its clients during periods of disruption.

“Reliability is the currency of advertising. When a brand invests in our network, their campaign must be on screen every single time — and rising energy costs and grid outages have been a real challenge for our entire industry, and so this partnership with Rush Hour Engineering aims to solve those issues permanently “ Wilson said.

“By taking our screens off-grid, we are eliminating downtime completely while protecting our advertisers’ investment, as we also build the kind of resilient, sustainable media infrastructure that Jamaica deserves. It is a multimillion-dollar commitment to our clients and to the environment,” he added.

The solar programme forms a part of broader upgrades and expansion of Visual Vibe’s network and coincides with the company’s latest quest to deploy its newest high-resolution screens to flagship sites and premium locations along some of the city’s busiest corridor.

Phase one of the solar installation is scheduled to begin this week in the new Kingston area before being rolled out across the wider network.

Visual Vibe was acquired by Kintyre (trading then as iCreate) about three years ago for more than $500 million. Since then, the company has continued to expand its digital advertising operations, which now account for a substantial portion of group revenue.

In addition to its outdoor signs, Visual Vibe operates more than 50 indoor screens. Through a multichannel model combining outdoor billboards, indoor screens, and mobile formats, the company seeks to give advertisers multiple ways of reaching their target audiences.

Rush Hour Engineering President and CEO Edwin Xiao, commenting on the partnership, said the project demonstrates the potential for renewable energy to transform commercial infrastructure.

“We are proud to partner with Visual Vibe on a project of this scale,” Xiao said.

“Powering Jamaica’s largest digital advertising network entirely with solar energy demonstrates what renewable technology can do for the country’s commercial infrastructure. This partnership sets a new standard for how media assets are powered across the region.”

Rush Hour Engineering is a provider of engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) services for residential and commercial projects. In addition to solar systems, its capabilities include electric vehicle chargers; LED lighting; and mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) design.

The Florida-based company, as a Tesla-certified partner, also provides energy-efficiency and renewable-energy solutions aimed at reducing electricity costs and carbon emissions.

As Kintyre doubles down on opportunities arising from the shift towards renewable energy, the Jamaica Stock Exchange-listed holding company earlier this year announced, through a separate partnership with Rush Hour Engineering, plans to strategically enter the EV market as it also positions to capitalise on developments in the transport sector.

“Renewable energy is the future, and we’re investing in it. It has been on our radar for a very long time, but we are now actively tapping into its potential,” Wilson said.

World.title: Raheem Sterling pleads guilty to dangerous driving after Lamborghini crash
World.content:
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - AUGUST 02: Raheem Sterling #17 of Chelsea FC looks on during the pre-season friendly match Borussia Dortmund at Soldier Field on August 2, 2023 in Chicago, Illinois. Justin Casterline/Getty Images/AFPJustin Casterline / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP

LONDON, United Kingdom (AFP) — Footballer Raheem Sterling pleaded guilty on Tuesday to dangerous driving after he crashed his Lamborghini on a motorway in May.

The 31-year-old also admitted possession of six nitrous oxide canisters for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen for analysis when he appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates’ Court, about 50 miles southwest of London.

Sterling, who attended court wearing a black suit jacket, black trousers, black shoes and a dark top, was arrested after crashing on the M3 on the morning of May 28.

Police said no other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported.

READ: Raheem Sterling arrested for suspected drug-driving

The winger won 82 England caps, the last of which came at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

Sterling made his senior debut at Liverpool before joining Manchester City in 2015, winning four Premier League titles and other silverware at the Etihad.

He left for Chelsea in 2022 but subsequently fell out of favour and spent the 2024/25 season on loan at Arsenal.

Sterling joined Feyenoord on a short-term deal in February, playing eight times in the Eredivisie.

World.title: JAMAICA gets Disney boost
World.content:
Disney Cruine Line’s Disney Destiny will make its inaugural call on Jamaica next month.

OCHO RIOS, St Ann — Jamaica’s tourism industry is set to receive a big boost on October 13 when one of Disney Cruise Line’s top modern vessels, Disney Destiny, makes its inaugural call at Falmouth’s historic cruise port bringing just under 2,800 passengers to the island.

The announcement was made by Jamaica Tourist Board (JTB) Deputy Director of Tourism for the Americas Philip Rose during Monday’s opening of the Jamaica Product Exchange (JAPEX) at Moon Palace Jamaica in Ocho Rios.

The arrival of Disney Destiny adds to the growing roster of Disney Cruise Line vessels calling on Jamaica, alongside ships operated by Norwegian Cruise Line, MSC Cruises, Royal Caribbean, Carnival, Princess Cruises, and Virgin Voyages.

From January to July this year, according to data shared by Rose, Jamaica recorded 234 cruise calls and 736,372 passengers. Montego Bay, Falmouth and Ocho Rios accounted for most visits, while four ships also called at Port Antonio and Kingston.

Rose pointed out that the cruise industry remains an important partner, particularly in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa — which hit sections of Jamaica last October — and reminded that it could provide a pathway to attracting visitors for longer stays.

“It’s often said you can come down, get a little taste of Jamaica on the cruise ship, then we can convert them, or they go back home and say that was too much of a teaser, and they come back,” he said.

The JTB official said cruise visitors are encouraged to venture beyond established resort centres, particularly towards Kingston and Port Antonio, to experience a wider range of the Jamaican product.

Reacting to news of Disney Destiny’s impending visit, Chukka Caribbean Adventures deputy executive chairman and Jamaica Tourist Board member John Byles pointed to the benefit it will bring to local artisans and attractions. According to Byles, Disney passengers tend to leave the ship and spend on Jamaican tourism experiences.

He welcomed the impending Disney Destiny call, describing it as a sign of the company’s growing trust in Jamaica.

“It is always very heartening to see the confidence that a brand like Disney continues to show for the Jamaica product and Jamaica destination,” Byles told buyers and suppliers attending the first day of JAPEX, a staple on the tourism calendar.

The trade show is being held under the theme ’Jamaica Reimagined’. Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association (JHTA) President O’Brian Heron used his address to stress that Jamaica’s recovery from Hurricane Melissa must lead to a stronger and more adaptable tourism industry.

“Resilience is not simply about recovering, It is truly about what comes next,” he said.

He noted that changing travellers, technology and artificial intelligence were reshaping how people discover and experience destinations, requiring Jamaica to embrace innovation without sacrificing its authenticity.

The JHTA head said Jamaica’s strongest differentiator remains its people, pointing to the warmth of the welcome, culture, creativity, music, spirit, and food.

Officially declaring the trade show open during an address delivered virtually, Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett stressed the importance of adapting to shifts in the global tourism marketplace, strengthening competitiveness and building resilience while safeguarding the characteristics that make Jamaica distinctive.

“An event like JAPEX is never just a trade show. Last year, JAPEX facilitated an estimated US$100 million in contracts and business negotiations. Behind that figure are real hotels, real workers, real families, and real communities. That is precisely why, in fact, we do this,” Bartlett said.

World.title: Veteran journalist Balford Henry passes
World.content:
HENRY... his quiet and composed demeanour belied his sharp wit, keen sense of discernment, hard work, and professional integrity that have been the hallmark of his more than four decades as a top print reporter

THE local media fraternity has lost one of its calmest and most easy-going veterans, Balford George Henry, who died on Monday after a brief illness.

He was 74.

Henry’s quiet and composed demeanour belied his sharp wit, keen sense of discernment, hard work, and professional integrity that have been the hallmark of his more than four decades as a top print reporter.

Henry served both national newspapers, The Gleaner and the Jamaica Observer, in several capacities. He also served as consulting editor at the Jamaica Information Service (JIS) and worked at

New York Daily News, WLIB Radio in New York as a correspondent.

Henry was also editor of Reggae Times in the 1990s and reporter for the Overseas Gleaner (North America Edition) in New York during the 90s.

In a 2011 interview with JIS the unflappable Henry said he simply loves to write, and responded to the call to the fourth Estate during the summer of 1971, while a sixth former at Wolmer’s Boys’ School in Kingston.

“At that time, The Gleaner advertised for trainee journalists. I was among scores of young people from across Jamaica who sat the initiative tests, coincidently held at Wolmer’s Boys’ School auditorium. Fortunately, I was among the handful of successful candidates,” he recalled.

At that time, The Gleaner was the only institutionalised daily newspaper in the country and, in the absence of a school of journalism in Jamaica and indeed, the wider region, the North Street facility prided itself as the nursery and training ground for print reporters.

“I was exposed to the veterans of the craft, people like Ken Allen, Calvin Bowen, LK Southerland, and Editor-in-Chief Theodore Sealy. Barbara Gloudon, in particular, discovered very early in my career that I enjoyed writing features, and encouraged and nurtured my efforts,” said Henry in the JIS interview.

He recalled that the training period was tough, with the late Fitzroy Nation “being the only other member of my group to survive that ordeal”.

Henry further honed his skills as a Commonwealth Press Union (CPU) Fellow, London, 1977; earned a journalism diploma as a Thomson Foundation scholar in Cardiff, Wales, 1977; and was one of 12 journalists from around the world chosen by the World Press Institute (WPI) for a fellowship at Macalester College, St Paul, Minnesota, in 1983.

Early in his career Henry reported on sittings of the then Kingston and St Andrew Corporation (KSAC), as well as major social and cultural activities and events.

Later, as a veteran labour relations reporter, he covered industrial relations issues including major strikes and disputes during the volatile 1970s.

The recipient of a number of professional awards, Henry had also been the winner of the Press Association of Jamaica (PAJ) Honorary Award for a series on the social and economic problems facing Jamaican youth in Britain’s inner cities, based on his own experience while living in that country in 1977.

He had also won the PAJ Best Story award for his coverage of the funeral of the late reggae icon Bob Marley in 1981; as well as the PAJ’s first Cultural Story Award for the feature entitled: ‘Fall of a Superstar’, on the rise and fall of Jamaican reggae singer Junior Byles.

In 2011 Henry was conferred with the Order of Distinction (Officer Class) for distinguished service to journalism.

Reacting to his passing, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness expressed sadness and said he remembers Henry as a committed journalist who understood the responsibility that comes with telling Jamaica’s story.

“His work reflected a deep knowledge of our politics, our people and the issues affecting our country,” Holness said in a post on Instagram.

“His passing is a loss to Jamaica’s media fraternity and to the many people who knew and worked with him over the years. I extend my heartfelt condolence to his family, friends, colleagues and the wider journalism community,” the prime minister said.

Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Minister Olivia Grange also expressed sadness at Henry’s passing, describing him as “a first-rate journalist” who was committed to his craft.

Grange said Henry was an “outstanding writer and questioner whose easy-going demeanour belied the penetrating nature of his questions”.

“I had great respect for Balford. He was always professional in his interactions and in his journalistic pursuits. He was sharp, he was keen, he could be tough, but he was always fair,” Grange said, and offered condolence to his family and colleagues.

Journalist Wilton Dyer, who was already at The Gleaner when a very young Henry arrived in 1971, remembers “a very quiet, contemplative man” who brought a “very dilligent, single-minded approach” to journalism.

“He was very efficient and driven,” Dyer said, recalling that Henry quickly developed a “mastery of labour relations and parliamentary reporting”.

Dyer also recalled that Henry was steeped in Jamaican music and also produced a record of his own called Bits of Paper.

By the mid-1970s Henry was among the leading Jamaican entertainment writers, said Dyer.

Fellow veteran journalist Garfield Myers remembered Henry as a workaholic.

“He was one of those who, when I went to The Gleaner in July 1973, had been there for a couple of years — very young man, a couple of years older than me — and he was one of those who showed me the way,” said Myers, a former Observer sports editor who still writes for the newspaper from St Elizabeth.

He said that Henry became very adept at labour relations and trade union coverage, which was a very important beat back in those days.

“Over time he graduated to Parliament and became one of the better parliamentary reporters, and mastered that beat. He was a very good reporter. Some journalists graduate to become editors but Balford was a reporter par excellence. Trying to make him into something else wouldn’t work,” Myers said.

Observer Executive Editor, Publications Vernon Davidson also commented on Henry’s mastery of parliamentary reporting, noting that he often returned from a long day of covering the legislature with stories missed by some of his colleagues.

“We could always depend on Balford to deliver, regardless of how long the sittings were, as he had an exceptional eye for detail and the type of patience required to cover Parliament,” said Davidson who also worked with Henry at The Gleaner in the early 1980s.

“Bally also provided excellent coverage of politics and would be our point reporter during the annual budget debates,” said Davidson who recalled that Henry joined the Observer in November 2003, left for JIS in 2009, and returned to the newspaper in 2012.

“He was a quiet fountain of knowledge and we are poorer for his passing. We extend our deepest condolence to his family, friends and colleagues,” Davidson said.

Henry is survived by his widow Claudia Stockhausen-Henry and was the father of two sons and two daughters.

World.title: Left on brink of victory in Swedish election
World.content:
The election is one of the closest in recent Swedish history, and offered voters a sharp choice between electing a new left-wing government or allowing far-right ministers into power for the first time.

Swedish public broadcaster SVT called the election for Andersson’s side on Wednesday night. Her Social Democrats are Sweden’s biggest party and have enjoyed the loose support of three other opposition parties who are seen as her likely coalition partners: The Greens, the Center Party, and the Left Party.

Kristersson’s conservative Moderates have been campaigning alongside the Christian Democrats, the Liberals and the far-right, anti-immigration Sweden Democrats. His allies do not expect him to concede defeat until Andersson wins a vote in parliament to prove she can command a majority. That vote won’t happen before Sept. 29 at the earliest.

Coalition negotiations will begin in earnest once the final outcome is confirmed. In theory any combination of parties can form into a government but in reality, the two-bloc system is likely to hold, meaning Andersson will seek to govern with some or all of her left-leaning partner parties.

Andersson’s Social Democrats stand on 99 seats, with her most natural allies in the Greens on 22. But that still leaves her 54 seats short of a majority and with a potentially difficult task persuading the other two parties in her bloc to cooperate with each other.

The Left Party, which has a historic association with communists, is emboldened by increasing its seat tally at this election to 30. And it has said the price of supporting a government will be gaining ministers inside the new top team.

World.title: EU blindsided by von der Leyen’s Canada ‘associate member’ pitch
World.content:
Ottawa has been exploring whether it can establish an unusually close relationship with the EU, the Wall Street Journal first reported last week. Carney publicly confirmed the broader ambition on Sunday, saying Canada was not seeking EU membership but rather a “unique alliance” with the bloc.

But von der Leyen’s decision to announce the proposal, at the biggest annual set piece of her political calendar, caught EU member countries off guard, according to four European diplomats who said their governments were not informed. They were granted anonymity, like others in this article, to speak candidly about their reactions to the proposal.

One diplomat slammed the secrecy as “dangerous” and “unwise,” pointing out that von der Leyen had not even raised the idea at a recent lunch with EU ambassadors. Another diplomat said the copy of the speech their government received in advance did not include the words associate membership.

Mark Carney said last week he wanted a “unique” partnership with Brussels but shied away from using the words associate membership. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images

And a different diplomat with knowledge of the discussions with Canada raised a different issue: “Nobody really knows what it [associate membership] means.”

While the Commission president is under no obligation to flag any of the speech's content to capitals in advance, they would need to approve any formal plan to grant Canada an exceptional status.

The idea has also raised questions about whether Britain could seek a similar deal. But EU officials have moved quickly to rule that out, stressing the model is intended for countries that cannot join the bloc. “Unlike Ukraine, Moldova, Georgia, Norway and the U.K., Canada is not in Europe,” one senior EU official said. “It cannot join the EU.”

World.title: Von der Leyen fleshes out Carney’s vision to paint Europe as leader of world’s middle powers
World.content:
“In this new world, we must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” von der Leyen said in the speech at the European Parliament building in Strasbourg. She added that the EU wanted to “build global coalitions for our resilience and democracies. And here too only Europe ― with its size and power ― can take the lead.”

For the head of the EU’s executive branch, who’s now two years into her second five-year term, the speech amounted to a declaration of geopolitical legacy.

Coming one year after she declared Europe’s “independence moment” from the same platform, von der Leyen expanded on that idea in a speech that seemed to echo Carney’s own address at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in which he called for the world’s “middle powers” to stand together against autocrats.

Ursula von der Leyen delivers her annual State of the Union address at a plenary session of the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France on Sept. 16, 2026. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images

In addition to offering Canada associate member status, von der Leyen suggested bringing the leaders of the U.K., Norway, Canada and Ukraine together in a newfangled “European Security Council” that would exist outside of NATO, offering a platform to discuss hybrid threats without the United States.

She also proposed that, with Europe in the role of coordinator, like-minded countries could jointly address challenges ranging from climate change to Chinese industrial overcapacity to the risks of frontier AI models.

“This speech was all about the big threats occupying European leaders: Russia and China, and to a lesser extent the United States,” said Mujtaba Rahman, Europe director at the Eurasia Group political consultancy. “It was all about how the EU can organize itself amid an imperialist Russia, a withdrawing America and a materialist China — it’s an attempt to draw those dots together.”

World.title: New EU security proposals risk fresh turf war with NATO
World.content:
“Our systems were made for a different world — they are driven by well-intentioned attempts at consensus and compromise,” she said. “But we need to consider whether they are still fit for purpose.”

The pitch is already stirring unease within NATO, which has bristled at any attempt by the EU to tackle military-adjacent threats and has warned against “unnecessary duplication.”

“I have seen many initiatives at the EU level during the recent years — none of them yet are really protecting member states,” said one senior NATO diplomat, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “Of course, any initiative has to be assessed on its merits, but I do feel that NATO has delivered much more in concrete terms for collective security.”

The EU proposals underscore a growing sense that Europe is failing to deal with proliferating airspace violations, cyberattacks and sabotage attempts amid tensions over Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

“Cyberattacks and sabotage, arson and drone incursions. They are ramping up every day. So, as the threat level climbs, so must Europe's preparedness,” von der Leyen said.

The security council is supposed to help the EU react more decisively. NATO itself has struggled with how to respond to Russian provocations below the threshold of direct military attack.

World.title: Azerbaijan insists it will preserve Christian heritage as part of its history
World.content:
Azerbaijan has warned that “revanchist forces” in Armenia and the Armenian diaspora “are still strong” and are trying to undermine the historic peace process between the former rivals.

 

In a wide-ranging panel at the Arab Media Summit in Dubai on Wednesday, Assistant of the President of Azerbaijan Hikmet Hajiyev told Euronews that “probably Armenian government and Armenian leadership should work to prepare their people for the peace as well.”

“Now we won the war, but we are also winning in peace which is an uphill struggle,” said Hajiyev, who is also Head of the Foreign Policy Affairs Department of the Presidential Administration.

“Throughout the years of occupation in Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur, our mosques, our Islamic cultural heritage were a subject of complete destruction by Armenia — even the pigs were put inside of the mosques."

“We are not taking it as a sign of revenge, but it's our history and our heritage and we cannot forget that;" he added.

The presidential advisor outlined that while his country is part of the broader Islamic civilisation, “currently, three religions — Islam, Christianity, and Judaism, with mosques, churches, and synagogues — are side by side” in Azerbaijan.

Hajiyev further said Azerbaijan is dedicated to “preserving the Christian heritage on the sovereign territory of Azerbaijan, regardless of their belonging, and that is a full stop because it's our cultural heritage.”

Speaking of Azerbaijan's history of cultural and religious coexistence, Hajiyev explained that he was "more than proud that my country is one of the first places of Zoroastrianism."

"It’s also one of the first places of Christianity since the fourth century: Christianity was adopted by the (Caucasian) Kingdom of Albania as an official religion,” while Azerbaijan was "also one of the first countries that adopted Islam.”

Caucasian Albania was an ancient kingdom in what is now Azerbaijan and parts of southern Dagestan, unrelated to the Western Balkan state of Albania — also once a kingdom — with which it shares only a name.

Armenian church authorities have disputed Azerbaijan's record on religious sites, accusing Baku of demolishing churches in Karabakh, claims Azerbaijan rejects.

'EU should embrace the entire region'

In the Euronews Forum panel at the Arab Media Summit, the top Azerbaijani official reiterated Baku’s firm position that even after securing peace, the South Caucasus country is still subject to “disinformation”.

“One such institution is the European Parliament which is not part of the solution, it's part of the problem,” along with certain Western media outlets, Hajiyev said.

“The European Parliament is adopting resolutions and decisions, humiliating and also undermining the agenda of peace of our region," he added.

"We are in the process of building regional peace, but the European Parliament is pursuing some completely different agenda."

Hajiyev pointed out the EU’s policy towards the South Caucasus “shouldn't be only a one-centric approach, it should embrace the entire region with balanced cooperation with the regional countries."

Furthermore, the EU policy should be about “building the concept of the new partnership ... and not to build into dividing lines," according to him.

Hajiyev reiterated that Azerbaijan contributes to the EU’s energy security by supplying gas to 16 EU member countries and other European countries as well, and in that sense, the Middle Corridor connectivity project could bring Azerbaijan and the EU even closer.

World.title: Rachida Dati in court: French ex-minister on trial over Renault-Nissan corruption case
World.content:
The trial of Rachida Dati opened on Wednesday afternoon before the Paris criminal court. The former justice and culture minister is facing charges of passive corruption, passive influence-peddling, and concealment of abuse of power and breach of trust.

 

At the heart of the case are the €900,000 she received between 2009 and 2013 from a Dutch subsidiary of Renault-Nissan, while she was serving as a Member of the European Parliament.

The opening day was marked in particular by the absence of Carlos Ghosn. The former head of Renault-Nissan, who has been in Lebanon since fleeing Japan in 2019, is also being prosecuted, notably for active corruption and influence-peddling.

Tried in absentia, he asked in a letter to the court for the hearing to be postponed, arguing that he had not been properly served. He said he was willing to take part in the proceedings via videoconference.

Over six half-days of hearings, up to 28 September, the court is to examine the relationship between Rachida Dati and Carlos Ghosn and, above all, the nature of the services said to correspond to the €900,000 paid by RNBV, the Dutch subsidiary of the Renault-Nissan alliance.

Carlos Ghosn in Tokyo, May 2012 AP Photo

Fees at the heart of the proceedings

Rachida Dati maintains she worked as a lawyer for the group and denies any lobbying activity in the European Parliament. Her lawyers denounce what they call an "intellectual construct" by the prosecution and insist their client has "exclusively" carried out legal work.

The prosecution, by contrast, argues that the fee agreement signed in 2009 was used to conceal lobbying activities. Investigating magistrates noted the paucity of documents that could, in their view, establish the reality and scope of the legal services provided. They also consider that the remuneration was "totally disproportionate" to the work for which evidence has been found.

Investigators are looking in particular at several interventions by Rachida Dati in the European Parliament, including three questions submitted in 2012 and 2013 relating to the automotive sector. The prosecution believes her parliamentary activity may have been influenced by her professional ties with Renault.

Rachida Dati faces up to ten years in prison and a €450,000 fine, as well as a possible ban on holding public office. She remains presumed innocent until the court reaches its decision.

Carlos Ghosn, for his part, will therefore not be in the dock. The former executive, who disputes the allegations against him, remains in Lebanon. His absence adds a particular dimension to a trial that is expected to help the court determine whether the €900,000 paid to Rachida Dati did indeed correspond to legal services or whether it concealed lobbying activity, which was banned at the time for MEPs.

World.title: US House votes for a third time to end the Iran war as conflict drags on
World.content:
The vote took place late Tuesday, and for a third time, the US House voted to end the war in Iran, attempting to cut President Donald Trump's ability to continue military action.

 

The roll call, 220-204, was similar to earlier efforts this summer, with a few more Republicans joining all Democrats voting to bring an end to the conflict. None of the resolutions have made it to the president’s desk, where Trump would almost certainly veto the measure.

"Remember when Donald Trump said that this war would last just a few weeks?" said Democrat Representative Seth Moulton, who served as a Marine during the Iraq War and pushed the resolution forward.

He said it’s time for Congress to "actually ask tough questions, as the Constitution directs us to do, rather than be subservient to another warmongering administration."

Republican Representative Brian Mast of Florida, the chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, questioned which military resources Democrats would want to remove from the region where he said Iran remains a threat.

Mast said Trump is against "forever wars, and that is what he is ending" — the decades of hostilities from Iran.

"They are a continuous ongoing threat to the United States," Mast said. "Enough is enough."

Last war powers vote before midterms

The action is likely the last House vote on the Iran war ahead of the midterm elections, where the conflict overseas is playing a substantial role in the political campaigns. The war that Trump launched on 28 February has dragged on, with on-again, off-again deadly missile strikes being exchanged and causing havoc in the region for nearly seven months.

Lawmakers are heading home at the end of the week to campaign nearly full-time, with less than 50 days to go before the elections that will determine control of Congress as Democrats try to wrest power from Republicans.

Voters are confronting high prices, particularly for gas at the pumps, as the conflict disrupts the flow of oil resources through the vital Strait of Hormuz.

The Congressional Budget Office said Tuesday that the war has cost more than $38 billion (€33 billion), as of 1 August, and is projected to be costing between $2 billion (€1.74 billion) and $3 billion (€2.62 billion) monthly, depending on the intensity of the fighting. The budget office projected inflation will be 0.5 percentage points higher than expected heading into 2027 due to the war.

Trump himself had promised not to involve the US in foreign wars when he won a second term in the White House, and his actions against Iran are weighing on the Republican Party that controls the House and Senate. Most Americans say the war in Iran has not been worth fighting, according to an AP-NORC poll in July.

In the previous House actions, four Republicans voted to halt the war in Iran, but that number rose to seven in Tuesday’s war powers vote, including GOP lawmakers from battleground Iowa, Representative Zachary Nunn and Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks, and retiring Representative Nancy Mace of South Carolina.

They joined GOP Representatives Tom Barrett of Michigan, Warren Davidson of Ohio, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky voting in favor of the war powers resolution, with all Democrats.

War powers put to the test

Congress has tried repeatedly to alter the trajectory of the war against Iran, but efforts to limit the Trump administration’s military action remain a long shot so long as the president is able to fend off or veto the measures.

The House first approved a war powers resolution in June, and followed up with another one in July, all seeking to halt US action in Iran. The Senate on its 10th try also approved a war powers resolution to end the conflict, but GOP senators quickly reversed course the next day after Trump berated them during a closed-door lunch.

While the Constitution gives Congress the authority to declare war, it also gives the president authority as the commander in chief to engage in some military actions. The War Powers Act, created in the aftermath of the Vietnam conflict, sought to put a more specific time limit on the president’s power, requiring congressional approval for sustained military actions after 60 or 90 days.

House Speaker Mike Johnson acknowledged at a press conference Tuesday the need to bring gas prices down.

But the Republican speaker said he believes the Iran conflict is entering a "new phase" as allies step up to help stabilize the region. When that happens, he said, "you’re going to see, as the president said, anytime gas prices will go down again, the cost of groceries will as well."

Johnson said Trump expects the shift after the election, and the speaker added, "I’d love it to happen today."

World.title: Mbappé, Vinícius and Konaté criticised for hiding Ceuta support message
World.content:
The La Liga president Javier Tebas criticised three Real Madrid players on Wednesday, including Kylian Mbappé, for not wearing a T-shirt properly in support of the people of Ceuta, a Spanish autonomous city in North Africa that has been hit by a migration crisis.

 

Mbappé, Vinícius Júnior and Ibrahima Konaté wore the commemorative T-shirt with the sleeves partially rolled up before Real Madrid's 3-2 victory over Elche in La Liga on Tuesday. The rest of the players wore it in the usual way.

In doing so, the three players partially hid the message "We are all Ceutans", referring to the inhabitants of this Spanish territory in North Africa. "We saw three players who decided not to put it on. Wearing it halfway is the same as not wearing it at all... it's bad, very bad," Tebas told reporters.

The initiative for the teams to wear these T-shirts came from a group of business leaders in the Valencian Community. Tebas explained that the proposal had been approved but not organised by La Liga, and stressed that "it is not a political act of any kind".

La Liga teams playing matches that do not involve clubs from the Valencian Community have not been using the T-shirt. Miguel Ángel Montaño, president of the supporters' club of Real Madrid in Ceuta, expressed his disappointment at the decision by the three players not to wear it properly.

No 'political purpose'

"We were really excited to see the players wearing the T-shirts because we need support, but we were left puzzled when we saw that these three players had covered up the message," Montaño told the Spanish media.

Villarreal hosted Real Betis on Monday and both teams wore the T-shirts in support of Ceuta. Levante also wore them before their match on Sunday against Barcelona, although the Catalan side chose not to wear it.

The controversy comes against a backdrop of mounting tension in Ceuta following the mass arrival of migrants. Tens of thousands of people entered the city from Morocco on 30 and 31 July. Most returned to Morocco a couple of hours after they arrived, but several thousand remained in Ceuta.

Local residents have been staging protests on a regular basis while the migrants continue camping on the beaches and sleeping in the streets. Protesters accuse the Spanish government of abandoning a city overwhelmed by a humanitarian crisis.

Abde Ezzalzouli, a Real Betis winger of Moroccan origin, came to the city's defence on Tuesday on social media after receiving criticism for wearing the T-shirt.

"I want to make one thing clear: at no point was the T-shirt with a message aimed at the inhabitants of Ceuta used for a political purpose or out of contempt for my people, the Moroccan people," Ezzalzouli wrote in a post on Instagram. The former Barcelona player described the gesture as an expression of social support for the city's residents, "regardless of their nationality".

World.title: Fed raises rates for the first time since 2023 in unanimous vote defying Trump
World.content:
Kevin Warsh has broken away from US President Donald Trump in his first Fed move, and he has done it with the entire committee behind him.

 

The Federal Open Market Committee lifted rates on Wednesday after holding them at 3.5% to 3.75% since December, ending a pause that had grown harder to justify as energy costs pushed prices higher.

Not a single member dissented in a unanimous 12-0 vote.

That matters because the pressure ran in both directions as three regional presidents had voted for a hike in July, while the White House spent months demanding cuts.

Nobody voted for either extreme.

At the time of writing, the market reaction to the decision has been fairly muted likely due to the fact that the hike was widely expected.

On the other hand, Trump has already reacted negatively on social media by stating that "interest rates in the United States should be 1%, or less [...]".

A statement stripped to the bone

The Fed's communication was as striking as its decision.

The statement ran to three short paragraphs, a fraction of the length markets are used to, with no forward guidance and no hedging.

"Inflation remains elevated," it read, adding that "today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal."

The word "timelier" carries an implicit admission that the return had been too slow.

Then a sentence the Fed almost never writes: "The Committee will deliver price stability." Not seeks to, not is committed to. Will.

The economic assessment was also confident throughout.

Activity is "expanding at a solid pace", domestic spending "has been resilient", productivity growth is "strong" and capital investment "robust", while job gains "have kept pace with the workforce".

Uncertainty remains elevated, the Fed said, owing partly to "geopolitical developments", its formulation for the Iran war.

By describing an economy in good health, the committee removed the argument that higher rates would damage growth, which is precisely the case US President Donald Trump has been making.

Boxed in by the data

The decision had been building for months.

Three regional Fed presidents dissented in July in favour of an increase, the most in one direction since 2016, and several others said afterwards they were ready to move unless inflation eased which it did not.

The Fed's preferred gauge, the personal consumption expenditures index, ran at 3.7% in both June and July, with core inflation at 3.3%. Before the Iran war sent fuel prices climbing, core stood at 3%.

Consumer prices held at 3.4% in August, but the monthly increase of 0.4% was the sharpest since May, evidence the energy shock is feeding through. Inflation has now been above the 2% target for more than five years.

Warsh had effectively committed himself at Jackson Hole in August, telling the symposium he "would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive" and warning that unless underlying inflation moved to target "clearly and at sufficient speed", the Fed had "work to do".

Markets took him at his word as the CME's FedWatch tool put the probability of a rate hike above 90% before today's decision.

Defying the president who chose him

US President Donald Trump had spent months demanding the opposite, insisting the country should have the lowest interest rates in the world and choosing Warsh partly on the expectation he would deliver them.

Warsh himself said while campaigning for the job that rates could come down.

The treatment of his predecessor sharpened the stakes as Jerome Powell was publicly attacked for moving too slowly, and the US Justice Department opened a criminal investigation into testimony he gave to Congress.

Today's decision could also have a restoring effect on the perceived independence of the Federal Reserve as an institution.

US President Donald Trump applauds Kevin Warsh, after being sworn in as Chairman of the Federal Reserve in the East Room of the White House, 22 May 2026 AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta

The technical details point to a Fed settling in at the new level.

The interest rate on reserve balances rises to 3.90% from Thursday, the primary credit rate to 4%, and standing repurchase operations will run at 4%. Seven regional reserve banks requested the discount rate increase.

The Fed’s new dot plot shows 12 of 18 officials expect another 0.25% hike by year-end, taking rates to 4.125%, while four see rates reaching 4.375%.

The hawkish signal extends well beyond 2026 as 14 officials see rates ending 2027 above today’s level, while the 2028 median stands at 3.9% versus 3.4% expected.

The longer-run rate also rose to 3.2%, suggesting officials increasingly believe neutral rates have moved higher while economists also expect more to follow.

World.title: Kosovo war crimes court jails ex-president Hashim Thaçi for 25 years, sparking mass protests
World.content:
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague sentenced former Kosovo president Hashim Thaçi to 25 years in prison on 16 September for war crimes during the 1998-99 Kosovo conflict. The 58-year-old former Kosovo Liberation Army commander was convicted of murder, torture, cruel treatment and arbitrary detention. He was sentenced alongside three other former KLA commanders: Jakup Krasniqi, also to 25 years, Kadri Veseli to 18 years and Rexhep Selimi to 13 years. All four were acquitted of crimes against humanity after judges found prosecutors had failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that civilians had been subjected to a widespread or systematic attack. They can appeal.

 

In Pristina, thousands gathered in the city centre to watch the verdict on a large screen, with many supporters weeping, booing and chanting “Thaci, Thaci” and “KLA” while waving Kosovo Liberation Army flags. After the judgment, some marched towards the EU rule‑of‑law mission (EULEX) headquarters, chanting and, in places, clashing with riot police.

Thaci resigned as Kosovo’s president in 2020 to face the trial.

World.title: English village votes to 'secede' from UK over asylum centre plan
World.content:
An English village of around 350 people has voted overwhelmingly to “secede” from the United Kingdom in a symbolic referendum held in protest against plans to house asylum seekers at a nearby former military site.

 

In Piddington, near Oxford, 285 of the 312 ballots counted backed the call for the village to seek self-determination. The referendum has no legal standing, but residents celebrated the result by putting up a sign declaring the area the “Principality of Piddington”.

Local residents pose with a "Principality of Piddington" sign in the village of Piddington, Oxfordshire, England PA Wire

The vote was organised by the parish council and was inspired partly by the 1949 British comedy film Passport to Pimlico, in which London residents discover their neighbourhood is technically outside the UK and declare independence.

Local council leader Tim McNally said the vote was intended to send a message about residents’ concerns over the government’s plans. The proposed centre at a disused military site is expected to house more than 1,200 single adult male asylum seekers for at least 10 years.

The government says the use of former military bases is part of its plan to reduce reliance on hotels for asylum accommodation.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would consider the concerns raised by the community, while the government has maintained that the site will go ahead.

World.title: France: TotalEnergies cut-price fuel spikes controversy among rivals
World.content:
French motorists are clogging TotalEnergies service stations to fill up with discount gasoline, but its rivals are crying foul, accusing the energy giant of distorting competition with the encouragement of the government.

 

TotalEnergies, which pumps crude oil and refines it into gasoline, also has an extensive network of filling stations throughout France, where retail sales are usually dominated by supermarkets selling gasoline at or near cost in order to pull in customers.

But as oil prices shot higher this spring due to the US-Iran war, the highly profitable company announced a cap of €1.99 per litre of E10 (€2.25 per litre for diesel), considerably less than the national average of around €2.15 per litre — and up to nearly €2.50 in other areas, including Paris.

The cap, which has been in place intermittently for the past five months, has already cost the company 250 million to 300 million euros.

While it is a hefty expense, higher oil prices helped the French company double its first-half profit to 11.2 billion euros.

TotalEnergies introduced the cap when political pressure was building to introduce a tax on windfall profits being made by energy companies.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu called on the company in May to put in place "a generous cap".

Its chief executive, Patrick Pouyanné, has made clear it will abandon the cap if a special tax is put into place.

"There's nothing forcing us" to keep the cap in place, Pouyanné said recently.

"If a tax is introduced, we'll draw our conclusions and TotalEnergies won't have any more price caps," he added.

Fear of widespread protest

With a presidential election seven months away and France's economic situation worsening, the government is keeping close watch.

"Today, the public authorities are quite happy a private company is doing the job, perhaps in their place," said Jacques Goisque, head of the FF3C trade association that represents a thousand independent service stations.

But there are limits to how much relief TotalEnergies can provide.

The most recent jump in fuel prices has prompted calls to demonstrate, reminiscent of the so-called yellow vest movement in 2018.

The public authorities are quite happy that a private company is doing the job, perhaps in their place. Jacques Goisque Head of the FF3C trade association

At the time, a plan to increase fuel taxes sparked widespread protests from low- and middle-income workers who stood to take the biggest financial hit, snowballing into a challenge to the economic policies of President Emmanuel Macron.

Macron called on the government on Wednesday to tackle the questions about fuel supplies and prices.

Government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon noted that around one in ten filling stations in France lacked at least one fuel, with the vast majority of them being TotalEnergies stations.

She said the government would seek to ensure sufficient supplies and gain some regulatory flexibility on refineries.

The goal is "to push prices down as much as possible, or at the very least to keep their increase under control", she said.

'Distortion of competition'

The FF3C group of independent petrol stations lodged a complaint in mid-July with France's competition regulator for unfair competition.

"There is an upstream player with a dominant position that takes advantage of it to set very aggressive prices that are below market levels," said FF3C's Goisque.

"We can't sell at a loss."

The supermarkets that usually sell gasoline as a loss leader to pull in customers are also furious.

Michel-Edouard Leclerc, head of the leading supermarket chain E.Leclerc, said "refiners are lining their pockets" while it is impossible for retail distributors to compete.

"We can't go any lower than what our prices are today," he said. "We don't have a cent of margin in our filling stations."

TotalEnergies are maintaining low price fuels in France while other gas stations are seeing their prices rise above €2 per litre threshold. AP Photo

More than a dozen filling stations closed over the past weekend on the island of Corsica.

"Despite the efforts of our supplier, our purchase price exceeds Total's retail price by several dozen cents," the stations said in a statement.

They denounced "the state failing to regulate prices", which "allows an integrated group that benefits from considerable upstream margins to dictate, to blackmail, leading to this distortion of competition."

While the price cap has financial costs for TotalEnergies, it pays well in terms of public image for a company that has frequently faced criticism for the low amount of taxes it pays in France in comparison with the profits it earns globally.

The price cap has "above all earned the company a large amount of goodwill among the French," Pouyanné, the chief executive, said recently.

World.title: How climate change worsened Nepal's deadly mountain collapse
World.content:
A glacier and rock collapse in Nepal killed nearly 1,400 people and left thousands missing. Scientists say decades of warming helped set the disaster in motion.

Nearly 1,400 people have died after a mountain slope collapsed and flash floods swept through the valleys of Nepal and Tibet. More than 5,000 people remain missing.

The collapse was initially thought to have been caused by an earthquake. Now, glaciologists and climate scientists have determined that a complex series of factors led to the disaster, with climate change laying the groundwork several times over: Warming temperatures receded the glacier, thawed permafrost and increased meltwater, destabilizing the slope until it gave way on August 26.

"This was not a single trigger event," Walter Immerzeel, a mountain hydrologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, told journalists on a press call. "The failure occurred at an elevation of about 5150 meters (about 16,896 feet) and there were several processes acting together over time scales of years to decades, rather than one factor acting alone."

With no time to prepare, families in Devighat returned to mud-filled homes days later to salvage whatever survived Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

How the disaster unfolded

The floods began upstream with a large rock avalanche on the north face of Langtang Lirung. That caused a section of the glacier to collapse at the same time, sending roughly 110 million cubic meters of rock and glacier ice, the size of 44,000 Olympic swimming pools, hurtling downward. That type of rock avalanche is rare, occurring at this size only once every 1,000-10,000 years.

The material fell about 1,400 meters (4,593 feet) from the mountain to the valley floor, picking up debris, water, ice, rock and sediment as it descended. The impact released as much energy as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. As it crashed into the valley, it also tore up buried glacier ice, adding up to 30 million more cubic meters of debris and water to the flow.

Within about seven minutes, the flood reached Nepal and China's Rasuwagadhi border, 20 kilometers (about 12 miles) downstream, moving at an average speed of 170 kilometers per hour (about 106 miles per hour). The flood continued downstream, traveling 200 kilometers in under seven hours.

Relatives are going through photographs of missing people, trying to find loved ones Image: Safal Prakash Shrestha/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance

How did this happen?

It was a complex combination of conditions, exacerbated by climate change, that allowed the slope to collapse in the first place. That's according to researchers with World Weather Attribution, an international collaboration of scientists that looks at the role of climate change in extreme weather and disaster events.

Rising temperatures, due to the burning of fossil fuels, have reshaped this stretch of the Himalayas for decades.

Near the failure site, the glacier's edge had retreated just 75 meters between 1964 and 2000. But between 2010 and 2026, it dramatically accelerated, retreating another 373 meters. That stripped away the ice supporting the rock wall above it.

Permafrost — or permanently frozen ground within the rock — had also started to thaw. That took place between 4,500 and 5,500 meters of elevation, a critical band that's most sensitive to warming. As it thawed, the mountain walls became more and more unstable.

In the immediate run-up to the collapse, conditions were extreme. July and August overall were the warmest on record in the area, with climate change adding about 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to the region. On August 24 and 25, temperatures ran roughly 2.5 to 2.7 degrees Celsius above the 10-year average. A day before the catastrophe unfolded, the maximum temperature was approximately 7 degrees Celsius above the reference mean.

An unusually snowy October in 2025 likely also played a role, generating more meltwater.

Researchers also believe a 2015 earthquake played a role. That magnitude-7.8 quake triggered an earlier avalanche at Langtang Lirung, which may have weakened the rock mass in the years since, priming the slope for failure.

A disaster beyond adaptation

Researchers also tried to find out whether this was a disaster the region could have prepared for and adapted to. They determined it was uniquely hard to detect, as Nepal's early warning systems are designed for forecastable rainfall-driven floods, not quickly developing, cascading events like this one.

Essentially, this kind of complex threat exceeds the limits of adaptation.

The flood outran Nepal's early warning systems and destroyed several monitoring gauges in its wake. The first mass SMS warning was sent about 38 minutes after the initial collapse, but the flood had already reached the border 7 minutes in.

"When warming destabilizes the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction," Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London, said.

"Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come."

World.title: US Congress passes Russia sanctions bill
World.content:
The sanctions package is considered the most substantial US legislative effort against Moscow since Trump returned to the White House. Measures in the bill could lead to secondary sanctions on India, China and Iran.

The US Republican-led US House of Representatives passed on Wednesday a package of broad new sanctions against Russia over its war in Ukraine.

The bill passed 262-159, after breezing through the Senate in an 86-11 vote last month.

The bill, considered the toughest legislative effort against Russia during US President Donald Trump's second term, awaits the president's signature to come into law. Trump has said he will sign it.

Russia's economy is growing, despite sanctions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What does the sanctions package against Russia entail?

The package targets Russia's energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials. It also targets Moscow's so-called shadow fleet, old tankers it uses to circumvent sanctions.

More controversially, the legislation allows Trump to impose secondary sanctions on countries that rely on Russian oil and gas, in the form of tariffs. China and India are expected to be the main targets of such measures.

The bill would also extend sanctions on Iran.

It was drafted in April 2025 by late Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly in July.

But Trump had delayed the bill's passage, as his foreign policy favors retaining control over tariffs and sanctions rather than leaving such decisions to Congress.

How much leverage does the US have over its adversaries? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Who opposed the bill and why?

Democrats who voted for the bill broke ranks with the party leadership, which argues the legislation expands Trump's tariff powers and that the president already has the power to sanction Russia should he choose to.

"What this legislation will do ​is give Donald Trump, perhaps, unfettered authority to unleash ⁠tariffs on the American people," House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said in a speech on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, some Republicans opposed to the bill were wary of compounded tariffs further increasing consumer prices ahead of the midterm elections in November.

The bill's supporters say it is integral to keeping up the pressure on Russia.

It has been celebrated by Ukrainian activists. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with lawmakers to urge its passage and even watched an early procedural vote from the chamber.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

World.title: Sweden's center-left bloc set to win election, STV reports
World.content:
The center-left opposition won the Swedish elections by a very slim margin, the public broadcaster reported after 99% of the votes were counted. Thorny negotiations await the bloc even if the result is confirmed.

Sweden's center-left opposition bloc looks set to win the most votes in the country's parliamentary election, albeit by the slimmest of margins, public broadcaster SVT said on Wednesday with 99% of the votes counted.

As of 1647 GMT, with fewer than 1% of votes left to count, the center-left bloc was ahead by just 26,169 votes.

The bloc is led by Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats, the party that ruled Sweden for most of the 20th century.

If the results are confirmed, it would usher in a change in government from the right-wing bloc led by Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson.

The election authority was now counting late incoming ballots, such as those from voters abroad Image: Christine Olsson/TT News Agency/REUTERS

What do we know about the Swedish election results so far?

Data from Sweden's election authority shows Kristersson's bloc was on track to win 174 seats, against 175 seats for the center-left. Both Kristersson and Andersson have said they would be open to exploring coalition options.

"The likelihood of a turnaround at this stage is so low that we ​can confidently state that the opposition will secure the most seats in this election," ⁠SVT ​said.

The election authority was counting late incoming ballots from home and overseas, a process expected to continue until Thursday.

Sweden awaits final outcome of razor's-edge election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Even with Andersson's slim lead, her bloc is bracing for tough negotiations before forming any government, especially amid deep divisions between the liberal Center Party and the socialist Left Party.

After the 2022 elections, it took 37 days to form a government, which was considerably shorter than in 2018, when the process took 134 days.

Parliament cannot vote in a new prime minister before September 29.
