World.title: “Don’t be a creep”: Polish ice cream company launches campaign against sexual harassment of staff
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish ice cream chain has launched a campaign to stamp out sexual harassment of staff by customers, including empowering employees to refuse to serve such clients. The campaign is based around the fact that the Polish word for ice cream, “lody”, also has an informal vulgar meaning, referring to oral sex. The company, Good Lood, which runs 37 outlets, says that its female staff regularly suffer lewd comments from male customers incorporating this double entendre. In response, in late August it launched a campaign titled “Nie bądź oblechem”, meaning “Don’t be a creep”, with information displayed prominently at its ice cream stands and on its social media platforms. The firm said it condemned “crude remarks, inappropriate jokes and verbal harassment directed at service workers” and promised to support its staff in dealing with them. “Everyone deserves respect, without exception!” Good Lood advised employees to respond to inappropriate comments with a short, firm retort such as “Great, that’s the 20th time I’ve heard that” or “Perhaps you could repeat that more loudly, so the rest of the queue can hear?” It also called on other customers to react if they witnessed such behaviour. In a follow-up social media post last week, the company confirmed that staff had its backing if they decided not to serve a customer. “If someone is a creep and makes inappropriate comments and verbally harasses them, our team have the right to refuse them service.” That post alone has so far garnered more than 50,000 likes or other positive responses on Facebook. Good Lood says that its messages posted as part of the campaign have already received over 10 million organic views on social media. Comments on the company’s posts show overwhelming support, with many commenters sharing their own experiences. “At last someone has spoken out about this!” wrote one, who said she worked in an ice cream parlour as a teenager. “I remember how outraged I felt when I heard comments like that from men who could have been my fathers, or even my grandfathers. I wonder what would happen if someone spoke to their daughters or granddaughters like that.” Good Lood says it want to start a broader conversation on the “global issue” of harassment and disrespect towards front-line staff in retail and hospitality. “Working in service or hospitality does not mean consenting to disrespect. The safety and wellbeing of our team will always come before profit. We are not afraid to lose a customer who cannot show basic human respect,” the company said in a press release. Founded 10 years ago in Kraków, Good Lood now has 37 outlets there as well as in the Warsaw area. It also sells its products throughout Poland at Biedronka, the country’s largest supermarket chain. Poland’s interior ministry has launched a TV campaign, including spots on public broadcaster TVP’s flagship morning show, aimed at educating the public about how to respond to emergency situations such as natural disasters and security threats. The initiative comes as Poland has faced growing threats from Russia, including acts of sabotage and the entry of missiles and drones into Polish airspace. Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned this week that there may be an “escalation” of such actions in the coming weeks and months. 📺 Dzisiejsza wizyta w programie „Pytanie na Śniadanie” odbyła się w ramach naszej nowej kampanii „ Minuta dla twojego bezpieczeństwa”! The weekend programmes will introduce topics such as floods, fires, extreme weather, power outages, chemical contamination, evacuation, cybersecurity, disinformation and first aid. Specialists will then discuss the subjects in greater detail during the morning segments. The ministry says the content is based on its official security handbook, which it sent to all 17 million Polish households earlier this year, and is intended to help people prepare for emergencies before they occur. “We only find out whether we’re prepared for difficult situations when they actually arise,” said Mateusz Jarecki, who is presenting the segments. “That’s why, in collaboration with specialists, we’ve produced a series of short, easy-to-follow videos that will help you prepare for various life scenarios.” The government is sending copies of a booklet advising how to prepare for and act in emergencies to all 17 million households in Poland. The guide includes information on what to do in the event of military attacks, terrorist threats and natural disasters https://t.co/xIaRQ2ie5N — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 12, 2026 According to Presserwis, a newsletter by media industry magazine Press, the ministry will spend 5.4 million zloty (€1.3 million) on broadcasting the campaign during Pytanie na śniadanie. The agreement with the public broadcaster, signed on 4 September, includes 16 short segments and seven commentary pieces, according to Presserwis. Pytanie na śniadanie’s website so far shows two segments with material from the series. One explains what to do when an evacuation order is issued, while the other covers what should be included in an emergency kit. The campaign comes following recent criticism from the opposition over how the government communicates with citizens during emergencies. Amid Russian mass attacks on western Ukraine this week, including strikes on a train and a truck near the Polish border, residents of eastern Poland received mobile phone alerts from the Government Security Centre (RCB) warning of air strikes and urging them to seek shelter. However, Beata Mazurek, a senior figure from the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, criticised the messages for “spreading panic without providing instructions” on where people should shelter. “Where are we supposed to go? World.title: Moose on the loose at Warsaw’s main station brings trains to a standstill

A moose wandered onto the tracks at Warsaw Central Station on Sunday evening, disrupting rail services in the Polish capital for more than 80 minutes before it was safely removed. The animal first appeared on a platform before moving onto the tracks, forcing Polish Railway Lines (PLK), the company responsible for Poland’s rail infrastructure, to suspend, cancel and divert several train services. View this post on Instagram A post shared by TVP3 Warszawa (@tvp3warszawa) Videos and photographs shared online showed the moose lying on the tracks and running along the railway line at Warsaw Central, the capital’s busiest station, which is mainly underground and therefore not easy for such a large animal to access. Police do not know how the moose ended up at the station, reports broadcaster TVN24. Officers were first alerted at 7:10 pm on Sunday and cordoned off the platform where the animal was located. When emergency services arrived, the moose was tranquilised. It was then placed on a large sheet and carried out of the station by police officers and emergency workers before being loaded onto a specialist vehicle to be returned to a forested area. PLK, which named the moose Emil, later confirmed that the animal had been safely removed and that normal train services were being restored. The company added that the disruptions lasted just over 80 minutes, using a pun combining the Polish words for moose (łoś) and 80 (osiemdziesiąt) to produce the word “łosiemdziesiąt”. ❗Aktualizacja❗Zwierze zostało bezpiecznie zabrane z torów. Przywracana jest rozkładowa organizacja ruchu pociągów. Utrudnienia trwały przeszło łosiemdziesiąt minut. https://t.co/Xui2B6SxyU — PLK SA (@PKP_PLK_SA) September 13, 2026 The Eurasian moose (also known as the Eurasian elk) has long been native to Poland, but by the mid-20th century hunting and habitat loss had brought the species close to extinction in the country. Its population subsequently recovered, reaching an estimated 6,000 animals by the 1980s and around 30,000 by 2019, helped by a moratorium on moose hunting introduced in 2001. Several hundred live in the Kampinos national park on the northwestern outskirts of Warsaw. They are therefore relatively frequent visitors to the capital, according to the Interia news website, although venturing onto train lines in the centre is unusual. The growth in the moose population, combined with urban expansion and changes to its habitat, has led to other high-profile encounters in areas inhabited by humans. In 2022, a moose was spotted on the roof of a shopping centre in the northern Polish city of Elbląg. A moose was this morning spotted on the roof of a shopping centre in Poland. World.title: Drone hits Kyiv-Warsaw train close to Polish border during Russian attacks on Ukraine

A drone has struck a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw, around two kilometres from the Polish border, amid the latest round of mass Russian attacks on Ukraine. In a separate incident, a truck was also hit in Ukraine around 800 metres from a border crossing with Poland. “This is Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO,” wrote Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha. “Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners.” 🚨 BREAKING: Russian drone targeted a passenger train on the border with Poland. "Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners. Act now: throw the full weight of your sanctions at Putin’s aggressive regime," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Sybiha wrote in response. pic.twitter.com/VsgQ2UGtPb — UNITED24 Media (@United24media) September 13, 2026 “Today in the Volyn region, two kilometres from the Polish border, the enemy struck the locomotive of a passenger train,” announced Ukrainian Railways in a statement. “A monitoring group warned the train crew of the threat in advance, ensuring that no one was injured.” Ukrainian media outlets report that the train in question was a service running between Kyiv and Warsaw. They shared a video purportedly showing the strike, in which passengers are seen fleeing a train as an explosion is seen and heard in the background. Ukrainian Railways’ deputy director for communications, Oleksandr Shevchenko, was quoted by media outlet Suspilne confirming that the strike had been carried out by a Russian drone. Meanwhile, Poland’s border guard on Sunday morning confirmed to news website Interia that a drone had struck a truck in Ukraine around 800 metres from the Dorohusk-Jagodzin border crossing between the two countries. Earlier reports and images shared on social media had indicated that a petrol station at that location had been hit, causing a fire. The spokeswoman for Poland’s interior ministry, Karolina Gałecka, said that no injuries had been reported on the Polish side of the border. The border guard said that traffic at the crossing was proceeding normally. 🚨 BREAKING: Russian drones struck a gas station near the Yahodyn checkpoint on the Polish border, setting off a massive fire that engulfed parked cargo trucks. Border guards suspended processing and sheltered visitors during the air alert. pic.twitter.com/SSUiXayBYS — UNITED24 Media (@United24media) September 13, 2026 The interior minister himself, Marcin Kierwiński, condemned the two “Russian terrorist attacks” near the border and declared that “Russia is the enemy of the free world”. Sybiha, meanwhile, said that the incidents highlighted why the world must take “uncompromising, powerful steps…[to] make Moscow feel the consequences of its terror”. “Full trade embargo. Full entry bans. World.title: Poland issued EU’s third most residence permits to immigrants in 2025
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland issued first residence permits to almost half a million immigrants in 2025, which was the third-highest figure in the European Union, behind Spain and Germany but ahead of Italy and France. However, the number of permits issued by Poland fell for the fourth year running, as the country continued to tighten its migration rules. Previously, between 2017 and 2022, Poland had led the EU figures for six years running, reaching a peak of almost one million permits in 2021. The new data, released on Friday by Eurostat, the EU’s statistical agency, show that Poland issued 467,314 first residence permits to immigrants from outside the EU in 2025. As was the case last year, Spain (635,438) issued the most, followed by Germany (605,292). Poland was then followed by Italy (433,099) and France (377,462). However, whereas in those four other countries the number of permits rose in 2025 (by 13.1% in Spain, 11.1% in Germany, 25.0% in Italy and 9.2% in France), in Poland the figure fell by 4.4%. That decline has come amid a tougher new migration strategy by the current government, a coalition that ranges from left to centre right, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Ahead of elections in 2023, Tusk, then in opposition, accused the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which had ruled Poland since 2015, of allowing “uncontrolled” migration, including through widespread abuses of the visa system. Shortly after coming to power in those elections, Tusk, a former president of the European Council, declared that the “survival of Western civilisation” depends upon preventing mass migration. His government has since introduced tougher entry requirements for foreign workers and students, suspended asylum rights for migrants who irregularly cross the border from Belarus, and stepped up deportations of immigrants who have committed crimes or entered the country unlawfully. Poland has introduced tougher new rules regulating the entry of foreign students and immigrant workers. “This is another step towards regaining control over migration and increasing the safety of Poles," says the government https://t.co/gYdikpc6pL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2025 The new 2025 data show that, in relative terms (the number of permits issued in relation to countries’ populations), Poland was only ninth in the EU (12.8 permits per 1,000 people), behind Malta (56.9), Cyprus (46.7), Portugal (27.3), Lithuania (18.5), Ireland (13.4), Croatia (13.2), Luxembourg (13.1) and Spain (12.9). That marks a significant decline since 2021, when Poland issued 967,345 permits, which was the highest in the EU in absolute terms but also second-highest in relation to population. In 2025, as in previous years, Poland issued the most first residence permits to Ukrainians (241,126, 51.6% of the total), who are by far the country’s largest immigrant group. They were followed by Belarusians (128,468, 27.5%), Georgians (10,249, 2.2%), Indians (9,230, 2%) and Turks (7,533, 1.6%) – the same top five nationalities as in 2024. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 Following a decade of unprecedented mass migration, the number of foreigners with residence permits in Poland this year passed two million for the first time, making up just over 5% of the country’s population. Around 1.5 million of those are Ukrainians. In June, the number of foreigners working in Poland reached 1.14 million, making up almost 7% of the workforce. While Ukrainians constitute two thirds of the total, the fastest-growing nationalities are Colombians and Indians, who are now the third- and fourth-largest groups of foreign workers. The rise in migration has come as Poland’s economy has boomed but the country has also faced a demographic crisis, with a shrinking, ageing population and one of the lowest birth rates in the world. In 2023, the state Social Insurance Institution (ZUS) calculated that, in order to maintain its ratio of working-age population to retirees, Poland would need to attract almost two million immigrant workers over the following decade. However, it admitted that that target was “unrealistic”. World.title: Two New Squares and a Tower Planned Around Holešovice Station
World.content:
The area around Prague’s Nádraží Holešovice station is set for a major redevelopment after the international architectural competition for the site was won by Czech studio Chybík + Krištof.

The winning proposal envisions turning the current transport hub and surrounding brownfield into a new urban district, with two public squares, improved connections between public transport services and a new high-rise building designed to become a landmark.



The redevelopment covers roughly eight hectares around the station. Its aim is not only to add new buildings, but also to reorganise one of Prague’s important transport nodes and connect it more closely with the surrounding neighbourhood.

The competition jury selected the proposal by Chybík + Krištof as the winning design.

From transport hub to urban district

Nádraží Holešovice is currently one of Prague’s major transport interchanges, but much of the surrounding area has traditionally been used primarily for transport and other infrastructure.

The redevelopment is intended to change that. Alongside new construction, the project places emphasis on making transfers between different modes of public transport easier and fully accessible.

The project forms part of the wider Nové Holešovice development, which brings together the Prague Public Transit Company and private investors.

CPI Property, EP Real Estate, Penta Real Estate and AKIPIA are among the companies involved. The City of Prague and Prague 7 municipal district are also participating in the project.

World.title: ČokoFest to Bring Three Days of Chocolate to Galerie Harfa
World.content:
Chocolate lovers will have plenty to discover in Prague this October as ČokoFest 2026 returns to Galerie Harfa for three days of tastings, workshops, competitions and sweet treats.

The festival will take place from October 16 to 18, 2026, at the shopping center in Prague 9. Admission is free.



Now in its 14th year, ČokoFest brings together Czech and international producers, including established chocolatiers and smaller makers.

Visitors will be able to sample and buy a wide selection of chocolates and confectionery, including handmade and bean-to-bar products, pralines, cakes, cookies and macarons.

The festival will also feature a range of less conventional chocolate and sweet specialties. Among the offerings will be a chocolate fountain, chocolate kebabs, chocolate-covered fruit, as well as chocolate-infused wine and beer. Other products on sale will include jams, liqueurs, syrups, dried fruits, honey products, coffee and tea.

Exhibitors from several European countries will join Czech producers, giving visitors the opportunity to discover different chocolate styles and specialties while shopping at international sales stalls.

ČokoFest will also feature a program of activities for both adults and children. Visitors can take part in tastings, competitions and creative workshops, while children can enjoy a dedicated zone and entertainment from performers dressed as popular children’s characters.

Cooking demonstrations will be another part of the program, with chefs from local restaurants sharing their experience and showing visitors how to prepare various sweet treats. Some workshops will also focus on chocolate-making techniques that can be tried at home.

The festival is designed as a family-friendly event, with activities taking place throughout the three days. In addition to tasting and shopping, visitors can watch pastry chefs at work, take part in competitions and learn more about the production and preparation of chocolate and other confectionery.

Opening hours:

Friday, October 16: 2:00–6:00 p.m.

Saturday, October 17: 10:00 a.m.–6:30 p.m.

Sunday, October 18: 10:00 a.m.–5:00 p.m.

World.title: Poznej Vltavu Festival Returns to Prague on September 28
World.content:
The second edition of the Poznej Vltavu (Get to Know the Vltava) festival will take place across Prague on September 28, 2026.

For one day, the banks of the Vltava will host a programme exploring the river from a variety of perspectives.

The festival will feature workshops, exhibitions, sports activities, boat trips, and tours of places that are not normally open to the public.



Prague’s riverfront embankments and other locations along the Vltava will offer activities for children, adults, and seniors.

The festival aims to highlight the Vltava as a natural part of Prague’s urban environment and an important ecological feature, while giving visitors the opportunity to spend a day exploring the river and its surroundings.

Experts from a range of fields will discuss the Vltava in its broader context and offer insights into lesser-known aspects of the river.

This year’s programme will involve organisations including the Prague Institute of Planning and Development, Prague City Tourism, the Prague City Gallery, the Vltava River Authority, Prague Waterworks and Sewerage Company, the Prague Water Management Company, ROPID, Prague City Forests, the Nature Conservation Agency of the Czech Republic, and many others.

The festival area will extend farther along the Vltava this year, reaching Žluté lázně and the new Dvorecký Bridge, which has quickly become a popular destination for Prague residents since opening.

Most events will be free to attend, although some activities will require advance registration due to limited capacity.

More information is available on the festival’s Facebook event.

World.title: Red Arrows to Fly Over Charles Bridge This Friday
World.content:
Prague will hear the roar of Royal Air Force jets on Friday, September 18, when the Red Arrows aerobatic team stages a flypast over the city.

Ten BAE Hawk T1 aircraft from the British RAF team are scheduled to pass over the Charles Bridge at around 2:00 PM. The jets will leave smoke trails in the colours of the Czech flag during the display.



The formation is expected to approach Prague from the north before reaching the area around Václav Havel Airport. The aircraft will then form an arrow-shaped formation and fly around the western and southern parts of the capital before turning north along the Vltava.

The jets are expected to fly at an altitude of roughly 300 metres above the ground. The engines will be clearly audible across parts of the city, although the flypast itself will last only a short time.

After passing through central Prague, the formation will turn northeast and continue toward Ostrava. The city is hosting NATO Days, one of the Czech Republic’s largest military and security events, this weekend.

The timetable and route could still change because of weather or other air traffic in the Prague area. A similar Red Arrows flypast was held in Prague last September, but poor weather delayed the aircraft by more than an hour.

The flypast is being held in connection with Czech Air Force Day, which is observed on September 15.

The Red Arrows are the official aerobatic display team of the Royal Air Force and regularly perform at air shows and military events in Britain and abroad.

World.title: Groovy Market Fest Returns to Riegrovy Sady on October 3
World.content:
Prague’s Groovy Market Fest will return to Riegrovy Sady on Saturday, October 3, bringing together food, independent brands, design and live music for its third edition.

The one-day event will take place at Energy Pub from noon until 10 p.m.

Following two editions held during the summer, the organizers are extending the concept into the autumn, with visitors able to browse local products, eat street food and listen to live music and DJs throughout the day.



The market is organised around three main areas. The Food Garden will focus on gastronomy and street food from local businesses, while Palm Street will feature bakeries, artisanal products and other local goods. The Design Zone will bring together fashion, design and products from independent Czech brands.

Live performances and DJ sets will run from the afternoon into the evening, providing the musical programme alongside the market stalls.

Marek Novák, founder of Groovy Market Fest, said the first two editions helped the team establish the format and identify what visitors respond to.

“After two editions, we know exactly what works at Groovy Market Fest: high-quality local brands, good food, and an atmosphere that keeps people coming back,” Novák said. “This third edition is an opportunity for us to show that Groovy isn’t just a summer event, but a festival that holds a firm place in Prague all year round.”

Visitors can buy tickets for either of the two five-hour sessions. The first runs from 12 p.m. to 5 p.m., followed by a second session from 5:30 p.m. to 10 p.m.

A ticket for one session costs 100 CZK, while an all-day ticket covering both sessions is available for 190 CZK. Tickets are sold through GoOut.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Groovy Market Fest (@groovymarketfest)

From Barcelona street food to a Prague market

Groovy Market Fest was founded by Marek Novák and Veronika Kracíková, a couple with experience in Prague’s food scene and Barcelona’s street-food sector.

One of their main inspirations was Barcelona’s Palo Alto Market, an urban market known for combining food, design, music and independent creative businesses.

World.title: Prague Run Day to Bring Six Races to Riegrovy Sady on September 19
World.content:
On September 19, runners of all levels can take part in a new running event combining track and park races in one of Prague’s best-known green spaces.

There are six different races to choose from, so whether you’re looking for a serious challenge or just want to get out and run, there’s an option for you.



Six races to choose from

The programme includes six races, ranging from a short family run to a one-hour challenge.

The day will begin with the 800m Family Run, designed for young runners and their accompanying adults. There will also be an 800m race on the athletic track, offering participants the opportunity to compete over a short distance in a traditional track setting.

For those looking for a longer challenge, the 1 Mile race will take place on the athletic oval. The organisers describe it as a special opportunity to race over the classic distance, with participation limited to a maximum of 30 runners.

The 5km Solo Run will offer a more familiar challenge for runners of different experience levels. It is followed by the 4x3km Relay, a team race in which four runners each complete two 1.5km laps.

The final event of the day will be the Golden Hour Race, a one-hour running challenge taking place during the golden hour.

The event will be based at the Sokol Vinohrady athletic oval, which will serve as the main hub for the day.

Find all race distances, times and registration details at praguerunday.cz

World.title: Prague Is Turning a Historic Factory Chimney Into an Observation Deck
World.content:
A glass elevator will carry visitors through the preserved chimney of a former distillery before emerging above its rim to reveal views of the city.

Inside the developing Lihovar district in Smíchov, a historic factory chimney is being transformed into a viewing platform, with visitors set to travel through the structure in a panoramic glass elevator.



The chimney, which stands approximately 50 meters tall, is part of the former Zlíchov distillery. Rather than demolishing the industrial landmark, developers have incorporated it into the redevelopment of the site.

The project is being developed by Trigema, which is building the new Lihovar district on the former distillery grounds.

The elevator itself is one of the project’s most unusual features. Once it reaches the top of the chimney, the cabin will lift a special cap weighing approximately 500 kilograms, allowing it to rise above the chimney’s opening.

The glass cabin will then serve as an observation deck, offering a 360-degree view of Prague.

From industrial site to new Prague district

The Lihovar development is being built on the site of the former Zlíchov distillery in Prague 5. The redevelopment includes new buildings alongside the preservation of selected elements of the original industrial complex.

The factory chimney is among the structures being retained. Another is the historic former brewhouse, which is planned for cultural use.

The opening date for the observation deck has not been announced.

World.title: Riegrovy Sady to Host Goodbye Summer Party With Three Live Acts
World.content:
Summer may be drawing to a close, but the music season at Riegrovy Sady is not over yet.

On Thursday, 17 September, Energy Pub will host the Goodbye Summer Party, organised by Ploom in cooperation with Energy Pub.



The evening will feature a DJ set by Forgen, a performance by Jirka Drtil and a live concert by Renne Dang, following his sold-out show at Forum Karlín.

Tickets cost CZK 100 and the event is open exclusively to guests aged 18 and over.

The last long days and warm evenings of summer will get a musical send-off at Riegrovy Sady. The Goodbye Summer Party is designed for everyone who is not quite ready to say a final goodbye to summer and wants to enjoy one of the last outdoor evenings of the season.

The evening will kick off with a set by DJ Forgen, followed by a performance by musician Jirka Drtil. The main highlight of the evening will be a concert by Renne Dang, Ploom brand ambassador, whose current music blends elements of rap, pop and pop-punk.

His distinctive personal lyrics and energetic guitar-driven sound have already taken him to some of the country’s biggest stages. His recent achievements include a sold-out concert at Forum Karlín.

The Last Party of the Summer

Music will not be the only reason to head to Riegrovy Sady in September. The evening will also feature a dedicated Ploom zone, where adult guests can take a break during the programme and enjoy the atmosphere of one last summer party.

Every ticket holder will also receive a complimentary welcome drink. A food pop-up by Pavel Berky will be part of the event as well.

When: Thursday, 17 September 2026, doors open at 6:00 PM

Where: Energy Pub, Riegrovy Sady 28, Prague 2

Line-up: DJ Forgen, Jirka Drtil, Renne Dang

Tickets: CZK 100, including a welcome drink

Entry: 18+ only

Capacity: Limited

World.title: Hungary tightens syphilis screening during pregnancy as congenital cases rise
World.content:
An increasing number of babies are being born with congenital syphilis in Hungary, prompting the National Public Health and Pharmacy Centre (NNGYK) to introduce new, nationwide procedures. The number of cases has risen significantly since 2021: 91 cases were recorded in 2025, while 100 were reported in the first eight months of 2026 alone.

New screening during the second half of pregnancy

According to the NNGYK, a coordinated response is needed because congenital syphilis can largely be prevented if the infection is detected and treated in time. One of the key changes under the new methodological guidance is that, from 1 September, pregnant women must undergo a second syphilis screening between the 24th and 28th weeks of pregnancy, in addition to the test carried out during the first trimester.

The requirement also applies to pregnancies where antenatal care began before 1 September. If the pregnancy has already progressed beyond the 24–28-week period, the screening must be carried out at the next antenatal care appointment. Women who have not received antenatal care, as well as those considered to be at high risk of syphilis infection, must undergo a rapid syphilis test when they give birth.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Strict deadlines for treatment

The NNGYK aims to ensure that no positive screening result is left without appropriate follow-up. In confirmed cases of syphilis, specific penicillin treatment must be started within 72 hours of the diagnosis at the latest.

Treating sexual partners is also considered essential to prevent transmission and reinfection. Identification and notification of partners must begin immediately, and no later than 48 hours after a confirmed infection. If a test is positive, immediate steps must also be taken to ensure appropriate care for both the mother and the newborn.

Hungary more than twice the WHO target

The World Health Organisation (WHO) has set a target of no more than 50 cases of congenital syphilis per 100,000 live births. Based on data recorded in Hungary in 2025, the rate was 126 cases per 100,000 live births. The seriousness of the situation is also reflected in the reported deaths: 26 children died from the infection in Hungary in 2025, while a further 23 deaths had been recorded by August 2026.

The new nationwide procedure standardises the steps to be taken from screening and treatment through to the management of sexual partners and the follow-up care of newborns. The NNGYK stresses that congenital syphilis is largely preventable, but this requires the infection to be detected and treated in time.

World.title: Budapest-Belgrade railway passenger services within sight, says minister
World.content:
Passenger services on the Budapest-Belgrade railway line could be launched in the near future, according to Hungary’s Minister for Transport and Investment, Dávid Vitézy.

Budapest-Belgrade line soon to become fully operational

In a Facebook post on Tuesday, Vitézy said the project had reached an important stage following months of testing and preparations involving the Hungarian and Chinese construction companies, the investment joint venture, MÁV and railway authorities.

A full-load test is scheduled for 3 and 4 October, when trains will operate without passengers for several hours at speeds of up to 160 kilometres per hour, following the daytime peak-hour timetable. The final decision on the launch of scheduled passenger services will only be made after the tests have been completed and their results evaluated.

Safety checks continue

According to Vitézy, stringent safety checks have been carried out on the Budapest-Belgrade line since the summer. Minor problems and faults have emerged, but most have already been corrected, while work on some issues remains ongoing.

Tuesday’s meeting brought together representatives of MÁV, the Hungarian and Chinese construction companies, MÁV Pályaműködtető, independent experts and the railway authority. Vitézy said the parties confirmed that no safety-critical fault had been identified in the train control system, including during the most thorough testing so far.

He nevertheless stressed that passengers would only be allowed to use the new line once all safety checks had produced positive results and these had been confirmed by the relevant authorities and independent experts. “The launch of passenger services is now within sight,” Vitézy wrote, while stressing that safety requirements would not be compromised.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Warning to residents

The October tests of the Budapest-Belgrade line will simulate a high level of traffic, with trains running for several hours according to the daytime peak timetable. Vitézy also warned residents living along railway line 150 that passenger facilities along the route will still be construction sites during the tests. Only authorised testing personnel and staff will be allowed to enter these areas.

He urged the public to exercise particular caution at railway level crossings as the number of trains using the line increases in October. Residents were asked to cross the railway only at designated crossings, obeying signals and following the applicable safety rules.

In case you missed it: Volánbusz scandal – what we know about why one of Hungary’s wealthiest was detained

Launch date not yet confirmed

The October full-load test represents another important stage before passenger operations can begin, but it does not guarantee that services will start immediately afterwards. The final decision will depend on the test results and their assessment by the relevant authorities and independent experts.

Vitézy’s announcement indicates that the Budapest-Belgrade railway is moving closer to passenger operation, but the exact launch date can only be decided after the successful completion of the remaining safety checks.

World.title: 16-year-old Hungarian boy discussed mass violence with AI chatbot, FBI alerts Hungarian authorities – Video
World.content:
A 16-year-old boy from Győr made statements about violent acts while communicating with an artificial intelligence chatbot. According to Hungarian police, his conversations included threats against groups and individuals, discussions about preparations for attacks and references to weapons that could be used. The case came to the attention of Hungarian authorities after a warning from the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).

AI company alerted US investigators

In mid-September, the National Bureau of Investigation (NNI) of Hungary’s Rapid Response Police received information from the FBI about a user believed to be connected to Hungary. The US investigators had been alerted by a company operating in the field of artificial intelligence after one of its users allegedly made threats involving violent and life-threatening acts.

Documents forwarded to the Hungarian authorities indicated that the user had discussed violent acts against groups and individuals with an AI-powered chatbot and had also talked about preparations for such attacks.

‘This will soon be a mass atrocity’

Hungarian police quoted two statements from the conversation. In one, the user reportedly wrote: ‘There can be no mercy, and you have to be able to carry out what you have planned.’ Another message stated: ‘This will soon be a mass atrocity.’

According to police, the conversations also included discussions about weapons suitable for the planned attack.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Electronic evidence led investigators to the teenager

NNI investigators identified the user based on electronic traces. According to police, the account belonged to a 16-year-old boy from Győr, western Hungary.

The teenager was arrested at his home on 15 September. Police searched the property and seized his mobile phone and computer. Forensic investigators have begun extracting and examining data from the devices.

The boy was taken into custody and questioned as a suspect on suspicion of making threats to commit an act of terrorism.

Have you heard? Hungarian police officer admits beating defenceless man, breaking several bones

Police warn of criminal consequences for online threats

Following the case, Hungarian police also warned that statements made on online platforms and in applications based on artificial intelligence can have criminal-law consequences. The authorities stressed that online statements concerning violence, attacks against people’s lives or acts of terrorism cannot simply be dismissed as a ‘schoolboy prank’.

The investigation is ongoing, with forensic investigators continuing to examine the electronic devices seized from the teenager.

World.title: Ursula von der Leyen points to Hungary as proof democratic decline can be reversed
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has pointed to Hungary as an example of how democratic backsliding can be reversed, saying the country has returned to the “heart of the European Union” following its April election.

A positive example

Speaking in the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Wednesday, 16 September, during her annual State of the Union address, von der Leyen focused on threats to European democracy, including disinformation, foreign interference and the rise of what she described as “anti-democratic, anti-European forces”. She argued, however, that such developments are not irreversible, highlighting Hungary as an example of political change restoring democratic institutions and strengthening ties with the EU.

Hungary as a democratic turning point

Von der Leyen referred specifically to Hungary’s 12 April parliamentary election, in which Péter Magyar’s Tisza Party defeated Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz after 16 years of Orbán-led government. “The Hungarian people took their future into their own hands. They chose democracy. They chose Europe. They brought Hungary back to where it belongs, to the heart of the European Union,” she said.

The Commission president presented the election as evidence that what she described as years of democratic and rule-of-law deterioration can be reversed. She also argued that progress is being made in areas including the fight against corruption and state capture, fundamental rights and academic freedom.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Billions of euros potentially unlocked

Von der Leyen linked Hungary’s political change to economic consequences, saying it had opened the way for billions of euros in investment. The European Policy Centre reported in May that von der Leyen and Prime Minister Péter Magyar had reached an agreement to unlock EUR 16.4 billion in previously blocked EU funds connected to rule-of-law concerns.

According to Index, von der Leyen nevertheless stressed that substantial work remains. Her message was that strengthening democratic safeguards, the rule of law and anti-corruption measures can produce tangible results.

Europe under pressure

The Hungarian example formed part of a broader assessment of the challenges facing the EU. Von der Leyen described Europe as both stronger and more vulnerable than before. She pointed to efforts to reduce dependence on Russian energy, strengthen European defence and maintain the EU’s position as a major global trading power. At the same time, she warned of external threats, including Russia’s war against Ukraine, hybrid attacks, disinformation and growing geopolitical competition.

Domestic pressures, including rising living and housing costs and rapid technological change, were also highlighted as factors affecting European societies and democratic systems. Von der Leyen also warned that political forces opposed to the European project are gaining strength within the EU.

Stay up-to-date: FM Orbán files criminal complaint over former FM Szijjártó’s countless private jet travels

A test of democratic resilience

The Commission president praised the EU’s efforts to protect democracy and the rule of law, including mechanisms designed to identify democratic deterioration in member states. Her central argument was that democratic decline should not be considered permanent.

Hungary, in her interpretation, demonstrates how voters can change a country’s political direction through an election. The longer-term impact of Hungary’s political transition will depend on how the new government implements institutional, rule-of-law and anti-corruption reforms.

World.title: Reader’s letter: The things I learned to appreciate about Hungary after leaving
World.content:
As a Paraguayan who lived in Hungary for six years, between 2018 and 2024, many things that once seemed unusual eventually became part of my everyday life. It was only after leaving the country and returning to South America that I began to see some of those ordinary experiences differently. Distance made me realise how much I had learned to appreciate the small details of life there that I once took for granted.

Author: Fabiola Sosa Torras

Emerging at Kossuth Lajos tér

It is an ordinary day in Budapest. You get on metro line 2. As usual, the atmosphere is quiet: some people are reading books on the distinctive red seats, others are listening to music, and a few tourists are staring intently at the route map above the doors. In the background, you hear a deep Hungarian voice announcing the next station.

Once at Kossuth Lajos tér, getting out means taking escalators so long and steep that you are not quite sure whether they are taking you to heaven or hell. But when you finally reach the top and walk through the exit, there it is, as if it were nothing unusual: the most majestic Parliament building in the world. These days, I would not complain about having to be patient on those endless escalators again.

The luxury of silence in Hungary

I remember that, at first, I found it quite surprising how quiet Hungary was compared with other places I had visited before. One Saturday afternoon, I was on my way to a park with a basketball, bouncing it as I walked along the pavement. Seconds later, a man appeared on a balcony and angrily went, “Shhhh”, while gesturing at me to be quiet.

Now, on the other hand, I sometimes go to certain places hoping to relax, such as a café, only to end up finding out why a complete stranger got divorced or even why they changed their shampoo brand. Apparently, silence can feel uncomfortable simply because some of us are not used to so much tranquillity.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

When Christmas began to smell different

Dressed in your warmest coat and the biggest scarf you own, you leave home while, if luck is on your side, a little snow falls outside. It is your first Christmas season in Hungary. At some point, a curious but unfamiliar smell catches the attention of any foreigner from a faraway land like mine. Wondering what it could be, you follow the scent wherever it leads, like the rats that blindly followed the Pied Piper of Hamelin.

Eventually, the trail leads to a traditional Christmas market, where familiar Hungarian dishes are everywhere. As the exploration continues, several large black cauldrons come into view, filled with liquids in different shades of burgundy, mixed with spices and slices of orange.

They look suspiciously like magical witches’ potions because, at that moment, you have no idea that the aroma you have been following, and which will come to define Christmas over the next few years, is called mulled wine.

In my country, Christmas is in summer, and the scent that represents it is the coconut flower. I am not complaining, because it is wonderful, deeply representative of this time of year in Paraguay, and brings back beautiful childhood memories. However, since returning, I sometimes wish that when I leave my flat, instead of enduring 40-degree heat and tropical humidity, I could feel a cold breeze while hearing the call of that divine substance.

Bars with tiny entrances

There, I discovered something I had never seen in any other country. Imagine being invited to a bar by a Hungarian friend and walking down the street together until, at some point, they say, “We’re here.” Confusion sets in as there seems to be no bar in sight, to the point that you start wondering what date it is just to make sure it is not April Fools’ Day. But no, it is not.

Then they point to a tiny entrance, explaining that getting in requires crouching down. For a few seconds, you wonder whether your friend really is just a friend and not a kidnapper, but decide to trust them and go inside. Suddenly, it feels less like entering a bar and more like stepping into another dimension.

Read another reader’s letter: Living in Budapest: Why a Swedish expat chose Hungary as his home

Sitting by the Danube with a beer

When I think about the summers I spent in Hungary, the first image that comes to mind is of me sitting by the Danube, drinking a plum-flavoured Szent András beer, my favourite, while watching the colours of the sunset and listening to the river flow as if it were ASMR for my body. On the surface, it was neither an expensive nor an elaborate activity.

Although I can still visit other rivers, none of them makes me feel quite the same as the Danube. If I ever returned to Hungary, I would no longer be able to have the same beer because I am now gluten intolerant, but I could definitely relive some parts of those moments, which were among the happiest of my life.

World.title: 10 Chinese guest workers and 37 bunk beds found at former restaurant building in Szeged
World.content:
Authorities found 10 Chinese guest workers and 37 metal bunk beds at a former restaurant in Szeged during inspections in late July. Officials subsequently determined that the building, in its current condition, was not suitable for use as accommodation.

Guest workers from China found in a dilapidated restaurant building

The inspections took place between 29 and 31 July at the former Kék Csillag Restaurant on Olajbányász Square. Authorities examined both the property and the foreign nationals present there. The Csongrád-Csanád County Government Office identified several irregularities at the property. There was no fire safety policy, while the operator could not demonstrate that the guest workers had received fire safety training, writes local outlet Szegeder.

Several safety problems uncovered

The building had neither an operating fire alarm control panel nor a built-in fire extinguishing system, and no fire extinguisher with a valid inspection was available. Officials also found that the operator could not prove that the kitchen ventilation system and electrical equipment met fire safety requirements, or that LPG cylinders were being stored properly. The property’s large kitchen gas appliances also lacked the required certificates of conformity.

The government office therefore concluded that the building was not currently suitable for accommodation. The operator was warned and instructed to remedy the irregularities. Officials said they had not identified circumstances posing an immediate threat to life, physical safety or property, so a warning was issued rather than a more serious measure.

Immigration proceedings launched

The presence of the 10 Chinese nationals led to a separate procedure by the National Directorate-General for Aliens Policing (OIF). All 10 guest workers had valid Chinese passports and valid Hungarian residence permits authorising them to work in Hungary. However, officials found that they were working at a location and in occupations different from those specified in their residence permits.

The OIF therefore launched immigration proceedings to examine whether their employment was lawful. The authority has not disclosed why the workers were at the former restaurant or whether they were staying there.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

But why were there 37 bunk beds?

The discovery of 37 bunk beds raised questions about whether the former restaurant was being used as guest workers’ accommodation. During its inspection, the local authority counted 37 metal bunk beds in the former dining area. However, officials said it was clear that the beds were not in use and that only their frames remained inside the building.

The municipality nevertheless warned the operator that the property could not be used as a guest workers’ hostel in its current condition. Such accommodation would have to meet legal requirements covering sleeping, washing and toilet facilities, as well as cooking, food storage and dining. Importantly, there was no registered accommodation service at the property.

Municipal records show that the Kék Csillag Restaurant had been registered as a catering establishment since 1997, but there was no record of accommodation services. The operator subsequently announced that the restaurant business would cease and that the property would be rented out. The establishment was later removed from the official register.

In case you missed it: Temu, Shein and AliExpress lose ground in Hungary after new EU customs charge

Was it actually a guest workers’ hostel?

Despite the bunk beds and the presence of the Chinese nationals, there is currently no official confirmation that the building was operating as a workers’ hostel or that the Chinese nationals were staying there. The OIF has not disclosed the purpose of the workers’ presence at the property or whether they had any connection with the bunk beds.

Questions about a possible connection between the property and BYD or its suppliers have also remained unanswered by the Szeged municipality. When journalists visited the site on 7 September, the building’s windows were covered from the inside, making it impossible to establish whether the bunk beds or other accommodation-related equipment were still there.

World.title: Travel across Hungary for less than EUR 3 during European Mobility Week’s Car-Free Day
World.content:
Hungary is offering special public transport discounts during this year’s European Mobility Week, including free bicycle transport on intercity trains and nationwide travel for just HUF 999 on Car-Free Day.

Free bicycle transport for a week

Dávid Vitézy, Minister for Transport and Investment, announced the measures on Wednesday, saying the aim is to encourage more people to choose public transport as an alternative to travelling by car.

From 16 to 22 September 2026, passengers can transport bicycles free of charge on trains available for intercity travel. Where a bicycle reservation is normally required, passengers will still need to obtain one, but the reservation itself will also be free during the promotional period.

Unlimited travel for less than EUR 3

The main promotion will take place on 22 September, Car-Free Day. Passengers will be able to purchase a special Car-Free Day ticket for HUF 999 (around EUR 2.74), allowing unlimited travel for one day on eligible intercity public transport services across Hungary. The ticket will have the same geographical validity as the Magyarország24 day ticket and will cost HUF 999 through all sales channels.

There is an important limitation, however: the ticket does not cover local public transport, including in cities where county passes are otherwise accepted on local services. Any additional supplements required for a particular journey, such as a seat reservation, must also be purchased separately.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Encouraging alternatives to driving

Vitézy said the measures were introduced to demonstrate that public transport can be a genuine alternative to the car for many journeys. In a Facebook post, he said that it was not enough simply to talk about alternatives to driving; they also needed to be made easier and cheaper to use.

He acknowledged that public transport cannot replace cars for every journey, but said that where trains, buses or bicycles provide a suitable alternative, the government wants more people to try them.

The HUF 999 day ticket is intended to make that particularly simple on Car-Free Day, allowing passengers to explore eligible intercity routes throughout the country for a single day. The promotions form part of Hungary’s participation in European Mobility Week, which runs from 16 to 22 September.

World.title: Volánbusz scandal: what we know about why one of Hungary’s wealthiest was detained
World.content:
Hungary’s long-running Volánbusz investigation has taken a major new turn after authorities brought in billionaire businessman Dániel Jellinek and former state asset manager Norbert Szivek for questioning.

The Central Investigative Prosecutor’s Office (KNYF) said investigators carried out searches and seizures at several locations on Tuesday, 15 September, in connection with a suspected bribery case involving passenger transport services and bus procurement at Volánbusz, reaching HUF billions. Four people were questioned as suspects and three were detained. The case centres on transactions dating back to 2015–2018, when more than 600 used buses were allegedly purchased at inflated prices.

HUF 10 billion in suspected damage

According to the National Bureau of Investigation (NNI), the suspected transactions caused around HUF 10 billion (EUR 24.7 million) in financial damage to Volán companies. Investigators are also examining the purchase of a Volán company’s headquarters in Kecskemét, which they allege was overpriced and caused at least HUF 550 million (EUR 1.5 million) in financial damage.

Authorities suspect that money originating from the disputed transactions was subsequently moved through intermediary companies and purported loan agreements. The NNI has said the funds may have been used for property projects, cash withdrawals exceeding HUF 1 billion (EUR 2.74 million) and the purchase of a high-value car.

The investigation has therefore expanded beyond the original Volánbusz purchases. Investigators are attempting to reconstruct a chain of transactions and establish who arranged particular deals, who approved them and who ultimately benefited. Earlier proceedings reportedly examined three main strands: a leasing transaction involving 138 buses, a maintenance contract connected to 250 buses, and the Kecskemét property transaction.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Who are Jellinek and Szivek?

Dániel Jellinek, the head of Indotek Group, is Hungary’s seventh wealthiest businessman, with major interests in property. He has also had business dealings with several prominent figures in Hungary’s business world. One company linked to Jellinek that has appeared in reporting about the case is Barwald Real Estate Ltd.

According to Telex, investigators suspect the company received a loan of around HUF 1.25 billion (EUR 3.4 million) from a person linked to the Volánbusz investigation. Telex reported that the money was subsequently placed in escrow with interest, although this happened after police searches and questioning had begun.

Norbert Szivek is also a significant figure in the Volánbusz case. He was the former chief executive of the Hungarian National Asset Management Company (MNV), which exercised ownership rights over the Volán companies during the period under investigation. His alleged role is therefore being examined in connection with decisions made within the state asset-management structure.

Could the investigation reach further?

The investigation of the Volánbusz scandal has also prompted reports about other prominent figures who have had business or institutional links to people already mentioned in the case. HVG.hu said the investigation could potentially reach figures including businessman István Tiborcz, son-in-law of former prime minister Viktor Orbán and former development minister Miklós Seszták.

Tiborcz has had business relationships with both Jellinek and Szivek, while Seszták was the minister responsible for the ministry overseeing the relevant state asset-management structure during part of the period under investigation.

These reports do not mean that either man has been charged with a crime in the Volánbusz case. Their names have emerged in reporting about the wider network surrounding the investigation. HVG has also reported that investigators are interested in whether those being questioned will provide information about other possible participants.

What can possibly come next?

The Volánbusz bribery case has been under investigation for years now, so this operation means a huge step. Jellinek’s Indotek Group has rejected the allegations against its chief executive, saying he has committed no crime and is co-operating fully with the authorities. The company said Jellinek had voluntarily complied with an NNI summons on 10 September and had remained available to investigators.

The authorities now face the task of determining whether the complex series of bus purchases, property transactions, loans and other financial movements amounts to criminal conduct and, if so, who can be held responsible.

It is important to note that being questioned as a suspect or detained does not mean that a person has been convicted or that the allegations have been proven. The investigation remains ongoing, and the precise roles of those involved — as well as whether further people will become suspects — remain to be established.

World.title: Kosovo Slams ‘Unjust’ Conviction of Hashim Thaci; Serbian Minister Applauds
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Kosovo’s Prime Minister Albin Kurti condemned the guilty verdict handed down to four wartime leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army in The Hague on Wednesday as “an unacceptable injustice”.

In a video on Instagram, Kurti declared that the war crimes ruling “must undoubtedly be overturned and rectified on appeal”.

Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci, former parliament speakers Kadri Veseli and Jakup Krasniqi and former MP Rexhep Selimi – all senior Kosovo Liberation Army officers during the 1998-99 conflict – were convicted of war crimes. Their lawyers say they will challenge the judgment.

Kurti’s statement was echoed by other senior Kosovo politicians, including Acting President, Albulena Haxhiu, who called the verdict handed down by the Kosovo Specialist Chambers “shocking”.

The opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK – which has been led by both Hashim Thaci and Kadri Veseli – also condemned the verdict, calling it “a great injustice, because it is based on claims and materials that we consider fabricated and nurtured over the years by the state apparatus and Serbian propaganda to criminalise the just war of the Kosovo Liberation Army [against Serbian forces]”.

Kosovo’s former Prime Minister Ramush Haradinaj, who was found not guilty of war crimes by the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia in 2012, slammed the verdict as “unacceptable and unjust”.

“The KLA carried out a liberation war. The battle for justice should continue. This battle should be won,” Haradinaj said in a Facebook post.

Kosovo Albanians who gathered to hear the verdict livestreamed in Pristina and The Hague were also furious. In Pristina, they rallied in front of the government building and some threw stones, shattering some windows, as well as tearing down some barriers and pushing police officers.

Thousands of Albanians who had travelled to The Hague for the verdict erupted in anger when the convictions were announced. There was a brief clash with Dutch police, who prevented them marching towards the Specialist Chambers.

In neighbouring Albania, President Bajram Begaj expressed “deep sadness” about the verdict. “For Albanians, no one and nothing tarnishes the KLA!” Begaj declared in a Facebook post.

Albania’s Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has repeatedly criticised the trial as unjust, posted a graphic on Facebook showing barbed wire over a European map and the one-word message “Marre” (“Shame”).

Head of Milosevic’s old party says verdict confirms KLA were ‘terrorists’

Thaci was sentenced to 25 years in prison for the war crimes of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder. His co-defendants Krasniqi, Veseli and Selimi were sentenced to 25, 18 and 13 years in prison respectively.

Serbia’s Interior Minister Ivica Dacic welcomed the guilty verdict, saying it represents a “clear, though long-overdue, confirmation of what Serbia and the Serbian people have been saying loudly for more than a quarter of a century – that the so-called KLA was a criminal and terrorist organisation”.

Dacic is the leader of the Socialist Party of Serbia, the party once headed by Slobodan Milosevic, who led a bloody campaign of ethnic cleansing and repression against Kosovo Albanians in 1998-99.

Dacic added that he thought it was a “direct insult to the victims” that the trial chamber had dismissed other charges against the KLA leaders that accused them of committing crimes against humanity.

During the delivery of the verdict, presiding judge Charles Smith III stressed that the case was “not about the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army”, saying that individuals were on trial, not the guerrilla force itself.

Some of Kosovo’s allies echoed this statement. The UK’s Minister for Europe, Lord Wood, said that “the court’s findings concern individuals and should not be used to inflame tensions between communities or across the region”.

Marta Kos, the European Commissioner for Enlargement, wrote on X that the verdict “is about individual accountability and justice for victims and their families from all communities in Kosovo”.

Responding to the verdict, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic told a press conference that it should not be received with “any kind of euphoria”, condemning the fact that the trial chamber had dismissed charges relating to crimes against humanity.

He compared the differing Western reactions to the verdict convicting the KLA leaders and the funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic in Belgrade last week. EU officials have repeatedly condemned the glorification of Mladic at his funeral, which was held with military honours.

Vucic cited statements by Kosovo officials claiming the defendants were innocent liberators, saying: “My question is – imagine if we had said that, about any accused or convicted person? How many resolutions and declarations would have been adopted against our country in various regional, European and international parliaments?”

During the Kosovo war, Vucic was serving as Serbia’s information minister in the government appointed by nationalist strongman Milosevic.

Meanwhile in neighbouring Croatia, which has a strained relationship with its wartime foe Serbia, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared that the verdict “does not alter the historical context of the war in Kosovo, nor the fact that Kosovo and its population were victims of repression and grave crimes committed by the Milosevic regime”.

World.title: Turkey Stages Wide-Ranging LGBT Crackdown for ‘Family Safety’
World.content:
Chanting “Long live the struggle for freedom!”, supporters of recently detained LGBTQ+ campaigners gathered outside Istanbul’s Caglayan courthouse on Tuesday, demanding their release.

Some reportedly unfurled a banner with the slogan: “Being LGBTQ is not a crime.”

The response was harsh: police moved in to detain more than 100 protesters, including activists and journalists.

The protests comes after Turkish authorities launched one of the country’s toughest ever clampdowns on LGBTQ+ groups.

Police have raided organisations, homes and entertainment venues. Activists have been detained and websites and social media accounts blocked.

World.title: North Macedonia Opposition Urges Deeper Probe into Independence Day Spending
World.content:
Spanish tenor José Carreras performs at an independence event in Skopje in September 2026. Photo: EPA/GEORGI LICOVSKI.

North Macedonia’s main opposition Social Democratic Union, SDSM, said on Wednesday that the State Anti-Corruption Commission’s decision to examine a possible conflict of interest over independence celebrations involving the composer and producer Nikolche Micevski was insufficient.

It instead called on the Public Prosecutor’s Office to investigate the whole financing and organisation of more than month-long celebrations marking the anniversary of September 8’s Independence Day.

“The opening of a case by the Anti-Corruption Commission for a possible conflict of interest involving one person is not an investigation into the 5.5 million euros,” the SDSM said, referencing the disclosed total cost of events.

Micevski was among three outside experts involved in evaluating the programme submitted by Stardust, the company selected to organise the celebrations. He later appeared in the programme himself as a performer and was involved in the musical arrangements for a concert featuring Spanish tenor Jose Carreras.

The state anti-corruption body has stressed that its case is limited to the possible conflict of interest and does not amount to an investigation into the entire 5.5 million euros expenditure. It said it was, nevertheless, monitoring other aspects of the organisation of the celebrations.

The SDSM said prosecutors should secure the full documentation concerning the spending and establish who authorised the use of the money, how payments were made and whether all procedures were followed.

It specifically questioned the use of some 4.9 million euros from the State Lottery’s undistributed profits to finance the celebrations. It asked whether the lottery’s shareholders’ assembly had approved the allocation and which institution had authorised the expenditure.

The SDSM also called for scrutiny of the contract with Stardust, the payments made to the company, the reported involvement of Avalon production, which is owned by Stardust, and the arrangements for the appearance of French DJ and producer David Guetta at the main September 8 concert in the capital, Skopje.

The government has said the celebrations, comprising 16 events, cost around 5.5 million euros, 4.9 million euros of which came from the State Lottery, which it completely owns. The rest was provided by companies described by the government as socially responsible.

It insists no money was taken directly from the state budget to finance the celebrations.

The government initially provided limited information about the overall cost of the celebrations – until BIRN reported that the state-owned lottery had played a key role in managing events.

The SDSM said questions raised by the Anti-Corruption Commission over Micevski’s role should not divert attention from the broader issue of how millions of euros were allocated and spent.

The anti-corruption body, meanwhile, has said other competent institutions should take action if they establish grounds for criminal or other legal proceedings.

Faced with prolonged public scrutiny, on Sunday Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski again defended the celebrations, dismissing the opposition’s criticism as “political theatre” and saying the events were on a world-class level that promoted North Macedonia internationally.

World.title: Hague Court Convicts Kosovo Liberation Army Leaders of War Crimes
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Rexhep Selimi, Hashim Thaci, Jakup Krasniqi, and Kadri Veseli in court on September 16, 2026. Photo: Screenshot/Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

Kosovo’s former head of state Hashim Thaci was sentenced to 25 years in prison by the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague on Wednesday for the war crimes of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder, committed from April 1998 to June 1999 during the Kosovo war.

“In the names of the people of Kosovo, the panel finds you, Hashim Thaci, guilty of arbitrary arrest and detention as a war crime against at least 385 persons; cruel treatment against at least 49; torture as a war crimes against at least 303 persons; murder as a war crimes committed against 96 persons,” presiding judge Charles Smith III announced.

Thaci’s co-defendants Jakup Krasniqi, Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi were sentenced to 25, 18 and 13 years in prison respectively. All four men were found guilty of bearing responsibility for the crimes while they were senior officials of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA during the war with Serbian forces.

The four men were found not guilty of the crimes against humanity of persecution, imprisonment, other inhumane acts, torture, murder and enforced disappearances because the crimes were committed after the end of the Kosovo war.

Thaci, along with former parliament speakers Veseli and Krasniqi, and former MP Selimi, had all pleaded not guilty to all charges.

Thousands of supporters of the defendants, who had travelled to The Hague for the verdict and listened to the livestream in a public park, erupted in anger when the convictions were announced. There was a brief clash with Dutch police, who prevented them marching towards the court.

The Specialist Chambers found that Thaci, Veseli, Krasniqi and Selimi were part of a joint criminal enterprise that aimed to exert control by targeting perceived opponents of the KLA.

These opponents included people associated with other political or military groups that had not pledged their loyalty to KLA – in particular the Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK party – as well as individuals alleged to be associated with the Serbian authorities and members of non-Albanian ethnic groups like Roma people and Serbs.

Hundreds were imprisoned and some killed, according to the verdict. “Some detainees died because of severe beatings from their KLA captors,” judge Smith said.

During the trial, the defence insisted that the KLA did not have a proper army command structure, so the defendants did not have genuine control over lower-ranking fighters. However, judge Smith said the court found that the KLA’s political directorate, which Thaci led, had huge authority over the guerrilla force.

The presiding judge said that the accused worked together with others to set up detention facilities and establish a military police force, intelligence service and special units, and tasked them with carrying out their “criminal plan” to establish their authority in Kosovo. They also “secured impunity for the perpetrators of these crimes as a matter of policy”, the judge added.

The time that the defendants have spent in detention since November 2020 will be counted against their sentences. They have the right to appeal.

This is the highest-level case to be heard at the so-called Kosovo Special Court and has been marred by delays and controversy, as well as a series of protests staged by supporters of the defendants in Pristina, Tirana, Skopje, Strasbourg and The Hague.

Many ethnic Albanians consider the court biased against the KLA’s war against repression by the Serbian authorities.

Delivering the verdict, judge Smith insisted that the case was “not about the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army”.

“This case is not concerned with crimes of Serbian army and paramilitaries that undoubtedly committed against the Albanians in Kosovo. This case is not concerned with any claims of self-defence. Instead this case is exclusively concerned if the crimes alleged in the indictment were committed,” he said.

The lengthy trial was marred by accusations of witness-tampering. As a result, Thaci faces judgment in another case for obstruction of justice. Judge Smith lamented that the trial had taken place in “climate of witness intimidation”, saying that some witnesses lied or changed their previous accounts in court, and that some may have been afraid due to concerns for their safety or out of loyalty.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies. The court is part of Kosovo’s justice system, but based in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s ability to try former KLA fighters, who are seen by many in the country as heroic liberators from Serbian oppression.
