That immediately runs into one of the Philippine manufacturing sector’s oldest weaknesses, with electricity still expensive and reliable supply essential for factories and data centers that cannot afford interruptions.

No less than Energy Secretary Sharon Garin has warned against simply plugging the full load of a built-out Pax Silica into the Luzon grid, calling that prospect “too dangerous for our usual consumers.” Once the project grows large enough, she said, it would likely need a large stand-alone power system rather than risk destabilizing supply for households and other businesses.

And the challenge isn’t merely finding enough megawatts. The Philippines also has to make electricity cheap enough to remain competitive with other countries chasing the same investments. (READ:[READOUT] The race to deliver cheaper power)

“On the single most important constraint for manufacturing in the Philippines, which is the price of electricity, the dealbook is silent,” Punongbayan said. “Beyond tax incentives, what does the government actually have on the table to bring advanced manufacturing here?”

In the end, all of these calculations may have to be reconsidered if Filipinos themselves reject the project.

That opposition was difficult to miss during the very forum where Marcos and foreign officials were selling the corridor’s future. Outside the Grand Hyatt hotel, protesters led by Bayan rallied against Pax Silica, raising concerns over its impact on communities, the environment, and Philippine resources. Demonstrators clashed with police as they tried to reach the hotel lobby.

Human rights group Karapatan said 27 people were injured and five paralegals were arrested.

Inside, investors were being asked to help build the Philippines’ technological future. Outside, protesters were demanding that one of its most ambitious pieces be scrapped. – Rappler.com

*$1 = P62.829 based on the September 14, 2026 rate of the Bankers Association of the Philippines.

World.title: [Pastilan] The curious case of Sara Duterte’s memory hole
World.content:
Sara Duterte tries to sweep under the carpet the corruption and anomalies that took place during her father's presidency, while blaming Ferdinand Marcos Jr. as though he and he alone were responsible for all the country's institutional rot

Somebody should tell Sara Duterte that people are swimming in floodwaters because her father Rodrigo and other presidents, Ferdinand Marcos Jr. included, failed to do enough to address this country’s chronic infrastructure failures and the corruption that has accompanied them for decades.

Her deliberate omissions as she addressed her supporters outside the court after her arraignment was reset were an insult to the intelligence of Filipinos, as she sought to pretend that this catastrophe began recently, or that it conveniently arrived with the administration she once supported and loved, but now wishes to blame.

The responsibility is collective, and her father had six years in Malacañang in which to confront these problems. He did not solve them. He contributed substantially to them. Decades of incompetent infrastructure planning, grotesque failures of execution, and allegations of corruption have left the country exactly where it is today.

And where was Sara while construction firms associated with then-presidential caregiver and now Senator Bong Go were reportedly collecting government contracts left, right, and center? Some of those contracts involved flood control and other public works. Where was the outrage then?

Where was Sara when the construction businesses of Sarah and Curlee Discaya, by their own admission, saw their government contracts balloon in 2016, when they expanded their attention from local governments to the Department of Public Works and Highways? That was the year her father began his presidency and placed extraordinary trust in figures such as Chinese ring leader Michael Yang a.k.a. Yang Hongming whom Duterte turned into an economic adviser.

The Duterte years also saw the extraordinary expansion of the Yang syndicate’s Philippine offshore gaming operations and a proliferation of criminal allegations and scandals surrounding parts of that ecosystem, including allegations involving smuggling, illegal drugs, etc.. These are not minor footnotes to history. They are part of the political inheritance that Sara Duterte now seems remarkably eager to edit.

Then came Yang and Pharmally. Billions of pesos in government contracts for COVID-19 pandemic supplies became the subject of investigations and allegations of anomalous procurement, excessive pricing, and substandard and questionable supplies. Filipinos were frightened, dying, unemployed, and confined to their homes while public money was being spent over deals that raised serious questions about who benefited from the national emergency. Sara was not exactly famous for making herself hoarse in protest.

And what did Sara say when her father himself publicly suggested that eliminating corruption was effectively impossible within the existing constitutional framework and floated the idea that the country might need “another Marcos” (dictator) to end it?

Silence. Sara Duterte did not call her father inutile and bangag (slow-minded) – by his own admission, he was using Fentanyl. Instead, she has been trying to sweep all the corruption and anomalies that took place from 2016 to mid-2022 under the carpet.

Now the ambitious Sara wants Filipinos to believe that Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is all to blame – he and he alone – for the country’s institutional rot. This is political amnesia if not intellectual dishonesty. Marcos did not invent decades of failed flood control, inadequate drainage, dysfunctional planning, or corruption. This may have been taking place since his father’s presidency or even much earlier. Nor did he inherit a blank sheet of paper in 2022. But neither does that absolve him of responsibility for what happened under his administration.

The adult position is to hold every administration accountable for its own failures, not to turn politics into a children’s game in which one family is permanently innocent and another is permanently guilty.

Sara’s propaganda is therefore not merely partisan. It is intellectually lazy. It asks Filipinos to forget everything that happened before 2022 and to treat the Duterte administration as though it had not been six years of terribly bad governance.

And now she wants Filipinos to believe that she is the greatest agent of change.

Really?

This is the same politician who could not even say Pax Silica right and then became the subject of ridicule for calling it something resembling “Fox sili.” If the phrase was unfamiliar, that is hardly a crime. But when someone presents herself as uniquely qualified to understand the future while displaying conspicuous unfamiliarity with a major geopolitical and economic initiative, Filipinos are entitled to ask whether the confidence is supported by competence.

“Fox sili” ka diha.

More seriously, why should taxpayers be expected to place unquestioning faith in Sara whose own offices have faced serious questions about the use of confidential funds?

The Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd), during Sara Duterte’s tenure as education secretary, are being scrutinized over their confidential fund expenditures.

The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) was asked to verify thousands of names appearing in the documents associated with those expenditures.

Information from PSA Assistant National Statistician Marizza Grande, presented before the Senate impeachment court, showed that of the 2,669 names submitted for verification, 1,685 had no corresponding birth, marriage, or death records. These are based on the PSA database.

The verification reportedly found 37 names corresponding to individuals with death records and 25 corresponding to minors, including infants. One listed individual was reportedly only two months old and had died in 1965.

Two months old. 1965. Let that sink in.

The OVP accounted for 1,992 of the names, of which 1,287 reportedly had no corresponding civil registry records.

The DepEd list contained 677 names, including 398 without matching records.

Those figures constitute precisely the kind of matter that should make any responsible citizen demand answers before handing even more public money to the people responsible.

So before Sara Duterte asks Filipinos to believe that she alone possesses the courage, competence, and moral authority to rescue the country, perhaps she should answer a simpler question.

Where was that courage when her own political house was being built?

Conflict of interest

And now we hear that a company linked to Sara secured over P15 million in food and catering contracts from the Davao City government and PhilHealth between 2022 and 2025, with its contracts peaking in the very year she became vice president.

Isn’t that an awkward coincidence for anyone preaching about corruption while demanding that Filipinos forget the record of her own political camp?

More awkward still are questions over her disclosed financial interest in the company and discrepancies between her Statements of Assets Liabilities and Net worth (SALN) and corporate records, because the fight against corruption is rather less convincing when the questions start knocking on your own door.

The country does not need another politician who discovers corruption only when it belongs to an opponent. It does not need another dynasty asking the public to forget the dynasty’s own record. It certainly does not need another presidential campaign disguised as righteous anger.

What the country needs is accountability that does not change according to surname.

That standard has to apply to Marcos, and it has to apply to the Dutertes.

In fact, it has to apply to everyone who has occupied Malacañang, everyone who has controlled a government agency, and everyone who has benefited from the machinery of the state.

The floodwaters do not care which political family is making the speech. Neither should the Filipino voter.

Saba diha, Sara! Pastilan. – Rappler.com

World.title: Divine Adili’s parents accept teammates’ account of son’s death: ‘We have known the truth’
World.content:
Seeking answers, Elias and Ifeoma Adili visit the Philippines for the first time and hear firsthand from Divine's teammates what happened in the June 8 incident that claimed the lives of their son and Rene Baterbonia

MANILA, Philippines – The parents of late Ateneo big man Divine Adili can return home to Nigeria having known the “truth” about their son’s death.

Visiting the country for the first time in search of answers, Elias and Ifeoma Adili heard firsthand from Divine’s teammates what happened during the June 8 incident that claimed the lives of their son and Rene Baterbonia during a team-building activity in Dipaculao, Aurora.

“We talked to the teammates, because they are the ones that will tell us what happened, because they were present at the place of the scene. So they explained everything,” Elias said. “That was our purpose of coming — to see the team, to talk with them, to tell us the truth.”

“It’s only the truth that will set you free. Okay? So we have known the truth and I think I can now go back to my kinsmen and tell them that this is what happened.”

Play Video

Elias and Ifeoma were in attendance as the Blue Eagles opened their UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball campaign at the Mall of Asia Arena on Wednesday, September 16, exactly 100 days since the two student-athletes’ deaths.

And Ateneo did not disappoint, breezing past the UE Red Warriors in a 101-74 rout starring Kieffer Alas, Jared Bahay, and Grayson Rogers.

While they are grateful to finally see their son’s team play in person, the moment is inevitably bittersweet for the Adilis.

Divine, after all, had once promised to bring Elias and Ifeoma to the Philippines so they could watch him in action for the Blue Eagles — a commitment that, in the end, was never fulfilled.

“I’m delighted to be here, but I wish I am watching my son. But I really appreciate what I see because I know that my son is there. Divine and Rene, they are there. They might be invisible, but I know my son is there,” said Ifeoma.

“I wish to come to the Philippines to watch my son play because that’s what I’ve been desiring. And I know my son desired that, to bring us to the Philippines to come and watch him live, though we have been watching his games [online]. We have been watching every of his games since he came to the Philippines and he desired to bring us here.”

Moving on has also been particularly difficult for the Adilis, especially now that they find themselves surrounded by things and people that were once close to their son.

“To be honest with you, it has not been easy. I tried to move on. But honestly, it has not been easy for me. Even as I entered the Philippines, the moment I stepped in at the airport, I felt so emotional,” said Ifeoma. “I don’t want to cry. But unfortunately today, the moment I stepped into the playground, I saw myself crying. But it’s fine.”

Ifeoma also expressed her disappointment that former Ateneo head coach Tab Baldwin only reached out to their family much later.

“He spoke to us very late, about four days after the incident, which is not proper,” said Ifeoma. “I am not okay with that. To be honest with you, since then, we’ve not heard from him. And it’s okay, it’s okay.”

As painful as Divine’s death is, though, the Adilis know they have to live with it and find the strength to move forward without their son.

“There’s nothing we can do. We can’t bring him back. We have cried, we have shed tears, we have complained. But there’s nothing we can do. Thank God we saw his remains — seeing his remains and laying him to rest,” said Elias.

Elias and Ifeoma will also be around when the Blue Eagles battle perennial finalist UP Fighting Maroons on Saturday, September 19, at the Araneta Coliseum. – Rappler.com

World.title: Rodrigo Duterte attends ICC hearing | The wRap
World.content:
Here are today’s headlines – the latest news in the Philippines and around the world:

Former president Rodrigo Duterte personally appears during the third status conference hearing of his case at the International Criminal Court.

Three of four retired Supreme Court justices consulted by the impeachment court say, the threshold to convict Sara Duterte is not fixed at 16 votes.

Former house speaker Martin Romualdez enters a not-guilty plea in his P7.44 billion plunder case related to the flood control mess during his arraignment on Wednesday, September 16. This means his plunder case now moves to trial.

The Bangsamoro people decide no single party will get absolute control over their first-ever elected parliament, following the historic elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.

In a landmark ruling, the Supreme Court unanimously grants the petitions that seek to compel Congress to pass a law against political dynasties. – Rappler.com

World.title: ICC orders Rodrigo Duterte’s continued detention
World.content:
DUTERTE. Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte appears before the International Criminal Court, as the court hears arguments regarding Duterte's health and ability to stand trial, while he faces murder charges related to his war on drugs, in The Hague, Netherlands, on September 16 2026.

'The Chamber therefore finds no notable change in circumstances that warrant the release of the Accused, with or without conditions,' says the order issued by the ICC Trial Chamber III

MANILA, Philippines – The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III ordered the continued detention of former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte at The Hague, Netherlands.

“The Chamber therefore finds no notable change in circumstances that warrant the release of the Accused, with or without conditions. For these reasons, the chamber hereby decides that the accused shall continue to be detained,” said the chamber’s decision on Wednesday, September 16.

In May, the chamber said Duterte is still not qualified to avail himself of temporary liberty, ruling that the former president shall continue to be detained.

At the ICC, chambers conduct a yearly review to check if detention is still warranted for an accused. Specifically, the judges will check for changed circumstances that would warrant temporary liberty for detained suspects.

After the May resolution, the chamber reviewed Duterte’s continued detention again.

According to the trial chamber, it found that there’s a likelihood that Duterte would “abscond,” “obstruct,” or “endanger” the court proceedings.

“In respect of the latter considerations, owing to the Prosecution’s submission of the Witness and Evidence Lists (thereby disclosing the identities of the witnesses and the contents of their expected testimony), this increases the Accused’s ability to interfere with witnesses, either directly or through his family or supporters in the Philippines,” the court explained.

The court is also assessing Duterte’s fitness for trial. But even though the results of this assessment are still pending, the “panel’s reports do not contain any information that warrants a modification of the accused’s detention,” the court said.

Under the Rome Statute, which created the ICC, suspects cannot be released if they present risk factors, which include the danger of fleeing, obstructing justice by intimidating witnesses, or recommitting the same alleged crimes.

“Accordingly, the Chamber finds that the risks under Article 58(1)(b)(i) and (ii) have increased and, in respect of the risks outlined in Article 58(1)(b)(iii), sees no change in circumstances,” the court explained.

The chamber held the third status conference on Duterte’s case on Wednesday, where the parties discussed the possible evidence for the upcoming November 30 trial. Duterte appeared during the hearing, marking his first personal appearance before the court since his arrest in March 2025. – Rappler.com

World.title: Rappler Recap: Martin Romualdez enters not-guilty plea in plunder case
World.content:
This means that Romualdez's plunder case will now move to trial

MANILA, Philippines – Former speaker Martin Romualdez pleaded not guilty in his P7.44-billion plunder case during his arraignment on Wednesday, September 16.

This means that the case will now move to trial.

Romualdez was allowed to join the arraignment online, but the Sandiganbayan 3rd Division deployed an official to personally read Romualdez the allegations against him.

Select members of the media were also allowed to personally witness the arraignment.

Jairo Bolledo reports from the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakh Foreign Ministry Informs Travelers as Visa Rules Change in Georgia, Thailand and Indonesia
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry has urged citizens traveling abroad to check visa, migration, transit and customs requirements before departure.

Kazakh citizens can continue to enter Georgia visa-free for up to 365 days. However, visa-free status does not permit employment. Since Sept. 1, working without the required legal authorization may constitute grounds for expulsion, with a possible re-entry ban of two to five years, Kazakh Foreign Ministry spokesperson Zhanbolat Ussenov said at a Sept. 16 briefing.

Thailand has reduced the visa-free stay applicable to Kazakh citizens from 60 to 30 days. As of Sept. 15, citizens can stay visa-free for up to 30 days per entry, with a maximum of 90 days within 180 days. Those planning longer stays should obtain an appropriate visa in advance.

Since July, Kazakh citizens can also enter Indonesia visa-free for up to 30 days. The regime is free and allows a single entry. Travelers must also complete Indonesia’s electronic arrival declaration.

The Foreign Ministry recommends checking passport validity and entry requirements, obtaining medical insurance, using official ticket services, complying with airline baggage and transit rules, and not carrying other people’s parcels or luggage.

Citizens traveling abroad for work, study or medical treatment should verify all required documents, contracts, invitations and permits in advance.

While Kazakhstan’s diplomatic and consular missions assist within their competence, each citizen is responsible for complying with the laws of the country they are visiting.

World.title: South Korea, Central Asia Target Deeper Industrial Ties at First Summit in Seoul
World.content:
ASTANA – South Korea and five Central Asian nations moved on Sept. 16 to deepen industrial and supply chain ties, seeking to combine Korean technology and manufacturing with the region’s critical minerals and push for more local processing and production.

Seoul hosted the first Korea-Central Asia summit at the leaders’ level on Sept. 16, where President Lee Jae Myung called for building “mutually beneficial” regional value chains, while Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed a new industrial and technological partnership focused on localization, technology transfer and exports to third markets.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said cooperation should move beyond individual projects and infrastructure construction toward jointly developing industrial capabilities and value chains. He described Central Asia’s resources and growing markets and South Korea’s manufacturing and technological capabilities as complementary, particularly as Seoul seeks to diversify its markets and supply chains.

For Central Asia, that objective is parallel to using foreign investment and technology to move further up the production chain rather than remaining primarily suppliers of raw materials.

Political upgrade

Tokayev commended more than two decades of the dialogue, saying the Seoul summit elevated the format to the “highest political level.”

“This is truly a culminating moment in our multifaceted cooperation, a testament to genuinely strategic relations and mutual trust. The current summit can rightly be described as a historic event,” said Tokayev.

The Korea-Central Asia Cooperation Forum was launched in 2007 and gained a permanent secretariat in 2017. The Sept. 16 meeting brought that dialogue to the presidential level for the first time.

The six countries adopted the Seoul Declaration setting out a longer-term framework for cooperation and agreed to hold leaders’ meetings regularly. Kazakhstan is expected to host the next summit in 2028.

Sabina Insebayeva, an assistant professor at the Department of Political Science and International Relations at Nazarbayev University, said the key outcome is “strategic rather than institutional.”

“You are right, much attention has been paid to the upgrade in format. But I think that misses the bigger point. The real outcome is strategic rather than institutional. What has really changed is how Seoul sees Central Asia,” Insebayeva told The Astana Times.

“Look at South Korea’s strategic environment. Its security rests on the United States. But with Donald Trump back in power, the alliance is changing. Seoul has to think harder about how much it can rely on the existing arrangement,” she added.

This “strategic environment” also involves balancing deep economic ties with China and growing cooperation between North Korea and Russia.

“Now, let’s look at where Seoul is putting its attention. The Korea-Central Asia summit is the only multilateral leaders’ level summit South Korea is hosting in 2026. That is significant for a country who traditionally focused its diplomacy on Northeast Asia. This fact tells us that Central Asia now has a different strategic value for Seoul,” she explained.

At the same time, Central Asian states are pursuing more diversified foreign policies and are increasingly reluctant to be viewed solely through the interests of larger powers, she said.

“And South Korea is responding to that. I think this is really important. Central Asia wants more choices, and South Korea wants more choices too. To me, that is the main outcome of the summit: Seoul is building its own relationship with an increasingly autonomous Central Asia,” said Insebayeva.

From critical minerals to deeper processing

Tokayev proposed a Central Asia-Korea industrial and technological partnership. It will be focused on localizing production, transferring technology, strengthening regional supply chains and exporting finished goods to third-country markets.

The summit gave that agenda an institutional framework. South Korea and the five Central Asian states signed a memorandum on industrial and supply chain cooperation, which covers manufacturing, infrastructure, critical minerals, energy and digital transformation and established a consultative mechanism among their industry ministers.

Tokayev called for deeper cooperation with South Korea on critical minerals, noting that all 10 minerals classified by Seoul as strategic are found in Kazakhstan.

He said the two countries should aim to build a full value chain, from research and extraction to advanced processing and the production of semiconductors, batteries, electric-vehicle components and robotics equipment. He also proposed creating a joint Kazakh-Korean company to support that effort and welcomed plans to establish a rare and rare-earth metals research center in Almaty.

“For now, this remains a proposal, alongside an agreement to establish the center, but together they provide a more concrete foundation for cooperation on critical raw materials,” said Aidar Kurmashev, head of the Asian Studies Department at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies.

South Korea, whose advanced manufacturing industries depend heavily on imported energy and minerals, has put supply-chain diversification near the center of its engagement with Central Asia. Lee also called for cooperation across the critical minerals value chain, from exploration and refining to materials processing and finished products.

“The next step will be to determine which materials can be processed competitively in Kazakhstan and who would buy the finished products. A Korean partner could provide technology and access to industrial customers, while the Kazakh side would need to assess the resource base and the cost of energy and water. In such projects, a long-term supply contract could be decisive: without predictable demand, even modern equipment may not make the operation commercially viable,” he explained.

Tokayev pointed to the Kia Qazaqstan plant, launched last year with an annual capacity of 70,000 vehicles, as a model for deeper industrial cooperation with South Korea. He said a similar approach could be extended to other industries by combining South Korean technology with Kazakhstan’s manufacturing capacity.

The broader economic relationship already has significant weight. In 2025, trade between Central Asia and Korea surpassed $10 billion, with Kazakhstan accounting for nearly half of that figure, Tokayev said. He added that South Korea is among Kazakhstan’s top 10 trading partners and ninth-largest investors, with more than $12 billion in gross investment. More than 1,000 companies with Korean capital work in Kazakhstan.

Kazakhstan and South Korea also signed commercial agreements worth about $19 billion during Tokayev’s state visit to Seoul, a day before the regional summit.

Connectivity

The ambition also requires reliable routes to move what it produces to international markets. That places transport at the center of the same industrial strategy.

Tokayev said Kazakhstan aims to increase total transit volumes through its territory to 100 million tons and expand the capacity of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or Middle Corridor, to 20 million tons.

He proposed linking the corridor more closely with other regional transport initiatives to create an integrated logistics chain connecting South Korea with Central Asia and Europe, including through greater cooperation between the Port of Busan and Kazakhstan’s Caspian ports.

Local processing becomes more commercially attractive if producers can reliably source inputs across the region and reach larger markets beyond individual Central Asian economies.

Lee also called for stronger railway, logistics and energy links alongside improvements in customs procedures, certification and intellectual property protections.

Energy security

The same push toward higher-value production extends to energy. Tokayev said Kazakhstan is ready to expand energy cooperation with South Korea, including by resuming energy supplies and increasing joint exploration and development of new deposits. But he also emphasized deeper processing, inviting South Korean companies to participate in Kazakhstan’s expanding petrochemical industry, including polypropylene and polyethylene production.

The two countries are pursuing large industrial projects. QazaqGaz, Hyundai Engineering and SICIM Kazakhstan signed an agreement during the visit to build a gas processing plant in western Kazakhstan. The facility is expected to process five billion cubic meters of raw gas annually, and

AI and technology cooperation

Kazakhstan and South Korea are expanding cooperation in artificial intelligence, research and higher education.

Alatau City is also emerging as a broader test of that partnership. During Tokayev’s visit, Kazakh and South Korean partners formalized plans for South Korea’s Korea Overseas Infrastructure and Urban Development Corporation (KIND) to help develop a master plan for the Alatau Smart City project in the Almaty Region. Three agreements were exchanged covering the master plan, investment cooperation and broader participation by KIND in the city’s development.

This is not the first project for the company in Kazakhstan. Earlier, KIND took part in the implementation of the Big Almaty Ring Road project.

The industrial strategy also requires skilled workers. Tokayev pointed to joint initiatives involving Woosong University branch in Turkistan, SeoulTech in Kyzylorda and the planned KAIST branch in Alatau City. He also proposed a regional AI Talent program with South Korea to train specialists across Central Asia and deepen links among universities, research institutions and technology companies.

Lee similarly put technology and skills within the broader economic strategy. The summit adopted a Korea-Central Asia initiative on AI, science and technology.

The emphasis on human capital is an important part of building a more sophisticated production chains: factories, processing facilities and technology projects require trained engineers, researchers and technical workers alongside capital and raw materials.

World.title: Vice President Karin Outlines Three Priorities for Kazakhstan’s Domestic Policy
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s domestic policy should focus on constitutional values, a new public ethic and an orientation toward the future, Vice President Erlan Karin said in a Telegram post on Sept. 16, outlining three key priorities for the country’s domestic policy.

Constitutional values

The first priority is constitutional values, which form the foundation of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s strategic reform agenda. These include the rule of law and order, national unity, interethnic and interfaith harmony, the values of culture and education, science and innovation, hard work and progress, environmental responsibility, and responsible and constructive patriotism.

Karin said relevant government bodies should focus on consistently implementing the Presidential Decree on Approving the Basic Principles, Values and Directions of the Domestic Policy and the Action Plan for promoting the Constitution.

“Systematic expert and methodological, informational, cultural and educational work is needed to explain the key provisions of the Constitution and promote constitutional values,” Karin said.

A new public ethic

The second priority is a new public ethic.

“It is about embedding progressive norms and patterns of behavior in society, strengthening our own value foundation, countering the archaization of public life and attempts to replace historical facts,” Karin said.

He also emphasized the need to implement the Law and Order principle in practice, as well as the Taza Qazaqstan (Clean Kazakhstan) project and the Adal Azamat (Honest Citizen) education program.

“New approaches and formats of work are needed. In particular, the President’s Taza Qazaqstan initiative should be scaled up through the creation of a unified digital platform, the introduction of a national cleanliness standard and a regional cleanliness ranking,” he said.

Focus on the future

The third priority is an orientation toward the future, focusing on developing human capital through science and education, innovation and technology, culture and public enlightenment.

According to Karin, strategic documents initiated by President Tokayev set the conceptual direction. The main goal is to build a strong state and a progressive society that looks to the future with optimism. Summing up the three priorities, Karin linked them to the broader question of what kind of society Kazakhstan is building.

“All three priorities answer the main question: what kind of society are we building and what kind of country will we live in. To achieve this, we need to follow a constructive agenda and constitutional values,” he concluded.

Kazakhstan’s first vice president

Karin, 50, was elected Kazakhstan’s first vice president on Aug. 31 after President Tokayev nominated him during a meeting with the leaders of political party factions in the Kurultai. A total of 141 out of 145 Kurultai members voted in favor of his candidacy.

The position was established under Kazakhstan’s new constitutional framework. Under the Constitution, the President appoints the Vice President with the consent of the Kurultai, and while in office, the Vice President may not be elected as a deputy of a representative body, hold other paid positions, engage in business activities or belong to a political party.

The Constitution also provides that the Vice President represents the President in interaction with the Kurultai, the Government and other state bodies and exercises other powers determined by the President.

Under the President’s outline of the role, the Vice President is also expected, at the President’s instruction, to represent the head of state in international forums and negotiations, engage with foreign and domestic political, scientific, cultural and educational organizations, represent the President in Parliament and carry out other assignments.

Karin has held several senior public-service positions, including director of the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, aide to the President, state secretary and state counselor. On June 30, he was appointed first deputy head of the Presidential Administration before becoming Vice President.

World.title: Experts Highlight Investment and Coordination Priorities for Middle Corridor
World.content:
ASTANA – The Middle Corridor is gaining strategic importance as countries across Central Asia and the South Caucasus seek to strengthen trade connectivity and diversify transport routes between Asia and Europe, experts said during a Sept. 15 British-Kazakh Society (BKS) Trade Group webinar on Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan-Middle Corridor Investments, Operations & Trade.

The webinar brought together experts from Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and the United Kingdom (UK) to discuss investment, operations, regional cooperation and the corridor’s development.

“The Middle Corridor is really maturing politically faster than it’s maturing operationally,” said Assylbek Nurgabdeshov, Assistant Professor of Strategy and director of Strategy Postgraduate Programs at Edinburgh Business School, Heriot-Watt University.

He noted that the route remains a multimodal system involving railways, ports, ferries and road networks across several jurisdictions. Improving coordination among the countries involved is therefore essential to its development.

“Reliability is the key aspect” for companies considering the route, Nurgabdeshov said, stressing the importance of predictable operations and long-term sustainability.

According to Nurgabdeshov, the UK could contribute through financial, legal and institutional expertise rather than directly building the corridor.

“UK’s main role will be to shape how it functions rather than to build the corridor,” he said.

Ahmad Alili, director of the Caucasus Policy Analysis Center in Baku, described the Middle Corridor as a “geopolitical necessity,” arguing that closer cooperation between the South Caucasus and Central Asia will become increasingly important.

He pointed to growing contacts between Azerbaijan and Central Asian countries, including cooperation in transport, trade and other areas, as part of a broader regional integration process.

Arzu Abbasova, research analyst at the Royal United Services Institute’s Center for Finance and Security, said geopolitical developments have made connectivity a strategic issue extending beyond trade.

“The war in Ukraine, the uncertainty in Iran, in the maritime trade routes, and the competition around the critical minerals and technology and supply chains have all made this connectivity very much of a strategic issue rather than a purely commercial one,” she said.

The experts also discussed digitalization, Caspian Sea infrastructure and Kazakhstan’s use of alternative routes for oil exports.

Nurgabdeshov stressed that cooperation should take precedence over competition among countries along the route.

“Let’s work on collaborating rather than on competing with each other,” he said.

World.title: Experts: Geopolitical Volatility Reshapes Kazakhstan’s Energy Strategy
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s energy security is increasingly tied to diversified supply routes, modern electricity infrastructure and deeper regional connectivity, while green hydrogen could open a new industrial opportunity if the country can turn its resource potential into commercially viable projects, experts said at the third Regional Central Asian and European Decarbonization Forum on Sept. 16.

The Energy Security in Volatile Geopolitics panel highlighted a fundamental shift in what energy security means. For Kazakhstan, it is no longer only about securing sufficient supplies of oil and gas, but also about developing multiple energy sources, strengthening electricity networks and creating alternative routes to regional and international markets.

“Dependency on single routes is not a good thing,” said Sanzhar Zharkeshov, deputy Energy Minister of Kazakhstan, stressing the need to diversify energy routes while expanding alternative electricity sources.

The country is pursuing nuclear power alongside renewable energy. At the same time, expanding renewables requires greater flexibility in the electricity system. Zharkeshov said Kazakhstan’s new legislation requires renewable energy projects to include battery storage.

“You can’t count on natural gas forever for balancing and manoeuvring power. We have to have a reliable battery storage system,” he said.

This highlights a key challenge for the energy transition: adding generation capacity alone is not enough. Transmission networks, storage and regional interconnections will determine how effectively new electricity can be integrated and delivered.

Building the infrastructure before demand peaks

Azerbaijan’s Deputy Minister of Energy Orkhan Zeynalov said stronger electricity links between Central Asia, Azerbaijan and Europe could provide additional resilience and flexibility.

He said that regional infrastructure should be developed with future demand in mind rather than based solely on current volumes, comparing energy connections with highways that need to be built ahead of traffic growth.

“Tomorrow, the biggest risk is not having this infrastructure,” Zeynalov said.

Plans for a green energy corridor linking Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan are part of this emerging regional approach. Greater interconnection could allow countries with different renewable-generation patterns to exchange electricity and provide additional routes to European markets.

The discussion also linked the growth of artificial intelligence to a potentially sharp increase in electricity demand. Zharkeshov said this could change the economics of different energy technologies, making it less relevant to view them as competing alternatives and more important to develop them in parallel. He argued that stronger demand could, in turn, help improve the economic case for hydrogen.

“There will be no battle between the energy sources. We’ll have to throw everything at it so that we can meet the demand. And that will drive the economic feasibility of hydrogen as an energy source,” he said.

Green hydrogen: from strategy to a market

Green hydrogen illustrates both Kazakhstan’s potential and the challenges of developing new energy technologies.

Zharkeshov identified metallurgy, chemicals, ammonia production and refining as potential applications, notably in sectors that are difficult to decarbonize. However, he acknowledged that production costs remain a major obstacle.

“One of the challenges we’re seeing in hydrogen is the price, the break-even price,” he said.

Kazakhstan has significant wind and solar potential that could support renewable hydrogen production. But the next question is whether this potential can be converted into projects with buyers and viable business models.

Hendrik Meller, program director of H2-diplo at the German Society for International Cooperation (GIZ), told The Astana Times that the clearest milestone over the next five years would be an operating or near-operating project with a committed buyer.

“In five years it would be great to have a project in operation or close to operation, producing green hydrogen, with a clear offtake customer to cater to,” Meller said.

He suggested that Kazakhstan could initially focus on domestic applications rather than relying entirely on exports, including replacing grey hydrogen at refineries and using green hydrogen in fertilizer production. Other applications, such as green steel and sustainable aviation or maritime fuels, could develop as the market matures.

Meller said the immediate practical step is to engage with project developers and technology providers to advance existing hydrogen projects and determine where they can secure an offtake agreement.

“I think that’s something where we have to bring businesses together,” he said.

Critical raw materials add another opportunity

For the European Union, Kazakhstan’s importance extends beyond energy to critical raw materials, connectivity and industrial processing.

EU Ambassador to Kazakhstan Aleška Simkić stressed that developing new technologies requires a long-term investment perspective.

“We have to invest now in order to have long-term benefits, even though it’s not commercially viable,” she said.

Simkić noted that 21 of the 34 critical raw materials the EU identified as important for its green transition are present in Kazakhstan. But she emphasized that cooperation should move beyond extraction.

“We actually want the processing and technologies to be here, locally managed and dealt with,” she said.

This could allow Kazakhstan to capture more value from its mineral resources while helping Europe diversify supply chains.

Taken together, the discussion suggests that Kazakhstan’s energy advantage will depend less on the scale of its resources alone and more on its ability to connect them to modern infrastructure, regional markets and higher-value industries.

The key indicators to watch will be progress on electricity interconnections, battery storage, grid modernization, critical-minerals processing and, particularly, the emergence of a green hydrogen project with a real buyer. If those elements begin to materialize, Kazakhstan’s energy transition could move from a collection of strategies and potential projects towards a more integrated regional energy and industrial model.

World.title: Kazakhstan Highlights New Stage of Nuclear Development at IAEA Conference
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is entering a new stage of nuclear sector development, focusing on nuclear energy, science, medicine and high-tech industry, Deputy Chairman of the Agency for Atomic Energy Gumar Sergazin said at the 70th session of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) General Conference on Sept. 15.

“Atom, placed at the service of peace, science and humanity, can become not a source of fear, but a source of energy, progress and hope,” Sergazin said, outlining Kazakhstan’s priorities in the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

He said Kazakhstan’s nuclear agenda is guided by the newly approved Strategy for the Development of the Nuclear Industry until 2050. The strategy envisages a national nuclear cluster bringing together energy, industry, science, education and high-tech manufacturing, the agency’s press service reported on Sept. 16.

Sergazin also highlighted Kazakhstan’s role in global nuclear supply chains and the country’s contribution to nuclear fuel security through the IAEA Low Enriched Uranium Bank hosted in Kazakhstan.

International cooperation remains a key priority. A Roadmap signed in 2026 to expand Kazakhstan-IAEA cooperation through 2036 covers nuclear energy, nuclear medicine, science, safety and workforce training.

The national statement also highlighted the 35th anniversary of the closure of the Semipalatinsk Nuclear Test Site. Kazakhstan reaffirmed its commitment to nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation and called for the early entry into force of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty.

Kazakhstan said it remains committed to strengthening its strategic partnership with the IAEA and advancing the peaceful use of nuclear energy for energy security, science, medicine and sustainable development.

World.title: One Plant Tripped in Kyrgyzstan, Four Countries Go Dark
World.content:
What the August 14 Blackout Revealed About Central Asia’s Shared Power System

The Almaty metro stopped, and the traffic lights went dark at around 14:37 local time on Aug. 14. The trigger occurred in Kyrgyzstan’s Toktogul Hydropower Plant, where two generating units had tripped, taking roughly 600 MW off the Central Asian grid during one of the year’s highest demand peaks. Within minutes, consumers across Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan lost power.

Reuters reported simultaneous outages across the region that afternoon, and investigators later traced the trigger to the loss of two 300 MW units at Toktogul. Kyrgyzstan’s Energy Ministry acknowledged the technological failure on August 17 while disputing responsibility for what followed in neighboring states. By then, emergency protection had already isolated Kazakhstan’s southern zone from the Central Asian unified power system to prevent a wider collapse, at the cost of outages across the region’s largest cities.

The individual infrastructure fault matters less than the overarching problem it reveals. A trip at one plant in one country reached millions of consumers across four countries, carried there by an aging electricity system already under strain from climate stress, rapidly growing demand, and thin regional coordination. All while Central Asia is positioning itself as a destination for digital infrastructure, including hyperscale artificial intelligence data centers that consume hundreds of megawatts of continuous power, matching an entire city’s demand.

Yesterday’s Grid Running Today’s Central Asia

Central Asia inherited an interconnected grid made for a different era. Under the Soviet Union, the five republics were designed to operate as a single integrated power system rather than as independent national grids, relying on a carefully balanced seasonal exchange. In summer, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan exported hydropower from snowmelt and reservoir releases. In winter, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan supplied coal and gas generation so upstream countries could conserve water.

After the 1991 collapse, coordination weakened because of commercial disputes, underinvestment, and Turkmenistan’s 2003 decision to disconnect and operate synchronously with Iran.

Consequences arrived in the winter of 2007 and 2008, when extreme cold, low water, and suspended supplies from neighbors left Tajikistan to freeze under subzero temperatures. Uzbekistan then withdrew from the regional system altogether in December 2009, exposing the absence of planning to manage such cross-border emergencies. Since then Uzbekistan returned to the grid, and Cooperation has improved considerably, but much of the underlying infrastructure has not.

Although melting glaciers and varying river flows erode hydropower availability, water was not this year’s problem.

Kyrgyzstan’s Energy Ministry estimated the Toktogul reservoir has enough water to support normal turbine operation through autumn and winter. The failure came instead from temperature stress beyond the climate the system was designed for. Extreme summer temperatures pushed demand toward seasonal peaks in several countries at once, reducing transformer cooling efficiency. As equipment temperatures approached safety limits, protection systems disconnected generators to prevent damage. Heat, combined with high energy use, caused high-voltage conductors to expand and sag, raising the risk of a line fault. When Toktogul abruptly lost 600 MW, the deficit spread through the grid and overloaded other parts of the network.

What Needs Investment

The system that lets Kyrgyz hydropower turn on the lights in Kazakhstan also lets a Kyrgyz fault turn them off. Kazakhstan remains reliant on Russian imports at system peaks, and plans to expand its own generation and end those imports by 2027. But that does not solve the infrastructure problem. Large portions of the region’s power plants and transmission infrastructure were built decades ago and are approaching the end of their effective life. This requires investment in asset renewal, control systems, and reserve capacity.

Basic asset renewal involves rehabilitating aging thermal and hydropower plants, replacing overloaded transformers and substations, and modernizing the high-voltage lines that carry power between them.

Fortunately, control system modernization is already underway in Tashkent’s Coordination Dispatch Center “Energiya,” the operational heart of Central Asia’s grid, with World Bank support. Modern dispatch depends on real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and automated contingency analysis to detect instability before it becomes an outage. Still, many of these capabilities remain limited within the existing regional system.

Expanding regional reserve capacity is crucial to preventing a repeat of August 14 by buffering the loss of a large generating unit. The Forecast Balance for 2026–2032 is often cited to show that generation will outpace consumption by 2032. But that measures energy over a year, not capacity at the hour of peak load, and on that measure, the roughly 3 GW deficit never closes.

Storage can close part of that gap, and it has already been tested. Uzbekistan’s Energy Ministry credited recently installed energy storage systems with limiting the domestic impact of the August 14 disturbance, and Kazakhstan is moving in the same direction. A draft law would establish capacity market auctions in which developers bid to provide guaranteed availability.

Efficiency remains the cheapest option at scale. Improved efficiency frees up capacity that would otherwise have to be built and increases gains from new generation. Modernizing industrial equipment, insulating old buildings, and upgrading aging heating and cooling systems lower stress at seasonal peaks and can postpone expensive investment in new capacity.

Data Centers Arriving Ahead of the Grid

Kazakhstan is trying to capitalize on the global shift into the AI era, and the commitments are growing quickly. Under the Digital Qazaqstan strategy approved by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in June 2026, NVIDIA and Firebird.ai signed a $10 billion package based in Ekibastuz’s Data Center Valley, and the UK-based consortium JMOT04 signed a memorandum to build a 200 MW facility paired with a 250 MW gas-fired plant to power it. Signed agreements already amount to roughly 650 MW of new load, and talks with Nasdaq-listed SuperX AI Technology over a 1 GW project would more than double that.

The location is a risk. The zonal tables from Kazakhstan’s Forecast Balance for 2026–2032 show the Northern Region, containing Ekibastuz, in official surplus, and the Southern Region, containing Shymkent and Almaty, in heavy deficit. Shipping power from North to South closes this gap, turning the North’s official surplus into an actual deficit. Thus Kazakhstan’s data center buildout is sited in a zone that only looks like it has power to spare.

According to S&P Global, Kazakhstan’s grid underinvestment is a returns problem, as years of tariff policy oriented toward keeping consumer prices low disincentivized private investment through low returns and unpredictable prices. A recent amendment now runs tariffs through a commission that includes the owner of Samruk-Energo, Kazakhstan’s largest power generator, which may make tariff decisions more sympathetic to producer economics.

The JMOT04 arrangement is the one worth repeating. New large-scale data centers should be required to invest in dedicated generation, storage, and substations rather than drawing on the existing public grid. A facility that brings its own power does not drain the surplus the South is already counting on. On that condition, Ekibastuz becomes the right site rather than the wrong one, and Kazakhstan can use the AI boom to attract the generation investment it needs regardless.

The Need for an Operating Agreement

World Bank projections estimate that electricity demand across Central Asia could triple by 2050, driven by population growth and rapid economic development. Technological investment alone is unlikely to eliminate the risk. The region also needs renewed political agreement on how the interconnected system should operate during normal and emergency scenarios. Normal operations should include transparent plans for cross-border flows, joint investment planning, and coordinated emergency protocols.

Central Asia’s interconnection is also a major strength, enabling it to pool diverse energy resources across borders. The task for the coming decade is to strengthen this grid together. August 14 served as an unplanned stress test, and power returned within hours. Why a local fault crossed four borders remains an open question about the system, not the plant. Every year of delayed investment raises the probability that the next local failure becomes a regional one.

The authors are Sobir Kurbanov and Amel Metjahic, experts and fellows at Nightingale Int. network.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Kazakhstan Plans Cross-Border QR Payments With 11 Countries
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is working to launch cross-border QR-code payments with 11 countries, including China, the United Arab Emirates, Uzbekistan, the Kyrgyz Republic and India, Deputy Governor and Digital Transformation Adviser of the National Bank Binur Zhalenov said at a Sept. 15 government briefing on the development of the digital assets ecosystem.

According to Zhalenov, separate road maps have been developed with each country to integrate national payment systems and establish cross-border QR payments.

“Among the countries we are working with, there are 11. I will not list all of them, but they include China, the United Arab Emirates, Uzbekistan, we signed a memorandum last week, the Kyrgyz Republic and India. We have a corresponding road map with each of these countries,” Zhalenov said.

QR payment pilot with China planned for 2026

The timeline for launching the service will vary depending on the country. Testing and pilot projects with some partners are expected to begin before the end of 2026. China is among the countries where such testing is planned this year.

If the pilot is successful, Kazakh citizens could be able to use the mobile application of any bank in Kazakhstan to make QR-code payments in China as early as next year.

“If testing and piloting go well, next year Kazakh citizens will have the opportunity to pay through the application of any bank using QR in China, and vice versa,” Zhalenov said.

The National Bank expects the pace of integration to differ across partner countries. While some systems could be connected next year, others may require up to two years to complete the necessary technical and regulatory work.

“When we have a clearer picture regarding all 11 countries or other countries that may be added, we will certainly provide a separate communication,” Zhalenov said.

World.title: Former Georgian security chief Grigol Liluashvili jailed for 13 years for corruption
World.content:
Georgia’s ex-security chief jailed

Former head of Georgia’s State Security Service Grigol Liluashvili was sentenced to 13 years in prison on 16 September on corruption charges. The ruling was handed down by Tbilisi City Court judge Nino Tarashvili.

Liluashvili headed the State Security Service for more than five years, from October 2019 to December 2025. He was found guilty on all four charges. Liluashvili denied the charges.

Charges against Grigol Liluashvili

Grigol Liluashvili was arrested on 23 December 2025.

He was accused of “accepting particularly large bribes as part of a group acting by prior agreement”.

Prosecutors charged Liluashvili over four separate bribery cases.

● The first dates back to October 2022. According to prosecutors, Liluashvili received $1m from Turkish investor Cagatay Ulker through then Deputy Economy Minister Romeo Mikautadze, who is also in custody. Prosecutors said the money was paid in exchange for lobbying for a wind farm construction project.

● According to the second case, in February 2022 Liluashvili, again through Romeo Mikautadze, demanded and received 1.5m lari (about $580,000) from Giorgi Khazhalia, founder of Express Service 2008, in exchange for helping the company secure tenders for household gasification projects.

● The third case concerned call centres operating in Georgia between 2021 and 2023. According to prosecutors, Liluashvili took bribes from “a small number of call centres that remained in Georgia” through his relative Sandro Liluashvili.

Prosecutors allege that Liluashvili received about $1.365m in connection with the call centres, with Sandro Liluashvili acting as an intermediary.

● The fourth case involved Kakha Gvantseladze, former director of the Tbilisi City Hall agency responsible for managing kindergartens.

According to prosecutors, Liluashvili used his official position to protect Gvantseladze’s alleged corrupt activities in exchange for payment. Prosecutors said Gvantseladze received particularly large sums in kickbacks from private companies in return for awarding them procurement contracts for kindergartens.

Georgia’s ex-security chief jailed

World.title: ‘How much money do you need each month to live comfortably?’ Street poll in Tbilisi. Video
World.content:
We asked passers-by on the streets of Tbilisi how much money they need each month to live a normal life. We also asked what they actually mean by “a normal life”.

The answers vary widely. Some young people believe the amount should be at least 5,000–8,000 lari around $1,900–3,000 per person. Middle-aged and older respondents, meanwhile, say that 2,000 lari around $769 is enough for one person.

Meanwhile, the subsistence minimum for the average consumer in Georgia is 250.9 lari around $97.

Responses to the question of what constitutes a normal life also vary by age. For middle-aged and older people, having enough money for food, medication and utility bills already amounts to a normal life.

Here are several examples of the answers we received:

“No excessive comfort, no leisure, just food and medication.”

“The basics, at least food, right? Proper food. Children need clothes and shoes. Basic school supplies.”

“To be able to go into a shop without worrying that if you buy this, you won’t have enough money left. Because absolutely everything is very expensive.”

Cafés and restaurants, trips out of town, shopping, leisure activities and travelling at least once a year, meanwhile, are all seen as part of a “luxurious life” among this age group.

We also asked our randomly selected respondents whether they had ever had to give something up because they lacked the money. It turned out to be a very common experience.

Cost of living in Georgia

World.title: Russian MoFA: Russia, Georgia ‘allies’ in defending ‘traditional values’ against West
World.content:
Russia on alliance with Georgia

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova devoted much of her 15 September briefing to Georgia. She spoke about the Georgiyevsky and Father Gabriel military units, which were formed by Georgians living in Russia to fight on the Russian side in the Ukraine war.

Zakharova also referred to the 1783 Treaty of Georgievsk, under which Georgian King Erekle II entered into an alliance with the Russian Empire.

“Russia and Georgia are allies in the fight to preserve the family and traditional values, while Western countries are trying to deprive Georgia of its historical memory,” Zakharova said.

Maria Zakharova on Treaty of Georgievsk

“The name of the unit, ‘Georgiyevsky’, reminded me of the 1783 Treaty of Georgievsk, when King Erekle II took a historic step and chose the Russian Empire, which at the time was the largest Orthodox state, as an ally. The signing of the treaty saved Georgia.

I think everyone understands this very well. For Georgia, the treaty was concluded at an extremely difficult point in its history, when the country’s very existence was under threat, and it made it possible to preserve its religion, culture and people. That is why I made this association,” Zakharova said.

The Treaty of Georgievsk became the focus of political controversy in Georgia in August. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze described King Erekle II’s decision as “wise” and said there had been no alternative, arguing that it had saved Georgia as a state and nation. His remarks prompted a strong reaction from the opposition. His opponents accused him of portraying Russian imperial policy as historically beneficial to Georgia and of distorting the country’s history. The Georgiyevsky unit was established in Russia in early September. Its commander was named as Otar Romanov-Partskhaladze, Georgia’s former prosecutor-general. He lives in Russia, is under US and UK sanctions, and faces criminal charges in Georgia over allegations that he organised a contract killing. Russia describes him as a veteran of the war against Ukraine. The Georgian Orthodox Church strongly opposed the creation of a military unit named after Georgian Archimandrite Gabriel Urgebadze. The head of the Georgian Patriarchate’s press service said it was “particularly unacceptable that individual clergy of the Russian Orthodox Church support this initiative”.

According to Zakharova, Georgians have “long been helping” Russian-backed administrations operating in occupied territories of Ukraine and in Russian regions bordering Ukraine.

“Since the start of the special military operation, a large number of ethnic Georgians have voluntarily gone to the front and continue to take part, including in combat operations,” the Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman said.

Asked about the Georgian volunteers in the Russian army whom she had mentioned, Zakharova suggested “looking not at who is on which side, but at what values each side stands for”.

She cited Georgians fighting alongside people of other nationalities during World War Two as an example.

“At that time, 700,000 Georgians went to the front. And how many people did Georgia take in during the evacuation?” she said.

Zakharova also recalled Georgian soldier Meliton Kantaria, who, together with Russian soldier Mikhail Yegorov, raised the Soviet banner over the Reichstag in May 1945.

“Their feat became a symbol of the brotherhood in arms between Russians and Georgians,” Zakharova said.

“Our grandfathers and great-grandfathers were not fighting for one side or another. They were fighting Nazism, an ideology which held that the world should be divided along racial and national lines into those who deserved everything and those who deserved nothing except what those who deserved everything allowed them to have. That is what they fought against. And that is exactly what we are fighting against now,” she also noted.

Zakharova on family values and West seeking to ‘take them away’

“We and the Georgians are also allies in the fight to preserve the family,” Zakharova said, pointing to what she described as spiritual and moral values shared by the two peoples, including their way of life, traditions, art and culture.

She went on to say accuse Western countries of “trying to impose anti-values on Georgia”.

“We can see that a real struggle is taking place on this front as well. Together, we are protecting children from destructive ideology. They say that children are supposedly neither boys nor girls, that there is almost some kind of third gender. Or that they can be whatever they want: perhaps a chair, perhaps a saucepan. They can decide later in life. That is the kind of ideology they have there in the West,” the Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman said.

“Western countries are now trying to deprive Georgia of its historical memory and undermine the Orthodox foundations of society. This is exactly what we were talking about in the case of Armenia. They do not understand that this is impossible. Georgia has responded in a way that has further strengthened its commitment to respecting its own historical heritage,” Zakharova added.

Zakharova also spotlighted volunteers of the Georgiyevsky unit. She said she was certain what its members, whom she described as ethnic Georgians, were fighting for: “They are fighting for truth, for love of their history and their ancestors.”

“It is terrible to imagine what my grandfathers would have gone through if they had seen how [in Ukraine] the remains of the scoundrels Yevhen Konovalets and Andriy Melnyk [Ukrainian nationalists] were reburied. How they glorified the memory of Roman Shukhevych and Stepan Bandera. How they portrayed them as heroes and erected monuments to them.

How can we not fight against this? What will they turn us into afterwards? People like them, who have had their sexual organs changed 33 times? No, thank you,” she concluded.

World.title: Preferential regime for Armenian exports to EU in response to Russian restrictions
World.content:
Preferential trade regime with the EU for Armenia

Customs duties on a wide range of goods exported from Armenia to the European Union will be temporarily suspended. The preferential trade regime is expected to remain in place for two years. The European Parliament approved the European Commission’s proposal the previous day.

A total of 583 MEPs supported the application of Autonomous Trade Measures to Armenian goods. Forty-nine voted against, while 39 abstained.

“This step is prompted by the restrictions that Russia has imposed since May 2026 on several key Armenian export goods,” the decision says.

The EU Council must now approve the regulation. It will enter into force afterwards.

The EU initiative aims to support Armenia’s economy and create additional opportunities for local exporters to access the EU market.

The Armenian Centre for Socio-Economic Research (ACSES) analysed the potential implications of the decision. The centre’s experts described the scale of trade liberalisation with the European Union as significant. At the same time, they believe further developments will depend on several key factors:

“Can Armenia overcome entrenched perceptions of dependence and restructure its export profile? Much will depend on the next steps taken by Armenian businesses and the government. Creating new, comprehensive logistics infrastructure is a necessity of the times.”

Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Trade believes the temporary trade preferences “will help diversify Armenia’s foreign trade, expand Armenian goods’ access to the EU market, and further deepen trade and economic cooperation with the European Union”.

Context

In early July 2026, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced in Yerevan that the EU could introduce autonomous trade measures for Armenia.

“I am here today to state clearly: if Russia closes its market to Armenian products, the EU will open the doors to its consumer market of 450 million people,” she said.

Since May, Russia has banned imports of Armenian fruit, vegetables, fish products, alcohol and many other goods. Russian authorities cited their alleged failure to meet quality standards. Meanwhile, the European Union, which has stricter standards, has decided to help Armenia.

Ursula von der Leyen said the autonomous trade measures would liberalise around 80% of Armenian exports. In other words, that share of goods would become exempt from customs duties.оло 80% армянского экспорта. То есть такой объем товаров будет освобожден от таможенных пошлин.

Details of the European Parliament’s decision

European lawmakers approved a proposal to liberalise exports of goods marked “Made in Armenia”. The decision will cover 324 product categories. According to EU estimates, Armenian businesses will save a total of €5.4 million over two years. This is the amount they would otherwise have had to pay in customs duties.

To benefit from the preferential terms:

Armenian products must comply with EU regulations on the origin of goods and customs procedures;

Armenia must cooperate with EU authorities to verify the origin of goods and prevent possible fraud.

In addition, the EU plans to introduce duty-free import quotas for eight types of Armenian agricultural products. The list includes apricots, grapes, plums, peaches, cherries, strawberries, cucumbers and pears.

The European Union believes that Russia’s restrictions have significantly limited Armenian goods’ access to their established market:

“The situation has had a severe impact on small and medium-sized enterprises, including agricultural producers, threatening Armenia’s economic resilience.”

The preferential regime will cover 99% of fresh agricultural exports and 91% of beverage exports.

Against the backdrop of these changes, the EU also intends to introduce safeguards for its own market:

“These mechanisms will allow the European Union to intervene if a rise in imports from Armenia negatively affects European producers.”

The European Commission may fully or partially suspend the regime if an increase in imports from Armenia destabilises the EU market. It may also do so if Yerevan fails to meet the agreed requirements.

Expert opinion

Experts at the Armenian Centre for Socio-Economic Research say the project approved by the European Parliament aims to reduce pressure on Armenia’s economy. According to their calculations, potential export losses in 2026 could reach $260 million.

However, goods that will receive temporary exemptions from customs duties account for a significant share of Armenia’s total exports:

“In 2025, Armenia exported around $3.5 billion worth of goods. More than two-thirds of this amount falls under the proposed preferential regime.”

The experts believe that the EU’s preferential trade regime, combined with business support programmes implemented by the Armenian government, could change the structure of the country’s exports. Exporters that previously supplied goods to Russia may redirect their products to the EU.

However, after analysing the tariff quotas that will apply to agricultural products, economists noted that some quotas are lower than actual export figures:

“For example, the quota for plums amounts to only 13% of actual exports, while the quota for apricots stands at 16%.”

In their view, these low quotas are due less to the EU’s desire to protect its own market than to the methodology used to calculate them.

In particular, the quotas were determined using export data from companies registered in Armenia. The information comes from the UN Comtrade database. However, the calculation did not account for the fact that individuals carry out a significant share of fruit and vegetable exports.

“Perhaps our government should have defended the interests of Armenian exporters of fresh fruit and vegetables more consistently,” the publication says.

Preferential trade regime with the EU for Armenia

World.title: Aliyev calls European Parliament ‘nest of corrupt figures’ and urges Muslim countries to unite
World.content:
Aliyev meets religious leaders

On 15 September, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev accused European institutions of bias during a meeting in Baku with representatives of Muslim religious organisations and participants in international conferences. He said the peace process with Armenia was continuing. At the same time, he stressed that Azerbaijan intended to strengthen its military capabilities.

The meeting was attended by members and observers of the Council of Heads of Muslim Religious Administrations of the Organisation of Turkic States, co-organisers of the Yahya Bakuvi International Conference, and representatives of the Supreme Religious Council of the Peoples of the Caucasus.

Allegations against European institutions

Aliyev accused the Council of Europe and the European Parliament of supporting Armenia and applying double standards towards Azerbaijan. He called the European Parliament a “nest of corrupt figures”.

“I say this with full responsibility: the European Parliament is a nest of corrupt figures. Millions of dollars in cash were found in the house of its vice-president, and they covered up the entire affair, as if it had never happened. Her name is known; she is a Greek member of the European Parliament.

How many years have passed since then? Has any measure been taken against her? No. Has she been held accountable? No. She was released.

Look, the European Parliament consists of these Islamophobes, and this must remain a matter of constant attention.”

The president linked Azerbaijan’s restoration of full control over Karabakh in September 2023 to a subsequent decision concerning the Azerbaijani delegation. In his account, the decision came in response to Baku’s military operation.

He was referring to a decision by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), which refused to ratify the credentials of Azerbaijan’s delegation in January 2024. PACE is a body of the Council of Europe and has no connection to the European Parliament, which is an institution of the European Union.

The report on which PACE based its decision cited a broader range of reasons, including Azerbaijan’s failure to fulfil its human rights obligations, reports of political prisoners, arrests of independent journalists, restrictions on monitoring, and the absence of an invitation for observers to attend the presidential election. The document also mentioned the military operation in Karabakh and the departure of the region’s Armenian population.

Peace process and military power

Aliyev expressed hope that the peace process with Armenia would last in the long term. At the same time, he said the war and destruction of the past would not be forgotten, and that Azerbaijan would remain vigilant on security issues.

The president described military power as one of the guarantees of the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. In his view, the growing role of military power in international relations requires Azerbaijan to further strengthen its defence capabilities.

The meeting also addressed the expansion of regional conflicts. Aliyev stressed the importance of joint efforts to preserve peace in the Turkic world and the Caucasus.

Call for religious solidarity

Aliyev said that an undeclared war was being waged against the Islamic world, and described Islamophobia as one of its components. According to him, Muslim countries’ main response to this pressure should be solidarity.

“Discrediting the Muslim world, tarnishing its image, equating it with terrorism, and committing such insulting acts against our values and the Holy Quran—do you think these things happen by chance? No. This is a deliberate and targeted policy. And what must we counter this with? Only our unity. Therefore, this call for unity is not merely a slogan.

This is what we have faced—that is, for over 30 years, both from a territorial point of view, as our territory was under occupation, and from a political point of view, as Azerbaijan is one of the very few Muslim countries participating in European organizations.

Therefore, we know what happens there. As a member of the Council of Europe, we have faced these injustices, we continue to face them, and we will likely continue to face them. This undeclared smear campaign against us will never stop. Why? Because we do not and will not bow before anyone. We speak our mind, we protect our national dignity, and we protect our way of life.

We do not allow certain trends that are alien to our people and our religion to take root in Azerbaijan. We are guardians of morality. Look, this is why these campaigns are being waged against us. I expanded the scope of our meeting somewhat simply to substantiate my points with evidence.

That is, once again, the main message is that we must all strive for unity. Again, I say, the words of religious figures carry special meaning for all Muslim countries.”

The president also announced that Baku would host a summit of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation next year. He called on religious leaders to promote peace and cooperation within their communities.

Aliyev meets religious leaders

World.title: Money transfers from Russia to Georgia plunge 88%, dropping from third to 11th place
World.content:
Russia-Georgia money transfers drop

The volume of money transfers from Russia to Georgia fell sharply in August, with just $5m transferred – almost 88% less than in August 2025. Russia dropped from third to 11th place in the ranking of countries sending money to Georgia.

According to the National Bank of Georgia, around $295m was transferred to the country from abroad in August 2026, about 8% less than in the same period in 2025.

The most significant change amid the overall decline was in transfers from Russia.

For the first time, Russia, which for years had been one of the main sources of money transfers to Georgia, did not even make the top 10.

The changes followed the introduction of a new package of European Union sanctions against Russia.

In late July, the Russian payment and money transfer system Zolotaya Korona suspended money transfers to Georgia.

In August, Georgia received the largest amount of money from the United States, at more than $64m, followed by Italy and Germany. Transfers from these countries, by contrast, increased year on year.
