Greece and Israel also remain important sources of money transfers, further indicating that the geography of transfers to Georgia is gradually changing, while Russia’s share is rapidly declining.

Countries from which Georgia received the largest amounts of money in August 2026:

United States — $64.14m (+8.17%)

Italy — $55.22m (+3.48%)

Germany — $31.31m (+6.84%)

Greece — $28.24m (+12.40%)

Israel — $27.92m (+24.88%)

Turkey — $10.56m (+11.88%)

Spain — $10.26m (+11.35%)

Kazakhstan — $8.04m (-9.74%)

United Kingdom — $7.29m (+13.02%)

France — $6.91m (+2.86%)

The National Bank also said that around $34m was transferred from Georgia abroad in August, down from the same period in 2025.

World.title: Turkish foreign minister visits Baku for talks on energy, peace and regional security
World.content:
Turkish foreign minister visits Baku

During Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan’s meetings in Baku, the two sides discussed Azerbaijani-Turkish relations, as well as energy and transport projects, the process of normalising relations with Armenia, defence co-operation and the situation in the Middle East. Experts see the visit as an attempt by Baku and Ankara to co-ordinate their positions amid a rapidly changing regional security environment.

On 15 September, Fidan was received by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. The Turkish foreign minister conveyed greetings from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, while Aliyev asked him to convey his greetings to the Turkish president.

A brief statement on the Azerbaijani president’s official website said the two sides expressed satisfaction with the development of the strategic alliance between Azerbaijan and Turkey, based on the principle of “one nation, two states”.

The meeting was held behind closed doors. A full transcript of the talks was not published, and neither side issued a separate statement.

Energy and new export routes

One of the issues highlighted in the official statement was energy co-operation and the development of new routes for supplying renewable energy to international markets.

Further details emerged later during Fidan’s meeting with his Azerbaijani counterpart Jeyhun Bayramov and at their joint briefing.

Bayramov said the projects discussed included supplying renewable energy generated in Azerbaijan to Europe via the Black Sea, as well as laying a new energy cable linking Nakhchivan with Turkey. Azerbaijan says these projects have significant potential not only for the two countries but also for the European energy market.

Trade between Azerbaijan and Turkey exceeded $3.2bn in the first eight months of 2026. However, this remains well below the $15bn target previously set by the two countries’ presidents.

Middle Corridor and Kars-Dilucu railway

The talks also covered the role of Azerbaijan and Turkey as a logistics bridge between Europe and Asia.

At the joint briefing, Hakan Fidan stressed the importance of the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars railway becoming fully operational. He also said construction of the Kars-Dilucu railway, which will provide Turkey with a rail link to the border with Nakhchivan, was expected to be completed by the end of 2029.

The line is regarded as the Turkish section of a future transport route that will run through Nakhchivan to Azerbaijan and onwards to Central Asia. Fidan said the development of the Middle Corridor was in the interests of Azerbaijan and Turkey, as well as other members of the Organization of Turkic States.

Peace process with Armenia

Following his meeting with Aliyev, Fidan said Turkey was closely following the process of normalising relations between Azerbaijan and Armenia and supported Baku on the issue.

A statement issued after an expanded meeting between the Azerbaijani and Turkish foreign ministers said the two sides discussed progress made in the peace process over the past year and practical steps aimed at developing regional co-operation.

They also discussed security and defence co-operation, their allied relations under the Shusha Declaration, and co-ordination within the UN, OSCE, Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and Organization of Turkic States.

The ministers also reaffirmed their shared position that ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and other regions should be resolved through political and diplomatic rather than military means.

How do experts assess the visit?

Turkey expert Mehmet Emin Iqbal Durre said that although the visit had been planned in advance, it had taken on particular significance amid tensions surrounding Syria and Iran, as well as the Russia-Ukraine war.

In his view, Baku and Ankara need to co-ordinate their approaches amid the rapidly changing situation in the region. He sees the Kars-Dilucu railway, energy projects and preparations for the next summit of the Organization of Turkic States as key elements of future regional integration.

Political commentator Chingiz Shahbazi offered a different interpretation. He suggested that growing tensions between Turkey and Israel, particularly over the situation in Gaza and Syria, may have been among the issues discussed behind closed doors.

Shahbazi believes Azerbaijan, which has allied relations with Turkey and strategic relations with Israel, could provide a platform for dialogue between the two countries. However, official statements on the meeting between Aliyev and Fidan make no mention of Turkish-Israeli relations. His interpretation therefore remains speculation.

World.title: Trump Tower project unveiled in Tbilisi
World.content:
Trump Tower presentation in Tbilisi

The Trump Tower project was presented at Mtatsminda Park in Tbilisi on the evening of 15 September. The 62-storey skyscraper will be part of the Downtown Tbilisi development planned on the site of the former hippodrome.

The event was attended by representatives of the Georgian government and ruling party, the president of the National Bank, the chairman of the Energy and Water Supply Regulatory Commission, the prosecutor general, business representatives and other invited guests.

Hundreds of people attended the presentation, leaving some guests standing throughout the event.

The event also featured a video address by Eric Trump, executive vice president of The Trump Organization and son of US President Donald Trump.

“When we undertake projects, the overall climate is very important to us. We build the best buildings in countries where there is a welcoming environment. We want to have outstanding buildings in different countries around the world. My father supports this,” Eric Trump said.

Eric Trump addresses Trump Tower presentation in Tbilisi remotely

The presentation featured speeches by executives of the companies involved in the construction of Trump Tower, as well as government representatives.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said the project would receive $2 billion in investment. The complex will have a total area of approximately 600,000 square metres.

Kobakhidze said Trump Tower will have 62 floors and stand 282 metres tall. Construction is scheduled to be completed in 2031, with the entire complex due for completion in 2033.

“This is a bold project that will give Tbilisi a new appeal, putting it on a par with the world’s leading urban centres,” Kobakhidze said.

Georgian government and business representatives at the Trump Tower presentation in Tbilisi

Economy Minister Mariam Kvrivishvili said the project “will create new jobs from day one”, facilitate the exchange of knowledge and expertise, introduce modern international standards, and “take cooperation between Georgian and international companies to a new level”.

During the presentation, government representatives and executives of companies involved in the project symbolically pressed a red button.

A drone show was held at the site, with the words “Trump Tower Tbilisi” appearing in the sky. The evening ended with a fireworks display.

During the Trump Tower presentation in Tbilisi, government representatives and executives of companies involved in the project symbolically pressed a red button

Project announced in April

Information about plans to build a Trump Tower in Tbilisi was released in April 2026. The Wall Street Journal was the first to report on the project.

According to the newspaper, a 70-storey skyscraper is planned for Tbilisi, with the design being developed by US architecture firm Gensler.

The Trump Organization’s partners are named as Georgian companies Archi Group, Biograpi Living, Bloxi Group and Finvest Georgia, as well as US-based The Sapir Organization.

According to The Trump Organization, once completed, the building will be the tallest in Tbilisi. The complex is planned to include luxury residential apartments, retail space and restaurants.

The organisation described the project as the first official use of the Trump brand in the region.

The exact location was not initially disclosed. The Trump Organization only said the skyscraper would be built in a “prestigious location” overlooking Tbilisi’s Central Park.

Local media immediately linked the project to a planned mixed-use development on the site of the former hippodrome. A development plan for the area has already been approved, providing for seven high-rise buildings. The tallest will be 79 storeys.

Central Park Avenue, the company developing the area, is linked to Wissol Group and Biograpi Living, which are involved in the Trump Tower project.

What The Wall Street Journal writes

On 13 September, The Wall Street Journal published an extensive article about the Trump Tower project in Tbilisi.

The headline was: “The Latest Spot for a Trump Tower: An Ex-Soviet Republic Moving Closer to Russia” In the subheadline, the newspaper highlighted the fact that the land designated for the skyscraper in Tbilisi was acquired from a fund linked to billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, who is under US sanctions.

The WSJ examines the project not only as a real estate development, but also in the context of deteriorating Georgia-US relations and Georgia’s domestic political situation.

The newspaper writes that despite a significant deterioration in relations between Tbilisi and Washington in recent years, one of the largest new projects involving a brand associated with the current US president is being developed in Georgia.

A significant part of the WSJ article focuses on the deal for the land designated for the project. According to the publication, the Trump Tower project provided a financial benefit to the family of Bidzina Ivanishvili, who was placed under US sanctions in late 2024.

According to the WSJ, in 2023 the developers agreed to purchase the land from a fund controlled by the Ivanishvili family, with the deal valued at up to $85 million.

World.title: Government bows to pressure to scrap allied health cap for veterans
World.content:
The Albanese government has bowed to pressure, scrapping a plan to cap allied health services for veterans at $5,000 a year.

The proposal would have imposed an "annual monetary limit" on services such as physiotherapy and dentistry, with veterans able to access more funding if they "demonstrated clinical need".

The May budget showed the measure would have saved the government roughly $750 million over three years but was rubbished by both the Coalition and veteran advocacy groups for making health services harder to access.

Minister for Veterans' Affairs Matt Keogh released a statement today confirming the threshold measure was "off the table".

Veterans healthcare change sparks fury Jacqui Lambie's emotional moment in the Senate taps into veteran fury over a government change to healthcare access.

"We have been consulting on this measure, and we have heard from veterans there are concerns about this approach," he said.

Mr Keogh had initially been under pressure after the Coalition accused him of declining to meet with veterans or properly understand their needs.

He later told the parliament he "got it wrong," with some government sources confirming the issue was being considered at the highest levels, including the prime minister's office.

Independent senator Jacqui Lambie, who is herself a veteran, made an emotional speech in the Senate last month about healthcare access following recent surgery for vaginal prolapse.

She turned to the Department of Veterans' Affairs (DVA) to pay for the surgery, but eventually footed the bill herself after facing serious administrative hurdles.

Senator Lambie linked her personal experience to the concerns being expressed by other veterans about looming changes to the way the DVA manages access to allied healthcare.

Today, she said scrapping the cap was a win that belonged to "every veteran".

"They knew what would happen to our most vulnerable veterans if this cap went ahead and they fought like hell to make sure it didn't," she said.

" This cap was cruel, it was dangerous and it should never have been announced in the first place. I'm relieved that the government has finally listened and scrapped it and I thank them for doing it. "

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the government had taken "too long" to drop the policy and called on Mr Keogh to step down.

Angus Taylor has called for Matt Keogh to step down. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"It has taken too long to scrap this cap. It should never have happened, and frankly, it's time for this minister to go," he said.

But advocacy group Fair Care for Veterans, which had pushed the government to drop the changes, said the minister had "made it right".

"This is what happens when a government listens to veterans," spokesman John Armfield, a former navy clearance diver, said.

"Veterans, families and doctors came from all over the country to say one thing: this cap would only ever hurt the most badly injured.

"The minister made the right call, and he deserves credit for it."

Government still wants to find a fix

The government had said it wanted to introduce the limit to stamp out "over-servicing" of veterans who were being charged for support they did not need.

Department figures suggest about 10 per cent of veteran cardholders spend more than $5,000 on allied health services each year.

A Senate estimates hearing in June heard examples of overcharging, including one case where a single patient was charged $101,000 in a single year by a dietitian, equivalent to 19 appointments a week.

The policy also aimed to reduce the administrative burden on veterans under the current system, which requires them to go back to a GP every 12 allied health visits for a new referral.

Mr Keogh said he would continue to engage the veteran and provider community to address those goals and "deliver on the objective of achieving better veteran wellbeing outcomes while ensuring integrity of the system".

"We will not change our commitment to improving access to allied health care through the fee increase to allied health providers," he said.

Mr Armfield said Fair Care for Veterans was open to further conversations.

"We welcome that, and we'll be there," he said.

"We'll also make sure whatever comes next doesn't bring the cap back under another name."

World.title: Book highlights abuse UK child migrants endured in WA
World.content:
It has taken seven decades for Norman "Johno" Johnston to trust someone with the full story of the abuse he endured as a child migrant from the United Kingdom.

His biography, titled Johno, has been painstakingly recorded, cross-referenced and written by his former wife, Kathleen O'Reilly Johnston, and released during Child Protection Week.

It shines a glaring spotlight on the brutality and abuse endured by Mr Johnston, now 83, and many others like him by the Christian Brothers in Western Australia.

"We were told quite emphatically, not only did your parents abandon you, your country's abandoned you as well," he said.

When he was seven, Mr Johnston was one of thousands of children sent from an orphanage after World War II to help rebuild Australia with "good British stock".

The story of UK child migrants has been the subject of a parliamentary inquiry in Britain, and the Christian Brothers apologised to West Australian victims in the 1990s and reached an out-of-court settlement with some of them.

Others successfully sued the institutions.

WA hearings of the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Sexual Abuse focused on four institutions run by the Christian Brothers, including St Vincent's Orphanage Clontarf in Perth and Castledare Junior Orphanage in Wilson.

Norman Johnston was sent to Australia aged seven. (Supplied: Family)

Mr Johnston spent more than six years at Castledare and later Clontarf, where he was stripped of his identity and suffered significant ongoing abuse.

"The brutal floggings that went on were ad hoc," he said.

"There was very seldom a reasonable reason for half of the pain that was meted out.

"For example, having a dirty jumper warranted, you know, six of the best on the stage in front of the whole school, sort of thing."

He describes being almost drowned after witnessing the sexual abuse of another boy.

"I've been told I've got PTSD from an incident where a brother, one of the brothers, tried to drown me because I caught him interfering with another boy at Castledare," he said.

"I was taken out into the middle of the Canning River, forced underwater, and he shot through, left me in the middle of the river and I couldn't swim a stroke."

Vietnam War and marriage

At 15, Mr Johnston was considered too old for school and was sent to work on a farm where he lived in a shed with no windows and very little pay.

"Working 100 hours a week for two pound five a week," he said.

"That was my lot for two and a half years until suddenly out of nowhere a welfare officer turned up."

Mr Johnston joined the army and served in Vietnam before meeting Kathleen O'Reilly in the 1960s.

While their romantic relationship was fraught, the pair always maintained civility for their three children.

"The children are definitely the glue to the relationship that exists today, and of course, that's been overtaken now by the grandchildren," he said.

"So yeah, we have an understanding, we have a mutual respect based on the family ethics of what we need to do."

Loading...

Ms O'Reilly Johnston said she had felt compelled for a number of years to write Norman's story.

"The older that I became, the more extraordinary I realised the story is," she said.

"And it is a part of our history, maybe not a very nice part, but I'm just wondering if you'd give me permission to write it.

"His initial response was 'no' and I didn't take no for an answer."

Ms O'Reilly Johnston would make the long drive from her home in WA's Wheatbelt to Mr Johnston's home in the southern suburbs of Perth each week.

She would ask questions, hand-write Mr Johnston's answers, cross-check and reference his memories with evidence from historical sources, and then return the manuscripts for him to check.

"It just occurred in increments until we ended up with a book," she said.

Norman Johnston checked the manuscript every step of the way. (Supplied: Kathleen O'Reilly Johnston)

Weeks before the book went to print, Kathleen checked again that Norman was OK with publishing, particularly in relation to the sexual abuse.

"His response was that yes, it does sort of put him in a more vulnerable light, but it is also such a part of the story, such a part of the truth, that he would prefer that it remain in there, which I thought was incredibly brave."

World.title: Breaking: Olympic authorities sign off on controversial rowing and canoeing venue
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

After months of fierce debate, the International Olympic Committee has approved rowing and canoe sprint events to be hosted on Rockhampton's Fitzroy River for the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic Games.

Premier David Crisafulli said the doubters had been proven wrong with today's announcement.

"The IOC assessment for the site is complete," Mr Crisafulli said.

" The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours. It's official, signed, sealed and delivered. "

It comes after World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide also backed an independent technical assessment of the Rockhampton flatwater course.

International rowing bodies had questioned the location's suitability for competition. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Comprehensive and independent technical assessment of the Fitzroy River was completed by the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA) and internationally renowned marine engineering experts WaterProof Marine Consultancy and Services B.V. (WaterProof).

The assessment included extensive on-water investigations and modelling to understand how the course would perform under a range of conditions, weather patterns, water levels and flood risk at both Games time and throughout the period leading into the event.

Having reviewed the assessment, World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland and Paddle Worldwide president Thomas Konietzko both endorsed the course.

Mr Rolland said it could provide a safe, fair and consistent field of play suitable for Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoe sprint competitions.

"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games, consistent with the requirements of Olympic and Paralympic rowing," he said.

Game on Rocky

Tony Williams has thanked the state government for its support of Olympic rowing in the city. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Rockhampton Mayor Tony Williams welcomed the confirmation of the Fitzroy River as the venue for rowing at the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

"This endorsement proves what we've always known. That Rockhampton's Fitzroy River will be the perfect venue for rowing at the 2032 Games," he said.

"Rockhampton is ready for the world stage. Now it's time to get to work and secure the infrastructure and opportunities that will benefit our community long after the Games have ended."

The Queensland premier said GIICA would now proceed with the detailed planning, design and construction of the Rockhampton site.

He also told state parliament there would be no widening or dredging and that the Fitzroy Barrage was Rockhampton's "secret weapon".

The Fitzroy River rowing course has faced intense scrutiny since it was selected as a venue for the Brisbane 2032 Olympics. (Supplied: Rockhampton Fitzroy Rowing Club)

Rowing Queensland chief executive Anthea O'Loughlin also welcomed the announcement, as the Rockhampton venue prepared to host more than 800 young rowers for the Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta this weekend.

"This is an important step to provide certainty to our athletes and community as we progress towards 2032," Ms O'Loughlin said.

"We note the references in the statement to legacy and investment in the sport and look forward to further information on this as it develops."

World.title: New laws on mining objections 'hacking at safety net'
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Queensland communities could find it harder to challenge new mining projects under proposed laws that would restrict who can object to a mine and give politicians greater control over whether objections are heard in court.

Resources Minister Dale Last introduced the Mineral Resources Objections Reform and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2026 on Tuesday, arguing the changes would cut red tape and stop "vexatious" objections from holding up projects.

Dale Last says the bill will put a stop to "vexatious claims". (ABC Rural: Brandon Long)

But farmers, environmental groups and lawyers said the reforms would instead make it harder for communities to have their say and weaken independent scrutiny of mines.

Under the proposed laws, objections would generally be restricted to landholders directly affected by a project and others living within 125 kilometres of a proposed mine.

Automatic referrals of objections to the Land Court would also disappear, with decisions about whether an objection went to court instead made through "a ministerial referral process".

'Benefit from an open process'

Barrister and University of Queensland adjunct professor Chris McGrath said the changes would undermine the approvals system.

"This is another step of this current government in really hacking at the safety net of laws that protect Queenslanders from bad development," Dr McGrath said.

"We all benefit from an open process with independent review, and they're really blowing holes in that process."

Under the proposed laws, objections would generally be restricted to landholders directly affected by a project and others living within 125 kilometres of a proposed mine. (Supplied: Ernest Henry)

Dr McGrath said the proposed 125km limit failed to recognise that the effects of a mine could travel far beyond its immediate footprint.

But mining industry group Queensland Resources Council chief executive Janette Hewson argued the 125km limit is an "arbitrary number".

She said the government uses different radii for different impacts, such as groundwater and air emissions.

"We think that it should be more of a sliding scale that's actually based on science and data."

Janette Hewson says people are fighting approvals on ideologies "really not relevant" to the issue. (Supplied: Queensland Resources Council)

Dr McGrath said the reforms could also restrict the ability of incorporated community groups to bring objections to the Land Court.

He said those groups had played an important role in protecting landholders during the long-running New Acland mine expansion battle on Queensland's Darling Downs.

He represented landowners involved with the Oakey Coal Action Alliance (OCAA), which challenged the expansion that was later approved.

Dr McGrath said incorporated groups such as OCAA could also provide landholders with protection against potentially significant legal costs.

OCAA president and Brymaroo dairy farmer David Vonhoff, who lives 6km from the mine, described the proposed changes as "very disturbing".

"The mining people … dictate terms to the government and the government's just listening to them and not listening to the people that are producing the food on the land," he said.

Mr Vonhoff questioned why people who lived further away should be excluded from the process if they had legitimate concerns about a project.

Mr Last said the bill would streamline the objections process without reducing environmental protections.

"[It's] to deliver a more efficient and targeted framework for objections to mining lease applications while putting a stop to those who lob vexatious claims and intentionally use this process to frustrate or delay project approvals," the minister said.

He said the existing system had left projects such as New Acland without certainty for almost 15 years.

Dale Last says the bill will streamline processes without reducing environmental protections. (Supplied: Arlie Felton-Taylor)

Ms Hewson said, for the mining industry, this was about cutting duplicated red tape.

"It's not about taking people's rights away," she said.

Ms Hewson said they were also seeing activists fighting approvals on ideologies "really not relevant" to the issue.

"Where objections are made … about a project simply for ideological reasons such as climate change."

The bill is the latest in a series of changes by the government aimed at accelerating resource and major-project approvals.

In June, the government launched a review of Queensland's mining rehabilitation financial safeguards.

Then in August, parliament passed critical-minerals laws giving the government new powers to fast-track projects declared "state strategic".

The government has also shown it can retreat from proposed changes, abandoning plans to remove a key approval protecting farmland and groundwater.

The new mining objections bill will now be debated by Queensland parliament.

World.title: Greene to leave Giants ahead of expected move to Cats
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The GWS Giants have confirmed Toby Greene will leave the club to potentially join Geelong ahead of the 2027 season.

The Giants released a brief statement on Thursday morning, announcing Greene's intention to return to his home state of Victoria.

Greene has told the Cats he wants to join the club from next season.

"The Giants have been advised by Toby Greene of his intention to move back to Victoria for family reasons with a view to joining the Geelong Football Club," the statement read.

Giants chief executive Dave Matthews told SEN radio Greene was leaving with the club's wishes.

"That's the decision he has made and we certainly respect that," Matthews said.

"He's been a celebrated figure at our club, a very important person and I know this has been a really tough decision, one he's largely made for family reasons."

Toby Greene (second from right) was a foundation player at the Giants. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Mark Kolbe)

The 32-year-old has been offered a lucrative three-year deal to join Geelong.

Greene can join the Cats as an unrestricted free agent once the free agency period opens on October 2.

"We are really excited Toby wants to join the Geelong Football Club," Cats executive general manager of football, Andrew Mackie, said in a statement.

"We know this was a significant decision for Toby and his family, and we recognise what the Giants have meant to him and respect the contribution he has made to their club.

"We are looking forward to helping Toby write the next chapter of his career at the Cats."

Last week, Greene spoke about his talks with the Cats.

"With Geelong, I've had an open discussion," Greene said last week.

"Told them what I think about and what I wrestle with and they then explained what it would look like for me.

Zak Butters nominates Bulldogs as preferred club Port Adelaide's three-time best and fairest winner announces his desire to join the Victorian team.

"Geelong would be a lot less travel and more time for family. They discussed aspects of the role and how it would look in the team."

The news comes after Zak Butters chose the Western Bulldogs, instead of the Cats, as his preferred destination following his exit from Port Adelaide.

Greene was a foundation player at the Giants, spending 15 seasons at the club.

He debuted in 2012 and kicked 450 goals across 282 senior matches.

Greene won the club's best and fairest award twice and is a three-time All-Australian.

He was named Giants' co-captain in 2022 before becoming the sole skipper the following season.

World.title: The Italian dog breed helping farmers protect their livestock
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

After losing all of his lambs to feral predators, Central West NSW farmer Leo Tompkins turned to livestock guardian dogs to protect his flock.

"We started with one [dog], and our numbers for sheep mortality and lamb mortality dropped drastically," Mr Tompkins said.

" Once we acquired our second dog … we found that we had barely any predation issues whatsoever. "

According to the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences (ABARES), pest animals such as wild dogs, feral pigs and foxes cost farmers almost $1 billion a year in livestock deaths and infrastructure damage.

Maremmano-Abruzzese sheepdogs, better known as Maremmas and named after the Italian regions they hail from, are guardian dogs bred to protect livestock.

The breed has been around for thousands of years.

While alpacas and donkeys are also used as guardian animals, recent research suggests more people could introduce Maremmas as a solution for predators.

Mr Tompkins said his guardian dogs had been an incredible addition to his Wattamondara property.

Maremmas are known to live with their flock to protect livestock from predators. (ABC Central West: Emily Middleton)

"[Wild] dogs were coming onto the property and either predating upon the lambs or the sheep themselves, or essentially playing with them and running them around to the point where they were stressed out and they would die from exhaustion and stress," he said.

"We were looking at losses for mature ewes up to 75 per cent of the flock … and then the entire lamb crop in multiple instances would be taken out by a neighbourhood wild dog."

Mr Tompkins looked at a number of options, including predator-proof fences, but found Maremmas were the most economical choice.

"They're not a silver bullet, but they are very effective at helping stop predation of livestock once trained and bonded appropriately," he said.

Research backed

University of Tasmania guardian dog researcher Linda van Bommel said the presence of a Maremma sent a message "to everything that's out there that there's a big dog there, and you'd better stay away".

Linda van Bommel says Maremmas can significantly reduce livestock deaths. (Supplied)

"It's up to the predator to decide whether it heeds that message or not, and sometimes they get a bit ballsy, and they go in anyway."

Ms van Bommel has researched Maremmas for 20 years and surveyed 150 producers who used livestock guardian dogs.

About 66 per cent of the farmers said predation stopped after their dogs started working, and a further 30 per cent said predation had significantly decreased.

Training guardian dogs is crucial to ensuring they are committed to protecting the flock and happy to be handled by owners. (ABC Central West: Emily Middleton)

"In a lot of cases, even that decrease in predation can make the difference for a farmer, whether they're able to keep running their business with a profit, or it's just not really viable anymore," Ms van Bommel said.

"[One farm] did not get any lambs whatsoever … because the moment they gave birth, the lambs were just eaten.

"They went into guardian dogs … their lambing went up to about 70 per cent … just that difference of the before and after dogs, it's really striking."

Using guardian dogs

Just as it is in a kelpie's nature to herd, it is in a Maremma's nature to guard.

But they require training to ensure they voluntarily want to live with and protect the flock, while also still being approachable to their owners for feeding and veterinary purposes.

It involves introducing the dog to the flock from a young age, and slowly ensuring a positive unsupervised time between them.

Maremmas on a chicken farm in Central West NSW. (ABC Central West: Emily Middleton)

But despite the high success rate, Ms van Bommel said the uptake was low due to lack of training and management information.

"They're probably one of the most effective predator control methods that Australia has, but you do need to manage them properly," she said.

"There's very little information available for farmers who actually want to try guardian dogs … everybody's pretty much left reinventing the wheel for themselves."

Maremmas have proven to help considerably against predation. (ABC Central West: Emily Middleton)

Farmer training

Paul Gibbs, senior biosecurity officer with Central Tablelands Local Land Services, said farmers were looking to manage the growing feral animal problem in every way possible.

He is running guardian dog workshops in the Central West later this month.

"What I'm trying to do is let people have a good think about whether this is an option for them, whether it fits into their enterprise," Mr Gibbs said.

"It's not all smooth sailing; you have to understand you've got another animal that needs looking after.

World.title: Country police dangle $20 reward for sober drivers
World.content:
Police patrolling the streets of a small town in southern Western Australia are taking a novel approach to reward good drivers, offering a $20 reward to those blowing zero when breath tested.

Officers in Manjimup, 290 kilometres south of Perth, are handing out 100 of the $20 vouchers during traffic stops throughout September to support a local road safety initiative.

The campaign to encourage safe driving will target footy finals in September. (Supplied: WA Police)

Officer-in-charge Sergeant Tyler Winter said the September timeframe was a deliberate call, with football finals and the looming school holidays seeing more people on the road.

"[We are] trying to recognise good driver behaviour because of the terrible road toll we are seeing this year," he said.

"If they are doing the right thing, if they are not breaking any laws, and they blow zero, then we may give them one of the $20 vouchers."

Manjimup police are rewarding drivers who stay sober with random $20 vouchers. (Supplied: WA Police )

He said the unique inversion of the no-tolerance approach to drink driving had emerged from the local road safety committee.

"[They] thought that maybe if we have a positive interaction and reinforce when people do the right thing, then maybe the message will get through," Sergeant Winter said.

Police are ramping up road safety efforts in Manjimup in September. (Supplied: WA Police)

Criminologist unconvinced

Criminologist Matthew Morgan, from the Australian Catholic University, agreed it was a novel approach, and said he would be interested to see the results.

But he said the vouchers would probably do more to build rapport between police and the community than reduce drink driving.

"It's definitely a PR exercise on behalf of police. I definitely think it's a good way of building interest with the community," Dr Morgan said.

" [Whether] it will prevent drink driving is the million-dollar question. I'm not convinced it will. "

However, Dr Morgan said research did indicate drivers tended to respond well to immediate feedback.

He pointed to roadside electronic speed checks, which displayed a smiling or frowning face in response to a driver's adherence to the speed limit, as a small-scale example.

"That instant feedback stimulates our reward systems in the brain, and it actually has been proven to limit speeding on our roads," he said.

Manjimup is a three-hour drive south of Perth. (ABC South West: Andrew Williams)

"Whether you go to the football and think I'm not going to speed because I might get $20, I don't know."

Community funding for new approach

The vouchers, worth $2,000, were funded through Drug and Alcohol support service Holyoake, which sits on the local road safety committee.

Team leader Jo Woodruff said the organisation would ask police to collect data to help them assess how effective the program had been.

"This effectively is our first run, so it is going to be our baseline, with the hope that we would do this in subsequent years and see some improvements," she said.

" It really does recognise people who are doing the right thing around Manjimup during the footy season. "

A WA police spokesperson said it supported a variety of local Blow Zero initiatives around the state, with Moora police in the Wheatbelt previously trying a similar voucher program.

Moora, about 170km north of Perth in WA's Wheatbelt region, has also offered incentives for safe driving. (ABC News: Herlyn Kaur)

"They are not WA police state-wide enforcement programs and are not typically subject to formal performance measures or statewide statistical reporting," the spokesperson said.

With next weekend's AFL Grand Final falling on the King's Birthday long weekend in WA, double demerits will be in force across the state.

World.title: Cheryl Grimmer's family 'deeply angry' as decision to drop case upheld
World.content:
Cheryl Grimmer's family says it is devastated after the NSW director of public prosecutions upheld the decision to abandon the case over the three-year-old's disappearance.

Cheryl disappeared from Fairy Meadow Beach near Wollongong on January 12, 1970.

Her body has never been recovered.

Her brother, Ricki Nash, has strongly criticised the outcome of a formal request under the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP) Victims' Right Of Review Policy.

"I am utterly disgusted, devastated and deeply angry at what our family has received," he said.

The review examined the decision to discontinue proceedings against a man known by the pseudonym "Mercury", who had been charged over Cheryl's disappearance.

The prosecution collapsed in 2019 after the NSW Supreme Court excluded admissions Mercury made to police when he was 17.

Cheryl Grimmer's family say they will continue fighting for answers. (ABC News)

Justice Robert Hulme found the interview did not meet legal requirements applying to admissions made by children, including safeguards concerning the presence of an adult.

DPP finds ruling cannot be challenged

In a two-page letter emailed to the family on September 16, director of public prosecutions Sally Dowling SC acknowledged the impact of the original decision and their patience while the review was conducted.

Ms Dowling said she had reviewed the case "afresh to determine if the decision not to proceed further was correct".

"As you appreciate, this question turns on whether the exclusion of the recorded interview with Mercury by the trial judge is reasonably open to challenge.

" After careful consideration I have concluded that it is not, and that therefore the original decision to take no further proceedings following that ruling was correct. "

She told the family her review led her to conclude 'there are not reasonable prospects of succeeding in a challenge to the trial judge's determination" on Mercury's admissions.

She said she appreciated the determination would be very disappointing for the family and offered to meet with them to discuss the decision.

UK-based geneticist Michael Grimmer compiled the family's detailed submissions seeking a fresh review of his cousin Cheryl's case. (Supplied: Polly Gibney)

Mr Nash said the family had provided 50 detailed submissions, setting out extensive evidence and legal arguments.

" We have received an extraordinarily brief determination. To describe the findings as disappointing is an understatement. "

Mr Nash said the repose provided little detail explaining how those matters were actually dealt with.

The family believed the review focused on whether the original ruling could be challenged, rather than fully reconsidering and responding to the issues it raised.

"That distinction matters enormously to us. There is also something else that cannot be ignored."

Serious admissions excluded from case

He said Mercury's admissions contained details about Cheryl and her disappearance that raised questions about how he could have known them.

Ricki Nash says the family is devastated and angry at the outcome of the DPP's review. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

''The fact that such extraordinary admissions were made is precisely why our family believes the circumstances surrounding them deserved the most rigorous examination possible."

He said the family did not expect the DPP to automatically agree with them, but did expect an application under the Victims' Right of Review Policy to provide "meaningful scrutiny".

"Our family is devastated and angry, but we are not going to stop asking questions.

" We owe that to Cheryl. She was only three years old. Cheryl deserves better. "

The review is separate from the family's request for NSW Police to assess what it describes as significant new evidence that emerged after the prosecution ended.

That material includes accounts from potential witnesses who came forward following renewed publicity generated by BBC reporter Jon Kay's podcast, Fairy Meadow.

The ABC has contacted the ODPP for comment.

World.title: Depleted, doubted and written off, yet somehow the Swans are just one win from another grand final
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Depleted, doubted and written off, yet somehow the Swans are just one win from another grand final September 17, 2026 — 11:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Sydney and Fremantle dominated much of the home-and-away season, yet it may have taken the events of the past few weeks to bring out their best finals football. Footballers often talk about embracing a backs-against-the-wall mentality. When expectations are stripped away and the outside world begins to doubt you, the task can suddenly become simpler. Roles become clearer, players turn towards one another and the focus narrows to what can be controlled. Friday’s AFL preliminary final pits Patrick Voss and the Fremantle Dockers against Tom Papley and the Sydney Swans. Matt Willis Both preliminary finalists have reached that point, although through vastly different circumstances. Sydney has spent the past few weeks under an intense – and deserved – spotlight after the Pullman hotel scandal. This should not be framed as adversity simply happening to the club; the damage was caused from within. Nor should the Swans’ football be used to excuse or erase what occurred.



The more revealing question now is how the remaining players have responded. The Swans have acknowledged the disappointment and its impact on the club and community, then turned their attention towards what they can control. Rather than allowing the situation to fracture the playing group, Sydney has galvanised and produced some of its most connected football of the season. Perhaps being depleted, doubted and largely written off has given the Swans the clarity they needed. They are no longer carrying the expectation of a dominant home-and-away team. Instead, they are playing like a group with its back against the wall and something to prove. Their football against Brisbane suggested exactly that.



Sydney’s 53-point qualifying-final victory was not built around individuals trying to compensate for the talent missing from the side. It came through role clarity, collective effort and complete commitment to the contest. Every player appeared to understand exactly what the team needed from them. Even when captain Callum Mills ruptured his ACL early in the match, the Swans did not lose their heads when they easily could have. Mills had shouldered much of the responsibility that comes with being captain throughout the previous few weeks, making his injury an even crueller blow. Yet Sydney remained composed and focused on what it could control: playing football that its supporters and the broader community could be proud of again. Loading The Swans’ performance at the centre bounce embodied that mindset. They scored 39 points from centre-bounce clearances against Brisbane – their third-highest return from that source across the past five seasons. Sydney won the centre clearances 19-9, first possessions 20-10 and hitouts to advantage 5-1. Most importantly, it outscored the Lions 39-6 from centre-bounce clearances.



Those numbers reveal more than midfield dominance. They demonstrate a team playing proactively. Sydney did not enter the final hoping to absorb Brisbane’s pressure and simply remain in the contest. The Swans attacked from the game’s most direct starting point, generating territory and scoreboard impact before the Lions could establish their defensive structure. That will be critical again against Fremantle. Sydney is equal-first in the competition for scoring from offensive one-on-one contests. Clean centre clearances allow Charlie Curnow and Logan McDonald to attack before opposition defenders receive support. If Brodie Grundy and the Swans midfield can again win first possession and move the ball with speed, Fremantle’s backs will be placed under immediate pressure.



However, the Dockers are one of the best-equipped teams to handle that challenge. Fremantle loses only 21 per cent of its defensive one-on-one contests, the second-best result in the AFL. Its defenders can hold up individually when required, and that starts with inspirational captain Alex Pearce. Charlie Curnow delivered the goods in his first final for the Swans, with five goals. Sam Mooy The Dockers understand when to roll across and help, when to remain accountable and how to delay the opposition long enough for their defensive system to assemble. That creates one of the preliminary final’s defining contests: Sydney’s ability to generate quick, isolated opportunities against Fremantle’s capacity to slow the ball and protect its defenders.



The battle at the opposite end will be equally important. Related Article Explainer

Draft Talent is just the start. What do footy recruiters look for in young players? Fremantle averages 39.4 points from defensive-half chains, ranking second behind Sydney. These are the AFL’s two best teams at turning defence into attack, so the quality of their forward entries will have consequences in both directions. A rushed kick inside 50m will not simply waste an attacking opportunity. It can quickly become the beginning of an opposition scoring chain at the other end. The team that uses the ball with greater composure going forward, while maintaining its defensive structure behind the play, will have an enormous advantage.



Like Sydney, Fremantle may have needed to feel vulnerable again before rediscovering its boldest football. After finishing minor premier, the Dockers carried enormous expectation into September. Their qualifying-final loss to Hawthorn intensified that pressure and created the possibility of a straight-sets exit after such a strong home-and-away season. Expectations were high at Fremantle training this week. Getty Images Suddenly, their backs were against the wall. The focus was no longer on what finishing first entitled them to achieve, but what they were prepared to do to keep their season alive. The victory over Geelong changed their September story.



It was Fremantle’s first finals win since 2022 and secured its first preliminary-final appearance since 2015. More importantly, the Dockers proved to themselves they could respond when a final began slipping away. They kicked six goals in the opening quarter, but Geelong recovered and moved eight points ahead during the third term. At that moment, Fremantle could easily have become consumed by the fear of “old Fremantle” resurfacing and another promising season disappearing in September. Instead, the “new Fremantle” reclaimed the game. Luke Jackson drove the response with 25 disposals, 35 hitouts and two goals. Caleb Serong, Andrew Brayshaw and Hayden Young helped restore control around the contest, while Patrick Voss kicked four goals and Josh Treacy responded strongly after a quiet qualifying final.



The battle between Jackson and Grundy will be the defining match-up on Friday night. Fremantle does not necessarily need to dominate at the centre bounce, but it cannot allow Sydney the same clean first possession and direct access it enjoyed against Brisbane. Jackson’s ability to influence the game beyond the ruck contest makes him especially dangerous. Grundy must match him at ground level and prevent him from becoming an extra midfielder, while still giving Sydney’s on-ballers the opportunity to attack. The duel between Sydney’s Brodie Grundy and Fremantle’s Luke Jackson will be critical to Friday night’s preliminary final. AFL Photos via Getty Images There is also another elephant in the room for the Swans. This is a club carrying the scars of its recent grand final record. Sydney has repeatedly been good enough to reach the final day of the season, only to suffer painful defeats once there. Could this campaign be different precisely because it feels so different?



The absence of several stars and the belief that Sydney’s premiership chance had disappeared may have removed some of the suffocating expectation that followed its previous campaigns. The Swans are not yet in another grand final, but playing as the hunter rather than the hunted could help them take the next step towards confronting that hoodoo. Sydney has found strength in the collective. Fremantle has released a different burden. Its first finals victory since 2022 has replaced anxiety with belief and allowed the minor premier to rediscover the bold football that carried it through the season. That is why I believe the Dockers will win. The mind is a powerful thing, and with the weight of expectation finally lifted, Fremantle can play with the freedom and confidence that made it the competition’s best team across the home-and-away season. Both teams have discovered how dangerous they can be with their backs against the wall. On Friday night, I expect Fremantle’s renewed belief to carry it into the grand final.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Cross-examination of complainant ‘M’ resumes as indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Alan Jones’ criminal trial in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney.

Jones, 85, is standing trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent relating to six male complainants over a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. He denies the alleged physical acts occurred.

Alan Jones’ trial resumed on Thursday after a one-day break. Wolter Peeters

On Monday, the third of the six complainants, a former athlete dubbed “M”, started giving evidence.

His cross-examination started on Tuesday, and he returns to the witness box today for further questioning by Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC. “M” has told the court:

Jones kissed him on the corner of his mouth at an event in Sydney about a decade ago. “I think I froze at that time,” “M” said.

He rejected suggestions by Bashir on Tuesday that the alleged kiss didn’t happen.

The court has heard Jones texted “M” after the function: “Great to see you. Sorry I didn’t catch up after, had to go back to work. You looked great. I love you, I hope you can feel my kisses darling xxxx.”

“M” replied: “Nice to see you too. I had a very long day today and I am pleased to be in bed now; thanks mate xoxo.” The conversation ended in “M” saying “let me know when we can catch up. Lots of love” and Jones replying: “I will darling. Big kisses forever.”

“M” agreed during cross-examination that he did not tell police in his statements that Jones kissed him on the lips at the event. But he said that “I believe I pointed to where it was”.

The complainant said he had “a close relationship with Jones over a period of time” and that “in certain areas” he could go to the broadcaster if he needed help.

The court has previously heard that Jones texted “M” on another occasion, after receiving a photo: “I love the photo. I love you. I want to kiss you for hours. That is beautiful. We must catch up darling [name] xxx”. “M” said he did not respond immediately. Hours later, Jones wrote: “I hope my message did not upset you. I love you.” The man said he responded the next day, writing: “Not at all mate. It’s nice to be loved.”

The complainant said he had used the word “mate” for many reasons. “I know I’d made it very clear that ... it wasn’t moving into a relationship, so ‘mate’ was my way of pushing back, I guess.”

Reflecting on the messages, “M” told the court that he believed “it’s a person that is in love with me”, adding that he did not return those feelings.

“M” said that on the last occasion he visited Jones at his harbourside apartment, the broadcaster kissed him on the cheek towards his lips and said words to the effect of, “I love you so much, you don’t know how much I love you.” The complainant said he could feel Jones’ genitals on his leg .

The complainant said he pushed the broadcaster away and said, “OK, mate”, in a tone intended to convey “get away from me”, and “got out of there as quickly as possible”.

The court heard Jones had sent the complainant gifts including weekly flowers for years and a dinner set. The complainant agreed he also sent Jones flowers at least once.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: The special one: why Longmuir is on the cusp of history
World.content:
NationalWAFremantle Dockers The special one: why Longmuir is on the cusp of history Justin Chadwick September 17, 2026 — 11:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In September 2006, Justin Longmuir was preparing for the biggest match of his life - a preliminary final against Sydney at the SCG. The Dockers lost by 35 points and, just two appearances later, Longmuir’s AFL career was over at the age of 26 due to a debilitating knee injury. Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir speaks to captain Alex Pearce during the team’s finals clash with Hawthorn. Paul Kane/Getty Images The game we love can be so cruel at times. Longmuir knows that more than most. His retirement at such a young age was described as a tragedy by then-Dockers coach Mark Harvey.



But as fate would have it, Longmuir will be back at the SCG on Friday night – some 20 years after that heartbreaking day when Fremantle bombed out of the premiership race. Longmuir’s knees didn’t allow him to reach his full potential as a player during his 139 games in the purple, a grand shame for a ruckman/forward selected with pick No.2 in the 1998 national draft. But his mind might end up being the crucial element that lands Fremantle an elusive flag. So what is it exactly that makes Longmuir so special? And how is it that the coach labelled overly cautious as recently as 2025 is now in charge of one of the AFL’s most electrifying outfits?



Judging Longmuir from the outside can be tough. Related Article Fremantle Dockers Tame Impala frontman reignites calls for end to Woodside’s Dockers sponsorship He’s awkward in front of the cameras; deadpan at times. The 1-0 mantra spruiked after every win this season sums up his public face. The 45-year-old lacks the fearful aura of coaching greats like Mick Malthouse, Denis Pagan and Leigh Matthews. But external perspectives are just that.



What is Longmuir truly like as a coach? The best insight is from his players. There is no shortage of love, admiration and respect for the new-school mentor, the way he backs himself and his players. Shai Bolton knows a thing or two about coaching quality, having won two flags at Richmond under master coach Damien Hardwick. Bolton, who won his second All-Australian blazer this year playing big stints through the midfield, describes Longmuir as “amazing”. “Everyone has different personalities and they coach differently,” Bolton says.



“Dimma is probably a little bit harder on the players. Related Article AFL 2026 Flight of the Dockers: More airline services deployed as purple army sets sights on Sydney “I feel like JL – he’s pretty chill. But when you haven’t played your way, or you haven’t done your role, he can obviously give you a little spray now and then. “But he’s also a kind man and is always willing to have our backs.” Retiring forward Sam Switkowski has spent seven of his nine seasons under Longmuir.



And while there have been external doubts about some of Longmuir’s tactics, especially whether he has been too defensive and conservative in the past, internally it has been 100 per cent faith. “We’ve been trusting him the whole way through,” Switkowski explains. “And just like we’ve improved on field, he’s also improved as a coach. “I love playing for him. I think he’s coaching the best he’s ever coached.” Switkowski has admired the way Longmuir has stuck to his guns even when the external criticism has come thick and fast.



There were even people calling for Longmuir’s head following the club’s embarrassing 61-point loss to St Kilda in round eight last year. “He’s just really confident in his philosophy and his mantra,” Switkowski says. Justin Longmuir, centre, with Leigh Brown and Matthew Pavlich in 2002. “He’s built such strong relationships with his players and his staff, and there’s just so much trust between the players and him.” Powerhouse forward Josh Treacy also admires the way Longmuir sticks to his guns.



“He’s been strong on his beliefs, he’s laid that right from the get-go when he started coaching,” Treacy says. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Purple haze and Friday lights: How Fremantle reclaimed their mojo and kept the dream alive “And that belief and trust has continued to build and grow within our group, and he’s continued to show that, which has allowed guys to flourish.” Midfielder Neil Erasmus is one of those many Dockers to flourish under Longmuir. “Team defence, that’s what gets him excited, and that’s what makes us such a strong team,” Erasmus says.



“He’s a very honest guy, and he’s grown so much as a coach during the five years I’ve been here. “He cares a lot about his players and he cares a lot about the club. “He’s an unreal human and unreal coach.” Former Demons defender Judd McVee has been impressed by what he’s seen and heard from “the best bloke” during his first season at the Dockers. “There is probably a bit of outside noise about him, but everyone internally loves him,” McVee says.



“My transition over, I couldn’t be more thankful for him. He backs me in, and he believes in me. “He’s just so smart with the levers he can pull, and he’s very tactical.” Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir addresses his charges during the round 23 clash with the Adelaide Crows. Getty Images Longmuir, whose first season as coach was spent in COVID hubs during 2020, isn’t afraid to hit back at critics. Whether they are taking a swipe at his handball happy game style or selection calls, Longmuir has full belief in himself and his players.



Fremantle were the clear trendsetters this year, snaring a club-record 14 consecutive wins on the way to the minor premiership. When the Western Bulldogs tried to flood Fremantle into submission in round 21, Longmuir quipped “good luck” when asked if he thought other teams would follow suit. It wasn’t arrogance – rather a sense of pride and confidence in what had been created at Fremantle. Longmuir believes his players possess the tools to overcome any challenge, and he’s encouraging them to play with freedom. After a wake-up call from Hawthorn and a pressure-laden passed test against Geelong, now a decimated Swans outfit stands in Fremantle’s way.



Longmuir couldn’t do it 20 years earlier at the SCG as a player. But it would be only fitting if he guides the current Flagmantle train into a grand final. AAP

World.title: Grass greener on the other side as Smith builds career-best team
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Grass greener on the other side as Smith builds career-best team Craig Kerry September 17, 2026 — 11:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Trainer Matt Smith says he has never had a better collection of elite horses as the one spearheaded by his line-up this week. And the Warwick Farm horseman, who had his first runner in 2003 after learning from racing royalty Aidan O’Brien and Bart Cummings, has no doubt his Luskin Park property and the help of “Dr Green” has made a difference. Warwick Farm trainer Matthew Smith with Everest hopeful Headwall. Janie Barrett/SMH At Randwick on Saturday in group 2 races, Smith has Headwall striving in The Shorts to cement a slot in the $20 million Everest, group 1-winner Idle Flyer aiming to bounce back in the 7 Stakes and Queen’s Gamble stepping up to the Tea Rose Stakes. On Friday, exciting stayer Aethelwulf rises to stakes grade in the group 3 Newcastle Cup (2300m) as the favourite. “I’ve never had a group this strong,” said Smith, who sits equal second on the Sydney premiership with nine winners at 23.1 per cent.



“It’s a nice bunch of horses to have all going at the one time. It’s not like that very often.” Smith’s stable collected a career-best $6.94 million in prizemoney last season, capping a rise in runners and success since 2020 when he and wife, Melissa, bought the 46-hectare Luskin Park, where champion Luskin Star was bred, in the Lower Hunter as a spelling and pre-training property. They are building a 25-box stable there and hope to increase their numbers and day-to-day training at the facility in a year. “It’s definitely made a big difference,” he said. “Mel and I had been looking for years for a place, we knew that’s what we wanted to do. “I’d worked over in Ireland and I’d followed that way of training, having that ability to freshen horses mid-prep and give them a break mentally as well.



“A lot of horses can feel the strain mentally and they start to fall apart, so if you can get them up there and back to nature, you can’t underestimate the value of a horse just putting his head down in a paddock and having a pick of grass. “It’s a bit like us doing something we like, going fishing or whatever. You are not thinking about anything except what’s in front of you. It’s the same thing for horse. Day in, day out galloping, galloping and racing, it just catches up with them. “I read a book on [legendary trainer of Northern Dancer] Horatio Luro and he used to call grass Dr Green. He was always wanting his horses to be picking grass. It’s great to give them a time out. It rejuvenates them. They come back in from the farm and they want to go.” Seven-year-old Headwall showed he was back with a bang in the Concorde Stakes after a year out because of a pastern injury, surging late to finish second to Tempted two weeks ago. An Everest slot beckons if Headwall ($3.30) can repeat the effort in The Shorts (1100m), where he has gate five. Headwall, right, chases home Tempted in the Concorde. Getty Images



“He came out of that run really good and he looks super,” Smith said. “We haven’t got an Everest spot yet, but I think if he ran well, he will get one. If he can back up that first-up run. It will be bloody exciting if we can get one. “We just need a bit of room, a split at the right time with him. He’s one of those horses that always gets back amongst them.” Queen’s Gamble ($8) enters the Princess Series for three-year-old fillies at the 1400m Tea Rose after dominant Warwick Farm wins at 1300m and 1400m, following three placings over shorter trips. “She’s a nice filly and she just keeps getting better and better,” Smith said.



“She’s got the advantage of having that run over the trip and at 1300. A lot of these horses wouldn’t have run 1400m, so if something goes hard in front, it will find a few of them out.” He was looking for a guide on where to go next with Idle Flyer ($26), which races third up in the 7 Stakes (1600m) after a disappointing effort last start. The Queen Of The Turf winner had every chance in the 1400m Tramway when finishing three lengths fourth. Zac Lloyd rides Idle Flyer to victory in the Angst Stakes at Randwick last October. Getty Images “She had no real excuses really,” he said of the run. “She just didn’t let go like she can do, but getting up to the mile will suit her better.



“After that we will make a decision on where we go. Probably Epsom.” The 7 Stakes, headlined by Autumn Glow ($1.15), was down to five runners with the scratchings of Lindermann and Lady Shenandoah. Stayer Aethelwulf is perhaps Smith’s most exciting prospect. The four-year-old has won four of his five starts by big margins this preparation, rising in distance and class each time. The Metropolitan or Bart Cummings beckon if he wins. Aethelwulf cruises to victory last start at Rosehill. Getty Images “He hasn’t missed a beat so far, he’s just got to run the trip,” Smith said. “We obviously like him a lot, but he’s just got to keep stepping up. You don’t know when they are going to hit their mark. If he keeps winning, you’re going to keep going.”

World.title: Symbolic ‘first mango tray of the season’ raises $70,000 for charity
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity life Symbolic ‘first mango tray of the season’ raises $70,000 for charity Neesha Sinnya September 17, 2026 — 11:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The season’s symbolic first tray of mangoes has sold at the Brisbane Markets for a whopping $70,000, with its buyer crowned this year’s “mango monarch”. The auction marks the beginning of the mango season, and raises money for charities Redkite and the Lady Musgrave Trust. Elijah Etri, the manager at 24/7 Wellington Point produce spot Skippy’s Fresh Frootz, took the crown of mango monarch. Elijah Etri from Skippy’s was crowned this year’s monarch after securing the symbolic first tray of the season. Neesha Sinnya “We don’t think about what it’s costing us, we think about what it’s going towards,” Etri said.



“Everyone keeps asking what we’re going to do with a $70,000 mango tray … we can’t sell it, we’d have to sell them at $5,000 a mango. “We will take it home, share it amongst ourselves, and relish in what we won today.” Thea Sitcheff from Redkite said their share of the funds would be able to support eight families for a year, including counselling and financial assistance. Redkite works with families dealing with childhood cancer, while the Lady Musgrave Trust is focused on supporting homeless women and children.



Lady Musgrave Trust chief executive Victoria Parker said the auction was her favourite fundraising event of the year. “It’s always a joy … the money raised is so valuable toward supporting young women and children across Queensland who are experiencing homelessness, which is a really big issue,” Parker said. The $70,000 mango tray, filled with 14 Kensington Prides, came from NT Happy in Darwin and is part of Australian Mangoes’ first crop of the season. “First season fruit is always the best,” Jenna McManus from Australian Mangoes said. “[This year’s] fruit set is looking phenomenal, flowering … it’s a good indication of a great season.”



Last year the first tray of mangoes sold for $66,000 to Chris Frame from the Standard Market Company. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ASX gains as oil prices ease; Wall Street falls as Fed chief spooks investors
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX gains as oil prices ease; Wall Street falls as Fed chief spooks investors Staff writers Updated September 17, 2026 — 11:10am ,first published September 17, 2026 — 4:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket opened higher on Thursday, shrugging off falls on Wall Street following the Federal Reserve’s first interest rate rise in three years, as oil prices dropped for a second day on signs of easing Middle East supply disruptions. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 26.3 points, or 0.3 per cent, at 8722.80 as of 10.55am AEST, with eight of its 11 sectors in the green. The upbeat morning - despite futures indicating a sharp fall - came after the local bourse added 0.3 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar traded flat at US70.90¢. Fed chair Kevin Warsh’s warnings on inflation spooked Wall Street. AP Photo/Seth Wenig West Texas Intermediate fell toward $US101 a barrel, after losing 3.2 per cent on Wednesday, the most since August 4. Brent crude was back below $US105, having reached almost $US110 in recent days. Saudi Arabia is seeking to return about half the capacity of its damaged East-West pipeline within days, and full operations in six weeks, a person familiar said. The oil price reprieve boosted shares of fuel-dependent companies such as airlines Qantas (up 1.7 per cent) and Virgin Australia (up 5 per cent), but weighed on the energy sector, sending oil and gas giants Woodside and Santos down 1.4 per cent and 2.2 per cent, respectively.



The ASX’s gains in early trade were bolstered by the big four banks, which were all up between 0.9 per cent and 1.4 per cent. Consumer discretionary stocks such as Bunnings and Officeworks owner Wesfarmers (up 0.8 per cent), electronics chain JB Hi-Fi (up 0.5 per cent) and furniture seller Harvey Norman (up 0.5 per cent) also did well. The mining heavyweights BHP (up 0.4 per cent), Rio Tinto (up 0.7 per cent) and Fortescue (up 0.9 per cent) also helped, all advancing as prices for iron ore strengthened overnight. Related Article Breaking

Media & marketing ABC slams watchdog finding that Four Corners program failed impartiality test Gold stocks, however, slumped after the Fed’s rate rise and its signals of more to come, making gold less attractive as an investment because it doesn’t pay interest. Northern Star Resources fell 1 per cent, Newmont lost 1.7 per cent and Evolution Mining dropped 0.8 per cent. On Wall Street, US stocks slipped after the Federal Reserve hiked its main interest rate for the first time in three years and suggested more may be ahead as it tries to get the nation’s high inflation under control.



The S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent after giving up a modest gain from earlier in the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite was nearly unchanged after edging down by less than 0.1 per cent. Investors generally prefer lower interest rates because higher rates slow the economy’s growth and undercut prices for stocks and other investments. The US stock market initially held on to its modest, early gains after the Fed announced its decision. The short-term pain of a slower economy may be worth it if it starves inflation of its fuel and gets further increases for the cost of living back to the Fed’s 2 per cent target. But stock prices weakened later in the session as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said repeatedly in a press conference that inflation remains too high and the US economy appears to be strengthening. That could imply the world’s largest economy is solid enough to withstand more hikes to rates, and other officials at the Fed provided their own forecasts suggesting rates may need to go still higher. “We removed a dose of accommodation so that financial and credit conditions would be more consistent with our ultimate objectives,” Warsh said. “Today’s action starts to show we’re serious about this, and we will deliver on the price stability objective.”



Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh speaks at a news conference following the decision. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein The median Fed official expects the federal funds rate to end this year at 4.1 per cent, according to forecasts published after the central bank’s meeting. That’s up from its current range of 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent following Wednesday’s increase, and it’s up from the median forecast of 3.8 per cent that Fed officials gave three months ago. Traders, meanwhile, suspect the Fed may go even further. They’re betting on a 38 per cent probability the Fed could hike the federal funds rate to a range of 4.25 per cent to 4.50 per cent by the end of the year, according to data from CME Group. “Clearly the Warsh commentary was much more bluntly hawkish than investors expected,” said Nathan Thooft, a senior portfolio manager at Manulife Investment Management. It’s the first hike by the Fed to interest rates in three years. The central bank had been on pause for months following cuts to rates in 2024 and 2025, even though inflation has consistently remained above the Fed’s 2 per cent target.



President Donald Trump has been lobbying for interest rates to go lower rather than higher. On Wall Street, bank stocks fell to some of the market’s sharper losses. A slower US economy could mean less demand for loans from them. Banks also get hurt when the gap narrows between short-term interest rates and longer-term ones because the industry makes profit off the difference. Related Article Updated

Federal Reserve Fed defies Trump, raises US interest rates for first time in three years Following the Fed’s announcements, the two-year Treasury yield jumped to 4.74 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Tuesday. It tends to closely follow expectations for what the Fed will do with the federal funds rate. The yield on the longer-term 10-year Treasury, meanwhile, takes into account expectations for economic growth and inflation years down the line. It had a more modest increase, ticking up to 5.01 per cent from 5.00 per cent late Tuesday.



Huntington Bancshares fell 5.6 per cent, Citizens Financial Group sank 4.8 per cent and JPMorgan Chase slipped 1 per cent. Helping to limit the market’s losses were gains for some influential stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry. Nvidia rose 0.8 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices climbed 1.6 per cent to recover more of their losses from earlier in the week. AI stocks slid worldwide Monday after leaders of the AI industry called for a slowdown in development to address safety issues for humanity. Microsoft slipped 1.4 per cent. Overnight, its artificial intelligence chief Mustafa Suleyman warned infusing tools like Anthropic’s Claude with humanlike characteristics increases the risks of such systems going rogue. In an essay, the longtime artificial intelligence developer took aim at some of the language in the guiding documents behind Claude, Anthropic PBC’s popular family of large language models. Claude’s constitution expresses ambiguity about whether the assistant is a moral entity, positing that the software may have “some functional version of emotions or feelings.”



In other international markets, indexes rose across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1.4 per cent for one of the world’s biggest gains. with AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
