World.title: ‘I was blocking that vision’: How Jess Fox helped her sister beat her to Olympic gold
World.content:
NationalGood Weekend ‘I was blocking that vision’: How Jess Fox helped her sister beat her to Olympic gold Tim Elliott September 17, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Noémie Fox, 29, and sister Jess Fox, 32, are Olympic champion kayakers, and have been both rivals and allies, in and out of the water. Noémie: Jess and I were born in Marseille, where our mum’s from, but came to Australia in 2000 when our dad became head coach of the Australian canoe slalom team for the Sydney Olympics. I was about two-and-half, and Jess was three years older, so she took care of me. She was good at music and sport and was dux of the school. She helped me with my notes, and teachers loved me because they’d had Jess who’d been a pleasure to teach. When we were young, Jess was always easy to live with, whereas I was the squeaky wheel. A lot of my childhood, she’d be like, “OK, if you want the bigger room, you can have it.” That’s something I never would’ve been able to let go. I’m still like that. I’ll lose my hair tie while kayaking and she’ll be like, “Have mine. I don’t need it.”



Jess began competing at school, and I started when I was a bit older. She made it look easy, but I wasn’t such a fast learner. There was a bit of jealousy, naturally. I was envious: I thought, why is she so good and I can’t get there? At her first world championships in 2013, she won the canoe. At my first world junior championships, I came 11th. Related Article Good Weekend She nearly quit the pool at 14. Now, Mollie’s the face of a new Australian era Our parents had both been Olympian kayakers and my sister was world number one, so I began feeling like the black sheep, like I didn’t belong because I wasn’t at their level. I was always watching from the grandstands and helping Jess train, so her wins kind of belonged to the whole family – but, still, I constantly felt like a disappointment, even after I started getting better results. Jess understood and tried to lift me up, but there’s only so much help you want from your older sister. It’s especially hard because in our sport, there’s only one spot at the Olympics, so I had to beat Jess to get in the team, and she was so far ahead. In 2020, I “quiet quit” kayaking and did other things: I worked with L’Occitane in Switzerland and visited my grandma in France. Then a new event, called kayak cross, was introduced for the 2024 Paris Olympics. It opened up extra spots in the Australian team, and it resonated with me because it’s more messy. It was only then that I got out of that victim mindset of “I’m never going to make it”. I thought, “This is going to be something that’ll be mine.” I also decided, when I began training, that I’d learn from Jess and her ability to compartmentalise, which I’m terrible at. I get distracted by my environment, but she’s a magpie: she takes the shiny things and leaves the shit. Even with her surgery in 2025 [for a kidney tumour that proved to be benign], I would’ve panicked but she just went, “What can I take from this to learn and grow?” Jess Fox shares the joy after Noémie wins a gold medal in the kayak cross at the Paris Games. AP



In the end, I qualified for the Paris Games. I actually knocked Jess out in the first round. She came over, gave me a hug and said, “Take it all the way.” When I won [gold], she was the first one running down to the finish line. I think Australia loved seeing that moment: me, the little sister knocking her out, and the sportsmanship that she showed in return. Jess: My first memory was of Noémie being about four, and wanting to be involved with whatever I was doing. I’d be reading a book, gently turning the pages, and she’d be jumping up and down, saying, “Let me read your book!” When we came to Australia from France, we lived in Glenmore Park [west of Sydney] for a year before moving to Emu Plains [near the Blue Mountains]. We liked sport – swimming, gymnastics. As the younger sibling, you always tag along to whatever the older one’s doing. Noémie would see me do something and try to copy. When I learnt to ride a bike, I spent ages on training wheels, building my confidence. But then, one day, I hear this banging and clanging in the garage, and there’s Noémie, about three years old, teaching herself how to ride a bike, no training wheels, nothing, just going at it. Jess Fox with her silver medal at the London Olympics in 2012. Reuters At the same time, she was super-girly. Our grandmother, who we visited every year in France, had this big jewellery box, and Noémie was always trying on her necklaces, or cooking with her. Meanwhile, I was a tomboy, running around in shorts and a T-shirt.



She didn’t enjoy paddling at the start. She had a traumatic experience when she was 10: she flipped over in a kayak and was upside-down, underwater, and couldn’t get back up. Her instructor rescued her, but she didn’t paddle for a year after that. Eventually, I told her, “It’s scary to get back in, but that’s how you overcome the fear.” I had success early on. I was a junior world champion at 16, and competed at the Olympics at 18. For a long time, she was on the riverbank, in the crowds, watching and supporting. It was hard for her, especially when she started competing. I wanted her to paddle to her potential, but she knew that to beat me, she had to beat the world number one. I also struggled with it! I thought, “Is it selfish to be hogging that position? Or is that just elite sport, and if you beat me, fair play?” It’s brutal. Either way, she was always there to support me and train, which was pretty selfless. ‘I knew that she’d never let herself dream of being an Olympian because I was blocking that vision.’ Jess Fox Noémie didn’t want paddling to be her only identity, which is amazing because, for a lot of athletes, it’s the only thing you know. She got an internship overseas with L’Occitane during COVID and commentated during the Tokyo Olympics. But when kayak cross was added to the Paris Olympics, I told her: “OK, you’ve got to commit. You might not qualify, but there’s three people who will, so why not you?” When she decided to have a go, we started training together like sparring partners. The day she qualified, in Prague, I was running along the bank, screaming. My heart rate was like 180, and I lost my voice. When she actually won gold, it was the most euphoric moment because I knew that she’d never let herself dream of being an Olympian because I was blocking that vision. It’s been a complex relationship: you can be jealous as the younger sister, or you can feel resentment but, at the same time, she has loved and supported me. Luckily, we’ve always been brought up knowing that our paddling career is only a certain number of years, but we’ve got our whole life as sisters.

World.title: Should I keep waiting for Mr Darcy? Jane Austen answers your most pressing questions
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It is a truth universally acknowledged that every new generation must be in want of their own set of Jane Austen adaptions. This year sees the release on Netflix of Dolly Alderton’s take on Pride and Prejudice (starring Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden) and a new film version of Sense and Sensibility (with Daisy Edgar-Jones), written by Australia’s Diana Reid. Alderton and Reid are two voices of our generation whose novels have tackled some of the great questions of our time: Why do men ghost? How do you recover from a toxic friendship? Why is there never any food at hen’s parties? Dating apps might be our ballroom and we join run clubs instead of practising the harpsichord, but at the end of the day, put a group of young women together in 1811 or 2026 and the agenda will still be: who we love, economic security, sibling and parent drama and irritating in-laws. These topics remain so current that we can still turn to the mother of the romance novel through the lens of an agony aunt, and ask the same question that women have asked for centuries… what would Jane Austen suggest? 1. I haven’t found my Mr Darcy. Should I settle for less? Colin Firth as Mr Darcy in the 1995 BBC adaptation of Pride and Prejudice. We all want Wentworth or Darcy (or Colin Firth or Paul Rudd) to declare they love us just the way we are – despite our lack of self-awareness or ridiculous family or muddy skirts or whatever our red flag is. Who doesn’t aspire to a love so great it transforms them? The best advice here is to channel Elizabeth Bennet, from Pride and Prejudice. Lizzie knows her value and is (with self-awareness and a sense of humour) uncompromising about demanding her worth and not accepting less, even when everyone around her is urging her to settle.



You deserve the guy who sees everything wrong with you and loves you desperately anyway. And the giant house. 2. I’ve been ghosted. How should I respond? Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood and George MacKay as Edward Ferrars in Sense and Sensibility. Focus Features Related Article Literature Sorry, Jane Austen, but these Australian novels had us at hello In Sense and Sensibility, Marianne Dashwood is ghosted by Willoughby. She’s devastated when she writes him letter after letter with no reply. The first thing you should do is to stop texting him. Then you’re allowed to cry, refuse to get out of bed and look terrible. Soon you, like Marianne, will lose your whole heart again to someone better – your own Colonel Brandon/ young Alan Rickman. Happiness will be the ultimate revenge. In the end Willoughby regrets ghosting Marianne and spends the rest of his life thinking of her as the perfect woman, holding her up on a pedestal. Let’s assume that the same thing will happen to the guy who ghosted you. 3. My friend is getting serious about a boring, egotistical know-all. What should I do? Jennifer Ehle as Elizabeth Bennet and Lucy Scott as Charlotte Lucas in the celebrated BBC adaptation of Pride and Prejudice.



Again, be a Lizzie. When Elizabeth Bennet’s best friend Charlotte announces she’s marrying Mr Collins, who is all ick, Lizzie calls her out on it. Once. Then, when she realises Charlotte has made up her mind, she pivots to silently judging her decision and outwardly supporting her friend. There’s an unspoken agreement to ignore Mr Collins (where possible). Pride and Prejudice gives us the perfect playbook for when your friends get serious with someone who’s mid. You get one chance to attempt an intervention. Then, you must fall back to a position of quiet disdain and open solidarity. After a while (usually after the wedding), you’ll both mostly pretend he doesn’t exist. 4. I’m single and can’t afford to buy a house. What are my options? This is a very Jane Austen coded dilemma – her plots are often real estate-centred. Many of her novels begin with a cost-of-living crisis. In Sense and Sensibility, the Dashwoods solve their housing crisis by moving into a distant relative’s cottage. A modern-day equivalent might be to move back in with your parents. In Persuasion, the Elliotts rent out their estate and move to Bath. Maybe you could move to a regional town where prices aren’t so insane? Either way, Austen promises that your new locale will be swarming with handsome eligible men (and a few rogues). Some of them might even have enormous (mortgage-free) homes of their own, which will solve your housing dilemma entirely. 5. Working mum life is destroying my soul. Should I become a trad wife? Jane Austen was clear-eyed about women’s economic realities, so she’d be sympathetic to the plight of the modern woman who’s trying to juggle the mental load of paid work, childcare and strength training, all in the same day. You could argue that she’d endorse trad wives’ performative femininity and celebration of marriage and family values. But Austen was critical of anyone who pretends to be something they aren’t (think Harriet in Emma or Brittany Murphy’s Tai in Clueless). From left, Brittany Murphy as Tai and Alicia Silverstone as Cher in Clueless. Paramount Pictures



Related Article Romance A period romance changed my life. I’m not the only one If she were writing today, she’d surely enjoy taking her literary scalpel to women who act (on camera) like they’re living the simple life while cooking their homemade sourdough in gazillion-dollar ovens and flogging expensive homewares to their followers. That said, Austen would be wholly supportive of the running away part. Her heroines are constantly forming parties, jumping into carriages and heading off to London or Bath or the Lake District. The takeaway for those of us on the edge of burnout (and who isn’t?) is not to milk a cow but rather to book a one-way ticket to Bali and return only once cortisol levels have been lowered. 6. Should I be nice to my irritating in-laws? Austen’s novels are full of survival strategies for navigating a spectrum of tricky in-laws. For the super toxic, controlling in-laws (think Mrs Ferrars) you might need to go low-contact. For a more moderately irritating mother-in-law like Mrs Bennet you might want to consider moving to the other side of the country (like Jane and Mr Bingley). If they’re just low-key annoying but ultimately good people, a solid option is to pretend to be deaf or asleep during family gatherings (as demonstrated by Mr Palmer in Sense and Sensibility). 7. I wasn’t picked to be a bridesmaid for a close friend. Should I confront her? Imagine your close friend is Jane Bennet. When you were kids you swapped ribbons, learned to dance the quadrille together and dreamed about your (double) wedding.

And now, finally, she’s engaged to Mr Bingley. Everyone is thrilled. You’re waiting for the call-up to be bridesmaid. Maid of honour even. Except Jane is very close to her sister Elizabeth. And Elizabeth’s husband is the groom’s best friend. So obviously she’s the maid of honour.



There are three other sisters too. Lydia is in disgrace (and can’t be trusted to plan a hen’s). And Mary won’t enjoy the dressing up. But Jane’s far too kind to only ask half of her sisters – so they’ll all be in the bridal party too. And there’s the sister-in-law – Miss Caroline Bingley. Obviously, she shouldn’t be a bridesmaid – she doesn’t even like Jane. If she could break up the couple, she absolutely would. But her brother loves her, so she’s in. Your friend might desperately want you by her side on her big day, but for some (logical or irrational) reason (he wants an equal number of groomsmen, she’s been a serial bridesmaid who feels she should return the favour, she can’t afford to pay for six sets of hair and make-up and bonnets) she hasn’t asked you. Give her another chance. 8. Influencers are making my life feel ordinary. Should I delete all my accounts and get a dumb phone? No! Don’t feel bad about enjoying social media. Austen would have loved social media – though as a lurker, not a poster. And she basically wrote the job description for an influencer at the opening of Emma - someone “handsome, clever and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition”. Emma Woodhouse, a modern hot, rich woman who doesn’t need or want to work, would have an enormous following on Instagram. Her aesthetic would be pastel-hued country chic. Her TikTok would feature themed seasonal dinner parties, unboxing swathes of cashmere and being temporarily enthusiastic about new hobbies. On her podcast (there would be a podcast) she’d give endless advice about dating in the modern world. Anya Taylor-Joy as Emma Woodhouse in Autumn de Wilde’s film of the Jane Austen classic. Universal Pictures You could look at Emma’s grid and think it’s perfect and that she has all the answers. But (as Mr Knightley, regularly tells her, swoon!) she doesn’t. Emma thinks she’s excellent at life. But she (like all the best influencers) has an inflated ego and a big dose of self-delusion. Her lifestyle should not be compared with your own. Her advice is not to be taken. That way misery lies. Just ask Emma’s matchmaking project, Harriet Smith. Treat a glimpse into Emma’s life, into influencers’ lives, as a treat. Then revel in the extraordinary ordinariness of your own.

World.title: Depleted, doubted and written off, yet somehow the Swans are just one win from another grand final
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Depleted, doubted and written off, yet somehow the Swans are just one win from another grand final September 17, 2026 — 11:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Sydney and Fremantle dominated much of the home-and-away season, yet it may have taken the events of the past few weeks to bring out their best finals football. Footballers often talk about embracing a backs-against-the-wall mentality. When expectations are stripped away and the outside world begins to doubt you, the task can suddenly become simpler. Roles become clearer, players turn towards one another and the focus narrows to what can be controlled. Friday’s AFL preliminary final pits Patrick Voss and the Fremantle Dockers against Tom Papley and the Sydney Swans. Matt Willis Both preliminary finalists have reached that point, although through vastly different circumstances. Sydney has spent the past few weeks under an intense – and deserved – spotlight after the Pullman hotel scandal. This should not be framed as adversity simply happening to the club; the damage was caused from within. Nor should the Swans’ football be used to excuse or erase what occurred.



The more revealing question now is how the remaining players have responded. The Swans have acknowledged the disappointment and its impact on the club and community, then turned their attention towards what they can control. Rather than allowing the situation to fracture the playing group, Sydney has galvanised and produced some of its most connected football of the season. Perhaps being depleted, doubted and largely written off has given the Swans the clarity they needed. They are no longer carrying the expectation of a dominant home-and-away team. Instead, they are playing like a group with its back against the wall and something to prove. Their football against Brisbane suggested exactly that.



Sydney’s 53-point qualifying-final victory was not built around individuals trying to compensate for the talent missing from the side. It came through role clarity, collective effort and complete commitment to the contest. Every player appeared to understand exactly what the team needed from them. Even when captain Callum Mills ruptured his ACL early in the match, the Swans did not lose their heads when they easily could have. Mills had shouldered much of the responsibility that comes with being captain throughout the previous few weeks, making his injury an even crueller blow. Yet Sydney remained composed and focused on what it could control: playing football that its supporters and the broader community could be proud of again. Loading The Swans’ performance at the centre bounce embodied that mindset. They scored 39 points from centre-bounce clearances against Brisbane – their third-highest return from that source across the past five seasons. Sydney won the centre clearances 19-9, first possessions 20-10 and hitouts to advantage 5-1. Most importantly, it outscored the Lions 39-6 from centre-bounce clearances.



Those numbers reveal more than midfield dominance. They demonstrate a team playing proactively. Sydney did not enter the final hoping to absorb Brisbane’s pressure and simply remain in the contest. The Swans attacked from the game’s most direct starting point, generating territory and scoreboard impact before the Lions could establish their defensive structure. That will be critical again against Fremantle. Sydney is equal-first in the competition for scoring from offensive one-on-one contests. Clean centre clearances allow Charlie Curnow and Logan McDonald to attack before opposition defenders receive support. If Brodie Grundy and the Swans midfield can again win first possession and move the ball with speed, Fremantle’s backs will be placed under immediate pressure.



However, the Dockers are one of the best-equipped teams to handle that challenge. Fremantle loses only 21 per cent of its defensive one-on-one contests, the second-best result in the AFL. Its defenders can hold up individually when required, and that starts with inspirational captain Alex Pearce. Charlie Curnow delivered the goods in his first final for the Swans, with five goals. Sam Mooy The Dockers understand when to roll across and help, when to remain accountable and how to delay the opposition long enough for their defensive system to assemble. That creates one of the preliminary final’s defining contests: Sydney’s ability to generate quick, isolated opportunities against Fremantle’s capacity to slow the ball and protect its defenders.



The battle at the opposite end will be equally important. Related Article Explainer

Draft Talent is just the start. What do footy recruiters look for in young players? Fremantle averages 39.4 points from defensive-half chains, ranking second behind Sydney. These are the AFL’s two best teams at turning defence into attack, so the quality of their forward entries will have consequences in both directions. A rushed kick inside 50m will not simply waste an attacking opportunity. It can quickly become the beginning of an opposition scoring chain at the other end. The team that uses the ball with greater composure going forward, while maintaining its defensive structure behind the play, will have an enormous advantage.



Like Sydney, Fremantle may have needed to feel vulnerable again before rediscovering its boldest football. After finishing minor premier, the Dockers carried enormous expectation into September. Their qualifying-final loss to Hawthorn intensified that pressure and created the possibility of a straight-sets exit after such a strong home-and-away season. Expectations were high at Fremantle training this week. Getty Images Suddenly, their backs were against the wall. The focus was no longer on what finishing first entitled them to achieve, but what they were prepared to do to keep their season alive. The victory over Geelong changed their September story.



It was Fremantle’s first finals win since 2022 and secured its first preliminary-final appearance since 2015. More importantly, the Dockers proved to themselves they could respond when a final began slipping away. They kicked six goals in the opening quarter, but Geelong recovered and moved eight points ahead during the third term. At that moment, Fremantle could easily have become consumed by the fear of “old Fremantle” resurfacing and another promising season disappearing in September. Instead, the “new Fremantle” reclaimed the game. Luke Jackson drove the response with 25 disposals, 35 hitouts and two goals. Caleb Serong, Andrew Brayshaw and Hayden Young helped restore control around the contest, while Patrick Voss kicked four goals and Josh Treacy responded strongly after a quiet qualifying final.



The battle between Jackson and Grundy will be the defining match-up on Friday night. Fremantle does not necessarily need to dominate at the centre bounce, but it cannot allow Sydney the same clean first possession and direct access it enjoyed against Brisbane. Jackson’s ability to influence the game beyond the ruck contest makes him especially dangerous. Grundy must match him at ground level and prevent him from becoming an extra midfielder, while still giving Sydney’s on-ballers the opportunity to attack. The duel between Sydney’s Brodie Grundy and Fremantle’s Luke Jackson will be critical to Friday night’s preliminary final. AFL Photos via Getty Images There is also another elephant in the room for the Swans. This is a club carrying the scars of its recent grand final record. Sydney has repeatedly been good enough to reach the final day of the season, only to suffer painful defeats once there. Could this campaign be different precisely because it feels so different?



The absence of several stars and the belief that Sydney’s premiership chance had disappeared may have removed some of the suffocating expectation that followed its previous campaigns. The Swans are not yet in another grand final, but playing as the hunter rather than the hunted could help them take the next step towards confronting that hoodoo. Sydney has found strength in the collective. Fremantle has released a different burden. Its first finals victory since 2022 has replaced anxiety with belief and allowed the minor premier to rediscover the bold football that carried it through the season. That is why I believe the Dockers will win. The mind is a powerful thing, and with the weight of expectation finally lifted, Fremantle can play with the freedom and confidence that made it the competition’s best team across the home-and-away season. Both teams have discovered how dangerous they can be with their backs against the wall. On Friday night, I expect Fremantle’s renewed belief to carry it into the grand final.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Cross-examination of complainant ‘M’ resumes as indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Alan Jones’ criminal trial in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney.

Jones, 85, is standing trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent relating to six male complainants over a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. He denies the alleged physical acts occurred.

Alan Jones’ trial resumed on Thursday after a one-day break. Wolter Peeters

On Monday, the third of the six complainants, a former athlete dubbed “M”, started giving evidence.

His cross-examination started on Tuesday, and he returns to the witness box today for further questioning by Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC. “M” has told the court:

Jones kissed him on the corner of his mouth at an event in Sydney about a decade ago. “I think I froze at that time,” “M” said.

He rejected suggestions by Bashir on Tuesday that the alleged kiss didn’t happen.

The court has heard Jones texted “M” after the function: “Great to see you. Sorry I didn’t catch up after, had to go back to work. You looked great. I love you, I hope you can feel my kisses darling xxxx.”

“M” replied: “Nice to see you too. I had a very long day today and I am pleased to be in bed now; thanks mate xoxo.” The conversation ended in “M” saying “let me know when we can catch up. Lots of love” and Jones replying: “I will darling. Big kisses forever.”

“M” agreed during cross-examination that he did not tell police in his statements that Jones kissed him on the lips at the event. But he said that “I believe I pointed to where it was”.

The complainant said he had “a close relationship with Jones over a period of time” and that “in certain areas” he could go to the broadcaster if he needed help.

The court has previously heard that Jones texted “M” on another occasion, after receiving a photo: “I love the photo. I love you. I want to kiss you for hours. That is beautiful. We must catch up darling [name] xxx”. “M” said he did not respond immediately. Hours later, Jones wrote: “I hope my message did not upset you. I love you.” The man said he responded the next day, writing: “Not at all mate. It’s nice to be loved.”

The complainant said he had used the word “mate” for many reasons. “I know I’d made it very clear that ... it wasn’t moving into a relationship, so ‘mate’ was my way of pushing back, I guess.”

Reflecting on the messages, “M” told the court that he believed “it’s a person that is in love with me”, adding that he did not return those feelings.

“M” said that on the last occasion he visited Jones at his harbourside apartment, the broadcaster kissed him on the cheek towards his lips and said words to the effect of, “I love you so much, you don’t know how much I love you.” The complainant said he could feel Jones’ genitals on his leg .

The complainant said he pushed the broadcaster away and said, “OK, mate”, in a tone intended to convey “get away from me”, and “got out of there as quickly as possible”.

The court heard Jones had sent the complainant gifts including weekly flowers for years and a dinner set. The complainant agreed he also sent Jones flowers at least once.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: The special one: why Longmuir is on the cusp of history
World.content:
NationalWAFremantle Dockers The special one: why Longmuir is on the cusp of history Justin Chadwick September 17, 2026 — 11:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In September 2006, Justin Longmuir was preparing for the biggest match of his life - a preliminary final against Sydney at the SCG. The Dockers lost by 35 points and, just two appearances later, Longmuir’s AFL career was over at the age of 26 due to a debilitating knee injury. Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir speaks to captain Alex Pearce during the team’s finals clash with Hawthorn. Paul Kane/Getty Images The game we love can be so cruel at times. Longmuir knows that more than most. His retirement at such a young age was described as a tragedy by then-Dockers coach Mark Harvey.



But as fate would have it, Longmuir will be back at the SCG on Friday night – some 20 years after that heartbreaking day when Fremantle bombed out of the premiership race. Longmuir’s knees didn’t allow him to reach his full potential as a player during his 139 games in the purple, a grand shame for a ruckman/forward selected with pick No.2 in the 1998 national draft. But his mind might end up being the crucial element that lands Fremantle an elusive flag. So what is it exactly that makes Longmuir so special? And how is it that the coach labelled overly cautious as recently as 2025 is now in charge of one of the AFL’s most electrifying outfits?



Judging Longmuir from the outside can be tough. Related Article Fremantle Dockers Tame Impala frontman reignites calls for end to Woodside’s Dockers sponsorship He’s awkward in front of the cameras; deadpan at times. The 1-0 mantra spruiked after every win this season sums up his public face. The 45-year-old lacks the fearful aura of coaching greats like Mick Malthouse, Denis Pagan and Leigh Matthews. But external perspectives are just that.



What is Longmuir truly like as a coach? The best insight is from his players. There is no shortage of love, admiration and respect for the new-school mentor, the way he backs himself and his players. Shai Bolton knows a thing or two about coaching quality, having won two flags at Richmond under master coach Damien Hardwick. Bolton, who won his second All-Australian blazer this year playing big stints through the midfield, describes Longmuir as “amazing”. “Everyone has different personalities and they coach differently,” Bolton says.



“Dimma is probably a little bit harder on the players. Related Article AFL 2026 Flight of the Dockers: More airline services deployed as purple army sets sights on Sydney “I feel like JL – he’s pretty chill. But when you haven’t played your way, or you haven’t done your role, he can obviously give you a little spray now and then. “But he’s also a kind man and is always willing to have our backs.” Retiring forward Sam Switkowski has spent seven of his nine seasons under Longmuir.



And while there have been external doubts about some of Longmuir’s tactics, especially whether he has been too defensive and conservative in the past, internally it has been 100 per cent faith. “We’ve been trusting him the whole way through,” Switkowski explains. “And just like we’ve improved on field, he’s also improved as a coach. “I love playing for him. I think he’s coaching the best he’s ever coached.” Switkowski has admired the way Longmuir has stuck to his guns even when the external criticism has come thick and fast.



There were even people calling for Longmuir’s head following the club’s embarrassing 61-point loss to St Kilda in round eight last year. “He’s just really confident in his philosophy and his mantra,” Switkowski says. Justin Longmuir, centre, with Leigh Brown and Matthew Pavlich in 2002. “He’s built such strong relationships with his players and his staff, and there’s just so much trust between the players and him.” Powerhouse forward Josh Treacy also admires the way Longmuir sticks to his guns.



“He’s been strong on his beliefs, he’s laid that right from the get-go when he started coaching,” Treacy says. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Purple haze and Friday lights: How Fremantle reclaimed their mojo and kept the dream alive “And that belief and trust has continued to build and grow within our group, and he’s continued to show that, which has allowed guys to flourish.” Midfielder Neil Erasmus is one of those many Dockers to flourish under Longmuir. “Team defence, that’s what gets him excited, and that’s what makes us such a strong team,” Erasmus says.



“He’s a very honest guy, and he’s grown so much as a coach during the five years I’ve been here. “He cares a lot about his players and he cares a lot about the club. “He’s an unreal human and unreal coach.” Former Demons defender Judd McVee has been impressed by what he’s seen and heard from “the best bloke” during his first season at the Dockers. “There is probably a bit of outside noise about him, but everyone internally loves him,” McVee says.



“My transition over, I couldn’t be more thankful for him. He backs me in, and he believes in me. “He’s just so smart with the levers he can pull, and he’s very tactical.” Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir addresses his charges during the round 23 clash with the Adelaide Crows. Getty Images Longmuir, whose first season as coach was spent in COVID hubs during 2020, isn’t afraid to hit back at critics. Whether they are taking a swipe at his handball happy game style or selection calls, Longmuir has full belief in himself and his players.



Fremantle were the clear trendsetters this year, snaring a club-record 14 consecutive wins on the way to the minor premiership. When the Western Bulldogs tried to flood Fremantle into submission in round 21, Longmuir quipped “good luck” when asked if he thought other teams would follow suit. It wasn’t arrogance – rather a sense of pride and confidence in what had been created at Fremantle. Longmuir believes his players possess the tools to overcome any challenge, and he’s encouraging them to play with freedom. After a wake-up call from Hawthorn and a pressure-laden passed test against Geelong, now a decimated Swans outfit stands in Fremantle’s way.



Longmuir couldn’t do it 20 years earlier at the SCG as a player. But it would be only fitting if he guides the current Flagmantle train into a grand final. AAP

World.title: Grass greener on the other side as Smith builds career-best team
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Grass greener on the other side as Smith builds career-best team Craig Kerry September 17, 2026 — 11:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Trainer Matt Smith says he has never had a better collection of elite horses as the one spearheaded by his line-up this week. And the Warwick Farm horseman, who had his first runner in 2003 after learning from racing royalty Aidan O’Brien and Bart Cummings, has no doubt his Luskin Park property and the help of “Dr Green” has made a difference. Warwick Farm trainer Matthew Smith with Everest hopeful Headwall. Janie Barrett/SMH At Randwick on Saturday in group 2 races, Smith has Headwall striving in The Shorts to cement a slot in the $20 million Everest, group 1-winner Idle Flyer aiming to bounce back in the 7 Stakes and Queen’s Gamble stepping up to the Tea Rose Stakes. On Friday, exciting stayer Aethelwulf rises to stakes grade in the group 3 Newcastle Cup (2300m) as the favourite. “I’ve never had a group this strong,” said Smith, who sits equal second on the Sydney premiership with nine winners at 23.1 per cent.



“It’s a nice bunch of horses to have all going at the one time. It’s not like that very often.” Smith’s stable collected a career-best $6.94 million in prizemoney last season, capping a rise in runners and success since 2020 when he and wife, Melissa, bought the 46-hectare Luskin Park, where champion Luskin Star was bred, in the Lower Hunter as a spelling and pre-training property. They are building a 25-box stable there and hope to increase their numbers and day-to-day training at the facility in a year. “It’s definitely made a big difference,” he said. “Mel and I had been looking for years for a place, we knew that’s what we wanted to do. “I’d worked over in Ireland and I’d followed that way of training, having that ability to freshen horses mid-prep and give them a break mentally as well.



“A lot of horses can feel the strain mentally and they start to fall apart, so if you can get them up there and back to nature, you can’t underestimate the value of a horse just putting his head down in a paddock and having a pick of grass. “It’s a bit like us doing something we like, going fishing or whatever. You are not thinking about anything except what’s in front of you. It’s the same thing for horse. Day in, day out galloping, galloping and racing, it just catches up with them. “I read a book on [legendary trainer of Northern Dancer] Horatio Luro and he used to call grass Dr Green. He was always wanting his horses to be picking grass. It’s great to give them a time out. It rejuvenates them. They come back in from the farm and they want to go.” Seven-year-old Headwall showed he was back with a bang in the Concorde Stakes after a year out because of a pastern injury, surging late to finish second to Tempted two weeks ago. An Everest slot beckons if Headwall ($3.30) can repeat the effort in The Shorts (1100m), where he has gate five. Headwall, right, chases home Tempted in the Concorde. Getty Images



“He came out of that run really good and he looks super,” Smith said. “We haven’t got an Everest spot yet, but I think if he ran well, he will get one. If he can back up that first-up run. It will be bloody exciting if we can get one. “We just need a bit of room, a split at the right time with him. He’s one of those horses that always gets back amongst them.” Queen’s Gamble ($8) enters the Princess Series for three-year-old fillies at the 1400m Tea Rose after dominant Warwick Farm wins at 1300m and 1400m, following three placings over shorter trips. “She’s a nice filly and she just keeps getting better and better,” Smith said.



“She’s got the advantage of having that run over the trip and at 1300. A lot of these horses wouldn’t have run 1400m, so if something goes hard in front, it will find a few of them out.” He was looking for a guide on where to go next with Idle Flyer ($26), which races third up in the 7 Stakes (1600m) after a disappointing effort last start. The Queen Of The Turf winner had every chance in the 1400m Tramway when finishing three lengths fourth. Zac Lloyd rides Idle Flyer to victory in the Angst Stakes at Randwick last October. Getty Images “She had no real excuses really,” he said of the run. “She just didn’t let go like she can do, but getting up to the mile will suit her better.



“After that we will make a decision on where we go. Probably Epsom.” The 7 Stakes, headlined by Autumn Glow ($1.15), was down to five runners with the scratchings of Lindermann and Lady Shenandoah. Stayer Aethelwulf is perhaps Smith’s most exciting prospect. The four-year-old has won four of his five starts by big margins this preparation, rising in distance and class each time. The Metropolitan or Bart Cummings beckon if he wins. Aethelwulf cruises to victory last start at Rosehill. Getty Images “He hasn’t missed a beat so far, he’s just got to run the trip,” Smith said. “We obviously like him a lot, but he’s just got to keep stepping up. You don’t know when they are going to hit their mark. If he keeps winning, you’re going to keep going.”

World.title: Symbolic ‘first mango tray of the season’ raises $70,000 for charity
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity life Symbolic ‘first mango tray of the season’ raises $70,000 for charity Neesha Sinnya September 17, 2026 — 11:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The season’s symbolic first tray of mangoes has sold at the Brisbane Markets for a whopping $70,000, with its buyer crowned this year’s “mango monarch”. The auction marks the beginning of the mango season, and raises money for charities Redkite and the Lady Musgrave Trust. Elijah Etri, the manager at 24/7 Wellington Point produce spot Skippy’s Fresh Frootz, took the crown of mango monarch. Elijah Etri from Skippy’s was crowned this year’s monarch after securing the symbolic first tray of the season. Neesha Sinnya “We don’t think about what it’s costing us, we think about what it’s going towards,” Etri said.



“Everyone keeps asking what we’re going to do with a $70,000 mango tray … we can’t sell it, we’d have to sell them at $5,000 a mango. “We will take it home, share it amongst ourselves, and relish in what we won today.” Thea Sitcheff from Redkite said their share of the funds would be able to support eight families for a year, including counselling and financial assistance. Redkite works with families dealing with childhood cancer, while the Lady Musgrave Trust is focused on supporting homeless women and children.



Lady Musgrave Trust chief executive Victoria Parker said the auction was her favourite fundraising event of the year. “It’s always a joy … the money raised is so valuable toward supporting young women and children across Queensland who are experiencing homelessness, which is a really big issue,” Parker said. The $70,000 mango tray, filled with 14 Kensington Prides, came from NT Happy in Darwin and is part of Australian Mangoes’ first crop of the season. “First season fruit is always the best,” Jenna McManus from Australian Mangoes said. “[This year’s] fruit set is looking phenomenal, flowering … it’s a good indication of a great season.”



Last year the first tray of mangoes sold for $66,000 to Chris Frame from the Standard Market Company. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ASX gains as oil prices ease; Wall Street falls as Fed chief spooks investors
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX gains as oil prices ease; Wall Street falls as Fed chief spooks investors Staff writers Updated September 17, 2026 — 11:10am ,first published September 17, 2026 — 4:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket opened higher on Thursday, shrugging off falls on Wall Street following the Federal Reserve’s first interest rate rise in three years, as oil prices dropped for a second day on signs of easing Middle East supply disruptions. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 26.3 points, or 0.3 per cent, at 8722.80 as of 10.55am AEST, with eight of its 11 sectors in the green. The upbeat morning - despite futures indicating a sharp fall - came after the local bourse added 0.3 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar traded flat at US70.90¢. Fed chair Kevin Warsh’s warnings on inflation spooked Wall Street. AP Photo/Seth Wenig West Texas Intermediate fell toward $US101 a barrel, after losing 3.2 per cent on Wednesday, the most since August 4. Brent crude was back below $US105, having reached almost $US110 in recent days. Saudi Arabia is seeking to return about half the capacity of its damaged East-West pipeline within days, and full operations in six weeks, a person familiar said. The oil price reprieve boosted shares of fuel-dependent companies such as airlines Qantas (up 1.7 per cent) and Virgin Australia (up 5 per cent), but weighed on the energy sector, sending oil and gas giants Woodside and Santos down 1.4 per cent and 2.2 per cent, respectively.



The ASX’s gains in early trade were bolstered by the big four banks, which were all up between 0.9 per cent and 1.4 per cent. Consumer discretionary stocks such as Bunnings and Officeworks owner Wesfarmers (up 0.8 per cent), electronics chain JB Hi-Fi (up 0.5 per cent) and furniture seller Harvey Norman (up 0.5 per cent) also did well. The mining heavyweights BHP (up 0.4 per cent), Rio Tinto (up 0.7 per cent) and Fortescue (up 0.9 per cent) also helped, all advancing as prices for iron ore strengthened overnight. Related Article Breaking

Media & marketing ABC slams watchdog finding that Four Corners program failed impartiality test Gold stocks, however, slumped after the Fed’s rate rise and its signals of more to come, making gold less attractive as an investment because it doesn’t pay interest. Northern Star Resources fell 1 per cent, Newmont lost 1.7 per cent and Evolution Mining dropped 0.8 per cent. On Wall Street, US stocks slipped after the Federal Reserve hiked its main interest rate for the first time in three years and suggested more may be ahead as it tries to get the nation’s high inflation under control.



The S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent after giving up a modest gain from earlier in the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite was nearly unchanged after edging down by less than 0.1 per cent. Investors generally prefer lower interest rates because higher rates slow the economy’s growth and undercut prices for stocks and other investments. The US stock market initially held on to its modest, early gains after the Fed announced its decision. The short-term pain of a slower economy may be worth it if it starves inflation of its fuel and gets further increases for the cost of living back to the Fed’s 2 per cent target. But stock prices weakened later in the session as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said repeatedly in a press conference that inflation remains too high and the US economy appears to be strengthening. That could imply the world’s largest economy is solid enough to withstand more hikes to rates, and other officials at the Fed provided their own forecasts suggesting rates may need to go still higher. “We removed a dose of accommodation so that financial and credit conditions would be more consistent with our ultimate objectives,” Warsh said. “Today’s action starts to show we’re serious about this, and we will deliver on the price stability objective.”



Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh speaks at a news conference following the decision. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein The median Fed official expects the federal funds rate to end this year at 4.1 per cent, according to forecasts published after the central bank’s meeting. That’s up from its current range of 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent following Wednesday’s increase, and it’s up from the median forecast of 3.8 per cent that Fed officials gave three months ago. Traders, meanwhile, suspect the Fed may go even further. They’re betting on a 38 per cent probability the Fed could hike the federal funds rate to a range of 4.25 per cent to 4.50 per cent by the end of the year, according to data from CME Group. “Clearly the Warsh commentary was much more bluntly hawkish than investors expected,” said Nathan Thooft, a senior portfolio manager at Manulife Investment Management. It’s the first hike by the Fed to interest rates in three years. The central bank had been on pause for months following cuts to rates in 2024 and 2025, even though inflation has consistently remained above the Fed’s 2 per cent target.



President Donald Trump has been lobbying for interest rates to go lower rather than higher. On Wall Street, bank stocks fell to some of the market’s sharper losses. A slower US economy could mean less demand for loans from them. Banks also get hurt when the gap narrows between short-term interest rates and longer-term ones because the industry makes profit off the difference. Related Article Updated

Federal Reserve Fed defies Trump, raises US interest rates for first time in three years Following the Fed’s announcements, the two-year Treasury yield jumped to 4.74 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Tuesday. It tends to closely follow expectations for what the Fed will do with the federal funds rate. The yield on the longer-term 10-year Treasury, meanwhile, takes into account expectations for economic growth and inflation years down the line. It had a more modest increase, ticking up to 5.01 per cent from 5.00 per cent late Tuesday.



Huntington Bancshares fell 5.6 per cent, Citizens Financial Group sank 4.8 per cent and JPMorgan Chase slipped 1 per cent. Helping to limit the market’s losses were gains for some influential stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry. Nvidia rose 0.8 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices climbed 1.6 per cent to recover more of their losses from earlier in the week. AI stocks slid worldwide Monday after leaders of the AI industry called for a slowdown in development to address safety issues for humanity. Microsoft slipped 1.4 per cent. Overnight, its artificial intelligence chief Mustafa Suleyman warned infusing tools like Anthropic’s Claude with humanlike characteristics increases the risks of such systems going rogue. In an essay, the longtime artificial intelligence developer took aim at some of the language in the guiding documents behind Claude, Anthropic PBC’s popular family of large language models. Claude’s constitution expresses ambiguity about whether the assistant is a moral entity, positing that the software may have “some functional version of emotions or feelings.”



In other international markets, indexes rose across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1.4 per cent for one of the world’s biggest gains. with AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
