World.title: ‘I was blocking that vision’: How Jess Fox helped her sister beat her to Olympic gold
World.content:
NationalGood Weekend ‘I was blocking that vision’: How Jess Fox helped her sister beat her to Olympic gold Tim Elliott September 17, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Noémie Fox, 29, and sister Jess Fox, 32, are Olympic champion kayakers, and have been both rivals and allies, in and out of the water. Noémie: Jess and I were born in Marseille, where our mum’s from, but came to Australia in 2000 when our dad became head coach of the Australian canoe slalom team for the Sydney Olympics. I was about two-and-half, and Jess was three years older, so she took care of me. She was good at music and sport and was dux of the school. She helped me with my notes, and teachers loved me because they’d had Jess who’d been a pleasure to teach. When we were young, Jess was always easy to live with, whereas I was the squeaky wheel. A lot of my childhood, she’d be like, “OK, if you want the bigger room, you can have it.” That’s something I never would’ve been able to let go. I’m still like that. I’ll lose my hair tie while kayaking and she’ll be like, “Have mine. I don’t need it.”



Jess began competing at school, and I started when I was a bit older. She made it look easy, but I wasn’t such a fast learner. There was a bit of jealousy, naturally. I was envious: I thought, why is she so good and I can’t get there? At her first world championships in 2013, she won the canoe. At my first world junior championships, I came 11th. Related Article Good Weekend She nearly quit the pool at 14. Now, Mollie’s the face of a new Australian era Our parents had both been Olympian kayakers and my sister was world number one, so I began feeling like the black sheep, like I didn’t belong because I wasn’t at their level. I was always watching from the grandstands and helping Jess train, so her wins kind of belonged to the whole family – but, still, I constantly felt like a disappointment, even after I started getting better results. Jess understood and tried to lift me up, but there’s only so much help you want from your older sister. It’s especially hard because in our sport, there’s only one spot at the Olympics, so I had to beat Jess to get in the team, and she was so far ahead. In 2020, I “quiet quit” kayaking and did other things: I worked with L’Occitane in Switzerland and visited my grandma in France. Then a new event, called kayak cross, was introduced for the 2024 Paris Olympics. It opened up extra spots in the Australian team, and it resonated with me because it’s more messy. It was only then that I got out of that victim mindset of “I’m never going to make it”. I thought, “This is going to be something that’ll be mine.” I also decided, when I began training, that I’d learn from Jess and her ability to compartmentalise, which I’m terrible at. I get distracted by my environment, but she’s a magpie: she takes the shiny things and leaves the shit. Even with her surgery in 2025 [for a kidney tumour that proved to be benign], I would’ve panicked but she just went, “What can I take from this to learn and grow?” Jess Fox shares the joy after Noémie wins a gold medal in the kayak cross at the Paris Games. AP



In the end, I qualified for the Paris Games. I actually knocked Jess out in the first round. She came over, gave me a hug and said, “Take it all the way.” When I won [gold], she was the first one running down to the finish line. I think Australia loved seeing that moment: me, the little sister knocking her out, and the sportsmanship that she showed in return. Jess: My first memory was of Noémie being about four, and wanting to be involved with whatever I was doing. I’d be reading a book, gently turning the pages, and she’d be jumping up and down, saying, “Let me read your book!” When we came to Australia from France, we lived in Glenmore Park [west of Sydney] for a year before moving to Emu Plains [near the Blue Mountains]. We liked sport – swimming, gymnastics. As the younger sibling, you always tag along to whatever the older one’s doing. Noémie would see me do something and try to copy. When I learnt to ride a bike, I spent ages on training wheels, building my confidence. But then, one day, I hear this banging and clanging in the garage, and there’s Noémie, about three years old, teaching herself how to ride a bike, no training wheels, nothing, just going at it. Jess Fox with her silver medal at the London Olympics in 2012. Reuters At the same time, she was super-girly. Our grandmother, who we visited every year in France, had this big jewellery box, and Noémie was always trying on her necklaces, or cooking with her. Meanwhile, I was a tomboy, running around in shorts and a T-shirt.



She didn’t enjoy paddling at the start. She had a traumatic experience when she was 10: she flipped over in a kayak and was upside-down, underwater, and couldn’t get back up. Her instructor rescued her, but she didn’t paddle for a year after that. Eventually, I told her, “It’s scary to get back in, but that’s how you overcome the fear.” I had success early on. I was a junior world champion at 16, and competed at the Olympics at 18. For a long time, she was on the riverbank, in the crowds, watching and supporting. It was hard for her, especially when she started competing. I wanted her to paddle to her potential, but she knew that to beat me, she had to beat the world number one. I also struggled with it! I thought, “Is it selfish to be hogging that position? Or is that just elite sport, and if you beat me, fair play?” It’s brutal. Either way, she was always there to support me and train, which was pretty selfless. ‘I knew that she’d never let herself dream of being an Olympian because I was blocking that vision.’ Jess Fox Noémie didn’t want paddling to be her only identity, which is amazing because, for a lot of athletes, it’s the only thing you know. She got an internship overseas with L’Occitane during COVID and commentated during the Tokyo Olympics. But when kayak cross was added to the Paris Olympics, I told her: “OK, you’ve got to commit. You might not qualify, but there’s three people who will, so why not you?” When she decided to have a go, we started training together like sparring partners. The day she qualified, in Prague, I was running along the bank, screaming. My heart rate was like 180, and I lost my voice. When she actually won gold, it was the most euphoric moment because I knew that she’d never let herself dream of being an Olympian because I was blocking that vision. It’s been a complex relationship: you can be jealous as the younger sister, or you can feel resentment but, at the same time, she has loved and supported me. Luckily, we’ve always been brought up knowing that our paddling career is only a certain number of years, but we’ve got our whole life as sisters.

World.title: Should I keep waiting for Mr Darcy? Jane Austen answers your most pressing questions
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It is a truth universally acknowledged that every new generation must be in want of their own set of Jane Austen adaptions. This year sees the release on Netflix of Dolly Alderton’s take on Pride and Prejudice (starring Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden) and a new film version of Sense and Sensibility (with Daisy Edgar-Jones), written by Australia’s Diana Reid. Alderton and Reid are two voices of our generation whose novels have tackled some of the great questions of our time: Why do men ghost? How do you recover from a toxic friendship? Why is there never any food at hen’s parties? Dating apps might be our ballroom and we join run clubs instead of practising the harpsichord, but at the end of the day, put a group of young women together in 1811 or 2026 and the agenda will still be: who we love, economic security, sibling and parent drama and irritating in-laws. These topics remain so current that we can still turn to the mother of the romance novel through the lens of an agony aunt, and ask the same question that women have asked for centuries… what would Jane Austen suggest? 1. I haven’t found my Mr Darcy. Should I settle for less? Colin Firth as Mr Darcy in the 1995 BBC adaptation of Pride and Prejudice. We all want Wentworth or Darcy (or Colin Firth or Paul Rudd) to declare they love us just the way we are – despite our lack of self-awareness or ridiculous family or muddy skirts or whatever our red flag is. Who doesn’t aspire to a love so great it transforms them? The best advice here is to channel Elizabeth Bennet, from Pride and Prejudice. Lizzie knows her value and is (with self-awareness and a sense of humour) uncompromising about demanding her worth and not accepting less, even when everyone around her is urging her to settle.



You deserve the guy who sees everything wrong with you and loves you desperately anyway. And the giant house. 2. I’ve been ghosted. How should I respond? Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood and George MacKay as Edward Ferrars in Sense and Sensibility. Focus Features Related Article Literature Sorry, Jane Austen, but these Australian novels had us at hello In Sense and Sensibility, Marianne Dashwood is ghosted by Willoughby. She’s devastated when she writes him letter after letter with no reply. The first thing you should do is to stop texting him. Then you’re allowed to cry, refuse to get out of bed and look terrible. Soon you, like Marianne, will lose your whole heart again to someone better – your own Colonel Brandon/ young Alan Rickman. Happiness will be the ultimate revenge. In the end Willoughby regrets ghosting Marianne and spends the rest of his life thinking of her as the perfect woman, holding her up on a pedestal. Let’s assume that the same thing will happen to the guy who ghosted you. 3. My friend is getting serious about a boring, egotistical know-all. What should I do? Jennifer Ehle as Elizabeth Bennet and Lucy Scott as Charlotte Lucas in the celebrated BBC adaptation of Pride and Prejudice.



Again, be a Lizzie. When Elizabeth Bennet’s best friend Charlotte announces she’s marrying Mr Collins, who is all ick, Lizzie calls her out on it. Once. Then, when she realises Charlotte has made up her mind, she pivots to silently judging her decision and outwardly supporting her friend. There’s an unspoken agreement to ignore Mr Collins (where possible). Pride and Prejudice gives us the perfect playbook for when your friends get serious with someone who’s mid. You get one chance to attempt an intervention. Then, you must fall back to a position of quiet disdain and open solidarity. After a while (usually after the wedding), you’ll both mostly pretend he doesn’t exist. 4. I’m single and can’t afford to buy a house. What are my options? This is a very Jane Austen coded dilemma – her plots are often real estate-centred. Many of her novels begin with a cost-of-living crisis. In Sense and Sensibility, the Dashwoods solve their housing crisis by moving into a distant relative’s cottage. A modern-day equivalent might be to move back in with your parents. In Persuasion, the Elliotts rent out their estate and move to Bath. Maybe you could move to a regional town where prices aren’t so insane? Either way, Austen promises that your new locale will be swarming with handsome eligible men (and a few rogues). Some of them might even have enormous (mortgage-free) homes of their own, which will solve your housing dilemma entirely. 5. Working mum life is destroying my soul. Should I become a trad wife? Jane Austen was clear-eyed about women’s economic realities, so she’d be sympathetic to the plight of the modern woman who’s trying to juggle the mental load of paid work, childcare and strength training, all in the same day. You could argue that she’d endorse trad wives’ performative femininity and celebration of marriage and family values. But Austen was critical of anyone who pretends to be something they aren’t (think Harriet in Emma or Brittany Murphy’s Tai in Clueless). From left, Brittany Murphy as Tai and Alicia Silverstone as Cher in Clueless. Paramount Pictures



Related Article Romance A period romance changed my life. I’m not the only one If she were writing today, she’d surely enjoy taking her literary scalpel to women who act (on camera) like they’re living the simple life while cooking their homemade sourdough in gazillion-dollar ovens and flogging expensive homewares to their followers. That said, Austen would be wholly supportive of the running away part. Her heroines are constantly forming parties, jumping into carriages and heading off to London or Bath or the Lake District. The takeaway for those of us on the edge of burnout (and who isn’t?) is not to milk a cow but rather to book a one-way ticket to Bali and return only once cortisol levels have been lowered. 6. Should I be nice to my irritating in-laws? Austen’s novels are full of survival strategies for navigating a spectrum of tricky in-laws. For the super toxic, controlling in-laws (think Mrs Ferrars) you might need to go low-contact. For a more moderately irritating mother-in-law like Mrs Bennet you might want to consider moving to the other side of the country (like Jane and Mr Bingley). If they’re just low-key annoying but ultimately good people, a solid option is to pretend to be deaf or asleep during family gatherings (as demonstrated by Mr Palmer in Sense and Sensibility). 7. I wasn’t picked to be a bridesmaid for a close friend. Should I confront her? Imagine your close friend is Jane Bennet. When you were kids you swapped ribbons, learned to dance the quadrille together and dreamed about your (double) wedding.

And now, finally, she’s engaged to Mr Bingley. Everyone is thrilled. You’re waiting for the call-up to be bridesmaid. Maid of honour even. Except Jane is very close to her sister Elizabeth. And Elizabeth’s husband is the groom’s best friend. So obviously she’s the maid of honour.



There are three other sisters too. Lydia is in disgrace (and can’t be trusted to plan a hen’s). And Mary won’t enjoy the dressing up. But Jane’s far too kind to only ask half of her sisters – so they’ll all be in the bridal party too. And there’s the sister-in-law – Miss Caroline Bingley. Obviously, she shouldn’t be a bridesmaid – she doesn’t even like Jane. If she could break up the couple, she absolutely would. But her brother loves her, so she’s in. Your friend might desperately want you by her side on her big day, but for some (logical or irrational) reason (he wants an equal number of groomsmen, she’s been a serial bridesmaid who feels she should return the favour, she can’t afford to pay for six sets of hair and make-up and bonnets) she hasn’t asked you. Give her another chance. 8. Influencers are making my life feel ordinary. Should I delete all my accounts and get a dumb phone? No! Don’t feel bad about enjoying social media. Austen would have loved social media – though as a lurker, not a poster. And she basically wrote the job description for an influencer at the opening of Emma - someone “handsome, clever and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition”. Emma Woodhouse, a modern hot, rich woman who doesn’t need or want to work, would have an enormous following on Instagram. Her aesthetic would be pastel-hued country chic. Her TikTok would feature themed seasonal dinner parties, unboxing swathes of cashmere and being temporarily enthusiastic about new hobbies. On her podcast (there would be a podcast) she’d give endless advice about dating in the modern world. Anya Taylor-Joy as Emma Woodhouse in Autumn de Wilde’s film of the Jane Austen classic. Universal Pictures You could look at Emma’s grid and think it’s perfect and that she has all the answers. But (as Mr Knightley, regularly tells her, swoon!) she doesn’t. Emma thinks she’s excellent at life. But she (like all the best influencers) has an inflated ego and a big dose of self-delusion. Her lifestyle should not be compared with your own. Her advice is not to be taken. That way misery lies. Just ask Emma’s matchmaking project, Harriet Smith. Treat a glimpse into Emma’s life, into influencers’ lives, as a treat. Then revel in the extraordinary ordinariness of your own.

World.title: Man reportedly seen covered in blood, screams heard after incident at Auckland's LynnMall
World.content:
A woman who works at a bar at Auckland's Lynmall says she saw a man bleeding in the carpark, and was told by security that he was stabbed.

A Hato Hone St John spokesperson said they were called shortly after 11am and found a person with serious injuries.

The person has been taken to Auckland Hospital.

The woman, who didn't want to be named said she saw the man bleeding in the mall's carpark, and didn't know what had happened.

She said the man looked like he was in his 30s.

A security guard told her the man was stabbed in the neck, she said.

"It's crazy that people can do that in broad daylight," she said.

The New Zealand Herald is reporting that a man was seen covered in blood and screams were heard.

Police are at the scene but are yet to respond.

World.title: Supermarket owners shouldn't make the rich list – supplier
World.content:
New Zealand is probably one of the only countries in the world where owning a supermarket can put someone on the rich list, a grocery supplier and distributor says.

Daniel Shields, owner of Naked Kitchen and Barrys Bay Cheese, as well as fresh chilled distribution company Cool & Fresh, spoke to Midday Report on Thursday.

He said breaking up Foodstuffs, as National has proposed, would be one of the most efficient ways to get more competition into New Zealand's grocery sector.

Could I run out of money in retirement and other questions experts wish you'd ask No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 15m

"It would force Pak'n Save and New World into competition with each other. At the moment, that relationship is very, very cosy.

"Foodstuffs commands the top and bottom position in grocery, they can take margin out of New World and volume out of Pak'n Save without either of their store owners being desperately penalised... it's given them so much control over New Zealand consumers."

He said Foodstuffs was able to demand high margins from suppliers but did not pass those on to shoppers.

Foodstuffs North Island had moved to a centralised buying model in recent years, he said, which allowed it to use its scale to put pressure on supplier prices.

"None of that margin improvement Foodstuffs has gained was passed on to consumers, it has all been absorbed as more profit."

He said if Pak'nSave and New World were in competition, it would increase pressure on them to pass savings to shoppers.

Shields rejected Foodstuffs' characterisation of its shops as 500 independent owner-operators in their local communities.

"Foodstuffs has been very good at playing 'hide the sausage' in terms of where the profit goes in that business. We're probably one of the only countries in the world where individual supermarket owner can be on the rich list. That's no accident - Foodstuffs has been able to combine the power of their scale with these owner-operators having very strong positions in the local economy."

Foodstuffs brands include Four Square, New World and Pak'nSave Supplied

He said many suppliers had to watch supermarkets add margin to their products, while importing cheaper products from overseas to be sold as competing home brands.

In a statement, Foodstuffs said the National proposal would have significant implications.

"Our immediate focus is supporting our owner-operators, our 3000 supply chain and support centre team members, and the many New Zealand businesses that work with us, all of whom are hearing proposals that could fundamentally change the co-operatives they own, work for and support, and the businesses they have spent years building in communities throughout New Zealand.

"We also recognise that New Zealanders will want to understand what these changes would mean for them. Any proposal of this scale raises important questions about how long a major restructure would take to implement, the level of disruption involved, the costs of making those changes, and whether those costs and disruptions would ultimately deliver meaningful savings at the checkout.

"These are significant issues that deserve careful consideration. We will take the time to thoroughly review the proposal and its implications before providing further comment."

World.title: New Zealand and Samoan nationals charged over alleged Vietnam murder
World.content:
A New Zealand national and a Samoan national have been charged by Samoa Police in relation to the alleged shooting murder of an Australian citizen and suspected gangleader in Vietnam in May.

In a joint statement, Samoa Police and the Australian Federal Police (AFP) said the two men, aged 31 and 33 years old, were charged with conspiracy to murder on 10 September. Under Samoa's Crimes Act, the offence carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment.

The two men appeared before a Samoan court on Wednesday and were granted conditional bail, the statement said.

Joseph Vaa, 27, admitted on Vietnamese television to gunning down suspected 'Coconut Cartel' ringleader Lorenzo Lemalu Tovia, outside a restaurant in Ho Chi Minh City on 21 May, while his associate, Steve Tofa, 23, then confessed to being his accomplice in the shooting.

"An investigation by international law enforcement authorities began following the death of an Australian citizen and serious injuries sustained by a second Australian citizen in a shooting in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, on 21 May, 2026," the joint police statement said.

"Vietnamese authorities arrested two Samoan nationals, aged 22 and 26, on 24 May, 2026, over their alleged roles in the shooting.

"On 27 May, 2026, Samoa Police first arrested and charged the 31-year-old in Samoa with misleading police and corruption offences as part of their investigation into the alleged murder. He was arrested while attempting to leave the country.

The statement said the AFP launched an investigation into the alleged murder to support international law enforcement authorities and identify any further individuals involved.

The AFP assisted the Samoa Police through the execution of a search warrant, financial inquiries, witness interviews and a forensic review of electronic material.

"These AFP activities, and further inquiries undertaken by Samoa Police, led to an additional charge of conspiracy to murder laid against the New Zealand man and 33-year-old Samoan national."

"Samoa Police will allege these men conspired with the Samoan men arrested in Vietnam to carry out the alleged murder in Vietnam," the joint statment said.

AFP acting commander Pacific Greg Davis said the charges reflected the strength of international law enforcement cooperation across the Pacific and broader region.

"Organised crime does not respect national boundaries, so law enforcement agencies must work together to combat them," he said.

"Criminal networks rely on international connections to facilitate serious offending, which is why regional partnerships are critical to disrupting and dismantling them.

World.title: "Just F. Meth": Government bets on blunt anti-drug campaign
World.content:
The government has launched a deliberately provocative anti-meth campaign with a blunt message - "F. Meth" - after an earlier effort fell flat.

The slogan has intentionally been left open to interpretation, with officials suggesting meanings including fight meth, face meth, forget meth or be free from meth.

But for some with lived experience of the drug, the message is more explicit: f*** meth.

Community advocate Tee Tanielu is one of the faces of the campaign, alongside her partner Flo Murray.

Speaking to RNZ at the launch in Porirua on Thursday morning, Tanielu picked a more complicated word: "forgive".

Flo Murray (L) and Tee Tanielu (R) with their child (centre) Craig McCulloch/RNZ

"For a lot of us, including myself, meth wasn't the problem; it was the solution. And so, sometimes we have to move past what it did in order to finally get to why we used it."

She paused before adding: "And just f*** meth too... that as well. Just f*** meth!"

Mental Health Minister Matt Doocey was also unapologetic about the branding.

"Meth is provocative, right? We've got to meet it head on."

The $1.6 million campaign - which will run across multiple platforms - will be funded from the Proceeds of Crime Fund.

One of the campaign posters. Craig McCulloch/RNZ

The Herald previously reported that an earlier $100,000 test video had "low engagement" on social media with an average view time of just two seconds.

But Doocey said the new phase had been tested in focus groups and shaped with feedback from people who had used meth and those working on the frontline.

"We wanted to know what will connect with them, what will get the cut-through."

He said the campaign would be evaluated after six months and tested against a target of reaching 2.5 million New Zealanders aged 18 to 59, as well as whether they remembered the message or sought help.

"It creates hope. It's planting seeds"

Also at the launch, addiction counsellor Michael Hogan told RNZ he first used the drug in a pub in the 1990s.

"I used to have a few beers on the weekend. Typical Kiwi bloke," he said. "I didn't know what I was getting involved in."

Michael Hogan Craig McCulloch/RNZ

His meth use escalated. Hogan said he lost the respect of his children, sold his house and became a low-level drug dealer.

"Hated myself, loathed myself. Lost respect for who I was," he said. "I'd lost all control."

Hogan eventually spent two years in residential treatment and is now 15 years free from meth.

He hoped a campaign as blunt as F. Meth might reach someone before their life unravelled - or at least give them a reason to think about getting out.

"It's normalising recovery. It creates hope. It's planting seeds."

But Hogan stressed advertising alone would not fix the problem.

"We're bandaiding a lot," he said. "We need more rehabs. We need to get some education into our youth."

Doocey said the campaign was just one part of a wider $30.6 million health-led response announced last year, including more treatment, early intervention and prevention programmes.

World.title: New Zealand economy grows by 0.2% in June quarter
World.content:
Economy grows 0.2 percent in June quarter, 2.6 percent on year ago

Data is in line with expectations

Previous quarter revised up marginally to 0.9 percent growth

Construction, manufacturing, wholesaling lead growth

Consumer spending, transport activity weaker

Financial markets narrowly picking Reserve Bank will raise cash rate to 3.0 pct next month

The economy has escaped significant damage from the Middle East war and spike in fuel prices with a modest rise in growth driven by stronger house building.

Stats NZ data showed gross domestic product (GDP) - the broad measure of economic growth - rose 0.2 percent in the three months ended June, to be 2.6 percent higher than a year ago. On an annual average basis the economy grew 1.7 percent over the year.

It had been expected New Zealand would dodged significant economic damage from the US-Iran war, caused by the fuel-price shock and disruption that dominated the quarter.

Stats NZ spokesperson Jason Attewell said the growth rate was a mixed bag.

"The 0.2 percent growth in economic activity ... reflects mixed results, with increases in nine of 16 industries."

Initial fears were the major spikes in petrol and diesel prices would all but wipe out the solid start to the year, sending consumers and businesses scurrying to cut costs and severely dampening activity.

BNZ senior economist Doug Steel said there has been a stronger than expected economic pulse.

Escaping an economic bullet

The quarter's growth was the fourth in a row, and annual growth rates were the highest in more than two years.

The surge in house building drove construction up 2.7 percent, while government services grew 2 percent, with wholesale trade especially for machinery and equipment rising 1.3 percent.

The weakest sectors were those strongly exposed to fuel prices.

Road transport and support services fell 1.7 percent, while retail trade such as hospitality and accommodation 1 percent.

Stats NZ said falls in fuel retail volumes pointed to the impact of higher fuel prices.

"Accommodation and food services fell 3.8 percent ... indicating a potential change in discretionary spending."

It also noted that household spending in restaurants and hotels also fell.

Services make up close to three quarters of the economy, but grew only 0.2 percent for the quarter, while goods producing sectors were up 1.3 percent overall.

Transport industries were also weaker coinciding with significant price increases for diesel.

Individual shares of the economy - per capita GDP - rose 0.1 percent for the quarter.

The country's purchasing power (disposable income) fell 0.4 percent for the quarter, to be 2.5 percent ahead of a year ago.

'People still got out'

Infometrics economist Brad Olson said the country was getting better at absorbing economic shocks.

Brad Olsen. LDR

"I think when we first looked at the Iran war and the conflict in the Middle East, Earlier this year, we saw those big increases in fuel prices. We really did expect not only for those higher prices to drive a lot of people to do less activity, but also for everyone to sit on their hands a whole lot more because of the uncertainty.

"And although there was definitely a bit of a pullback in that momentum, people still got out - and did quite a bit."

The most surprising he said was perhaps construction, which despite rising costs had "momentum" behind it with the growing number of consents being issued.

"At the same time, the other parts of the economy that you might expect would face a bit more of a pullback, did. The likes of accommodation and food services, so hospitality and parts of the tourism sector not going quite as well because - of course - for a lot of Kiwi households, they were having to pay more for fuel. They then didn't want to travel around as much because they'd already spent their money on paying for the fuel and everyone went back into their shells a bit more."

He said it wasn't clear yet which way the Reserve Bank might go at its next review of the official cash rate.

"The biggest worry at the moment, right, is these GDP figures we're talking about, they're three months old. Whereas at the moment, you've got these pretty high levels of prices coming through for global oil, still above US$100 a barrel. It's those pressures the Reserve Bank will probably be focused on more in making their assessment."

Derailed recovery?

Economists are expecting growth to continue unevenly through to the end of the year, and gather more momentum next year, with global events remaining a significant influence.

Business and consumer confidence have improved but still remain pessimistic with uncertainty driving caution, but with growth still occurring.

Forecasts are now picking modest growth going into 2027.

The Reserve Bank last month raised the official cash rate (OCR) at 2.75 percent and signalled rates will rise further to combat 4 percent inflation, although it has said it is also balancing the need to support the economic recovery.

World.title: How much damage will athlete's incontinence do to $1b Hyrox brand?
World.content:
Over the course of this week, the high-intensity fitness racing world has been focused on Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk's performance at an event in Beijing, in which she suffered sudden faecal incontinence but continued to race.

Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste has apologised "to all who were directly or indirectly involved".

"Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race," Fürste said in a statement on Instagram.

But will it put others off competing, and what could it mean for Hyrox, which was rumoured to be valued at US$700 million (NZ$1.2b) when Investment firm L Catterton and WndrCo took a stake this month.

University of Auckland senior lecturer in marketing Drew Franklin said he thought the brand would recover from the incident.

"I think it's more of a short-term hit to Hyrox's brand equity… not necessarily a lasting one.

"We often call it a spillover effect - but I see that might have double meaning in this sense - to other partnerships or potential partnerships that Hyrox might engage in.

"The athlete's accident isn't really the issue, it was Hyrox's failure to intervene and I suppose for the community at large it challenges some of those core associations of safety, hygiene, fair competition.

"There is a bit at stake because Hyrox enjoys quite a lot of co-branding with gyms, sponsors and commercial partners that may otherwise worry the spillover effects may carry into their brand equity to their brand… but Hyrox have responded appropriately. They've apologised, changed the rules. If those safeguards are applied consistently the brand awareness they enjoy and have enjoyed to date and the loyal community following should contain or buffer the damage.

"Perhaps a bit of bruising but not a permanent loss of value unless these sorts of operational failures occur again."

Lou O'Reilly, of communications firm O'Reilly & Co, agreed it should not cause lasting damage for the brand.

"Even though the incident was significant, it's not going to wipe millions off the value of the brand. Hyrox itself is built around providing a professionally run, consistent experience for athletes all over the world.

"During that particular event, they lost control of that experience. The upside is they've responded, changed the rules, and you'd expect them to be much more stringent in future."

Franklin said with community-based brands like Hyrox "your people are your ambassadors and it's a big part of their own social identity, as opposed to something that may be a little bit more transactional, like your brand of cereal or toothpaste or that sort of thing".

Northland Activ8 gym owner Miranda Harrison coaches Hyrox participants and said most people were laughing about the incident.

World.title: Dame Noeline Taurua reappointed as Silver Ferns coach through to 2027 World Cup
World.content:
Dame Noeline Taurua has been reappointed as Silver Ferns head coach through to the 2027 Netball World Cup, a year after her relationship with Netball New Zealand broke down in a bitter dispute over the team's high-performance environment.

The move comes after Taurua led the Silver Ferns to Commonwealth Games gold in Glasgow last month, ending a 16-year wait for the title.

In a statement, Netball NZ said the decision reflects the organisation's confidence in Taurua's "leadership, coaching ability, integrity and vision" as well as a shared ambition to re-establish the Silver Ferns as the world's number one-ranked team.

The reappointment represents a remarkable turnaround in the relationship between Taurua and the national body, which has undergone a significant leadership change this year.

This time last year the veteran coach was stood down as Silver Ferns coach after a what began as a discreet cultural review of the team environment erupted into a fraught employment dispute.

A 51-day standoff followed, with Taurua and her coaching team challenging the process used to examine the concerns, while Netball NZ maintained that changes were needed to improve the environment and strengthen player voice.

Taurua was eventually reinstated in October, with both sides agreeing to changes designed to support player wellbeing and performance.

However, the 2019 World Cup winning coach remained sidelined for the Constellation Cup against Australia and the Ferns' end of year tour to the UK, meaning the Commonwealth Games was Taurua's first campaign back at the helm following her reinstatement.

Netball NZ chief executive Jennah Wootten, who is just a month into her role with the national body, said she was delighted to retain Taurua.

"The Silver Ferns programme is a world-class high-performance environment and we are thrilled to have retained the services of Dame Noeline. She is one of the greatest coaches in world netball," said Wootten.

"Netball New Zealand is proud of the Silver Ferns programme and is confident in its people, systems and high-performance environment. We look forward to further success with a huge 12 months ahead."

Dame Noeline Taurua led the Silver Ferns to Commonwealth Games gold in Glasgow, ending a 16-year drought. www.photosport.nz

Taurua said it is an "honour and a privilege" to lead the Ferns.

"This team has a proud history and a legacy that has been built over generations by the coaches, players and people who have gone before us," she said.

"I'm also incredibly proud of what this team achieved at the Commonwealth Games. The opportunity now is to build on that success, continue to grow our game and our people, and keep adding to the legacy of the Silver Ferns."

Taurua's reappointment will extend a remarkable career with the Silver Ferns that has spanned almost a decade, and survived one of the most serious ruptures between a New Zealand coach and their national body.

The veteran coach took the helm in 2018, replacing Janine Southby in the aftermath of an independent review in to the Silver Ferns' Gold Coast Commonwealth Games campaign, in which the team failed to win a medal for the first time.

What followed was one of the most dramatic turnarounds in Silver Ferns history. Taurua took a team that had finished in fourth place at the Commonwealth Games and transformed it into world champions within a year.

But the years that followed have produced more mixed results at pinnacle events.

New Zealand took bronze at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham, before suffering their worst ever finish at a Netball World Cup in Cape Town in 2023, when they ended the tournament in fourth place.

Taurua was retained following a recruitment process in 2024, signing a contract that ran through the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

Following their victory in Glasgow last month, the Silver Ferns will now turn their attention to next month's Constellation Cup against the Australia Diamonds. The series has taken on an even greater edge after the Diamonds took home bronze at the Commonwealth Games after failing to make the final for the first time, which meant New Zealand did not face their trans-Tasman rivals at the tournament.

World.content: But before that could happen, Ardern had to pick a song that captured who she was as a person and as a leader. When she finally settled on ‘Stars’ by local band Shapeshifter, she wasn't sure how people would react.

World.title: Broncos NRLW stars credit 'Princey blow-up' for season turnaround
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Brisbane Broncos NRLW stars Romy Teitzel and Tamika Upton insist an emotive half-time address from coach Scott Prince was the catalyst for the team's return to form.

The defending premiers host Newcastle in an elimination final on Saturday at Brisbane's Langlands Park.

They enter the match on a three-match winning streak, which followed a mid-season slump.

The Broncos' last loss was a 28-20 defeat to the Gold Coast Titans on August 23.

Broncos, Titans record wins The Broncos thrash the Warriors to hit peak form before the finals, while the high-flying Titans beat the Knights in the concluding round of the minor premiership.

It was their third consecutive defeat.

Trailing 14-4 at half-time in that match, TV footage showed Prince laying down the law in no uncertain terms.

"We are a great team with great standards and we weren't living up to them," Teitzel said.

"We deserved every single word that he threw at us.

"The response comes from having a lot of respect for Princey and believing in his game plan.

"Everything is driven from that respect factor and believing in what he is trying to drive here at the Broncos."

Following the loss to the Titans, the Broncos beat Parramatta 44-10 and St George Illawarra 24-16, before thrashing the Warriors 52-18 at home last Sunday.

Tamika Upton says the players have deep respect for their coach, Scott Prince. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Broncos captain Upton said Prince, who coached the team to the premiership last year, told the players home truths they needed to hear.

"We had a few little things we had to fix, and we weren't doing it, hence the Princey blow-up," Upton said.

"To be honest, we are used to it. He is a very passionate coach. That's the thing, we are all competitors."

Upton said she and her teammates had enormous respect for Prince, who captained the Wests Tigers to the 2005 NRL premiership during his decorated playing career.

"I would rather him be yelling at us than not speaking to us," she said.

"Honestly, you feel that because he was a player.

"When he is talking like that, you feel the energy, and you respect that a lot because he has been there and done it before.

"He wouldn't do it if he didn't care. I respond to that."

AAP

World.title: WTA Finals hoped to become 'Super Bowl of women's sports'
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The season-ending WTA Finals will be held in North Carolina for at least three years from 2027, as the tour seeks to take greater control of its flagship event amid financial concerns.

The finals, featuring the season's top-eight singles players and doubles ​teams, will be played in Charlotte at the venue which hosts the Hornets NBA team.

WTA chair Valerie Camillo said the tour wanted to build ‌the finals into the "Super Bowl of women's sports".

Camillo said the WTA would operate the event itself rather than rely on the type of outside-promoter arrangement previously used.

"The WTA will be taking greater ownership and control of the event and investing ⁠alongside our partners," Camillo said.

Financial details ​of Charlotte's package were not disclosed ‌ahead of a planned announcement by local partners.

Rybakina downs Sabalenka for US Open title Elena Rybakina already took Aryna Sabalenka's world number one ranking, now she takes her US Open title as well.

Camillo said it represented a "meaningful investment" that gave the WTA confidence to commit to the city.

The move follows the WTA's decision to relocate the November 2026 finals to Indian Wells, California, after ending an agreement under which Riyadh had hosted the event with the backing of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment ​Fund.

British newspaper The ‌Telegraph reported last week internal WTA projections showed the tour could run out of cash next year and move into debt by autumn 2027 if its spending pattern continued.

The report said the WTA expected operating ⁠losses of $US23 million ($32 million) in 2026 and cited the loss of ‌revenue associated with the Saudi finals deal ‌as a major contributor.

Camillo said 2026 was a transitional year and the tour was tightening spending while absorbing ‌the unexpected cost of moving the finals to Indian Wells.

The WTA has not yet set prize money for the 2027 finals.

Camillo said equal prize money remained an important goal, but added the tour was considering alternatives, including ⁠a profit-sharing model with players.

"We want this event to be built together with the players," she said.

"Why stop at equal prize money?"

The WTA also plans to establish a greater operational presence in Charlotte as it builds the event.

Reuters

World.title: Aussie F1 Grand Prix loses season-opening honour but gains sprint race
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Melbourne's Australian Grand Prix will not have the privilege of opening the 2027 Formula 1 season, but it will boast two races in its biggest weekend yet.

After landing the chance to open the F1 year in 2026 as it once traditionally did for two decades, the Albert Park event will be the third stop on next season's record-equalling 24-race program.

The main race will take place later than usual on April 4, with Bahrain replacing Melbourne as the season-opening venue on March 14.

Jeddah will host the Saudi Arabia Grand Prix a week after the Bahrain race.

Antonelli edges closer to historic title as teammate concedes the fight Kimi Antonelli is on the brink of becoming the youngest F1 champion in history, while his nearest rival says he is out of the fight.

But the key development will be the introduction of a sprint race in Melbourne on Saturday, on the eve of the grand prix itself.

Instead of two sessions of practice on the Friday before the grand prix, there will be just one with sprint race qualifying taking place in the afternoon.

On the Saturday, there will be the double attraction of a sprint race, followed later by qualifying for the main event.

Melbourne will be one of 10 circuits to stage a sprint race in 2027, four more than this year.

F1 bosses clearly believe the 30-minute shorter races on the Saturday are the way forward.

They claim data showed broadcast viewership of sprint weekends was 12 per cent higher than non-sprint weekends, with qualifying three times more popular with fans than free practice.

Portugal (June 20) and Türkiye (October 3) are additions to the program, with the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort and Barcelona having dropped off.

AAP

World.title: Daly Cherry-Evans has arrived at the end of forever
World.content:
Years ago, when Daly Cherry-Evans was merely in his early 30s, he'd say that he was going to play forever and he was only ever half-joking.

Every time he'd be asked about his future, be it at the beginning of a season or at the end, he'd grin widely and assure whoever wanted to know that he, in fact, would never, ever stop.

Most of the time it felt like a gag, a way for one of the slickest operators in the NRL to disarm the inquiry and Cherry-Evans follow with all the usual patter we hear from the greybeards — that he'd play as long as his body held up or as long as he was still enjoying it.

Plenty say that but Cherry-Evans has lived it. He lived it long enough that he reached the end of the "lifetime" deal he once signed with Manly, long enough that younger men than him succumbed to the ravages of age and long enough that maybe the joke was on us the whole time for not believing him in the first place.

Cherry-Evans has enjoyed another consistent season after joining the Sydney Roosters this year. (Getty Images: Matt King )

It is only now, a few months before he turns 38 years old, that Cherry-Evans has finally arrived at the end of forever.

Win or lose, the Sydney Roosters sudden-death semifinal against Cronulla on Saturday is the beginning of the last days, the ones that seemed like they would never arrive.

A defeat will mark Cherry-Evans's final NRL match before he links with Hull FC in Super League next year where's he's odds on to, at least once, play with or against someone a full two decades younger than him.

A win will push the Roosters into a preliminary final against the Dolphins and keep the dream of a farewell premiership alive.

If the Tricolours do manage to go all the way, Cherry-Evans will break Lote Tuqiri's record for the longest gap between grand final wins by one season.

That premiership back in 2011 is still definitional to Cherry-Evans and what he's been for all this time.

In becoming the first rookie halfback to win a grand final since 1978 and because he was one of Manly's best through the finals and on the big day in their win over the Warriors, Cherry-Evans was able to transcend many of the slings and arrows launched during the rise of franchise playmakers.

Cherry-Evans made history in his very first NRL season. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan )

Instead of the typical hero journey most halfbacks endure, with its peaks and valleys and rises and falls, Cherry-Evans's success as a rookie gave him a kind of instant validation.

There was never any talk of what he might be one day once he matures, or what he would eventually become once he developed this part of his game or not.

There was no debate whether he would one day be enough to lead a team to glory because he had already done it. It was instant proof of concept.

So many of young halfbacks are defined by their future, the possibility of what they might be, but ever since that first season, Cherry-Evans has instead existed in a blissful and seemingly eternal present.

His game has changed in subtle ways since that first year with Manly but through a bird's-eye view the similarities of his 16-year career is remarkable.

Why Daly Cherry-Evans is rugby league's ultimate survivor At 33, Daly Cherry-Evans might only be one more series loss away from his last game for Queensland – but if the decider was anything to go by, the Maroons' skipper isn't going anywhere.

This season was the 15th of those years where he managed at least 20 games and he has as many try assists this year at age 37 as he did the year he turned 25.

Old halves are supposed to run less but his return in that part of his game this year (51 run metres per game and five line breaks from 24 matches) is not miles away from his return as a rookie (57 per game and 11 line breaks from 27 matches).

They're meant to be worse at defending as well, but this year Cherry-Evans has had the third-best tackle efficiency of his career.

That's not to say there hasn't been some ups and downs for Cherry-Evans through his long career, but because of where he started and how long he's been there it was always easy to ride out the downs because, even as he reached his mid-30s, he had more time.

A bad option or a poor game or a sprayed kick, as rare as they were, or even a season where his team didn't make the finals were easier to accept because there was always more to come. He could always come back to what he had always been.

The end of that reality was put into stark relief in Sunday's qualifying final loss to Penrith even as, at the end of all things, Cherry-Evans can absolutely still cut it in a game of such quality and intensity.

It was only a month ago that he scored both tries in a 12-6 Tricolours win over the Panthers that remains their best performance of the season.

This time, with Sam Walker sidelined, Cherry-Evans slotted back into halfback and taken the lion's share of the kicking game and his field position chess match with Brian To'o as he hunted a 40/20 in the second half was a highlight.

Cherry-Evans missed the mark with what would have been an equaliser against Penrith last week. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

In the end, two kicks Cherry-Evans got wrong cost the Roosters badly.

First it was a screwball torpedo of a thing with ten minutes left that he launched from his own 40 metre line that found the grass and seemed perfect until it took one bounce too many and trickled dead.

It was unfortunate and nothing more. Not even someone as experienced as Cherry-Evans, who will likely bring up his 450th first class game next year, can predict how a ball bounces.

Penrith rolled up the field on the seven-tackle set and took the lead through a Nathan Cleary one-pointer but it was not necessarily a death blow given Cherry-Evans is the modern day field goal king.

He's kicked 31 of them in his career, the most of anyone in the NRL era.

He's kicked them to cap off big wins and to break stalemates at the last second — seven of them came in golden point extra time and his most recent match-winner was just a few weeks back against Newcastle.

Cherry-Evans is the player to look to when the scores are close. (Getty Images: Matt King )

He's kicked them off both feet, in howling gales and monsoonal rain.

He's never met a way he couldn't do it and he's met all the ways it can be done.

But this time his only attempt, from inside 20 metres and right in front, was a shank the likes of which we've rarely seen during his career.

Even the best can get it wrong, but both moments brought into stark relief just how things have changed for Cherry-Evans.

Roosters coach Trent Robinson was circumspect about it after the match, pointing out that Cherry-Evans had iced games before for the Roosters and would do so again.

Manly face uncertain future as Cherry-Evans comes home With Manly's season teetering on the edge, the Sea Eagles faithful welcomed former skipper Daly Cherry-Evans to Brookvale Oval in enemy colours for the first time. But it was the prodigal son who won the day.

The former is a fact but the latter is closer to a prediction than a guarantee.

There might still be a next week for Cherry-Evans, but it only might be. There will not be a next year.

On Saturday night against Cronulla, with Walker still out, Cherry-Evans must become the system once again.

He will play sharp and smart, like he always does, like he always has, and maybe it will be enough to earn another day.

But after seeming ageless for so long, he is running out of tomorrows. He has reached the end of forever and after seeming immune to time for so long it is coming for him at last.

The story might not have its final chapter against the Sharks or the Dolphins, but the last page is nigh and the final days of Daly Cherry-Evans in the NRL are a reminder of how the present, after seeming fixed for so long, becomes history wholesale — not at all and then all at once.

World.title: Australia's 43-year MotoGP streak continues with Senna Agius signing
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

There will be a full-time Australian rider in motorcycle racing's premier class for the 43rd consecutive year with 21-year-old Senna Agius signing on to race for KTM Tech3 next year.

The Sydneysider currently sits fourth in the Moto2 standings after placing 10th in 2025.

He has four grand prix wins in Moto2, including at the Circuit of the Americas in the United States and Jerez in Spain earlier this season.

He won his home Moto2 grand prix at Phillip Island last year, and will be in MotoGP for next year's maiden Australian Grand Prix at the new Adelaide street circuit.

Agius has signed on for KTM Tech3, which has former F1 team principal Guenther Steiner has the team's chief executive.

"Today a lifelong dream of mine has come true, reaching MotoGP," Agius said.

"So many years of hard work have gone into this moment and I'm incredibly grateful to Guenther and everyone at Tech3 for believing in me and giving me this opportunity.

"I can't wait to repay their faith. I know the challenge ahead, but I'm ready to learn, work hard, and become the best version of myself with this team."

Australia has had a full-time rider in the premier class since 1985.

In the modern era of grand prix motorcycle racing, which began in 2002 when 500cc two-stroke bikes were replaced with 990cc four-stroke engines, Agius will become the 11th full-time Australian rider.

He will also be the only Australian on the grid next season, with Jack Miller ending his 12-year MotoGP stint and moving to World Superbikes in 2027.

World.title: Alex de Minaur readies for Davis Cup tie between Australia and Poland
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A Davis Cup tie has come at the perfect time for Alex de Minaur as he searches to recapture a spark after nearly a decade on tour.

The Australian, ranked as high as number five in the world earlier this year, fell to ninth after his shock second-round US Open loss earlier this month.

A quarterfinalist at the Australian Open this year, the 27-year-old has missed golden opportunities to go further in majors since, with Alexander Zverev instead netting two titles as Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz both endured injury-hit seasons.

De Minaur headed straight to Brisbane after his Flushing Meadows disappointment, training with Australian Cup captain Lleyton Hewitt for more than a week before their qualifying tie against Poland begins on Saturday.

De Minaur crashes out of US Open Alex de Minaur has crashed out of the US Open at the second-round stage, beaten in straight sets by Botic van de Zandschulp.

"Back here, around the boys, some good practice, a great team environment; it's been a great little change-up for me," de Minaur said.

"This is exactly what I need to get that spark back that maybe I was missing.

"I've had that spark for 10 years, every single day, right?

"There are stages through your career where things happen, and maybe you don't feel your best. But the timing of this week, it feels like everything's clicking together."

De Minaur has previously taken his losses hard; he copped his most recent defeat to Botic van de Zandschulp with uncharacteristic nonchalance.

But he is adamant the competitive edge remains as he prepares to head a team that includes doubles ace Max Purcell fresh off an 18-month ban for an anti-doping breach.

"Physically I'm great, and mentally I'm in great shape," de Minaur said.

"A rough patch … I've been very fortunate in my career to not have many of those.

"The tennis is still there, mentally there's been matches I haven't played the way I would like.

"But I've got a lot to give, a lot left in the tank, and hopefully I can show it.

"I haven't plateaued in my career. I'm hungry for more and feel I've got the opportunities to achieve it."

De Minaur burst onto the scene when, after being handed a late wildcard, he surged to the Brisbane International semifinals in 2017.

A year later he made his Davis Cup debut at the same venue, losing in a fifth-set tie-break to Zverev.

"I love team competitions … it brings that extra oomph in my game," said de Minaur, who is 17-10 in Davis Cup singles matches.

Poland are without former world number six Hubert Hurkacz, who has skipped the tie as he manages his return from injury, and will be led by world number 73 Kamil Majchrzak.

Rinky Hijikata and Purcell trained together, against Hewitt and de Minaur, at Wednesday's training in a sign they will contest Sunday's doubles tie.

The full draw will be announced on Friday.

AAP

World.title: Tszyu changes tune on controversial draw, eyes off fights in US
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Believing his domestic duties are done, Nikita Tszyu is ready to take on America after changing his tune and claiming victory in his controversial draw with countryman Ben Mahoney.

Tszyu surprisingly but sportingly conceded he thought he had lost the pair's Brisbane bout last month after the judges, with three vastly different scorecards, declared a stalemate.

Mahoney danced around the ring like he had won a world title, prompting derision from Tszyu's brother Tim, before his team cried highway robbery.

But after watching replays of the super-welterweight stoush, Tszyu is now adamant he should have been awarded the contest.

Tszyu's stunning admission, says Mahoney 'edged' thrilling draw Nikita Tszyu and Ben Mahoney have fought themselves to a standstill in thrilling contest that was scored a split decision draw on the Gold Coast on Wednesday night.

"I'm not a very good judge," he said of his initial verdict.

"I scored it 7-3. In a good way, 8-4. I thought I won the majority of the middle rounds. I gave him the first two rounds and the last two rounds, but [I won] everything else in between.

"I don't regret it, because it was what I felt at the time."

The still-undefeated Sydney slayer hopes his best nights lie ahead of him — and ideally in the US.

The 29-year-old and his team have always been happy to take things slowly and not rush into taking big fights in the boxing mecca.

But Tszyu (12-1-0, 10KOs) finally feels ready, despite Tim relinquishing his IBO super-welterweight belt in the US to Sebastian Fundora, as well as losing a rematch and copping a brutal beat down in another world-title loss in America to Bakhram Murtazaliev.

"I think I can figure it out," Tszyu told AAP.

"This fight was a great learning curve for me and it puts things a lot into perspective. I've got to be a lot more professional with the way I do things.

"I can't be landscaping close to the fight. I can't be doing woodworking close to the fight. Just some bad habits I do.

"Yeah, I've got to be a professional athlete."

No Limit Boxing is known to be pushing for Tszyu to feature on the undercard to the David Benavidez-Michal Cieslak unified blockbuster in Phoenix, Arizona, on December 12.

But if a US date does not eventuate, No Limit has confirmed Tszyu will fight at least once more in 2026 in Australia.

AAP

World.title: Bazzana whacks two home runs in vital MLB win for Guardians
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Australian Travis Bazzana has continued his impressive rookie season with two home runs, helping Cleveland secure a crucial 7-6 win over the Chicago White Sox in its battle for a Major League Baseball play-off berth.

The Guardians have beaten the White Sox at home in their last two games, meaning they trail Chicago by just half a game in the American League Central standings.

Whoever finishes their division on top will go through to the post-season. Cleveland has topped the AL Central standings for the last two years.

Even if they finish second behind the White Sox, the Guardians are also well placed to progress with a wildcard berth.

It was the second time in his debut MLB season that Bazzana has hit two homers in a game. The first Australian number one baseball draft pick has racked up hits in his last five games.

On Wednesday (AEST), the all-star second baseman hit a solo homer in the first inning to give Cleveland a 3-0 lead.

The Guardians were 6-4 down in the bottom of the sixth when Bazzana hit another solo shot.

Brayan Rocchio ripped a two-run double with two outs in the ninth inning, scoring two runs to win the game.

The shortstop, nicknamed "Rocctember" and "Playoff Rocchio" for his late-season heroics, starred with two for three, including a walk and two runners batted in (RBIs).

Bazzana hit two for four with two RBIs.

The Guardians improved to a 77-75 record and have 10 games left in the regular season, while the White Sox are at 77-74.

AAP

Tech.title: Snap is launching a new Specs AI tool, and it’s coming to iOS and Mac
Tech.content:
SPECS Intelligence builds an understanding of your goals, priorities, relationships, and routines from the apps and tools you choose to connect. The service is designed to carry that personal context across devices and deepens its understanding over time, helping you move between work, personal responsibilities, and the things you care about.

SPECS Intelligence is designed to anticipate when help would be useful and surface relevant information and actions without waiting for a prompt. Before a meeting, it could highlight decisions to make, questions to ask, and things to remember. For an upcoming trip, it could bring together flight, hotel, and dinner plans while flagging a work deadline that falls during the visit.

Tech.title: I wore Snap’s $2,200 smart glasses
Tech.content:
My favorite part of wearing the Specs, Snap’s new augmented reality glasses, was playing dominoes. Sitting across the table from a Snap employee wearing the same pair of chunky glasses, I could select a virtual domino with a pinch and then move my hand to drop it in place, watching the tile snap down in front of us on a real table. It was unlike anything I’ve tried in other VR headsets or smart glasses — the ability to sit with another person and have a shared digital experience.

Snap really believes in AR glasses. The company has spent more than half a decade developing the technology, producing two generations of glasses that only ever shipped to a small number of developers. The company seems to want to untether itself from the limitations of being just one app in a big store and instead pioneer the next great platform.

Now, Snap is nearly ready to launch its first pair of AR glasses for consumers, the Specs, sometime this fall. That suggests Snap thinks these meet its vision well enough for regular people to enjoy using the $2,195 glasses. They’re certainly full of big ideas. But after an afternoon of testing at Snap’s offices this week, I’m skeptical of whether they’ll be fully ready for primetime.

Photo: Naohmi Monroe / The Verge

The Specs are big, black, bold glasses that come in two lens sizes, 47mm and 52mm. Part of why they’re so bold is almost certainly to make a statement — there’s no mistaking these for a regular pair of glasses, like you might with Meta’s Ray-Bans. (They’re a little too conspicuous for me personally; my glasses style is squarely “Elder Millennial Who Shops At Warby Parker.”) But they’re also so chunky because they house all the hardware necessary to let the Specs function as a standalone computer, meaning they don’t need to be tethered to a phone, compute puck, or external battery.

They may be chunky, but the Specs aren’t quite as heavy as they look. They’re heavier than my Warby Parker glasses, of course, which I can comfortably wear for most of the day. But the Specs didn’t drag on my face like a full-on VR headset. The Specs felt sturdy, too: I shook my head around and they didn’t fall off or even really slip. I wouldn’t suggest playing pickup basketball in these, but they’ll stay on your face while walking around. They made my ears sag just a little, though. And I wasn’t able to use the Specs enough to tell you if they’d start to feel uncomfortable over the course of a full four-hour battery cycle.

Actually using the Specs is kind of like using a hybrid of smart glasses and a VR headset. In front of your eyes, you can see menus, app windows, and elements of whatever app (“lens”) you’re using, like the digital dominoes. Those elements appear over whatever you’re looking at with your eyes through the lenses of the glasses, which have waveguide displays that can show “16 million colors” and “sharp, high-resolution visuals” (Snap hasn’t specified the exact resolution).

Thanks to hand-tracking tech in the Specs, you can pinch and drag to manipulate parts of the interface, such as resizing a window or moving a domino onto the game board, and Snap says you can even snap your fingers to take a picture in the Specs’ Snapchat app. Clever. You can also have windows follow along as you move your head, in case you want to keep a window in your vision no matter where you’re looking. You can access a home button, a Control Center-like menu, and status information like the time by holding up your palm in a setup that reminds me of the ill-fated Humane Pin.

In my limited testing, it was all rather finicky. I often had to pinch a few times or make sure my hand was placed in just the right spot to get something to work the way it should. I never quite nailed the two-part action of flipping my hand up and then using my other hand to press the home button. While standing in the sun, it was much harder to see the augmented reality graphics.

Snap has beaten competitors like Meta to shipping a pair of glasses with displays in both lenses, letting it deliver a true AR effect and not just another flat screen. But by putting the AR display dead center in your vision, the Specs’ 51-degree field of view becomes a major limitation. It meant that digital elements kept slipping out of sight during my demos, which ruined the illusion that they were actually in the real world. While watching Lanterns on HBO Max in a browser in a moving car, I had to shrink the window to make it easier to see in front of me. While playing dominoes, I had to keep physically turning my head to see my dominoes and the playing board and back again.

Because it’s 2026, the Specs also have a dedicated AI chatbot assistant, but in my limited experience it was slow and inconsistent. With a “Hey Specs” command, I asked it to show me funny cat videos on YouTube, as suggested by a Snap rep. I had to ask it twice because it didn’t pick up the command the first time. When the command worked, it then took about 15 seconds for the Specs to pull up a YouTube page with search results for funny cat videos.

Watching that video also revealed to me a bizarre social interaction that people will have to come to grips with if AR glasses gain any sort of traction. On that YouTube page, I picked some random cat video collection, and it played in the background while the Snap rep kept talking to me. Even though the Specs were playing audio through the onboard speakers, the Snap rep standing right next to me said they couldn’t hear anything. That made me feel weird — these glasses theoretically let you watch and listen to a private video while staring somebody else straight in the eye. Even when I wasn’t watching the video, I found myself constantly distracted from the in-person conversations I was having during the demo because my eyes were caught up with what they were looking at while my hands were focused on arcane gestures for tasks that only I could see. I didn’t feel very present.

Like Meta glasses, which are currently grappling with a “pervert” glasses reputation, the Specs also let you take photos and record video. They too have a privacy indicator light, and it’s arguably more prominent than Meta’s take: Instead of a light that’s off to the side, the Specs’ light is right in the center of the glasses. But I don’t know if, given the growing pushback against Meta’s glasses, a blinking light is enough to deter concerns about potential unwanted recording.

That bar in the middle is the privacy indicator light.

In 2024, Snap CEO Evan Spiegel told The Verge that there is an opportunity for computers to evolve to “support the ways that humans have long interacted socially by looking at each other eye to eye with much more natural interaction.” Today, Snap has a simpler message: It says that its vision with Specs is to “make computing more human.” But even in my controlled demos, I found that Specs were actually more computer than other hardware; the glasses are unmissable on my head, and the digital content that only I could see was getting in the way of me interacting with the other people in the room.

Still, these headsets are coming. Meta is working on a pair, Google has a new glasses initiative, OpenAI has reportedly considered smart glasses, and Apple is apparently planning to announce Ray-Ban Meta-like smart glasses next year (and it’s worth noting that former Apple CEO Tim Cook has repeatedly praised AR in the past). It’s clear they all see the next frontier as glasses with tech like cameras and screens that sit on your head. Specs will be the first real test of what AR glasses can be. But even after Snap’s years of work, they still might be coming out too soon.

Tech.title: The 2.5-hour AI-generated Odyssey movie is 2.5 hours too long
Tech.content:
Christopher Nolan’s engrossing take on The Odyssey dominated at the box office and spurred a newfound interest in classic literature among filmgoers. But a new retelling of the story made entirely with AI is so bad that it might just make viewers hate the original tale altogether.

The new film, called Odysseus: The Fall, comes via AI firm Fountain 0 and is written and directed by company cofounder Ash Koosha, who also lent his likeness to the title character and created all of the music. (The film’s credits are very short.) The studio’s only previous work is an AI film called Dreams of Violets that made it into Tribeca earlier this year. The Fall is, on its face, a much more ambitious project, billed as “the first completely AI generated film produced at the level of a Hollywood blockbuster.” In reality, it’s nothing close to “the level of a Hollywood blockbuster.” That may not necessarily be surprising, but after watching the entire 2.5-hour production I nonetheless found myself constantly surprised by just how much worse things could get. The Fall is the opposite of a glimpse at the future of AI filmmaking — it’ll make you wonder if there’s really any future in it at all.

The movie is available to rent now for $9.99 and, as far as I can tell, you can only watch it via a web browser. In order to view it on my living room TV I had to mirror the screen from my phone, which is not exactly IMAX in 70mm. Things didn’t get much better once I pressed play.

The Fall is plagued by two main issues. The first is consistency. The world of the film is constantly morphing, to the point that it’s incredibly distracting. The height of the cyclops that traps Odysseus and his men changes from shot to shot, waves move in the opposite direction of the wind, mouths don’t match the words spoken (and sometimes they move without producing a sound at all), and oars bend and twist as sailors row. In one scene a huge fleet of boats is racing through the ocean and one of them is inexplicably moving sideways. The AI-produced voice-overs can be incomprehensible, and at various points the names of both Odysseus and Zeus are pronounced wrong.

If it were just the odd hiccup it might be understandable, but there are so many faults in The Fall that it can be hard to focus on anything else. I watched the movie with my 13-year-old kid and it basically became a game of finding the weirdest mistakes. I noticed that a sword magically turned into a dagger, and then she one-upped me by spotting an alien carcass roasting over a spit. The Fall seems like a film designed to prove why script supervisors exist.

The thing is, while all of the AI-induced errors are distracting, they’re also the most entertaining part of the movie. There isn’t really much to distract from in The Fall because it is so dull. Because current AI models are really only capable of generating scenes that last a few seconds, the movie feels like a disjointed collection of moments from the odyssey that have been stitched together with little rhyme or reason. If you didn’t already know the story going into this, I don’t think you’d have any idea of what was going on, because the film explains very little. You don’t even learn about Penelope’s suitors until the movie is almost over.

I also can’t think of a single aspect of The Fall that feels improved because of AI. The “acting” is bafflingly bad, with characters pausing for seconds at a time for no apparent reason and bursts of laughter that jolt you out of nowhere. There’s no weight to the action, as if this takes place in a world where things like physics and gravity are suggestions rather than constants. Similarly, there aren’t any cool or impressive effects that wouldn’t be possible without the technology. The monsters look like shabby stop-motion creatures from the 1930s, which is all the weirder when they’re put beside the smooth, hyperreal human characters that AI spews out. It’s not just jarring, it’s boring and ugly.

Koosha claims that he adapted this story because he “always felt passionately about Homer’s epic tale since [he] originally read it years ago.” It seems much more likely that he’s trying to skate by on the hype and energy created by Nolan’s film, turning AI slop into a modern-day iteration of direct-to-video cash grabs. But this also puts the film at an incredible disadvantage from the very beginning, inviting comparisons to one of the most critically and commercially successful movies of the last few years, one that was especially beloved because of the director’s insistence on human craftsmanship. Nolan is someone who cares deeply about film, and his passion and enthusiasm is why stars want to work with him and viewers flock the theaters to see his movies.

The existence of The Fall, meanwhile, shows utter contempt for the medium, attempting to boil the work of hundreds of skilled workers into slop produced by a tiny team. It’s so terrible it’ll make you appreciate human-made art all the more.

Tech.title: The AI data center e-waste problem is huge — and getting bigger
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

E-waste from the AI boom has been vastly underestimated, a new report warns. By 2050, it could become enough trash to fill 23 million shipping containers — roughly enough 40-foot containers to circle the world six times if lined up in a row.

It’s a significantly higher estimate of AI’s e-waste than previous studies have found because the authors of the new report factor in all the infrastructure needed to support servers in data centers. The broader scope provides a clearer picture of junk AI leaves behind, according to the nonprofit Basel Action Network (BAN), which published the paper today.

”AI may feel weightless, but every model depends on an enormous amount of highly specialized, cutting edge hardware,” Jim Puckett, founder and chief of strategic direction at BAN, says in a press release. “If companies and governments do not begin planning for this new waste tsunami, today’s AI buildout could become an even more cataclysmic toxic waste crisis than we are already experiencing.”

“Today’s AI buildout could become an even more cataclysmic toxic waste crisis than we are already experiencing.”

Less than a quarter of the 68.3 million tons of e-waste created each year worldwide is formally collected and recycled. Most e-waste is ultimately dumped into shadowy “informal” waste collection where burning or burying equipment can expose workers and the local environment to toxic materials like lead and chromium.

BAN predicts e-waste generated globally will triple in amount to up to 211 million metric tons a year by 2050. It attributes about 15 to 20 percent of that garbage to AI. Unlike previous AI e-waste estimates that focused on servers and GPUs, BAN expands its count to include other categories of equipment: power supply and distribution, cooling systems, backup power, and networking equipment. Notably, BAN also counts what it calls “AI Waste Contagion” — a wide-ranging category that incorporates everything from telecommunications infrastructure to personal devices likely to become obsolete and replaced earlier as a result of advances in AI.

Counting it all up, BAN expects 70,000 metric tons of e-waste per gigawatt of data center capacity. It cites a McKinsey projection of total data center capacity reaching up to 219GW by 2030.

Considering AI-related electronic equipment retired between 2025 and 2050, BAN concludes that’ll add up to between 395 to 617 million metric tons of e-waste by the middle of the century. It breaks down to about 8.6 million to 13.1 million metric tons of equipment retired each year as a result of AI.

Previous estimates of AI’s e-waste have been more conservative. But by focusing on servers and accelerators, past studies miss about 87 percent of a data center’s electro-mechanical infrastructure, according to BAN.

A separate study published in 2024 predicted that e-waste from AI could reach between 1.2 million and 5 million tons by 2030. Another study published in February found that AI servers could create between 131,000 and 225,000 tons of e-waste annually by the end of the decade — an amount that’s still comparable to all the e-waste produced by a country the size of Denmark.

Tech.title: Resident Evil is a comedy first and a thrilling nightmare second
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

When Paul W.S. Anderson’s Resident Evil hit theaters in 2002, video game movies were largely seen as a niche. Films like Mortal Kombat and Tomb Raider had proven that big-screen game adaptations could be successful, but the commercial and critical failure of projects like the 1993 Super Mario Bros. still cast a long shadow.
